sampleAnswers.answer: The carbonised loaf from a Herculaneum house is organic remains, preserved by heat and ash. The wall painting of a fish market is art, since its purpose is decorative. The painted election notice from Pompeii is writing, because it conveys a public message. The floor plan of a house with a peristyle garden is evidence from buildings, recording the layout of a domestic space. Each classification shows what the item can reveal about life in the cities.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: classifies all four items correctly, with a reason for each, linking the classification to the kind of information each item gives.

sampleAnswers.answer: The loaf is organic remains and the fish market painting is art. The house plan is buildings. The election notice is art because it is painted on a wall.

prompts.scenario: A Year 12 student has four items from a hypothetical museum display (invented for this task): a carbonised loaf found in a Herculaneum house, a wall painting of a fish market, a painted election notice from Pompeii, and the floor plan of a house with a peristyle garden. prompts.question: Evaluate the value and limitations of art, buildings, organic remains and writing as sources for everyday life in Pompeii and Herculaneum.
markerNotes: Evaluate needs a judgement on reliability and usefulness. Each source needs a value and a limitation tied to the question of everyday life.
The strongest answers judge the sources against each other, for example by noting that organic remains show everyday practice while art shows what the wealthy wanted to display.
commonStudentErrors: Describing each source type without saying what it can or cannot show about everyday life.
Treating writing as the most reliable evidence simply because it is written, without considering who wrote it.
prompts.markingCriteria:
8 marks: Evaluates the value and limitations of each source type for everyday life, weighs their reliability against one another, and reaches a supported judgement on their combined use
7 marks: Evaluates the value and limitations of most source types with supported reasons, reaching a partly developed judgement
5-6 marks: Explains the value and limitations of several source types with some evaluation
3-4 marks: Describes the value or limitations of some source types with limited evaluation
2 marks: Identifies source types with minimal comment on value or limitations
1 mark: Makes a general statement about sources

sampleAnswers.answer: Each type of source offers a distinct value for understanding everyday life in Pompeii and Herculaneum, and each has limitations that the historian must acknowledge. Art, mainly wall paintings and mosaics, is valuable because it shows domestic scenes, religious images and the tastes of wealthy householders, such as the scenes of banquets and mythology in elite houses. Its limitation is that it was produced for a patron or a market and often idealises life, so it cannot be taken as a simple record of ordinary experience. Buildings offer a more reliable record of how space was used, because the arrangement of rooms, shops and workshops reveals the household economy and the division of public and private life. Their limitation is that many buildings were altered or repaired before 79 CE, and that their function can be inferred only from their layout, so the evidence needs to be interpreted with care. Organic remains, including carbonised bread, figs and wooden objects found at Herculaneum, give a rare insight into diet and material culture, and they show the value of the surge deposits. Their limitation is that such remains are unevenly preserved, so they cannot be used to reconstruct the full range of food consumed in either city. Writing, including graffiti, election notices and the wax tablets of the banker Caecilius Iucundus, gives direct voices from ordinary people, which is a major value because it reveals opinions and transactions. Its limitation is that most surviving texts were written by men, and that the literate minority was small, so the writing reflects a narrow section of society. Taken together, the sources are most valuable when used in combination: art and buildings show what the wealthy wanted to display, while organic remains and writing provide evidence of everyday practice. The historian must therefore weigh each source by its purpose, its preservation and its authorship.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: evaluates the value and limitation of each of the four source types, weighs them against one another (what the wealthy displayed against everyday practice), and reaches a supported judgement on combined use.

sampleAnswers.answer: Art shows the wealthy and their tastes, such as banquet scenes, but it is idealised. Buildings show how houses were arranged and used, which helps understand daily life. Organic remains from Herculaneum include food, so we know what people ate. Writing like graffiti is useful because it shows what ordinary people thought, but it is not very common. These sources all have some value and some limitations, so they should be used together.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a value and a limitation for most sources, but the judgement that they should be used together is not argued against their relative reliability. It sits in the 5-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Art and buildings are sources about Pompeii and Herculaneum. Writing is also a source.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies source types with no comment on value or limitations, so it fits the 2-mark band.

prompts.scenario: A Year 12 student is writing an essay on everyday life in the cities and must judge which kinds of evidence are most reliable. The essay must weigh the usefulness of each kind of evidence against its limits.

markerNotes: The top answer states the value of graffiti (what it reveals about life) and uses Source A as evidence for a specific point, such as how common graffiti was in the Basilica.

Source A also attests to the sheer amount of graffiti in this location. Graffiti from the amphitheatre and palaestra are valuable in providing evidence about public entertainment. sampleAnswers.answer: Graffiti is useful evidence for life in Pompeii because it shows what ordinary people wrote about their daily concerns. Source A, found at the Basilica, shows that writing was common in public buildings.

markerNotes: The top answer judges how far the sources can be trusted for religion, comparing a painting, an epitaph and buildings.

Treating the wall painting as a neutral record of a real sacrifice rather than an artistic representation.

sampleAnswers.answer: The sources for religion in Pompeii and Herculaneum are valuable because they show ritual in action, yet their value and limitations depend on who made them and why. Source C, a wall painting from Herculaneum showing a sacrifice at an altar with robed figures and ibises, records the ritual itself: the altar, the ceremonial dress and the onlookers show a public act of worship. The ibises may suggest eastern cults such as Isis, though a painting cannot name its deity. Painters also idealised scenes for wealthy patrons, so the image shows the religion of the household that commissioned it rather than the practice of every citizen. Source D, a Pompeian inscription for Gnaeus Alleius Eros, a freedman appointed Augustalis, is useful for a different reason. It records that the Augustales and the inhabitants of the country district decreed 1000 sesterces for his funeral rites, which shows that religious and civic life were linked and that freedmen could be honoured through the cult of the emperor. Its limitation is that it is a single formulaic epitaph, which records a wealthy freedman and not the beliefs of the poor. Other sources, such as the Temple of Isis in Pompeii and the household shrines known as lararia, reveal religious practice in public and private settings, but these buildings were damaged by the earthquake of AD 62 and later restored, so their evidence is incomplete. Writing on the walls, including graffiti, adds evidence of ordinary belief, but it survives unevenly and favours the literate. Organic remains and votive objects add more, though they too survive by chance. Overall, the sources are highly valuable when used together, but each carries limitations that historians must test against one another.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sources such as wall paintings and inscriptions are valuable for religion in Pompeii and Herculaneum, because they show ritual. Source C shows a sacrifice at an altar at Herculaneum, which shows public worship, but painters idealised scenes for wealthy patrons. Source D records that the Augustales decreed funeral money for a freedman, which shows links between religion and civic life. However, it is one epitaph, so the sources are limited in what they show about the beliefs of ordinary people. Temples such as the Temple of Isis at Pompeii, and household shrines, add evidence for religious practice, but these buildings were damaged by the earthquake of AD 62 and later restored, so their evidence is incomplete.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6–8 row: some judgement of the value and limitations of the sources, referring to Sources C and D. Developing a clearer judgement about which source is most reliable would lift it to the 9–10 row.

prompts.question: Describe the social position of freedmen and freedwomen in Pompeii, using evidence from the houses of wealthy freed families.
markerNotes: Describe needs both sides of the position: the mobility of freedmen (wealth, houses, decoration) and their continuing dependence on former owners.
The House of the Vettii is the expected example. Naming it and linking its decoration to status earns the specific evidence mark.
commonStudentErrors: Describing freedmen as fully equal to free-born citizens.
Writing about enslaved people when the question asks about freedmen and freedwomen.
prompts.markingCriteria:

sampleAnswers.answer: Freedmen and freedwomen occupied a distinctive place in the social organisation of Pompeii. Many had been enslaved and were freed by their owners, and some built wealth through trade and manufacturing. The House of the Vettii, which belonged to freed owners, shows how a freedman family could display wealth and status through decorative schemes that rivalled those of the old elite. Yet freed status carried limits: former slaves remained tied to their patrons through obligations of service and respect, and enslaved people in these households had no legal standing of their own. The position of freedmen therefore combined upward mobility with continuing dependence.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: describes the mobility of freed families using the House of the Vettii, and explains the continuing obligations to former owners and the lack of legal standing of enslaved people.

sampleAnswers.answer: Freedmen were people who had been slaves and were then freed. The House of the Vettii was owned by freedmen and was richly decorated.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Accurate definition and one example, but no analysis of the position or its limitations. It fits the 2-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Enslaved people were not free in Pompeii.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement about enslaved people rather than freedmen, so it does not answer the question and earns only the 1-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The graffito suggests that manumission was one route by which enslaved people could move into a new social position in Pompeii. Its public display on a wall indicates that the household wanted to show its generosity, and that the change of status was socially meaningful rather than private. Giving a freed man a shop shows that freedmen could take on economic roles that kept them connected to the household and benefited the owner through profit and loyalty. However, this is a single hypothetical source, and it cannot show whether such manumissions were common or typical. The evidence therefore suggests that social relationships in Pompeii were flexible at the margins but still rested on the owner's power over the household.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: interprets the graffito as evidence of manumission and of freedmen's economic roles, explains the owner's interests, and evaluates the reliability of a single hypothetical source.

sampleAnswers.answer: The graffito shows that some enslaved people were freed. A freed slave could run a shop for their former owner. This shows that owners could be generous, but it probably was not common.

prompts.question: To what extent do Sources B and C help historians to understand the roles of slaves and freedmen in Pompeii and Herculaneum? Support your response using evidence from these and other relevant sources.
markerNotes: The top answer makes a judgement about how far Sources B and C help, and keeps that judgement through the response rather than only in the conclusion.

It reads each source for what it shows (the freedman and social mobility in Source B, the servants in Source C) and then for the limits of the perspective, since both were produced by and for the elite.
Other sources are used to show what the two given sources cannot reveal about the lives of enslaved people and freedmen.
commonStudentErrors: Describing Sources B and C without answering the 'to what extent' part of the question.
Treating Source B as a neutral record of a freedman's life, without considering that the dedication is family propaganda.
Using 'slaves' and 'freedmen' as one group, so that the different positions of enslaved people and freedmen are not separated.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Provides a reasoned judgement about the extent to which the given sources help historians to understand the roles of slaves and freedmen in Pompeii and Herculaneum; Supports the response using evidence from the sources provided and refers to other relevant source(s); Communicates ideas and information using appropriate historical terms and concepts
5-6 marks: Provides some judgement on the extent to which the given sources help historians to understand the roles of slaves and/or freedmen in Pompeii and/or Herculaneum; Refers to the sources provided and other source(s); Communicates using some historical terms and concepts
3-4 marks: Demonstrates some knowledge and/or understanding of sources or slaves/freedmen in Pompeii and/or Herculaneum; May refer to the sources provided; May use some historical terms and/or concepts
1-2 marks: Makes general statements about sources or slaves and/or freedmen in Pompeii and/or Herculaneum

sampleAnswers.answer:
Sources B and C help historians to a moderate extent. Both reveal the roles of slaves and freedmen in Pompeii and Herculaneum, but each was created by the elite, so their value lies partly in showing how the powerful wished to be seen.

Source B, an inscription from Herculaneum, records that Marcus Nonius Volusianus, a freedman of Balbus, paid for a monument to his former master, a praetor. This shows that a freedman could acquire wealth and that social mobility was possible. However, the dedication is propaganda: it presents the freedman as a grateful and loyal client, so historians must read it critically.

Source C, a wall painting from Pompeii, shows enslaved people serving diners at a banquet. It confirms that slaves performed domestic service in wealthy households, but it is painted from the perspective of the master and says nothing about how the servants experienced their work.

Other sources fill some of these gaps. Epitaphs, graffiti and the wax tablets of the banker Caecilius Iucundus record the buying and selling of slaves and the activities of freedmen. Even so, historians rarely hear the voices of enslaved people directly, so their understanding remains partial.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7–8 row: a reasoned judgement on how far Sources B and C help, supported by both sources and by other evidence such as epitaphs and the Caecilius Iucundus tablets, with historical terms used accurately.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sources B and C give some insight into the roles of slaves and freedmen. Source B shows that a freedman named Volusianus could afford a monument to his former master Balbus, which suggests that freedmen could gain wealth and standing. Source C shows enslaved people serving at a banquet, which confirms their domestic role, but it is painted from the master's view. Other sources such as epitaphs would help historians understand these groups more fully.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5–6 row: some judgement on the sources, with reference to both and to another source type, though briefly. Weighing the propaganda in Source B and stating how far the sources help would lift it to the 7–8 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Source B shows a freedman who paid for a monument to his master. Source C shows slaves serving at a banquet.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1–2 row: general statements that describe the sources without judging how far they help. Stating a clear judgement and explaining why it is qualified would lift it to the 3–4 row.

markerNotes: The top band uses both sources together but keeps them distinct, saying what the inscription (Source C) reveals and what the fresco (Source D) can and cannot show.
It explains status through property ownership, religious office and dependence on male relatives, rather than simply calling women equal or oppressed.

prompts.markingCriteria:

sampleAnswers.answer: Sources C and D help historians to understand the status of women in the social structure of Pompeii, although neither source gives a full picture on its own. Source C is an inscription recording that Mamia, daughter of Publius, was a public priestess who built a structure on her own land at her own expense. It shows that a Pompeian woman could hold a religious office, own property and spend her wealth publicly. Yet the inscription still names her father, so her standing was semi-independent and tied to a male relative. Source D is a fresco of a woman playing a stringed instrument beside seated figures. It suggests that women took part in social and domestic life and may have worked as entertainers, but the image cannot show whether this woman was free, enslaved or a freedwoman. Taken together, the sources show that women of wealthy families could act as property owners and religious leaders, while women of lower status are much harder to see. Historians must therefore combine these sources with wider evidence, such as graffiti and household remains, to judge how representative this status was across Pompeian society.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6–7 row: a detailed explanation of how the two sources reveal property, religious office and dependence, integrating both sources and using historical terms. To lift it, test the representativeness of elite evidence more explicitly.

sampleAnswers.answer: Source C shows that Mamia, a public priestess, could own land and spend her own money on a building, so women in Pompeii could hold property and religious roles. Source D shows a woman playing an instrument, which suggests women had a role in social life. Together, Sources C and D show that the status of women was not the same for everyone, and that wealthy women had more power than others in the social structure.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4–5 row: an accurate explanation that refers to Sources C and D and uses some historical terms. To reach 6–7, explain what the fresco cannot prove and identify the limits of elite evidence.

sampleAnswers.answer: Source C shows a woman who was a priestess, and Source D shows a woman with a musical instrument, so women had some roles in Pompeii.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1 row: general statements about women in Pompeii with a basic reference to the sources. To lift it, explain what the inscription reveals about status and how the fresco helps historians understand it.

prompts.question: Explain how elections worked in Pompeii and what the painted election notices reveal about political competition in the town.
markerNotes: Explain needs the mechanism (annual elections for the magistrates, notices urging voters) and the significance (patronage, endorsement and a limited franchise).

sampleAnswers.answer: Elections in Pompeii were held each year for the magistrates, and candidates ran public campaigns on the walls of the town. Supporters painted notices that named a candidate and urged voters to elect him, often adding the name of a trade association or neighbourhood group that endorsed him. These notices show that political life was organised around patronage and local networks rather than programmes, and that candidates needed the support of wealthy men and guilds to win. The competition was intense but narrow: only adult male citizens could vote or stand, so most inhabitants, including women and the enslaved, were excluded from the formal process although they were affected by its outcomes. The notices therefore reveal both the openness and the restrictions of local politics in Pompeii.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: explains the annual election process and the notices, analyses patronage and endorsement as the basis of competition, and assesses the restricted franchise against the openness of the campaigns.

sampleAnswers.answer: Elections happened every year and candidates put up notices on the walls asking people to vote for them. Some notices were from guilds. This shows that people were involved in politics.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the notices and their endorsement, but does not explain the competition or the limits on participation. It sits in the 3-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Elections were held in Pompeii.

prompts.question: Explain the nature of local political life in Pompeii and Herculaneum. Support your response using evidence from Sources C and D and other relevant sources.
markerNotes: The top band explains local political life as competitive, popular and rewarded with public honour, and integrates Sources C and D as evidence for each point.
Source C is read for what the notices reveal about campaigning, such as their placement on busy streets and their annual timing, rather than only described.
Other relevant sources, such as the programmata and Cicero's remark about the council, widen the explanation, and a caveat about who commissioned the evidence shows judgement.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the map and the inscription without explaining what they reveal about political life.
Treating Pompeii and Herculaneum as one political system, rather than explaining the evidence from each town.

9-10 marks: Provides a well-developed and detailed explanation of local political life in Pompeii and Herculaneum; Integrates evidence from Sources C and D and uses other relevant sources to support the response; Uses a range of appropriate historical terms and concepts

sampleAnswers.answer: Local political life in Pompeii and Herculaneum was competitive and popular, and it reached into everyday public space. Cicero remarked that it was harder to win a seat on the council at Pompeii than at Rome, which suggests how contested local office was. Source C shows this competition. The electoral notices for one candidate in Pompeii are concentrated along major thoroughfares and shopping streets, where the most people would see them. Politicians therefore chose places of heavy foot traffic to promote their cause. Because elections were held annually, the notices come from a single campaign rather than a permanent presence in the city. Programmata, the political graffiti found across Pompeii, extend this picture. They show that a wide range of people took part, from the tavern owner Aselina to guilds and professions, so local politics was not confined to the wealthy. Source D reveals the other side of public life, the reward of office. The decurions of Herculaneum voted to erect a statue to Marcus Nonius Balbus in a busy place, paid for by public funds, and recorded his titles as praetor, proconsul and patron. This shows that local politicians gained honour, and that they were expected to serve the town in return. Taken together, the sources show a political culture in which competition for office, popular participation and public honour for service were central to civic life in both cities. The caveat is that inscriptions and graffiti reflect those who could afford to commission them, so historians must treat them as evidence of an elite and popular political culture rather than of the whole population.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 9-10 row: a well-developed explanation of competition, popular participation and public honour, integrating Sources C and D with other evidence such as Cicero and the programmata. The caveat about who commissioned the evidence shows the critical judgement that the top band requires.

sampleAnswers.answer: Local political life in Pompeii was competitive. Source C shows many electoral notices for one candidate along major streets, so politicians could reach the people who shopped and walked there. Source D shows that successful politicians were honoured, because the decurions of Herculaneum set up a statue to Marcus Nonius Balbus in a busy place at public expense. Programmata also show that many people took an interest in elections, not only the wealthy. Historians should note, however, that these sources come from those who could afford to put up notices or statues, so they show the views of a particular group.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-6 row: some explanation of local politics that refers to Sources C and D. Explaining what the evidence shows about competition or honour, rather than only describing it, would move it to the 7-8 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Local politics involved elections and public honours. Source C shows electoral notices for one candidate in Pompeii, and Source D shows a statue set up to honour a politician in Herculaneum.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-2 row: a general statement about local politics, with references to Sources C and D. Explaining what the notices show about competition would reach the 3-4 row.

1-2 marks: Makes general statement(s) about public buildings in Pompeii and/or Herculaneum; May refer to Source D and/or Source E and/or other source(s)

sampleAnswers.answer: Public buildings help historians understand society in Pompeii and Herculaneum because they show how the community organised its political life, who paid for it and which values it displayed. The Forum of Pompeii, shown in Source D, was the centre of public life. Its temples, including the Temple of Jupiter, show that public religion was central to civic identity, while the macellum shows that buying and selling were organised in public space. The Temple of Vespasian, or Temple of the Genius of Augustus, shows that the imperial cult had reached local religion. The Building of Eumachia, which was dedicated by a wealthy woman, reveals that women could gain public influence through patronage, and its association with the fullers' guild shows the importance of trade in the town. Public buildings also show local political life. Inscriptions name the magistrates and the benefactors who paid for buildings, which reveals that political status was won through giving to the community. Source E makes the same point about Herculaneum. Although the town is largely unexcavated, Wallace-Hadrill argues that its public monuments imitated imperial Rome and that it was disproportionately well endowed. A missing macellum, built at the expense of a duumvir, reveals the importance of political patronage even in a small town. Historians must still be cautious. Public buildings were built by and for the elite, so they show the values of local leaders more than those of ordinary people. Nevertheless, they remain one of the most valuable ways to understand how Pompeii and Herculaneum were governed and how society was structured.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 9–10 row: a well-developed explanation of how public buildings help historians understand political, religious and economic life, integrating Sources D and E with other evidence. This is the top band; keep every building tied to a specific inference about society.

sampleAnswers.answer: Public buildings reveal political, religious and economic life. The Forum at Pompeii contained temples, a basilica and the macellum, a market, which show how these areas of life were organised together. The Building of Eumachia reveals that women could play a public role through their wealth. Source E shows that Herculaneum, although unexcavated, had public buildings and a macellum paid for by a magistrate, which reveals political patronage. Inscriptions on public buildings show who paid for them, so historians learn that wealthy men and women gained status by giving to the community. Baths and amphitheatres show that leisure was also a marker of social rank. Public buildings therefore show the elite's role in society, although they say less about ordinary people.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5–6 row: an explanation of how public buildings help historians understand political, religious and economic life, drawing on Sources D and E. To reach 7–8, integrate the sources more closely and add a second building type with its implication for society.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Forum at Pompeii shows that public buildings such as temples and markets were important to the town's life. Source D depicts the Forum, so historians can study how it was arranged.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1–2 row: a general statement about public buildings that refers to Source D without explaining how they help historians understand society. To lift it, state what buildings reveal about political, religious or economic life.

dotPoints.description: Economic activities, including commerce, industries and occupations

prompts.question: Deduce the main economic activities of Pompeii from the evidence of its workshops, shops and amphorae.
markerNotes: Deduce means reasoning from the evidence to a conclusion. Naming the fullery is description. Saying what its basins imply about scale and organisation is deduction.
Strong answers separate production (fulling, garum) from retail (bakeries, shops) and draw a conclusion about the balance between them.
commonStudentErrors: Listing workshops without explaining what they reveal about the economy.
Deducing that all Pompeian workshops were run by enslaved workers, which the evidence does not establish.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Deduces several economic activities from specific types of evidence (fullery, bakeries, garum production, amphorae), explains what each reveals about commerce and industry, and reaches a conclusion about the economy
4 marks: Deduces several activities from specific evidence, with explanation of their significance
3 marks: Identifies activities from the evidence with limited deduction
2 marks: Lists evidence of activities without linking it to the economy
1 mark: Makes a general statement about Pompeii's economy

sampleAnswers.answer: The economic activities indicated by the workshops and shops of Pompeii point to a diverse local economy based on manufacturing, food production and commerce. The fullers' basins and treading areas show that cloth was finished on a commercial scale, since fulling required a steady supply of water and urine, so it was an established industry rather than a household task. The bakeries, with their mills and ovens, show that much of the population relied on bread produced for sale. The garum shops and amphorae point to a substantial trade in processed food and drink, some exported beyond the region. The occupations shown by this evidence were concentrated among artisans and small traders, many of them freed people. Taken together, the evidence shows that commerce and small-scale industries formed the core of the local economy, supplemented by agriculture in the surrounding countryside.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: deduces several activities from specific evidence (fullery basins, bakery mills and ovens, garum and amphorae), explains what each implies about scale and organisation, and concludes about the balance of commerce and industry.

sampleAnswers.answer: Pompeii had many shops and workshops. There was a fullery, which cleaned clothes, and bakeries that made bread. There was also trade in wine and fish sauce, which was sold in amphorae. So the town had a lot of business.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the activities from the evidence, but the deduction stops at general business activity and does not reason about scale or organisation. It fits the 3-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Pompeii had shops.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement with no evidence or deduction, so only the 1-mark band applies.

prompts.scenario: A student is shown a hypothetical street plan (drawn for this task from the types of evidence found at Pompeii) showing a fullery, several bakeries, a shop selling fish sauce and a row of wine-shops. The student must draw conclusions about the local economy.

prompts.question: Describe the form and function of a Pompeian thermopolium, and what it reveals about street-level commerce.
markerNotes: Describe needs the form (masonry counter, jars, street frontage) and the function (sale of food and drink) with accurate detail.

sampleAnswers.answer: A thermopolium was a food and drink shop with a masonry counter opening onto the street. Large jars set into the counter held wine, water and prepared food, so customers bought take-away meals and drinks from passers-by. Its counter reveals street-level commerce in Pompeii, since many residents lacked kitchens and depended on shops such as this one.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: describes the counter and jars (form) and the sale of food and drink to passers-by (function), and explains the place of the shop in street-level commerce.

sampleAnswers.answer: A thermopolium was a shop that sold food and drink to passers-by. It had a counter with jars set into it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Accurate on form and function, but does not connect the shop to street-level commerce or the wider economy. It fits the 2-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: A thermopolium was a place where people ate.

prompts.question: What does evidence reveal about industries in Pompeii and Herculaneum? Support your answer using Source B and your own knowledge.
markerNotes: The top answer says what the evidence reveals about the economy (for example that Pompeii's industries served local needs and wider trade), not only that an industry existed.
Source B is a single object. The strongest answers interpret it as evidence for fishing and link it to other evidence, such as the marine remains from the Herculaneum sewers.
The stem asks what evidence reveals, so a list of industries stays in the lower rows unless each one is explained.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the fish hooks in detail (their size or shape) without saying what they show about industry.
Listing several industries with no link to Source B and no evidence for each.
Treating the fish hooks as proof of a large commercial fishing trade without saying how far the evidence supports that.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Provides a detailed and informed explanation of what evidence reveals about industries in Pompeii and Herculaneum; Supports the response using Source B; Communicates effectively using appropriate historical terms and concepts
5 marks: Provides an informed explanation of what evidence reveals about industries in Pompeii and Herculaneum; Refers to Source B; Communicates using appropriate historical terms and concepts
4 marks: Provides an explanation about industries in Pompeii and/or Herculaneum; Refers to Source B; Communicates using some historical terms and concepts
2-3 marks: Provides some information about one or more industries in Pompeii and/or Herculaneum; May refer to Source B; May use some historical terms and/or concepts
1 mark: Makes a general statement(s) about one or more industries in Pompeii or Herculaneum

sampleAnswers.answer: Evidence from Pompeii and Herculaneum reveals thriving industries that catered to the needs of both locals and trade networks. Numerous pistrina, with preserved mills and ovens, indicate the large-scale production of bread, a staple of the Roman diet. The fish hooks, shown in Source B, reflect the existence of the fishing industry in Campania. The importance of this is seen in the garum industry and the marine remains from the Herculaneum sewers. The presence of garum factories, particularly in Pompeii, highlights the significance of food processing and trade, as garum was highly sought-after across the empire. Excavations have uncovered fullonicae for textiles, with looms and dyeing vats suggesting a vibrant cloth-making industry. In addition, inscriptions and frescoes depict commercial transactions, advertising goods and services, from wine to metalwork. The discovery of wine presses, olive oil production facilities, and pottery kilns further demonstrates the variety of economic activities. These industries not only supported local communities but also linked Pompeii and Herculaneum to broader economic networks in the Mediterranean.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row: a detailed interpretation of what the evidence reveals about the industries of both towns, supported by Source B and by the garum and textile evidence.

sampleAnswers.answer: Source B, a group of bronze fish hooks from Pompeii, suggests that fishing was one of the town's industries. Pompeii also had bakeries, with mills and ovens, and fullonicae for cleaning and dyeing cloth. These show that the town produced food and textiles as well as objects for sale.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: some information about several industries, with a reference to Source B. To reach 4 marks it would explain what the fish hooks reveal about fishing and its links to trade, rather than listing industries.

sampleAnswers.answer: Pompeii had several industries, such as bread-making and cloth-making.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: a general statement about industries in Pompeii with no source and no explanation. Naming one industry with evidence from Source B would lift it.

dotPoints.description: Features and functions of houses

prompts.question: Explain how the features of a typical Pompeian house, such as the atrium, peristyle and street-front shops, reflected the functions of household life, business and display.
markerNotes: Explain needs the link between feature and function: the atrium served reception and display, the peristyle served private life, and the shops served income.
Strong answers note that one house combined domestic, economic and social functions, which is the central point of the question.
commonStudentErrors: Listing features without stating what each one did for the household.
Describing the atrium as a kitchen or bedroom, which confuses its function as a room for reception and display.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Explains how specific features (atrium, peristyle, tabernae, decoration, lararium) reflected the functions of domestic, economic and social life, and how the layout balanced privacy and display
5 marks: Explains how several features reflected their functions, with relevant evidence
4 marks: Describes several features and explains some of their functions
3 marks: Describes features with limited reference to their functions
2 marks: Identifies one feature and a use, with minimal explanation
1 mark: Makes a general statement about Pompeian houses

sampleAnswers.answer: The features of houses in Pompeii reflected the different functions that a household had to serve. The entrance (fauces) led into the atrium, an open-roofed room with a central pool (impluvium) that collected rainwater, and whose layout let visitors be received and seen by the household, so the atrium functioned as a space of public display and social status. Behind it, the peristyle, a colonnaded garden, gave private space for family life, for dining and for leisure, and the rooms around it show the division between public and private activity. Many houses had shops (tabernae) opening onto the street, which generated income and linked the household to commerce, so the front of a house could be both home and business. Wall paintings and mosaics in reception rooms and dining rooms displayed the owner's taste and wealth, while a lararium, or household shrine, expressed religious devotion within the house. Together these features show that Pompeian houses were designed to serve domestic, economic and social purposes at once, and that their functions shaped the way their spaces were arranged. The layout therefore reveals how the owners balanced privacy and display in a crowded town, and it shows that the same building could hold a family, a workshop and a visible claim to status.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: links specific features (atrium, peristyle, tabernae, decoration, lararium) to domestic, economic and social functions, and explains how the layout balanced privacy and display.

sampleAnswers.answer: A Pompeian house had an atrium, which was a central room with a pool, and a peristyle garden at the back. The atrium was for guests and the peristyle was for the family. Some houses had shops at the front that were rented out to make money. The paintings showed the owner's wealth.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes several features and some of their uses, but does not explain how the features together reflected household life, business and display. It fits the 4-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Pompeian houses had gardens and rooms.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement with no feature explained and no function, so only the 1-mark band applies.

prompts.question: Clarify the relationship between the street-front shops (tabernae) of a Pompeian house and the household that owned it.
markerNotes: Clarify means making the relationship clear: name the connection (an internal door, a shared building) and what it meant for the household.
Two supporting features (street location, access to rooms behind, income) move the answer into the top band.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the shops as separate businesses with no connection to the household.
Treating the tabernae as public buildings owned by the town rather than as part of private houses.

2 marks: Describes the shops and their location, with one link to the household
1 mark: Makes a general statement about shops in Pompeii

sampleAnswers.answer: The tabernae were shops opening onto the street from the front of many houses in Pompeii. They often connected to the rooms behind through an internal door, so the household and the shop shared one building. This shows that the features of a house, including its shops, served the functions of both domestic life and income. The street-front shop also gave the household a public face, linking its reputation to its trade.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: clarifies the physical link (internal door, shared building) and the economic link (income, household trade), with the street frontage as a public face.

sampleAnswers.answer: The tabernae were shops at the front of houses. They made money for the owners.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Accurate on location and income, but with no link to the household itself. It fits the 2-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Shops were built in Pompeii.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement that does not address the relationship with the household, so only the 1-mark band applies.

prompts.question: How useful are the private buildings in Pompeii and Herculaneum in providing evidence about the economy? Support your response using evidence from Source A and other relevant sources.
markerNotes: The top answer weighs how useful private buildings are for the economy, and says where their evidence stops, such as large-scale commerce or public markets.
Source A should be used as specific evidence, for example the rental of shops and apartments, rather than mentioned in passing.
Other evidence, such as the wall paintings in the House of the Vettii, lifts the answer above a single-source response.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the rooms and decoration of houses without linking any feature to the economy.
Treating Source A as evidence of a whole economy when it shows only one owner's estate.
Saying private buildings are useful without saying what they cannot show.
prompts.markingCriteria:

2 marks: Provides limited information about how useful private buildings are in providing evidence about the economy in Pompeii and Herculaneum; Makes limited reference to Source A

sampleAnswers.answer: Private buildings are useful for understanding the economy of Pompeii and Herculaneum, because many houses were also places of commerce. Source A, an inscription advertising Julia Felix's estate, offers baths, shops with upper rooms and apartments to let, showing that one property could earn rent from several activities. Wall paintings in the House of the Vettii in Pompeii show cupids working as goldsmiths and wine-makers, which suggests the production and sale of goods. However, private buildings say little about large-scale commerce or the public marketplaces, which were civic spaces. They reveal the economy of individual owners more than that of the cities as a whole.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row: accurate information on how private buildings show the economy, supported by Source A and other evidence, with the limits of that evidence stated. Adding a point about how far the houses reflect the wider economy would make the judgement more developed.

sampleAnswers.answer: Source A shows that Julia Felix let shops with upper rooms and apartments, so private buildings reveal how owners earned rent. The House of the Vettii in Pompeii also has wall paintings of wine-making, which show local trade, but they say little about public markets.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3–4 row: sound information on how private buildings show rental income and trade, with some reference to Source A. Explaining what the buildings cannot show about Herculaneum and the wider city would lift it to the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Private buildings show something about the economy of Pompeii.

dotPoints.description: Leisure activities, including entertainment and baths

prompts.question: Describe the riot at the amphitheatre of Pompeii in 59 CE and its consequences for the entertainment of the town.
markerNotes: Describe needs the core facts: 59 CE, the amphitheatre, the rivalry with Nuceria, the violence and the Senate's response.
Explaining what the ban meant for entertainment and public order is what earns the top band.
commonStudentErrors: Dating the riot to 79 CE and confusing it with the eruption.
Stating that the ban was permanent, when Tacitus records a ban of ten years.
prompts.markingCriteria:

3 marks: Describes the riot accurately with one consequence
2 marks: Describes the riot with limited detail
1 mark: Makes a general statement about an event at Pompeii

sampleAnswers.answer: In 59 CE a riot broke out at the amphitheatre of Pompeii during a gladiatorial show. According to Tacitus, a quarrel between Pompeians and people from neighbouring Nuceria escalated into the throwing of stones and bloodshed, with many killed or injured. The Senate banned such gatherings at Pompeii for ten years, and the organiser of the games was punished. The ban shows how the state acted to restore public order and control the entertainment of provincial towns. Tacitus presents the affair as a product of local rivalry, so it also shows how important entertainment was to the life of the town.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: describes the riot accurately (date, setting, parties, violence) and explains the consequences for entertainment and public order, including the ten-year ban.

sampleAnswers.answer: There was a riot at the amphitheatre in Pompeii in 59 CE between Pompeians and people from Nuceria. The Senate stopped such gatherings at Pompeii for a while.
sampleAnswers.feedback: An accurate outline of the event and one consequence, with no detail of the violence and no account of what the ban meant for entertainment. It fits the 2-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: A riot happened in Pompeii.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement with no date, parties or consequence, so only the 1-mark band applies.

prompts.question: Analyse the role of the public baths in the leisure life of Pompeii, including how bathing related to social status and the wider community.
markerNotes: Analyse needs relationships: how the mix of users and the patronage of wealthy men connected leisure with status and community.
Specific evidence (the Stabian Baths' sequence of rooms, the palaestra, the sections for men and women) carries the top bands.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the baths only as hygiene facilities, which misses their leisure and social role.
Assuming the baths were used only by the wealthy, when the evidence of mixed use and attached shops suggests a wider public.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses the baths' role in leisure, including bathing as exercise, conversation and entertainment, the expression of social status, and the creation of community ties, with specific evidence
5 marks: Analyses two of these roles with relevant evidence and some connection between them
4 marks: Describes the leisure role of the baths with some analysis of status or community
3 marks: Describes the baths and their facilities with limited analysis
2 marks: Identifies one feature or use of the baths with minimal explanation
1 mark: Makes a general statement about the baths

sampleAnswers.answer: The public baths were central to leisure in Pompeii because they combined bathing with exercise, conversation and entertainment. The Stabian Baths offered a sequence of heated, warm and cold rooms, as well as a palaestra for exercise, so bathing was an organised routine rather than simply hygiene. Baths brought together people of different social status, but status was still expressed in them: wealthy patrons who sponsored public facilities displayed their generosity and influence, and the separation of men's and women's sections regulated who could mix with whom. The baths also created community ties, since residents gathered there for conversation and commercial dealings, and the palaestra gave young men a place to display physical skill before their neighbours. Bathing usually took place in the afternoon, which made the baths one of the most regular points of contact between people of different occupations and households. The baths therefore show leisure as both a private pleasure and a public institution through which social status and community ties were displayed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: analyses the baths' leisure role (exercise, conversation, entertainment), the expression of social status through patronage and structured access, and the creation of community ties, with specific evidence.

sampleAnswers.answer: Baths in Pompeii were used for relaxing and exercise. The Stabian Baths had hot, warm and cold rooms. People went there to talk, and wealthy men could show their status. This made the baths part of the community.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Accurate on the facilities and social functions, but the link between status, display and community is asserted rather than analysed. It fits the 3-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: People went to the baths to wash.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement that misses the leisure, status and community roles, so only the 1-mark band applies.

prompts.scenario: A student is studying the Stabian Baths and notes that one of the public bath complexes in Pompeii had separate sections for men and women. The student is asked to analyse how bathing shaped the town's leisure and social life.

prompts.question: Explain the importance of leisure activities in everyday life in Pompeii and Herculaneum. Support your response using evidence from Sources D and E and other relevant sources.
markerNotes: The top band argues that leisure was central to social life in both towns, and that access to it depended on social status.
Integrate Source D (gladiatorial combat) and Source E (the Rufus inscription) with other evidence such as the amphitheatre and the baths.
Explain why leisure mattered, not only which activities existed: what it did for individuals, for cities and for wealthy benefactors.
commonStudentErrors: Describing gladiatorial fights or baths without explaining why they mattered in everyday life.
Reading Source E as evidence of entertainment alone, without noting the self-promotion of the benefactor.
Assuming all residents shared equally in leisure, without addressing the poor and the enslaved.
prompts.markingCriteria:
9-10 marks: Provides a well-developed and detailed explanation of the importance of leisure activities in everyday life in Pompeii and Herculaneum; Integrates evidence from Sources D and E and uses other relevant sources to support the response; Uses a range of historical terms and concepts appropriately
7-8 marks: Provides a detailed explanation of the importance of leisure activities in everyday life in Pompeii and Herculaneum; Uses evidence from Sources D and E and other relevant source(s) to support the response; Uses historical terms and concepts appropriately
5-6 marks: Provides some explanation of the importance of leisure activities in everyday life in Pompeii and Herculaneum; Refers to Sources D and E; may refer to other source(s); Uses some historical terms and concepts appropriately
3-4 marks: Provides some description of leisure activities in everyday life in Pompeii and/or Herculaneum; Refers to Source D and/or Source E and/or other source(s); May use historical terms and/or concepts
1-2 marks: Makes general statements about leisure activities and/or everyday life; May refer to Source D and/or Source E

sampleAnswers.answer:
Leisure activities were central to everyday life in Pompeii and Herculaneum, but access to them depended on social status. Source D, a fresco of gladiators, shows that gladiatorial shows were a popular form of entertainment that drew large crowds. The amphitheatre in Pompeii seated upwards of 20 000 people, and the seating itself reflected rank, with the wealthy in the front rows. Entertainment was not limited to spectacles. Pompeii had four public bath complexes and Herculaneum had two, and visits to the baths were social occasions with separate areas for men and women. The Odeion and theatre in Pompeii formed an entertainment quarter, so leisure was built into the physical fabric of the towns.

Source E shows that giving to leisure was also a form of self-promotion. The inscription records that Rufus paid for the theatre and orchestra from his own money, alongside his political offices, which suggests that wealthy men gained status by funding public entertainment. Gambling, dining and brothels were further features of daily life, so leisure filled many hours and many public spaces.

Yet leisure was not equally available. The poor and slaves had less time and money for the baths, the theatre and the games, so the importance of leisure in everyday life depended on a person's status. The evidence therefore shows that leisure was vital to the social life of both towns, but that it also reinforced the hierarchy within them.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 9–10 row: a well-developed explanation of the importance of leisure, integrating Sources D and E with the amphitheatre, the baths and the theatre. Keeping the link between leisure and social status holds the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Leisure activities were important in everyday life in Pompeii and Herculaneum because people went to shows and to the baths. Source D shows gladiators fighting, and gladiatorial shows drew large crowds to the amphitheatre in Pompeii. The public baths were social places, and Pompeii had several bath complexes where people met, bathed and exercised. Source E shows a benefactor paying for a theatre and orchestra from his own money, which suggests that wealthy people paid for entertainment and gained status by doing so. However, not everyone could take part in these activities, and the poor and enslaved had less access to them, so leisure reflected social status.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5–6 row: some explanation of leisure in both towns, with Sources D and E referred to and social access noted. Explaining what Source E shows about status and self-promotion would reach the 7–8 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: People in Pompeii went to the baths and watched gladiators, which was a common activity. Source D shows a gladiator fight, and the games were popular with many people in the town.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1–2 row: general statements about leisure with a reference to Source D and no explanation of importance. Saying why leisure mattered to social life, using one example, would lift it.

dotPoints.description: Health, including diet, water supply and sanitation

prompts.question: Explain how Pompeii's water supply and sanitation systems shaped the health of the town's residents.
markerNotes: Explain needs the chain from system to health: clean water and drains reduced some diseases, while lead pipes and unequal access created new risks.
Naming the Aqua Augusta, the castellum and the lead pipes accurately earns the specific evidence mark.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that the water system made Pompeii disease-free, which the evidence does not support.
Describing the aqueduct without linking it to Augustus or to the town's supply arrangements.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Explains how the water supply and sanitation systems worked and assesses their effect on residents' health, including the risks of lead pipes and unequal access, with specific evidence
4 marks: Explains the systems and their effect on health with relevant evidence and some assessment of risk
3 marks: Describes the water supply and sanitation with limited reference to health
2 marks: Identifies one feature of the water or sanitation system
1 mark: Makes a general statement about Pompeii's water

sampleAnswers.answer: The water supply of Pompeii came from the Aqua Augusta, an aqueduct that brought water from springs near Serino to a distribution tank (castellum) at the edge of the town. Lead pipes carried water from there to public fountains and some private houses, so most residents depended on fountains. The water system also made flushing latrines and drains possible, which carried waste away from the centre, so sanitation was better than in many ancient cities. However, lead pipes posed a health risk, since lead could accumulate in the body. The water supply and sanitation therefore improved the health of many residents while leaving real dangers unresolved. Benefits were also unevenly spread, since households far from the main pipes relied on public fountains. Households also collected rainwater in cisterns, so the quality of water varied with its source.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: explains how the aqueduct, castellum and lead pipes delivered water, how drains supported sanitation, and assesses the health effects, including the risk of lead and unequal access.

sampleAnswers.answer: Pompeii had an aqueduct that brought water from the hills. Water went to fountains and some houses through pipes. There were also drains and latrines, which helped with sanitation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the system accurately, but does not explain how it affected health. It sits in the 3-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Pompeii had running water.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement with no system and no health link, so only the 1-mark band applies.

prompts.scenario: A student is reading a summary of the water system: an aqueduct from the hills around Serino, a distribution tank at the town's edge, and lead pipes running to fountains and some houses. The student must explain how the system affected people's health.

prompts.question: Identify two foods that the organic evidence from Herculaneum shows were part of the local diet, and the type of evidence for each.
markerNotes: Two foods and the type of evidence for each are required. Naming foods alone is incomplete.
Stronger answers say what the evidence shows about diet and health, not just what the items were.
commonStudentErrors: Naming foods such as fish or olives that come from general or literary evidence, without stating the site evidence that supports them.
Confusing organic remains with art or buildings because they were found in the same houses.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Identifies two foods, each with a correct type of evidence (for example carbonised bread or figs as organic remains)
1 mark: Identifies one food, or one type of evidence, correctly

sampleAnswers.answer: Two foods in the diet at Herculaneum are bread and figs, each shown by organic remains: carbonised loaves and charred figs. This evidence of food shows what the diet was and supports conclusions about health.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: identifies two foods, each with a correct type of evidence (carbonised bread and charred figs as organic remains), and notes what the evidence shows about diet and health.

sampleAnswers.answer: Bread was eaten in Herculaneum.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One food with no type of evidence, so only the 1-mark band applies.

prompts.question: Explain the importance of water supply and sanitation to everyday life in Pompeii and Herculaneum. Support your response using Source B.
markerNotes: The top band explains why water supply and sanitation mattered to daily life, linking practical needs such as drinking, cooking and waste removal to social and public life.
It uses Source B: the private fountain shows how control of water in the home could display wealth and status.
It names the infrastructure precisely, such as aqueducts, pipes, latrines and cesspits, rather than writing that water was simply important.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the Herculaneum fountain without explaining why it mattered for everyday life.
Listing aqueducts and drains as facts without linking them to the question.
Giving only functional benefits and ignoring social or status meanings.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Provides a detailed and accurate explanation of the importance of water supply and sanitation to everyday life in Pompeii and Herculaneum; Supports response using evidence from Source B; Communicates using appropriate historical terms and concepts
4 marks: Provides an accurate explanation of the importance of water supply and sanitation to everyday life in Pompeii and Herculaneum; Refers to Source B; Communicates using some historical terms and concepts
3 marks: Provides some explanation of the importance of water supply and sanitation to everyday life in Pompeii and Herculaneum; May refer to Source B; Communicates using some historical terms and/or concepts
2 marks: Provides some information on the water supply and/or sanitation in Pompeii and/or Herculaneum; May refer to Source B; May use some historical terms and/or concepts
1 mark: Makes a general statement about water supply or sanitation in Pompeii and/or Herculaneum; OR; Makes general reference to Source B

sampleAnswers.answer: Water supply and sanitation were important for a variety of reasons in both public and private domains. For private citizens having water supplied to the home or business for practical purposes such as drinking, cleaning and cooking was important but to do so also demonstrated one’s wealth and social status through activities such as private bathing and ornamental fountains as shown in Source B. Water supply via aqueducts and pipes to baths, latrines and fountains, and carried away to cesspits and the sea, played an important functional role, while in the public sphere baths, for example, served a social role as a meeting place.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5 row: a detailed explanation of why water supply and sanitation mattered in practical, social and public life, supported by Source B and using appropriate historical terms. To extend it, it could weigh the health risks of poor drainage.

sampleAnswers.answer: Water supply and sanitation mattered in daily life. Households needed water for drinking, cooking and cleaning, and a private fountain, as shown in Source B, displayed a household’s wealth. An aqueduct brought water to the towns, and drains and cesspits carried waste away, which made the towns more pleasant and healthier to live in.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3 row: explains why water and sanitation mattered and refers to Source B with some historical terms. To reach the 4 row, explain how the source supports the point in more detail and use more precise terms such as aqueduct and cesspit.

sampleAnswers.answer: The towns had water pipes and latrines that were important for everyday life.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1 row: a general statement about water or sanitation with no explanation of importance and no use of Source B. To lift it, explain why water and drainage mattered for daily life and refer to Source B.

prompts.question: Explain what human remains reveal about the people of Campania.
markerNotes: The top band explains several findings about the people of Campania, such as diet, disease and labour, and says what each reveals about their lives.
Accurate, specific evidence such as pleurisy, brucellosis and differences in diet earns the detailed row; general claims that people were unhealthy do not.
Strong answers connect findings to the population: the differing diets of men and women, the signs of hard physical labour and the range of ages in the remains.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the eruption or the destruction of the cities instead of what the remains reveal about people.
Stating that 'the people were unhealthy' without naming a disease, a diet or a physical sign.
Claiming that the social status of the people found at Herculaneum is known, when the evidence does not settle it.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Provides a detailed and accurate explanation of what human remains reveal about the people of Campania
3 marks: Provides an accurate explanation of what human remains reveal about the people of Campania
2 marks: Provides some information about human remains and/or the people of Campania
1 mark: Makes a general statement about human remains or the people of Campania

sampleAnswers.answer: Human remains from Campania show us how the people there both lived and died. Remains at the boatsheds of Herculaneum indicate a range of the population; it is difficult to say for certain their social status. Some skeletons have been found with indications of pleurisy, which may be indicative of the polluted interiors of houses. These skeletons also indicate that women generally ate more meat and eggs, while men ate more fish and seafood. Human remains from Pompeii and other towns indicate a range of ages and diseases such as brucellosis. Their teeth were generally healthy, indicating a good diet; however, many skeletons have markings of malnutrition or hard physical labour.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4 row: a detailed and accurate explanation of what the remains show about diet, disease, labour and social uncertainty in Campania. Linking each finding to what it says about the population is what separates it from the 3 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Human remains from Campania show that people suffered from disease, such as pleurisy, which may have come from the polluted interiors of houses. Skeletons also show differences in diet between men and women, with women eating more meat and eggs. Remains from Pompeii show a range of ages, and many people bore the marks of hard physical labour.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3 row: an accurate explanation with several findings about health and diet. Explaining what the difference in diet between men and women reveals about their lives would reach the 4 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Human remains from Campania tell historians about the people who lived there.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1 row: a general statement about human remains. Naming one finding about health, such as pleurisy or diet, would lift it to the 2 row.

prompts.question: Explain what archaeological evidence reveals about food and dining in Pompeii and Herculaneum. Support your response using Source A and your own knowledge.
markerNotes: The top band explains what the evidence reveals about food and dining in both cities, not just what was eaten, and uses Source A to support its claims.

Source A is a price list from a food stall in Regio II at Pompeii, so the strongest answers read its items (wine, cheese, oil, bread and pork) and draw an inference about who bought food and at what cost.
Own knowledge should go beyond the source to the dolia, triclinia and carbonised food at Herculaneum, linking each to what it shows about daily life.
commonStudentErrors: Retelling the items in Source A one by one without drawing a conclusion about dining.
Describing dining with modern assumptions, such as tables and chairs in a restaurant, instead of the benches and dolia of Pompeian taverns.
Writing about Pompeii and Herculaneum as if they were one place, or using only one city without saying so.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Provides a detailed and informed explanation of what evidence reveals about food and dining in Pompeii and Herculaneum; Supports the response using Source A; Communicates effectively using appropriate historical terms and concepts
4 marks: Provides an informed explanation of what evidence reveals about food and dining in Pompeii and Herculaneum; Makes reference to Source A; Communicates using appropriate historical terms and concepts
3 marks: Provides some explanation of what evidence reveals about food and dining in Pompeii and/or Herculaneum; May make reference to Source A; Communicates using some historical terms and/or concepts
2 marks: Provides some information about food and/or dining in Pompeii and/or Herculaneum; May make reference to Source A; May use some historical terms and/or concepts
1 mark: Makes a general statement(s) about food and dining in Pompeii and/or Herculaneum

sampleAnswers.answer: Archaeological evidence at Pompeii and Herculaneum reveals much about food and dining. Common people would dine in taverns, selecting food from dolia set into benches, and Source A depicts a price list of food available for a food stall, including pork, bread, oil and cheese. This indicates that public dining using disposable income was available in Pompeii and Herculaneum. Frescoes and mosaics depict the types of food available to the local peoples. Carbonised seeds, bread and nuts from Herculaneum show us what people ate. Private houses contained triclinia, often highly decorated, showing that dinner parties were a common form of entertainment for wealthier people. Studies of bones have revealed that men in Herculaneum enjoyed a diet richer in seafood than women.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5 row: a detailed, informed explanation of what the evidence reveals about food and dining in both cities, drawing on Source A, the taverns, the triclinia and the carbonised food. This is the top band; keep each claim linked to a specific piece of evidence.

sampleAnswers.answer: Source A shows that food was sold ready-to-eat in Pompeii, with wine, bread, cheese, oil and pork priced for a food stall. This suggests that ordinary people with spare money could buy meals in the street. Taverns at Pompeii set dolia into their benches, so commercial dining was common. Such evidence shows how food was part of everyday life.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3 row: an explanation that uses Source A and the evidence from taverns, but the link to what it reveals about society is brief. To reach 4 or 5, compare Pompeii with Herculaneum and explain what the prices show about who could afford to eat out.

sampleAnswers.answer: Source A shows that bread and wine were sold in Pompeii.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1 row: a general statement about food in Pompeii that names the source without explaining what it reveals. To lift it, explain what the price list shows about dining and why it matters.

dotPoints.description: Public and private religion

prompts.question: Distinguish between public and private religion in Pompeii, using the Temple of Jupiter and household shrines as examples.
markerNotes: Distinguish needs a difference in organisation or purpose, not just two examples: civic and state-linked against domestic and personal.
The top band comes from explaining how the two levels related, for example civic cult projecting the state's authority while households kept their own devotion.
commonStudentErrors: Presenting public and private religion as entirely separate, with no link between them.
Calling the lararium a temple, which confuses household and civic religion.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Distinguishes the purpose and organisation of public religion (civic cult, magistrates, the Temple of Jupiter) from private religion (household shrines, personal devotion), using specific evidence and explaining the relationship between them
4 marks: Distinguishes both with specific evidence and some explanation of their purpose
3 marks: Identifies the two forms with examples but limited explanation of the difference
2 marks: Describes one form with accurate detail
1 mark: Makes a general statement about religion in Pompeii

sampleAnswers.answer: Public religion in Pompeii was organised by the city's magistrates and expressed the collective identity of the community. The Temple of Jupiter, the Capitolium, stood at the northern end of the forum and was dedicated to the Capitoline triad of Jupiter, Juno and Minerva, so its cult tied the town to the Roman state. Its festivals and sacrifices were overseen by the magistrates, who reinforced civic loyalty and their own authority. Private religion, by contrast, took place in the household. Household shrines, or lararia, honoured the Lares and the family's ancestors, and offerings were made at home rather than through civic officials. The two levels worked together: public religion projected the authority of the city, while household worship gave families a direct and personal relationship with the divine.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: distinguishes public religion (magistrates, the Temple of Jupiter, civic loyalty) from private religion (household shrines, the Lares, a personal relationship with the divine), using specific evidence, and explains how the two levels related.

sampleAnswers.answer: Public religion was for the whole town and was run by magistrates. The Temple of Jupiter was an example of public religion. Private religion happened in houses with shrines that people used for their own gods.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Accurate examples and a basic distinction, but the purpose of each level and their relationship are not explained. It sits in the 3-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Pompeii had both public and private religion.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement with no examples or distinction, so only the 1-mark band applies.

prompts.scenario: A student is working from a plan of Pompeii's forum, where the Capitolium (a temple of Jupiter, Juno and Minerva) stands at the northern end, and from a plan of a house with a small household shrine in its kitchen area. The student must explain how the two kinds of religion differed in their organisation.

prompts.question: Describe the cult of Venus Pompeiana and what its prominence in the town reveals about religion and civic identity.
markerNotes: Describe needs the cult itself (Venus Pompeiana as patron goddess, her sanctuary) and a link to civic identity.

commonStudentErrors: Treating Venus Pompeiana as a purely personal cult, when her prominence was civic.
Describing Venus as the goddess of Pompeii's trade only, without the civic role.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes the cult of Venus Pompeiana, including her role as patron goddess, and explains what its prominence reveals about civic identity and religion
2 marks: Describes the cult accurately with limited explanation
1 mark: Makes a general statement about religion in Pompeii

sampleAnswers.answer: Venus Pompeiana was the patron goddess of Pompeii, and her cult was closely tied to civic identity. Her sanctuary and her images on public and private walls show that the goddess linked the town's religion to its self-image as a prosperous Roman community. Her prominence therefore reveals how religion and civic pride were combined, and how the town expressed its collective identity through its protector goddess.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: describes Venus Pompeiana as patron goddess with her sanctuary, and explains how her cult linked religion to civic identity at both public and private levels.

sampleAnswers.answer: Venus was the patron goddess of Pompeii and had a temple in the town.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Accurate basics, but no explanation of what the cult reveals about civic identity or religion. It fits the 2-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Pompeii worshipped many gods.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement with no cult named and no explanation, so only the 1-mark band applies.

prompts.question: Outline the features of household religion in Pompeii. Support your response using Source A.
markerNotes: The top band names specific features of the shrine, such as the lares and the genius, rather than only saying that households prayed.
Source A has to support the answer: describe what the painted shrine shows and link it to household religion.
Keep to an outline; a full account of Pompeian religion is not needed for 3 marks.
commonStudentErrors: Describing Pompeian religion in general without referring to household shrines.
Mentioning Source A without saying what it shows.
Treating the lares and the genius as the same spirit.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Provides accurate information about features of household religion in Pompeii; Supports response using Source A; Communicates using appropriate historical terms
2 marks: Provides some information about features of household religion in Pompeii; Makes reference to Source A; May use historical terms
1 mark: Makes a general statement about household religion in Pompeii

sampleAnswers.answer: Household religion centred around shrines where the household gods were worshipped and presented with offerings. Source A is a lararium (shrine) that portrays two dancing youths (the lares) whose spirits protected the household and the spirit of the head of the household (the genius) in the centre. The paterfamilias (head of the family) conducted religious ceremonies at the household shrine to ensure the family’s good fortune.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3 row: accurate features of household religion, with the lares, the genius and the paterfamilias identified and Source A used as support. It is already at the top band; keep each feature tied to the source.

sampleAnswers.answer: Households worshipped their gods at small shrines, where offerings were made to protect the family. Source A shows a painted shrine with figures and a serpent, which reflects these beliefs.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2 row: some features of household shrines and a reference to Source A, but the figures are not identified. Naming the lares and the genius would reach the 3 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Families prayed to their gods at small shrines in their homes.
