prompts.question: Which culture had more influence in Pompeii and Herculaneum: Greek or Egyptian? Support your response using evidence from Sources B and C and other relevant sources.
markerNotes: The top band makes a clear judgement about whether Greek or Egyptian culture had more influence, and tests that judgement against Sources B and C.
Source C is Mary Beard's comment that a statue of Isis is 'hardly Egyptian at all', which strong answers use to show that Egyptian influence was often shaped by Greek style.
Other sources such as the Odeon, the Alexander Mosaic and the Temple of Isis should be used to show the breadth of each culture's influence.
commonStudentErrors: Describing Greek and Egyptian culture without making a judgement about which had more influence.
Treating Source B as evidence of Egyptian culture, or missing that Hercules and the Greek gods in it show Greek influence.
Using only the two sources and no other evidence, so the response cannot reach the 6-7 band.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6-7 marks: Provides an informed judgement about whether Greek or Egyptian culture had more influence in Pompeii and Herculaneum; Supports the response using evidence from Sources B and C and refers to other relevant source(s); Communicates ideas and information using appropriate historical terms and concepts
4-5 marks: Provides a judgement about the influence of Greek and/or Egyptian culture in Pompeii and Herculaneum; Supports the response with reference to Sources B and C and other relevant source(s); Communicates using some historical terms and concepts
2-3 marks: Provides some relevant information about Greek and/or Egyptian culture in Pompeii and/or Herculaneum; May refer to Sources B and/or C and/or other sources; May use some historical terms and/or concepts
1 mark: Makes a general statement(s) about Greek and/or Egyptian culture in Pompeii or Herculaneum

sampleAnswers.answer: Greek culture had more influence in Pompeii and Herculaneum than Egyptian culture, although Egyptian influence was real and visible. Greek influence was older and deeper. Greek colonists had settled the Bay of Naples from Cumae long before Rome took control of Campania, and this shaped the architecture, language and religion of both towns. Source B, a fresco from Herculaneum, shows Hercules on Mount Olympus with the Greek gods. Hercules was the patron god of the town, and his presence shows that Greek deities adopted by the early settlers were still celebrated when the towns were destroyed in AD 79. Egyptian culture was more exotic and more limited. The Cult of Isis was established in Pompeii, with a temple and statues of the goddess, and Egyptian-style figures appear in household shrines. Source C, by Mary Beard, describes a first-century CE statue of Isis which is hardly Egyptian at all, because it follows a Greek sculptural style several hundred years older. This suggests that Egyptian religion was absorbed into a Greek artistic tradition. The Odeon at Pompeii and the Alexander Mosaic from the House of the Faun reflect Greek architecture and art, while the Temple of Isis reflects Egyptian religion. Greek influence was therefore more pervasive, reaching architecture, art and religion, while Egyptian influence was more striking but more limited.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6–7 row: an informed judgement that Greek culture had more influence, supported by Sources B and C and by other sources including the Odeon and the Alexander Mosaic. This is the top band; to keep it, state the judgement at the start and test the Egyptian case against Source C.

sampleAnswers.answer: Greek culture was more influential in Pompeii and Herculaneum because both towns had Greek roots and Greek art and religion were widespread. Source B shows Hercules, the patron god of Herculaneum, with the Greek gods on Mount Olympus. Egyptian culture was also present, through the cult of Isis and Egyptian statuettes found in household shrines. Source C suggests, however, that even Egyptian imagery was shaped by Greek style. The Egyptian influence was therefore more limited. Overall, the Greek presence reached architecture as well as religion, so it was deeper than Egyptian influence.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4–5 row: a judgement about the relative influence of Greek and Egyptian culture, supported by Sources B and C. To reach 6–7, bring in more other sources and argue more fully why Greek influence was deeper.

sampleAnswers.answer: Egyptian culture was present in Pompeii through the Cult of Isis.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1 row: a general statement about Egyptian culture in Pompeii with no use of the sources. To lift it, refer to Source B or C and make a judgement about which culture was more influential.

dotPoints.description: The practices and challenges of excavation and conservation at the sites in the 20th and 21st centuries

prompts.question: Explain the main challenges of excavation and conservation at Pompeii and Herculaneum in the 20th and 21st centuries, and how practices have responded to them.
markerNotes: Explain needs the causal link: fragile material and visitor numbers create problems, and each conservation response carries its own trade-off.
The strongest answers show change over time, for example from earlier excavation practices to 21st-century stabilisation and management.
commonStudentErrors: Treating conservation as a 21st-century issue only, and ignoring the damage caused by early excavation.
Describing the House of the Gladiators collapse without relating it to the wider conservation problem.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Explains the challenges of excavation and conservation across the 20th and 21st centuries (past excavation practices, weathering, collapse, visitor pressure) and how practices have responded, with specific evidence
4 marks: Explains the challenges and responses with relevant evidence, with some attention to change over time
3 marks: Describes challenges with examples and limited explanation of responses
2 marks: Identifies one challenge or response with minimal explanation
1 mark: Makes a general statement about the sites

sampleAnswers.answer: The challenges of excavation and conservation at Pompeii and Herculaneum have been shaped by the fragility of the material and the scale of the sites. Earlier excavation practices, including large-scale digging and the removal of objects to museums, damaged the context of finds and left exposed walls vulnerable to weather. In the 21st century the main challenge has been deterioration, as rain, heat and large numbers of visitors affect exposed structures, and the collapse of the House of the Gladiators in 2010 showed how fragile some buildings had become. Conservators have responded with stabilisation, improved drainage and roofing, and funding such as the Great Pompeii Project, launched in 2012. Herculaneum, partly covered by the modern town, faces different difficulties, so the practices of conservation combine technical repair with decisions about how much of the sites to expose to the public.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: explains the challenges across the 20th and 21st centuries (early excavation damage, weathering, the 2010 collapse, visitor pressure), the responses (stabilisation, drainage, the Great Pompeii Project), and the trade-offs in the practices of conservation.

sampleAnswers.answer: The international community has contributed to Italian efforts in conserving the cities of Vesuvius through expertise, funding and direct leadership, although these contributions have depended on outside priorities and money. Source E shows one form of contribution. Gabriel Zuchtriegel, a German archaeologist, took part in the Great Pompeii Project, an Italian and European Union initiative begun in 2012 to save a site that had suffered years of neglect. He was then appointed director of Pompeii, the first non-Italian to hold the role, and he stated that new excavation would not be a priority because what is excavated must also be conserved and protected. This shows how international expertise shifted the emphasis from discovery to preservation. Source F shows a different model. The Pompeii Sustainable Preservation Project, founded in 2014, works in the necropolis of Porta Nocera and is funded entirely by fundraising and private investors. Its existence shows that private investment has filled gaps left by public budgets, and that donors now form part of the conservation effort. Other contributions extend this picture. Foreign institutions and foundations, including the Getty Foundation and the Packard Humanities Institute’s Herculaneum Conservation Project, have funded conservation work and research, while academic partners such as the University of Sydney worked with the Pompeii Archaeological Park on the Pompeii Cast Project. Together these examples show that international collaboration has been substantial and wide-ranging. However, it has relied on a mix of public, private and academic funding, so its long-term sustainability remains uncertain and depends on continued commitment from both Italy and its partners. Taken together, Sources E and F show that the international contribution combined expert leadership with direct funding.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 9–10 row: a well-developed explanation of several international contributions, integrating Sources E and F with other named examples and assessing their sustainability. prompts.question: Discuss whether archaeologists should reconstruct the sites of Pompeii and Herculaneum. Support your response using Sources A and B and other relevant sources.
markerNotes: The top band weighs points for and against reconstruction and reaches a judgement, such as digital records being defensible while physical reconstruction is risky.

Sources A and B are used as evidence: Source A for the benefits of digital copies, and Source B for the point that restored buildings are a re-presentation shaped by the excavator's own interpretation.
Other relevant sources, such as the debate over spending on conservation at Pompeii, are needed to reach the top row, and the answer should weigh the cost of physical work against preservation.
commonStudentErrors: Summarising Sources A and B without deciding whether reconstruction should happen.
Treating digital reconstruction as free of problems, and ignoring the uncertainty about how accurate any model of the past can be.
Writing about excavation or conservation in general rather than the question of reconstruction.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Demonstrates a thorough understanding of key issues and points for and against reconstructing the sites of Pompeii and Herculaneum; Supports the response using evidence from Sources A and B and refers to other relevant source(s); Communicates ideas and information using appropriate historical terms and concepts
5-6 marks: Demonstrates a sound understanding of key issues and points for and/or against reconstructing the sites of Pompeii and Herculaneum; Refers to Sources A and B and information from other source(s); Communicates using some historical terms and concepts
3-4 marks: Demonstrates some knowledge and/or understanding of reconstruction at Pompeii and/or Herculaneum; May refer to Sources A and/or B; May use some historical terms and/or concepts
1-2 marks: Makes general statements about reconstructions of Pompeii and/or Herculaneum

sampleAnswers.answer: Archaeologists should reconstruct the sites only with care, because both physical and digital reconstructions can serve the public while altering the evidence. Source A shows the case for digital reconstruction: laser scanning records every surface of Pompeii, and the replica can be shared with experts around the world. It preserves the city as a record even if the site is damaged, and it avoids the physical handling that wears away original remains. Source B, however, shows the danger of physical restoration. Maiuri's work at Herculaneum left fragments pieced together and restored, and architects calculate that no more than 50 per cent of the House of the Telephus Relief is antique. Wallace-Hadrill's warning that visitors see a re-presentation rather than raw evidence is a strong argument against reconstruction. Physical reconstructions also use modern materials, and they can take funds away from conservation, which is the more urgent need. Reconstruction still has value for visitors, who gain a clearer sense of how buildings once looked, and the large conservation programmes at Pompeii in recent decades show the scale of the challenge. On balance, digital reconstruction should be pursued as a permanent record, while physical reconstruction should be limited, clearly marked and based on careful evidence.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7-8 row: a thorough discussion of points for and against reconstruction, using Sources A and B and other evidence to reach a judgement. Making the judgement more precise, such as which kinds of physical work are acceptable, would strengthen it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Archaeologists should reconstruct Pompeii and Herculaneum only in limited ways. Source A supports digital reconstruction, because laser scanning preserves the city and can be shared with experts, and it takes no physical toll on the site. Source B shows the risks of physical reconstruction, since Maiuri's restorations at Herculaneum mean that much of what is standing is not ancient. Restoration of this kind can also use money that would otherwise go to conservation, and the sites are a re-presentation rather than raw evidence.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-6 row: a sound discussion with points for and against that refer to Sources A and B. Adding a point from other relevant sources, such as the cost to conservation, would move it to the 7-8 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Archaeologists should reconstruct the sites because digital copies help visitors. Source A says the digital replica can be shared with experts around the world.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-2 row: general statements about reconstruction with a reference to Source A. Weighing this against a point from Source B, and explaining why, would reach the 3-4 row.

prompts.question: Analyse how recent technology has changed interpretations of Pompeii and Herculaneum, with reference to at least two specific techniques.
markerNotes: Analyse needs the link between technique and interpretation: radar changes what is known about the city plan, and scans change what can be read.
Naming techniques is description. The top band asks what each technique changed in the historical picture, and where it has limits.
commonStudentErrors: Claiming that technology has solved the historical questions, rather than changing the evidence available.
Naming technologies such as scanning without saying what was scanned or what was learned.
prompts.markingCriteria:

5 marks: Analyses changes in interpretation using two or more specific techniques, with some explanation of their effect

3 marks: Describes techniques with limited analysis

sampleAnswers.answer: Recent technology has produced changing interpretations of Pompeii and Herculaneum by allowing sites and objects to be studied without destructive excavation. Ground-penetrating radar and LiDAR survey have mapped buried structures and features of the wider urban landscape, which has changed the view that the cities were fully known. Three-dimensional modelling allows researchers to test how light, space and movement worked in houses, shifting interpretations of domestic life towards dynamic accounts of use. X-ray tomography of carbonised papyrus scrolls from the Villa of the Papyri at Herculaneum has opened the possibility of reading texts that were previously unreadable, which could change understanding of the library and intellectual life of the Roman elite. Each technique changes the evidence available rather than simply confirming earlier conclusions. However, scrolls can be read only when imaging is combined with careful digital reconstruction of their damaged layers, and each method has limits, so changing interpretations depend on the quality of the data and the questions historians ask.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: analyses several techniques (radar and LiDAR, 3D modelling, tomography of scrolls) and what each changed in the historical picture, and evaluates the limits of the methods.

sampleAnswers.answer: New technology such as ground-penetrating radar lets archaeologists see buried parts of Pompeii without digging. Three-dimensional models help people understand how houses were used. Scanning of scrolls from Herculaneum may allow the texts to be read. So technology is changing how historians think about the sites.

prompts.question: Assess the extent to which changing interpretations of Pompeii and Herculaneum since their rediscovery reflect changes in archaeological method, rather than changes in the questions historians ask.
markerNotes: Assess needs a judgement on extent. The strongest answers argue which factor was more decisive and give examples of each.
Use the shift to plaster casts in the 19th century and recent questions about gender and enslaved people as contrasting examples of method and question driving change.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the history of excavation without assessing what drove the changes.
Treating new technology as producing objective interpretations automatically, without considering the questions asked of it.
prompts.markingCriteria:
8 marks: Assesses the relative importance of archaeological method and historians' questions in changing interpretations, using specific examples, and reaches a supported judgement
6-7 marks: Explains changes in interpretation and their causes, with relevant examples and a partly developed judgement
4-5 marks: Describes changes in interpretation and some of their causes, with little evaluation of method or questions
2-3 marks: Describes changes in interpretation or in archaeological technique, with limited explanation of their causes
1 mark: Makes a general statement about the sites

sampleAnswers.answer: Changing interpretations of Pompeii and Herculaneum since their rediscovery in the eighteenth century reflect both changes in archaeological method and changes in the questions that historians ask, and the balance between these two has shifted over time. Early excavation was driven by the search for art and luxury objects, and the 19th-century work of Giuseppe Fiorelli, who introduced the technique of pouring plaster into voids left by victims' bodies, changed interpretations by making the human figures visible. Those methods were concerned with the spectacular rather than the ordinary, so the early picture of the cities emphasised wealth and display. Changes in method have been important: stratigraphic recording, scientific analysis of organic remains and remote sensing have made it possible to reconstruct daily life, diet and urban infrastructure. These developments have produced new evidence for ordinary people, including the enslaved and freed, which would have been missed by earlier excavators. Yet the questions have changed as well. Modern historians ask about gender, social inequality and the experience of enslaved people, and they use methods that are designed to answer these questions. The evidence has been reinterpreted in the light of these questions, so a shift in method alone cannot explain every change. Therefore the changing interpretations of the sites reflect a combination of new technology and new historical questions, with the second often driving the choice of method. A useful test is to ask whether a given interpretation would have been possible with earlier methods, or whether it became visible only once a new question was asked, and many changes fall into the second category. The most persuasive cases combine both, as when imaging techniques were applied to material that scholars had begun to study for new social questions. On balance, the change in questions is at least as significant as the change in method, although each has been essential to the reinterpretation of the cities.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: weighs archaeological method (Fiorelli's casts, stratigraphy, scientific analysis) against the shift in historians' questions, uses specific examples of each, and reaches a supported judgement that the questions were at least as significant.

sampleAnswers.answer: Interpretations of Pompeii changed because archaeologists found new evidence. Early digs looked for art and treasure, but later excavators recorded everyday objects. Fiorelli's plaster casts made the victims visible. Modern science has also helped, with techniques for organic remains. But historians now ask different questions about women and slaves, so they read the evidence differently. Both method and questions have changed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies changes in method and in questions with relevant examples, but does not weigh their relative importance or support the verdict. It sits in the 5-6 mark row.

prompts.question: How have new technologies contributed to an understanding of Pompeii and Herculaneum? Support your answer using evidence from Sources C and D and other relevant sources.
markerNotes: The top answer explains a contribution for each technology in turn: DNA changed the account of the 'mother and child' casts, AI made the scrolls readable, and radar and reconstruction changed what is known about the buildings.
Sources C and D are integrated, not only described: say what each shows, then what that changes in historians' understanding. Other technologies answer the 'other relevant sources' part of the stem.

sampleAnswers.answer:
New technologies have changed what historians can know about Pompeii and Herculaneum, because they allow evidence that the eruption preserved to be examined without destroying it. Source C shows how DNA analysis has challenged older interpretations. Researchers extracted DNA from fragmented skeletal remains mixed with fourteen plaster casts, and found that the person thought to be a mother was actually a man unrelated to the child. This shows that earlier narratives were built on how the bodies were found, which reflected modern assumptions as much as ancient reality. Researchers also confirmed that Pompeii's citizens came from diverse backgrounds and were mainly descended from eastern Mediterranean immigrants, which challenges a simple picture of a uniform population.

Source D shows a different contribution. Artificial intelligence has been used to identify writing in charred scrolls from Herculaneum that could not be unrolled safely. The scroll's probable author, the Epicurean philosopher Philodemus, wrote about music, food and pleasure, which gives historians direct access to the intellectual life of a Herculaneum household. Source C's warning that people look at the ancient world 'through modern eyes' applies here too, because the texts were unreadable until these methods were used.

Other technologies extend this picture. Ground-penetrating radar has mapped buildings and streets beneath the volcanic deposits without invasive excavation, and digital reconstructions show how homes, temples and shops looked before 79 CE. Portable X-ray fluorescence has analysed frescoes, pottery and residues, which sheds light on trade networks and diet, and CT scans of the casts have added to knowledge of who died in the eruption.

Together these methods have changed the study of the sites. They correct earlier assumptions about identity and society, and they add evidence about texts, diet and the built environment that the eruption preserved but earlier generations could not read.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 10-12 row: a well-developed explanation of how DNA analysis, AI reading and other technologies changed understanding, with Sources C and D integrated into the argument. Stating the limits of each method more directly would make the judgement sharper.

sampleAnswers.answer: New technologies have helped historians understand Pompeii and Herculaneum in several ways. Source C describes DNA evidence taken from fragmented skeletal remains mixed with fourteen plaster casts. The researchers found that the person thought to be a mother was actually a man unrelated to the child, which challenges the earlier interpretations of how the victims were found. Source D shows artificial intelligence being used to identify writing on a scroll from Herculaneum, which means that texts can now be read. Ground-penetrating radar has also found buildings under the volcanic deposits without digging, and 3D reconstructions show what the houses looked like before the eruption. Each method adds a different kind of evidence about the victims, the texts and the buildings of the two cities.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7-9 row: an informed explanation of several technologies, with Sources C and D used. The phrase ‘Each method adds a different kind of evidence’ lists what each method found without weighing how far it changed understanding. Explaining the limits of each method, and which earlier interpretation it overturned, would lift it to the 10-12 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Technology such as DNA testing and artificial intelligence has been used to study Pompeii. Source D shows writing being identified on a scroll, and this has helped historians.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-3 row: general statements about new technology and a reference to Source D. Explaining what one method revealed, and how it changed understanding, would move it up the ladder.

sampleAnswers.answer:
New research has changed understanding of Pompeii and Herculaneum mainly by extending what can be known from the material remains and by revealing new evidence within old finds. It does so in two main ways: through technology applied to the bodies and buildings, and through imaging of written evidence.

Source D shows the director Massimo Osanna embracing 21st-century technology. Drones produce three-dimensional images of houses and record the progress of excavation, while CAT scans look inside the plaster casts made by Giuseppe Fiorelli in the nineteenth century, revealing the victims more clearly. The Muleteer shows how a changing interpretation can alter what was believed. The figure was long read as a crouched man shielding his face, but the arms that gave this impression were later found to be twentieth-century additions.

Source E shows that new imaging can recover text on the Herculaneum scrolls. Greek writing by Philodemus, buried by the eruption, could be read more clearly, and one word once read as charmed or bewitched turned out to mean enslaved. This changes how scholars read Philodemus' portrayal of famous thinkers, and it shows that a single correction can alter an interpretation.

Other research supports these changes. A graffito discovered in recent decades suggests that the eruption may have occurred in autumn rather than in summer, and studies of material from the sewers have altered understanding of diet and health. These changing interpretations show that historians must treat older accounts as provisional rather than settled.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 9–10 row: a well-developed explanation of how new research changed understanding, with detailed reference to Sources D and E and other evidence, and a clear sense of what the methods can prove.

sampleAnswers.answer: New research has changed the understanding of Pompeii and Herculaneum. Source D shows that drones and CAT scans have produced new images of houses and of the victims inside the plaster casts. The Muleteer shows how an interpretation can change, because its arms were later found to be additions. Source E shows that imaging has allowed Philodemus' scroll text to be read more clearly, and one word now reads enslaved rather than charmed. Other research on the date of the eruption also shows changing interpretations of the sites.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5–6 row: a sound explanation that refers to Sources D and E with a few examples, but develops little of what each change alters in understanding. Explaining what each finding changes about historians' view of the sites would lift it to the 7–8 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: New technology has helped archaeologists learn more about Pompeii and Herculaneum. Source D describes scans of the plaster casts, and Source E describes imaging of a scroll.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1–2 row: general statements that refer to Sources D and E without explaining how the research changed understanding. Explaining one specific change, such as the Muleteer's arms, would lift it to the 3–4 row.

prompts.question: Discuss the ethical issues raised by the study and display of human remains at Pompeii and Herculaneum in the 21st century.
markerNotes: Discuss needs both sides of the ethical trade-off: the educational and scientific value of display and study, against dignity and consent.
Naming the plaster casts and the skeletons from the Herculaneum boathouses as examples earns the evidence marks.
commonStudentErrors: Stating an ethical issue without explaining whose interests it affects.
Treating the plaster casts as human remains, when they are plaster made from the voids left by bodies.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses ethical issues (dignity, consent, scientific value, display and tourism) with examples from the sites, and reaches a supported position on the trade-off
5 marks: Discusses at least two ethical issues with examples and some reasoning
4 marks: Describes the ethical issues with some discussion of why they matter
3 marks: Identifies an ethical issue with limited discussion
2 marks: Identifies a relevant issue without explanation

sampleAnswers.answer: The study and display of human remains at Pompeii and Herculaneum raise ethical issues that must be weighed against the value of the evidence. The ethics of display are sharpest for the plaster casts of victims, made by Fiorelli's method, which have become some of the most powerful images of the eruption. Yet displaying the dead as spectacle raises questions of dignity and consent, because the victims' final moments are reproduced for tourists. At Herculaneum, where skeletons from the boathouses on the shore have been studied, the question of how to present the dead is equally pressing. Scientific study of remains provides information on health, diet and disease, which is valuable for understanding ordinary lives, but it must be carried out with respect and proper protocols. Tourism adds pressure, since growing visitor numbers increase demand for display while also increasing wear on the sites. On balance, the casts should remain on display only with interpretive context that presents the victims as individuals, because this balances education and remembrance against dignity and the protection of the site.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: discusses dignity, consent, scientific value and tourism pressure with examples (the plaster casts, the Herculaneum boathouse skeletons), reaches a supported position that the casts stay only with interpretive context, and weighs education and remembrance against respect and site protection.

sampleAnswers.answer: Human remains from Pompeii are displayed as plaster casts, which some people find disrespectful. Scientists also study bones to learn about health. Tourism means more people see the casts, which can damage the site. The ethics of displaying remains are debated.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the main issues of display, study and tourism, but asserts that the display is disrespectful without weighing either side. It also treats the casts as remains, when they are plaster made from the voids left by bodies. It fits the 4-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Human remains should be respected.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general value statement with no issue or example, so only the 1-mark band applies.

prompts.scenario: A museum curator at Pompeii is deciding whether to continue displaying plaster casts of victims, and a student is asked to consider the arguments on each side. The student must consider the claims of education, dignity and the protection of the site.

sampleAnswers.answer: I recommend that Pompeii limit access to the most fragile houses and manage visitor numbers through timed entry and set routes, which reduces physical wear on frescoes and supports conservation. Plaster casts of victims should remain on display, but only with interpretive signage that presents the victims as individuals and explains the ethics of display, so the human remains are treated with dignity. Timed entry would also let staff monitor sensitive spaces and reduce crowding around the casts. Tourism brings essential revenue, and the trade-off is some lost ticket income from restricted rooms, which is outweighed by the protection of fragile houses and the dignity owed to the dead. The policy can be reviewed each year against visitor data and conservation reports.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: a specific policy (contextual display, timed entry, route planning) justified by both conservation and ethics, and weighs it against the tourism revenue the site depends on.

sampleAnswers.answer: The site should limit the number of visitors so the houses are not damaged. Human remains should be displayed respectfully. Tourism is important for money, but it should not cause too much damage.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Sensible recommendations with general justification, but no specific mechanism and no reasons drawn from ethics. It sits in the 3-mark band.

prompts.question: To what extent is tourism valuable to Pompeii and Herculaneum? Support your response using evidence from Sources B and C and other relevant sources.

prompts.markingCriteria:

5-6 marks: Provides some judgement on the extent to which tourism is valuable to Pompeii and Herculaneum; Refers to Sources B and C and other source(s); Communicates using some historical terms and concepts
3-4 marks: Demonstrates some knowledge and/or understanding of the value of tourism in Pompeii and/or Herculaneum; May refer to Sources B and/or C; May use some historical terms and/or concepts

sampleAnswers.answer:
Tourism is highly valuable to Pompeii and Herculaneum, although its benefits come with costs that the sites must manage. Source B shows the scale of this value: visitor numbers at Pompeii rose from 2 336 188 in 2012 to 3 418 733 in 2017, and Herculaneum grew from 310 072 to 487 540 over the same period. Tourists pay entry fees and spend money on transport, accommodation and food, which funds the upkeep of the ruins.

Source C shows this value being reinvested. The Great Pompeii Project restored more than 130 000 square feet of the city, sidewalks were built to make the site accessible, and the Archaeological Park of Pompeii can now keep all of its ticket revenue. Tourism also raises awareness of the sites and builds public support for their conservation.

However, the value of tourism is limited by the damage it causes. Source C reports that there are not enough guards and that visitors have stolen objects, while the growing crowds in Source B increase wear on floors and frescoes. The closure of the sites during COVID-19 in 2020 showed how heavily they depend on visitors. On balance, tourism is valuable, but only when its income is used to protect the sites from the visitors it brings.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7–8 row: a reasoned judgement on the value of tourism, supported by Sources B and C and by the 2020 closure, with historical terms used throughout. Keeping the conclusion tied to the evidence holds the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Tourism is valuable to Pompeii and Herculaneum because visitor numbers grew from 2012 to 2017. Source B shows Pompeii's visitors rising from 2 336 188 to 3 418 733, and tourists pay entry fees and spend money in the region. Source C shows that revenue now stays with the Archaeological Park of Pompeii, which can use it for the sites. However, tourism also causes problems. Source C says there are not enough guards to stop misbehaviour, and large crowds can wear down the ancient sites.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5–6 row: some judgement on the value of tourism, with Sources B and C and the stated problems. A clear conclusion weighing the revenue against the damage would reach the 7–8 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Tourism is good for Pompeii because many people visit and pay to see the ruins. Source B shows that visitor numbers went up, and Herculaneum had visitors too, so tourism brings money to both towns.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1–2 row: a general statement with limited reference to Source B and no judgement. Adding one cost of tourism from Source C would lift it toward the 3–4 row.

markerNotes: The top answer explains the ethical tension between research, display and respect for the dead, rather than simply describing the boatshed.

sampleAnswers.answer: The central question of ethics here is whether human remains should be displayed and studied at all. Source B, a photograph of skeletons and skulls in the boatshed at Herculaneum behind a metal barrier, shows the problem: these were people who died in AD 79, and their display raises questions about dignity and consent that do not arise with artefacts. Archaeologists must weigh the scientific value of studying remains, which can reveal diet, health and disease, against the respect owed to the dead. A second issue is display. Exhibiting remains may educate visitors, but it can also turn victims into spectacles, and tourism brings crowds and income that can outweigh careful conservation. The plaster casts of victims at Pompeii, first made in the 1860s, show the same tension, as they recorded the dead yet became popular exhibits. Reconstruction raises a further issue, since a misleading interpretation of the victims can distort public understanding of the eruption. Archaeologists therefore have to balance research, conservation and respect when deciding how Pompeii and Herculaneum are presented. Public interest in the victims can also encourage sensationalism, which conservators and ethicists regard as a serious concern.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7–8 row: a well-developed explanation of the ethical issues of research, display and tourism, supported by Source B and the wider evidence. Weighing the ethical arguments against each other more explicitly would make the judgement sharper.

sampleAnswers.answer: Archaeologists face ethical problems over displaying human remains. Source B shows skeletons and skulls in the boatshed at Herculaneum behind a barrier, which raises questions about respect for the dead. Tourism also puts pressure on the sites, because visitors want to see remains, so conservation must balance access with protection. Studying the remains can reveal diet and health, but the benefit must be weighed against how the dead are treated. This is why the ethical debate is still ongoing.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5–6 row: a sound explanation of the ethical issues of display and tourism, which refers to Source B. Explaining why the study of remains is also contested, and linking this to conservation, would lift it to the 7–8 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Source B shows human remains at Herculaneum, which raises an ethical question about display. Archaeologists must consider it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1–2 row: refers to Source B and names one ethical issue without explaining it. Explaining why displaying remains is a problem would reach the 3–4 row.

prompts.question: Explain the political organisation of New Kingdom Egypt in this period. Support your response using evidence from Source G and other relevant sources.
markerNotes: The top band explains the pharaoh’s position at the top of a hierarchy sustained by Ma’at, control of the army and delegated administration, rather than only describing the pharaoh.
It uses Source G, the statue of Amenhotep, son of Hapu, to show how officials and priests exercised power under the king, and refers to other sources such as the vizier and the Amun priesthood.
It tests the picture against its limits: the pharaoh depended on the elite who administered Egypt, so royal power had to be managed.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the pharaoh as absolute without explaining the role of officials and the elite.
Describing Source G as a picture of the pharaoh rather than of an official.
Explaining Ma’at as a concept without linking it to political order.
prompts.markingCriteria:
10-12 marks: Provides a well-developed explanation, demonstrating detailed knowledge and understanding relevant to the question; Integrates evidence from the source provided and other relevant sources to support the response; Communicates ideas and information logically and coherently using appropriate historical terms and concepts
7-9 marks: Provides an explanation, demonstrating knowledge and understanding relevant to the question; Uses evidence from the source provided to support the response and refers to other relevant source(s); Communicates ideas and information logically using appropriate historical terms and concepts
4-6 marks: Provides a description demonstrating some knowledge relevant to the question; May refer to the source provided and/or to other source(s); Communicates ideas using some historical terms and/or concepts
1-3 marks: Makes general statement(s) in relation to the question; May refer to source(s); May use historical terms and/or concepts

sampleAnswers.answer:
Political organisation in New Kingdom Egypt rested on a hierarchy with the pharaoh at its apex, supported by a large body of officials drawn from the elite. The pharaoh was the living king, who held authority to rule, to command the army and to maintain Ma’at, the principle of order, truth and justice that held the cosmos together. Ma’at linked kingship to religious duty: the king mediated between the gods and the people, and his temple-building and offerings kept the cosmos in balance. This ideology gave the state its legitimacy, and royal images showing the king as a warrior and a divine ruler reinforced his position at the top of the pyramid.

Source G shows that the pharaoh’s authority was exercised through people. The statue of Amenhotep, son of Hapu, a priest and official under Amenhotep III, presents a man who held high office in both administration and religion. He was associated with royal building projects and rose through royal service, so the statue shows that a man could gain great influence by serving the king. The source therefore demonstrates that the political system relied on delegated power: the pharaoh governed through trusted officials who managed the palace, the treasury, the temples and the provinces.

Other evidence confirms this delegated structure. The vizier was the highest official, responsible for the administration of the state, the courts and the records, and he reported directly to the king. Below him, provincial governors and a network of scribes collected taxes and recorded labour, which allowed Egypt to manage its resources. The military also formed part of this system. The pharaoh led the army on campaigns to maintain control of Nubia and Syria-Palestine, and the rewards of victory, including land and wealth, bound soldiers and commanders to the crown. The Amun priesthood at Thebes controlled large estates and wealth, which gave the religious elite a powerful voice in the state.

These arrangements also created tensions. The elite’s wealth and religious influence could rival that of the king, while the pharaoh’s authority depended on his ability to balance officials, temples and the army. Royal appointments, building programmes and religious patronage were the means by which the king maintained that balance. The political organisation of New Kingdom Egypt was therefore a system of concentrated kingship supported by a wide administrative and religious elite, and its stability depended on the continued alignment of these groups with the pharaoh’s authority.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 10–12 row: a well-developed explanation of the pharaoh’s authority and delegated administration, integrating Source G with other evidence such as the vizier and the Amun priesthood. To lift it, weigh the tensions between king and elite more explicitly.

sampleAnswers.answer: The pharaoh stood at the top of Egypt’s political organisation. He was the king, who ruled through officials and maintained Ma’at, the order of the cosmos. Source G shows Amenhotep, son of Hapu, a priest and official under Amenhotep III, which illustrates how the pharaoh governed through trusted officials. The vizier and other administrators managed the state, while the army and the priests supported royal power. This system depended on the pharaoh’s control of the elite, so the political order was stable when the king managed these relationships well. The vizier and the Amun priesthood reinforced this structure, so that the state could manage its land, its labour and its religion through a network of trusted elites.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7–9 row: an explanation of the political structure that uses Source G and refers to other sources. To reach 10–12, develop the roles of the vizier and the army with specific examples and explain the tensions within the system.

sampleAnswers.answer: Egypt had a pharaoh who ruled the country. Officials helped him run the government and the temples, as the statue of Amenhotep, son of Hapu shows.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1–3 row: a general statement about political structure with a brief reference to Source G. To lift it, explain how the pharaoh governed through officials and what Ma’at meant for kingship.

sampleAnswers.answer: The pharaoh was the central figure of New Kingdom Egypt, and his role combined religious, political and military duties. As the living god, the pharaoh was responsible for maintaining Ma’at, the cosmic order, through religious rituals and offerings to the gods. Egyptian religion depended on the king to appease the gods and secure their protection, so the pharaoh's ritual role was essential to the stability of the state. The pharaoh was also a builder of monuments, from temples for the gods to palaces for the royal household and forts for defence. Amenhotep III, for example, built on a huge scale, including the temple at Luxor and the statues known as the Colossi of Memnon. Militarily, the pharaoh led expeditions to foreign lands, as Thutmose III did in his campaigns in the Levant, and this brought plunder and tribute into Egypt. Images of the pharaoh as a triumphant warrior on temple walls reinforced his authority. Politically, the king ensured the succession and was responsible for providing for and protecting the people through the Nile floods and the harvest. Diplomacy with foreign rulers, recorded in the Amarna Letters, was also part of the pharaoh's role, as foreign kings sent gifts and sought alliances. The pharaoh's role therefore linked religion, empire and the economy, and the king's authority depended on success in all three.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7-8 row: a well-developed explanation of the pharaoh's religious, building, military and diplomatic roles, linked to Ma’at and the economy. Naming one specific image or monument in more detail would strengthen the treatment of the pharaoh's images.

sampleAnswers.answer: The pharaoh was responsible for maintaining Ma’at, the order of the cosmos, through religious rituals and offerings to the gods. He also protected the people, which meant securing the frontiers and leading expeditions abroad that brought tribute and plunder into Egypt. Pharaohs such as Amenhotep III built temples and palaces for the glory of the royal household, and they received gifts from foreign rulers, which the Amarna Letters record. Images of the king as a warrior or a god reinforced his authority. The role of the pharaoh therefore linked religion, empire and the economy, and the king had to show success in each.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-6 row: an explanation of the pharaoh's roles with some specific examples. Developing one role with more evidence, such as a named campaign, would move it to the 7-8 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The pharaoh was a god-king who built temples and led armies. He was expected to keep the gods happy and keep order in Egypt.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-2 row: general statements about the pharaoh with little explanation. Naming one role and explaining how it maintained Ma’at would reach the 3-4 row.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The role of women in New Kingdom Egypt was shaped by social status. Women of the elite supervised the household as the Mistress of the House, while women of lower status often managed and worked in the home and on the land. Across society, the central expectation was that women would bear and raise children, and women could inherit, own and sell property in their own right.

Women had only a limited direct role in politics. Royal women could hold influence, as Hatshepsut did when she served as co-regent, and Queen Tiye corresponded diplomatically with the Mitanni court, but these were exceptions. Political power remained largely in male hands.

Religion was the area where women were most prominent. The God's Wife of Amun held large economic and religious influence over temple estates, and non-royal women could serve as priestesses or as musicians and singers at festivals and funerals. Source F shows female musicians at a funeral feast in the Tomb of Rekhmire, which indicates that women's performance was an important part of mourning and of the offerings made to the dead.

Women's economic and religious roles were therefore significant. Non-royal women helped with farm work and the harvest, as tomb reliefs show. Overall, the role of women depended on status: the household and religious life gave most women their most important functions, while political power was reserved for men and for a few royal women.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 9–10 row: a well-developed analysis of how status shaped women's roles, integrating Source F with the God's Wife of Amun and property rights. Keeping the judgement about status at the centre holds the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Women's roles in New Kingdom Egypt depended on their social status. Religion was an important area for women, and Source F shows female musicians at a funeral feast, which suggests that non-royal women had a role in funerary rites. Women could also own and inherit property, but political power was held mainly by men. Royal women, such as Hatshepsut, could hold influence in the state, although such cases were exceptions to the general pattern of women's roles in the household and religion.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5–6 row: some analysis of women's roles by status, with Source F used and religion and property noted. Explaining what Source F shows about funerary practice, and the God's Wife of Amun, would reach the 7–8 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Scribes played an important role during the New Kingdom Period. They studied for many years to learn to read and write and they were provided opportunities in the administrative, political and religious life in Egyptian society. Due to the complex nature of Egyptian administration, scribes were tasked with recording everything from royal decrees, religious texts, to correspondence with foreign rulers. The Amarna letters, many of them written by scribes, show how Egyptian scribes were involved in maintaining foreign relations during the reign of Amenhotep III. Many scribes were employed by temples to copy religious texts, write hymns, and maintain temple archives such as preparing mortuary texts, which were important for ensuring the deceased’s successful journey to the afterlife. The Papyrus Lansing ‘Be A Scribe’ refers to the high status of scribes in society. They were exempt from conscription and paying taxes. They could achieve high office, even serving the Pharaoh. Scribes were indispensable and high-ranking members of New Kingdom Egyptian society, fulfilling critical roles.

sampleAnswers.answer: Scribes were literate officials who recorded administrative and temple records, and their training was long. Some also handled correspondence with foreign rulers, as the Amarna letters show.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Archaeological and written sources show that the Egyptian economy under the New Kingdom depended on agriculture, state control of production and the wealth brought by empire. Together they reveal how far the state directed production, even though the surviving evidence is uneven and tends to come from elite tombs and temples.

Agriculture was the foundation of the economy. Nilometers recorded the flood levels on which crop yields depended, and the prayer to Hapi, the god of the Nile flood, shows how closely the state linked the harvest to religion. Tomb scenes, such as those in the tomb of Menna, show fields being measured and grain being recorded for the state granaries. These images, which are evidence as well as art, show a centralised system of collecting produce.

Booty and tribute from campaigns in Nubia and Syria-Palestine were a second source of wealth. Annals inscribed at Karnak record the goods taken from defeated peoples, and tomb reliefs of high-ranking officials show tribute bearers and their gifts. Much of this wealth was donated to the temple of Amun, so temples and their estates became major economic institutions. Archaeological evidence from Karnak shows the scale of the temple complex and its estates.

Trade also mattered. Expeditions to Punt, shown in reliefs at the Deir el-Bahri temple of Hatshepsut, brought luxury goods such as incense and exotic woods, which were a form of exchange as much as commerce. Tomb biographies and tomb paintings show a range of occupations, including sculptors, goldsmiths and viziers, which points to a specialised economy.

The evidence has limits. Most written sources come from state and temple propaganda, which exaggerates the wealth of the king and the gods, while the archaeological record is weighted towards tombs and monuments rather than ordinary households. Historians therefore combine both kinds of evidence to build a picture of a state economy based on grain, booty and tribute.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 10–12 row: a well-developed explanation of the Egyptian economy that integrates archaeological and written evidence from a wide range of sources, and weighs the propaganda in the texts against the archaeology.

sampleAnswers.answer: Archaeological and written sources show that the Egyptian economy depended on agriculture and on state control of grain. Nilometers and tomb scenes of farming and grain collection show that the state surveyed production and stored grain for its granaries. Written sources such as the Annals at Karnak show booty and tribute from campaigns, which were given to the temple of Amun. Trade with Punt is shown in reliefs at Deir el-Bahri, which suggests imports of luxury goods. Together these sources give a picture of an economy that was centrally managed rather than market-driven. Historians have to be careful, as much of the evidence comes from temples and the tombs of the elite.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7–9 row: a sound explanation of the evidence from archaeological and written sources, with several examples. Explaining how one source type limits another, and integrating more sources, would lift it to the 10–12 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Archaeological and written sources show that the Egyptian economy relied on farming. Temple reliefs show trade and tribute.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1–3 row: general statements about the economy, with the sources mentioned only briefly. Explaining what one source shows about production, and how it does so, would lift it to the 4–6 row.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Economic exchange in New Kingdom Egypt was based on agriculture and a centralised system of taxation. Most people worked the land, and the state collected grain as tax. This grain was stored in royal granaries and redistributed through a large bureaucracy of scribes, who recorded every quantity so that the state could feed its officials, workers and temples.

Wealth also came from outside Egypt. Thutmose III's campaigns in the Levant brought booty, and subject rulers in Nubia and the Levant paid tribute in gold, goods and luxury items. This material wealth was delivered to the king and the temples, which redistributed it through the economy.

Within Egypt, exchange also took place in local markets, where goods were bartered and valued in the deben, a unit of weight used for copper and silver. Trade with foreign powers, shown in the Amarna letters, involved gifts of gold, horses and goods between royal courts. Exchange was therefore centralised and royal, but it also moved goods through ordinary markets. Scribes kept the records of grain, goods and labour that linked these markets to the administration, and the royal granaries and temples received the bulk of the flow. The result was an economy in which the state controlled the main channels of exchange while ordinary people still bartered for their daily needs.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6–7 row: a well-developed and detailed explanation of taxation, tribute, booty and barter, using historical terms such as the deben and the royal granaries. Keeping each mechanism linked to who benefited holds the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Economic exchange in Egypt was based on agriculture, and the state collected grain as taxation and stored it in royal granaries. Scribes recorded the grain, and officials and workers were paid from these stores. Goods were also exchanged in local markets, where people bartered using the deben as a unit of value. Tribute and booty from campaigns in Nubia and the Levant added to royal wealth. Trade with other kingdoms, such as the gifts recorded in the Amarna letters, brought more goods into the country, so exchange was shaped by the royal court.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4–5 row: a clear explanation of taxation, markets and tribute, with historical terms used. Explaining how the royal granaries redistributed grain would reach the 6–7 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Egyptians paid taxes to the king in grain, and some goods were traded in markets. Tribute also came from other lands, and the grain was stored in royal granaries for officials and workers.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2–3 row: some information relevant to the question in a general account. Explaining what the grain was used for, or how the deben worked, would lift it.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Egyptian empire in the early New Kingdom led to an influx of plunder, tribute, tax, trade and gifts into the Egyptian economy. The annals of Thutmose III record the plunder of 340 captives after the Battle of Megiddo. The Amarna Letters from the reign of Amenhotep III demonstrate the practice of diplomatic gift giving, possibly arising due to Egypt’s increased prominence eg the king of Mitanni sending Amenhotep III teams of chariots. Much of this income was administered by temple estates. Another impact of empire was the increased cost of provisioning a standing army. This was partly achieved through the redistribution of land administered by temples.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5 row: an informed outline of plunder, tribute, trade and temple income, supported by the annals of Thutmose III and the Amarna Letters. Explaining in more detail how temples redistributed imperial income would make the economic link more precise.

sampleAnswers.answer: Empire brought plunder and tribute into the Egyptian economy. Thutmose III recorded the captives taken after the Battle of Megiddo, and Amenhotep III received gifts from foreign kings, as the Amarna Letters show. sampleAnswers.answer: Evidence from New Kingdom Egypt reveals that religion was centred on the pharaoh and organised through the state. Egyptian religion was polytheistic, and the gods and goddesses were worshipped through cults that were tied to the king. Horus, the sky god associated with kingship, showed the pharaoh as the divine ruler of Egypt, and the living king was regarded as Horus on earth. Osiris, god of the dead and of renewal, offered the promise of an afterlife, and funerary texts such as the Book of Amduat show that the afterlife was organised around status, which reveals the stratified nature of Egyptian society. Amun-Re, the chief god of the state, was served by a major temple estate at Karnak, and his priesthood functioned as part of the state bureaucracy. The priesthood of Amun-Re controlled land and goods, so the cult was also an economic institution. Festivals show the same connection between religion and the king. The Heb-Sed festival renewed the pharaoh's power, and the Beautiful Festival of the Valley at Thebes linked the living to the dead and the gods, revealing the importance of renewal and prosperity. Varying creation myths, such as the Memphite theology, reflect the political nature of religion, since creation was linked to the authority of a particular city and its god. Temples played an important redistributive role, acting as banks for the state and as a means of paying the bureaucracy. Private devotion also appears in the evidence, with offerings and votive stelae left at temples by officials and their families, which shows that the cults reached beyond the court. This personal religion, however, was framed by the king's ritual role, so that private hopes for protection and an afterlife depended on the pharaoh's maintenance of order. Taken together, the evidence shows a religion that legitimised the pharaoh, structured society and secured prosperity through ritual, with the gods and the king working as one system of authority.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 10-12 row: a well-developed account of what the evidence reveals about religion, using gods, funerary texts, festivals, temples and myths. Weighing how far religion was a tool of the state, rather than private belief, would make it more precise.

sampleAnswers.answer: Evidence reveals that religion in New Kingdom Egypt was closely tied to the pharaoh. The king was the central figure of the state cult, and gods such as Horus and Amun-Re were linked to his rule. Funerary customs and texts show a stratified society, in which the afterlife reflected rank. Priests of Amun-Re were part of the state bureaucracy, and the temples redistributed wealth, which means religion was also an economic institution. Festivals such as the Heb-Sed renewed the king's power and linked the people to the gods. Private offerings at temples show that the cults also reached officials and their families, who sought protection and an afterlife through the king's order. Taken together, the evidence shows that religion supported the authority of the pharaoh and the order of the state.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7-9 row: a clear account of religion in relation to the pharaoh, the state and the economy, using several sources. Adding a source from private religion, such as personal devotion, would extend the answer toward the top row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Myths and legends were important for Egyptian religious beliefs in this period. The myth of Osiris focused on renewal and rebirth after death, providing a framework for religious beliefs that helped Egyptians to deal with difficult times and the catastrophe that could accompany the annual flood, which could bring both life and destruction. The myth was an explanation for the succession of kingship, as the living king, seen as the embodiment of Horus. Creation myths reinforced the religious notion of ma’at, that the gods had decreed good order and set things in their place. The most prominent myth involved Atum-Re creating Shu and Tefnut by himself, followed by a series of other sibling couples, representing various aspects of creation. Myths influenced Egyptian beliefs and practices regarding royal sibling marriages, possibly undertaken to mimic the relationships of the gods. These myths of renewal and rebirth also influenced festivals, such as the Opet festival, or the festival of Ptah, which celebrated his role in creation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6 row: a detailed, informed explanation of how several myths shaped religious beliefs, including renewal, kingship and order. This is the top band; keep each myth tied to a belief or practice.

sampleAnswers.answer: The myth of Osiris, who died and was restored to life, gave Egyptians a framework for renewal after death, and it explained how the living king was seen as Horus. Creation myths, in which Atum-Re made the first gods, reinforced ma’at, the order that the gods had set in place. Myths also shaped festivals such as the Opet festival, which renewed religious life and the king's divine role.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Egyptian beliefs and practices about death were highly significant in New Kingdom society, because they shaped how the elite built their tombs, how the king's power was presented and how people understood the order of the world. Ian Shaw argues that the old cliché that Egyptians were 'totally obsessed with death' is being replaced by a new one, because tombs contain 'endless daily life' scenes showing people 'working in the fields, making wine, banqueting'. The evidence he cites is convincing as far as it goes. These scenes show that Egyptians expected the deceased to continue to enjoy food, drink and activity in the afterlife. However, they do not show that death was unimportant. The scenes were placed in tombs precisely because the afterlife was where the owner's most valued life would continue.

Other evidence confirms how central death was to the period. Mummification preserved the body so that the ka and ba could recognise and return to it. Funerary texts such as The Book of the Dead gave the deceased spells to pass the judgement of the heart before Osiris, and the outcome of that judgement determined whether the individual could enter eternal life. Shabti figures were placed in the tomb to perform labour for the deceased, so the fieldwork scenes also represented the future work and provision that the dead could rely on. Tombs of officials, such as Nakht and Nebamun, show banquets, harvests and hunting, which the owners hoped to enjoy in eternity.

The royal dimension was the most significant. The mortuary temple and tomb of Amenhotep III were designed to ensure that his divine kingship would continue eternally, so the king's afterlife was a public matter as well as a private hope. A king who was sustained in the afterlife guaranteed the continued stability of maat, which the pharaoh was responsible for maintaining in the living world. The beliefs therefore reinforced the state's ideology, and death was a concern of the whole kingdom because the king's afterlife underpinned the order the living depended on.

Shaw's reinterpretation is therefore a useful correction, because it shows that Egyptian funerary art was concerned with life as much as with death. Yet the two views are not opposed. The emphasis on continued life was itself a belief about death, and it drew on the same ideas of judgement, continuity and maat. The significance of these beliefs lay in how they organised the living, the elite and the king around the expectation of an ordered existence after death, rather than in any single obsession.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 13-15 row: a well-developed judgement on significance that interacts with Shaw's reading of the daily life scenes and supports it with the Book of the Dead, shabti figures and the royal mortuary complex.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Egyptian beliefs about death were significant because they shaped tombs, burial practices and royal ideology in New Kingdom Egypt. Ian Shaw argues that Egyptians were obsessed with life rather than death, and his point about the 'daily life' scenes is valid. Scenes of people working in the fields, making wine and banqueting suggest that Egyptians wanted these activities to continue after death.

Mummification and the Book of the Dead were also important. The Book of the Dead contained spells to help the deceased in the afterlife, and tombs were decorated with scenes that reflected the beliefs of their owners. The mortuary temple of Amenhotep III also reflected beliefs about the afterlife, and these ideas mattered to the people who could afford such tombs.

Overall, the beliefs were significant because they gave meaning to life in Egypt, even though they were not the same as an obsession with death.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7-9 row: some judgement on significance, with reference to Shaw and other sources. To reach 10-12 it would test Shaw's argument against other evidence, such as the judgement scenes, and explain why the beliefs mattered to the state.

sampleAnswers.answer: Egyptians believed in an afterlife, so they built tombs and were buried with goods. The Book of the Dead was an important text. Shaw says that tombs show life, not death.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-3 row: general statements about burial with only a passing reference to the interpretation. Explaining what the beliefs did for society, with evidence, would lift it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Funerary customs and rituals reveal the beliefs, wealth and hierarchy of Egyptian society, because the care taken over death was a public statement about status as well as a personal hope for the afterlife. Mummification was the most visible custom. The body was preserved so that the ka and ba could return to it, which shows that Egyptians believed the individual continued after death and needed a physical home. Mummification was costly and was carried out by specialists, so the process reveals that access to the afterlife was tied to wealth. Tombs and grave goods extend this evidence. Elite tombs were built with chapels, statues and offerings, and the shabti figurines placed in the tomb were to labour for the deceased, which shows an expectation that the afterlife would involve work as well as rest. Source E, the facsimile of a funeral procession from the Tomb of Ramose, a vizier, brings these customs into view. Mourners and attendants carry offerings and furniture, and the procession shows the coffin moving toward the tomb, which demonstrates both ritual movement and the social status of those who attended. Rows of people, arranged by rank, express the hierarchy of Egyptian society: the deceased is honoured by the household and officials who are shown following him. The procession also reflects the concept of a journey to the afterlife, in which the dead had to travel through the west safely. Rituals such as the opening of the mouth ceremony, which restored the senses of the mummy, reveal that Egyptians believed these acts could make the afterlife possible. Offerings made at the tomb chapel show that the living continued to supply the dead, which tied family duty to the afterlife. Funerary spells were written on coffins and papyri, and their wide use suggests that the afterlife was a concern for many, although the wealthiest could afford the most elaborate equipment. The Book of the Dead expands this evidence, because its spells and prayers show a belief that a moral life and the approval of Osiris and Anubis would decide the fate of the dead. However, the evidence has limits. Source E is a copy of an elite tomb made by modern artists, so it shows the rituals of the wealthy rather than those of ordinary farmers or workers, who were often buried simply. Funerary evidence therefore tells historians much about the values and hierarchy of Egyptian society, but much less about the poor, who rarely left monuments.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 13–15 row: a well-developed and accurate explanation of funerary belief, status and ritual, integrating Source E with other evidence and stating its limits. Linking the procession more directly to the function of the tomb would sharpen the argument.

sampleAnswers.answer: Funerary customs show that Egyptians believed in an afterlife and that status shaped access to it. Mummification preserved the body so the ka could return to it, and tombs held offerings and shabti figures to labour for the dead. Source E shows a funeral procession from the Tomb of Ramose, with mourners carrying offerings and furniture, which reveals the rituals of the elite. Rituals such as the opening of the mouth ceremony show that the dead were expected to receive food and attention. The Book of the Dead shows that moral conduct mattered for the afterlife. The evidence shows the hierarchy of society, but it mainly reflects wealthy families rather than ordinary people. Source E is a facsimile, so historians need to consider how far the copy reflects the original painting before drawing conclusions about society.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7–9 row: a sound explanation of funerary belief and social status, using Source E and referring to other evidence. Developing the link between the procession and the hierarchy of society, and noting the limits of elite evidence, would lift it to the 10–12 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Funerary customs show that Egyptians cared about the dead. The procession in Source E shows mourners carrying offerings, which suggests respect for the deceased and a belief in an afterlife. Mummies and tombs were expensive, so these customs also suggest that wealth affected how people were buried, although the answer does not explain this.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1–3 row: general statements about funerary customs that refer to Source E without explaining what it shows about society. Linking the offerings and mourners to social status would reach the 4–6 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Tombs were central to New Kingdom society because they prepared the deceased for the afterlife. sampleAnswers.answer: Art in New Kingdom Egypt reveals a society organised around the king, the gods and the afterlife, and increasingly connected to an empire. The clearest evidence comes from tomb decoration. In the Valley of the Kings, the walls of royal tombs show the sun god's journey through the underworld, which reveals the Egyptian belief that the dead could be reborn with the sun. These images show a society that invested heavily in preparation for death and in the priestly rituals that made the transition possible. Art also reveals how the state wanted the king to be seen. Reliefs at Karnak show Thutmose III as a warrior smiting enemies, and the booty of his campaigns in Syria-Palestine, including chariots and precious stones, is depicted in detail. These scenes present pharaonic power as military and divine, and they show that empire brought wealth to the court. At Deir el-Bahri, the temple of Hatshepsut has reliefs of the expedition to Punt, which show incense trees and other goods brought back from the land. These scenes reveal a society that valued trade and exotic goods, and that presented these acquisitions as gifts of the gods to the king. Art also reveals the social life of Egypt. Tomb paintings show clothing, banquets, music, hunting, and the work of farmers and craftsmen, so historians can reconstruct daily life and the place of different groups. Women of the elite are shown at banquets wearing fine linen and perfume, which suggests that elite women had a visible social role. The art of the reign of Amenhotep III, including the colossal statues of the king at Thebes, reveals a court that was confident and prosperous. Statues and inscriptions present the king as the embodiment of order, reflecting the ideal of ma’at. Taken together, the evidence shows that New Kingdom society was hierarchical and religious, and that its art was intended to legitimise pharaonic authority rather than to record ordinary life.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 10–12 row: an informed explanation of what art reveals about religion, kingship, empire and daily life, integrating several sources. This is the top band; to keep it, weigh whose society the art represents and not only what it shows.

sampleAnswers.answer: Writing and literature reveal a society that valued learning and shared moral values, and that had a rich cultural life, although this culture was largely confined to an educated elite. The most important evidence is wisdom literature such as the Instruction of Ani, a text in which a father advises his son on how to behave, work and worship. Its advice to be honest, to avoid quarrels and to respect superiors shows the values that shaped ordinary life and the hierarchy of Egyptian society. Scribes were the people who produced and copied such texts, and their training in reading and writing shows that literacy was a route to status and office. Other texts reveal a broader cultural world. Love poetry, which survives on papyri, suggests that personal emotion and leisure were part of the culture of the period, while the Papyrus Ebers, a medical text, shows practical knowledge of healing and the body. These works show that Egyptians valued knowledge not only for administration but for everyday survival and enjoyment. However, these sources must be treated with caution. Most literature was written by and for scribes and the elite, so it reveals their ideals rather than the lives of farmers, workers or women, who are less visible in the record. Writing and literature therefore reveal a sophisticated culture, but one whose everyday life must be reconstructed with other evidence. Overall, the writing and literature of the period illuminate cultural and everyday life in Egypt, even though the evidence is partial.

prompts.question: Assess the impact of the pharaoh on Egyptian society during this period. Support your answer with reference to the following interpretation and other relevant sources.
markerNotes: The top answer separates cultural influence (building, art, ritual) from political influence, and tests Wilkinson's claim about each.
Evidence must show the limits of royal power as well as its reach. The Deir el-Medina strike and the tomb robberies do this; Ramesses II's campaigns and treaty with the Hittites add to the picture.
