Her building at Deir el-Bahri and Karnak gave her rule a visible presence and supported her legitimacy as king. The reliefs of the Punt expedition show that trade was important to her government, and the goods brought from Punt added to the prestige of the court. Her chief steward Senenmut was a major figure in her administration, which shows that she used capable officials to govern. However, she inherited a system built by earlier kings, so not all of the changes were her own. After her death her images were defaced, which suggests that her influence was contested. The Punt and Karnak projects were the clearest expression of her policies, and they show a ruler who made the most of her position. Overall she influenced her time through her monuments and policies, but the extent of that influence is hard to measure, because the sources that describe it were produced under her own direction.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Hatshepsut’s legacy is significant mainly because she showed that a royal woman could hold full power, and because her building programme shaped how later rulers expressed kingship. Her reign was not a complete break with the past, and some of her achievements were reversed soon after her death, so the lasting significance of her legacy must be judged with care.

The most important element of her legacy was her claim to legitimacy. She ruled first as regent for Thutmose III and later as pharaoh in her own right. Her monuments show her with the full royal titles and, in some images, with the regalia and false beard of a king. Her temples proclaimed that she had been chosen by the god Amun, which allowed her to rule without challenging the divine order. This created a model of royal authority that later rulers could draw on, even though it was unusual.

Her building programme provided the most visible part of her legacy. The mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari, with its terraces and colonnades, displays the link between the king and the gods in a striking way. At Karnak she erected obelisks and expanded the temple of Amun, and these projects made the cult of Amun central to royal ideology. Her expedition to Punt is recorded in the reliefs at Deir el-Bahari, which present trade and divine approval as signs of a successful reign. These images are also a lasting record of Egypt’s contacts with the wider world.

Her legacy was also limited, and the evidence for this is clear. Many of her images were later defaced, probably on the orders of Thutmose III, who wished to erase her role from the official record. His later campaigns in the Levant, including the battle at Megiddo, show a return to a military emphasis in foreign policy. Modern scholars therefore debate how far her achievements were valued at the time, since much of the surviving evidence comes from her own monuments.

Overall, Hatshepsut’s legacy was significant because it demonstrated that a royal woman could hold full power and use religion, architecture and trade to support her rule. Its long-term impact was uneven, however, because her successors reshaped the record of her reign. Her most enduring contribution was the building programme and the model of legitimacy that it displayed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 13–15 row: it makes a well-developed assessment of legitimacy and the building programme, integrates the Deir el-Bahari reliefs and the Karnak monuments, and weighs the later defacement against her achievements. Testing the claim about the surviving evidence against a specific source would make the judgement sharper.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Hatshepsut’s legacy is significant mainly for its legitimacy and its building programme. She ruled as pharaoh and presented herself as chosen by the god Amun, which made her rule acceptable to the priests and the wider population. Her temple at Deir el-Bahari and the work at Karnak were visible signs of her authority, and they show how kingship was linked to religion. The expedition to Punt, shown in the reliefs, adds to her image as a successful ruler.

However, her legacy was partly reversed. Many of her images were later defaced, which suggests that her successors did not want her reign to be remembered in full. The Egyptian army remained important in foreign affairs after her death, so her peaceful reputation did not last. Her reign is nonetheless one of the clearest examples of a woman holding full royal power in ancient Egypt, and this part of her legacy was not undone.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Judged by her own aims, Hatshepsut was highly successful. She secured her position as pharaoh, ruled for about two decades in relative peace and prosperity, and left monuments that expressed a clear programme of legitimacy. Her impact on later Egyptian kingship was more uneven, because some of her names and images were later reduced or removed. The judgement therefore depends on whether success is measured by what she achieved during her reign or by what survived of her work.

Her success in securing power is the first measure. Hatshepsut moved from regent to full pharaoh and used religious ideas, especially the reliefs at Deir el-Bahari showing her divine birth from Amun, to make that transition acceptable. These reliefs show that she understood how kingship was represented and used that understanding deliberately. Tyldesley's reading, that she sought to recreate the splendours of the 12th Dynasty, fits this evidence well, because the stability she presented was itself a form of political argument. She claimed the authority of the kings who had prospered before her, and her reign was presented as a return to order.

Her building and trade provide the second measure. The mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari was a major project, and the architect Senenmut is linked with it in the sources. The expedition to Punt, shown in the same complex, brought exotic goods to Egypt and displayed the wealth of her reign. Her obelisks at Karnak were a visible contribution to the temples of Amun, and they show that her programme was ambitious. These achievements were largely successful during her own lifetime, and they show how a ruler could convert trade and building into a public record of legitimacy.

The third measure is lasting influence, and here the evidence is more mixed. Some of her images and monuments were later defaced or removed, so her reputation was not secured by her successors. Her reign also did not change the way Egyptian kings ruled in any lasting way, since the New Kingdom continued along the path of expansion and temple building that she had supported. Her success was therefore real but was measured mainly in her own time. On balance, Hatshepsut was very successful as a ruler who made her position secure and left a rich building record, but her long-term impact on the kingship that followed her was limited.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 13-15 row: a well-developed and reasoned judgement that weighs legitimacy, building and trade against long-term impact. It would lift further by testing the interpretation directly against the building evidence and by stating more precisely what the later treatment of her monuments shows.

These achievements show a ruler who knew how to turn her position into a public record of success.

Her long-term influence was less certain. Some of her monuments were later removed or defaced, and the kings who followed her returned to the path of conquest that she had not emphasised. This means that her reputation depended on her own presentation of her reign, which was carefully constructed, rather than on a settled tradition that her successors wanted to continue. Her success is therefore clearest in her own lifetime and less clear afterwards.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Cooney’s view that Hatshepsut ‘did everything right’ is largely justified in its emphasis on her competence, but its claim that she made no waves of discontent rests on an argument from silence that the evidence cannot fully support. Hatshepsut ruled Egypt for roughly two decades, first as regent for the young Thutmose III and then as pharaoh in her own right. Her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari is a masterpiece of architecture, and she commissioned expeditions to Punt, which brought incense and other goods to Egypt. Her reign was a period of stability and prosperity, and the monuments she built, including the obelisks at Karnak, show a ruler who could manage the state, the priesthood and the army. In this sense the source correctly identifies a skilled and successful leader.

The assessment is weaker when it treats the lack of recorded opposition as evidence that opposition did not exist. The record is largely shaped by Hatshepsut’s own building and inscriptions, and by officials who benefited from her rule. Silence in such a record is not proof of unanimous support. The source also suggests that later kings took the credit for her achievements, and this is supported by the fact that Thutmose III later had many of her images and names erased or defaced. The erasure shows that her memory was contested after her death, even if the ancient sources do not describe active rebellion. A modern reader must therefore weigh the claim that she was an exemplary ruler against the evidence that her legacy was deliberately reshaped.

The judgement is also strengthened by the evidence of her building programme, which was not confined to Deir el-Bahari. Her obelisks at Karnak, raised to honour Amun, show that she could work with the priesthood rather than against it, and the expedition to Punt displayed the wealth that a stable reign could generate. A reader who accepts the source’s claim of competence can point to these works as evidence that her reign was effective, and this is a fair basis for the source’s judgement.

A balanced reading must also recognise that the source’s judgement is shaped by its own purpose. Cooney writes a popular history, and her emphasis on Hatshepsut’s success serves a narrative that rewards a competent woman who was later overlooked. The judgement is therefore useful for restoring Hatshepsut’s reputation, but it is not a neutral measure of the evidence. The historian must weigh the claim against the monuments, the inscriptions and the later erasure, and conclude that the assessment is justified in its emphasis on competence rather than in its claim of universal approval.

Overall, the assessment can be justified in regard to her skill and success, but not in its claim of universal approval. The source is a useful statement of one modern view, and it should be read alongside the evidence of erasure and the limits of the surviving sources.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 13–15 row: a well-developed and reasoned judgement that integrates the source with the evidence of erasure and the surviving monuments. To lift it further, cite a specific inscription or monument in the second paragraph.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Hatshepsut's reputation as a successful and peaceful ruler is largely deserved, although it has been shaped by her own propaganda and by later interpretations. Her reign brought trade with Punt, large building projects and a period of stability. The reliefs at Deir el-Bahari, the Karnak obelisks and the Speos Artemidos inscriptions show a ruler who was confident in her right to govern, and the evidence for prosperity is strong.

However, the sources that praise her were commissioned by her own officials, so they reflect royal ideology rather than an independent judgement. The evidence for military success is limited, and the claim that she was a great conqueror is not supported. Her reputation as a peaceful builder rests largely on the monuments that she herself chose to build.

Later treatment also complicates the picture. Many of her images and names were defaced, most likely during the reign of Thutmose III, and this suggests that some of her contemporaries or successors wanted to diminish her memory. Modern interpretations have varied. Some historians have admired her as a capable pharaoh who ruled with skill, while others have seen achievements exaggerated by the monuments themselves. The extent to which she deserves her reputation therefore depends on which sources are trusted.

On balance, Hatshepsut deserves much of her reputation as an effective ruler who sustained the Egyptian state, but not the claim that her reign was a period of military greatness. The sources most useful for her achievements are the monuments that record her building and trade, while the defacing of her images shows that her standing was contested even in antiquity.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 9–10 row: a detailed and well-developed assessment of how far she deserves her reputation, using a range of sources. To lift it, the response could weigh modern interpretations against the ancient evidence more explicitly.

sampleAnswers.answer: Hatshepsut's reputation as a successful ruler is partly deserved. Her building program and the Punt expedition show that her reign was prosperous. The later defacing of her monuments, probably under Thutmose III, suggests that her reputation was contested even in antiquity, so historians should be cautious about accepting her own version of her reign. Modern historians have generally accepted the evidence for her trade and building, but have been more cautious about her claims to kingship. A balanced judgement accepts her achievements while recognising the self-serving nature of the sources.

sampleAnswers.answer: The surviving evidence for Hatshepsut is shaped by the fact that almost all of it was produced by the state. As Joyce Tyldesley notes, Hatshepsut lived in a literate age but in a society that did not keep personal records, so the sources are overwhelmingly official documents that rarely express private opinion. There are no intimate letters, diaries or memoirs from her court, and the historian is left with a figure who remains an enigma. The major sources are monumental. The mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahri contains reliefs showing her divine birth and her expedition to Punt, and the obelisks and inscriptions at Karnak present her building work. These monuments were commissioned to legitimise a woman who ruled as king, so they stress her divine right and her achievements and say little about the opposition her rule may have faced. This royal propaganda is the central problem. The record is also incomplete because of what happened after her death. Many of her images and inscriptions were defaced, probably under her successor and stepson Thutmose III, so the surviving evidence is partly the product of erasure. Historians must reconstruct her reign from fragments, using the reliefs and inscriptions with caution and testing them against administrative documents and the dating of the monuments. The problems are real, but they do not make Hatshepsut unknowable. Careful cross-checking of official records, monuments and the traces of erasure lets historians identify what the state wanted people to believe, and infer some of what was left out.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 9–10 row: presents a well-developed explanation of the official, monumental and erased evidence, and integrates the Tyldesley source with the Deir el-Bahri and Karnak monuments. To go further, weigh the evidence more explicitly against the problem it creates for each claim.

sampleAnswers.answer: Hatshepsut's evidence is a problem because most sources are official. Tyldesley says there are no personal letters or diaries, so historians rely on monuments such as the temple at Deir el-Bahri and the obelisks at Karnak. These were built to show her as a legitimate king, so they present a favourable picture. Later erasure of her images also makes the record incomplete, and historians must be careful about what these sources show. Tyldesley's point that the real Hatshepsut remains an enigma follows directly from this. Her reliefs say little about the political opposition her rule may have faced, so a historian must read them as statements of royal ideology rather than as reports of events.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5–6 row: refers to the source and gives a sound explanation of the official nature of the evidence. To reach 7–8, use the source's point about personal records more fully and bring in a second type of evidence, such as administrative records, linked clearly to the problem.

sampleAnswers.answer: The value and limitations of sources on Hatshepsut lie in the fact that most evidence was created by her own court and was later altered, so historians must read it as propaganda as well as record. Scholarly interpretations add a further layer. Matić’s article, cited in the stimulus, examines how the binary categories of modern scholarship shape the reading of Hatshepsut. Szpakowska argues that the male royal regalia Hatshepsut wore, including the false beard, does not mean cross-dressing. Her comparison is that female barristers in the United Kingdom wear the same wigs and robes as male barristers without pretending to be men, so the regalia represented kingship. This is a valuable argument because it shows how modern assumptions can distort the reading of ancient images. Its limitation is that it is an interpretation, and the historian must decide whether the ancient evidence supports it. The royal monuments themselves are valuable sources. The reliefs at Deir el-Bahri present Hatshepsut as the daughter of Amun, whose divine birth legitimised her rule, and show the expedition to Punt, which gave her reign a claim to success. These sources show how the queen wished to be seen, so they are a valuable guide to royal ideology. However, they are limited: they were made to present a particular image of the queen, and many were later defaced or removed after her death, so the surviving record is incomplete and biased. The erasure of her name and images under Thutmose III makes it hard to know how she was viewed by her contemporaries. Other sources, such as the tomb in the Valley of the Kings, add evidence, but they were also shaped by royal intentions. The texts call her king and use masculine royal forms, which shows that royal ideology presented her as a king rather than as a woman who had taken male power. Some of her statues combine male regalia with female forms, which invites careful reading rather than a single answer. Historians therefore need to combine the monuments, the texts and modern interpretations, testing each against the others. The most reliable evidence is the consistent picture across sources, while the least reliable is any single image. Used carefully, the sources allow a reasoned understanding of Hatshepsut as a powerful ruler, but never a complete one.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 13–15 row: a well-developed and reasoned judgement of the monuments and the modern interpretations, integrating the stimulus and stating the limits of each. Committing more firmly to which evidence is most reliable would strengthen the judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: The value of sources on Hatshepsut lies in the royal monuments, which show how the queen wished to be seen, such as the reliefs at Deir el-Bahri and the claim to be the daughter of Amun. Matić’s argument, as the stimulus presents it, shows how modern binary categories shape the reading of these images. Szpakowska’s comparison with female barristers suggests that the regalia represented kingship rather than cross-dressing. The limitation is that monuments were made as royal propaganda, and many were later defaced after her death, so the evidence is incomplete. The defacement of her images under Thutmose III means that contemporary attitudes are hard to recover, so the judgement must be cautious. The Punt reliefs add to the picture of a successful reign, but they too present an idealised view. Historians need to test interpretations against the surviving evidence.

sampleAnswers.answer: The reliefs carved on the walls of Hatshepsut's mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari are a valuable ancient source for a historian studying her. sampleAnswers.answer:
Akhenaten was shaped by the context of his father's reign and by the religious world of Egypt that he inherited. O'Connor and Cline argue that the Amarna episode should be set within the wider background from which Akhenaten was born and against which he reacted, and this is a strong starting point. Their claim that the king was not necessarily the only prime mover is also important, because it shows that his reform drew on existing antecedents as well as on his own will.

The reign of Amenhotep III was the most direct context. It was a period of wealth, international diplomacy and monumental building, and it gave the kingship a strong solar identity. The sun disc had long been linked with royal power in Egyptian theology, so the emphasis on the Aten did not appear from nowhere. O'Connor and Cline's point about antecedents fits this background: many of the elements Akhenaten later made central had roots in earlier religious practice, and the Egyptian king built on them.

The second context was the temple of Amun at Karnak, whose priesthood had grown rich and powerful. The Amun cult was the largest religious institution in the kingdom, and its wealth and political influence gave Akhenaten a clear target for reform. His decision to move the court to a new city and to elevate the Aten above the older gods can be read as a reaction against that power. This is why the context matters: it shows what Akhenaten was responding to, not only what he believed.

Yet the interpretation also reminds us that the king himself mattered. The reform was carried out through his authority, and the new style of art and worship was his own creation in its details. Context explains the shape of the Amarna episode, but it does not fully explain why Akhenaten chose to push these ideas so far. Shaped by his inheritance and his opponents, he nonetheless made choices that set his reign apart.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 9-10 row: a well-developed and informed explanation that interacts with O'Connor and Cline's claim about antecedents and supports it with the reign of Amenhotep III and the Amun cult at Karnak. It would lift further by giving one concrete example of an earlier solar element.

sampleAnswers.answer: Akhenaten was shaped by his father's reign, which had given the kingship a strong solar identity and a wealthy temple system. O'Connor and Cline suggest that the Amarna episode had antecedents in earlier religious practice, so his reforms were not wholly new. They also place the king among the causes rather than making him the only one. The power of the Amun priesthood at Karnak gave him something to react against, and this helps explain the move to a new capital. His context therefore included both an inheritance he could draw on and a rival he wished to displace.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-6 row: an explanation relevant to the question that refers to the interpretation and to the context of Amenhotep III and Karnak. It would reach 7-8 by using a second source and explaining how the antecedents shaped his art or worship.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Akhenaten's building program developed in stages, moving from the Thebes area to a new capital in Middle Egypt. The earliest work was at East Karnak, where he built a series of structures dedicated to the Aten, the sun disc. These buildings were made of small sandstone blocks called talatat, which were later reused in other monuments, and their decoration showed the king and queen worshipping the Aten under its rays. The East Karnak work is important evidence because it shows that the new religion was first expressed within Amun's great temple precinct, which the king then left behind.

The building program then shifted to a new city, Akhetaten, founded at the site now called Amarna. Boundary stelae around the city, which record its foundation, show that Akhenaten planned it as a religious and administrative centre dedicated to the Aten. Temples, palaces and tombs were built there, and the city was laid out on a new plan. The Amarna evidence, including the boundary stelae and the excavated city, shows a more complete program than the early Karnak work.

The development can therefore be understood in three phases: experimentation at East Karnak, the foundation of Akhetaten, and the continuation of the Aten cult in the capital. Although the early work is less well preserved, the surviving talatat blocks show that the program was planned as a series of structures rather than a single project. Together, these sources show how Akhenaten used architecture to express his religious reform.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 9–10 row: a detailed and well-developed explanation of the development of the building program, supported by a range of sources. To lift it, the answer could weigh how far the fragmentary evidence limits the conclusions.

sampleAnswers.answer: Akhenaten's building program began at East Karnak, where he built temples to the Aten using talatat blocks. These blocks show the royal family worshipping the sun disc, which supports the claim that the program was religious. The program later moved to Akhetaten, a city founded as the centre of the Aten cult. The sources show that the program developed from experimental work at Karnak to a planned capital city, although the early works survive only in fragments. Historians therefore see the development as a change in scale and ambition rather than a sudden break.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5–6 row: a sound explanation of the development of the building program that refers to sources. To lift it, the answer should use more detail from the sources and show how the stages connect.

sampleAnswers.answer: Akhenaten built temples at Karnak to the Aten. He later built a new city called Akhetaten. The blocks used are called talatat.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1–2 row: a general statement about the buildings, with little explanation of the development. To lift it, the response needs to show the order of the stages and cite one source.

sampleAnswers.answer: The founding of Akhetaten in about regnal year 5 was the most significant event of Akhenaten's reign because it made his religious reform physical and political. He changed his name from Amenhotep IV, a name honouring Amun, to Akhenaten, and built a new capital, Akhetaten, meaning Horizon of the Aten, on a site between Thebes and Memphis. Leaving Thebes weakened the priesthood of Amun at Karnak, whose wealth and influence were centred there. The city gave the Aten its own sacred ground, with the king at its centre. Few followers went with him, and the reform did not outlast him: Tutankhamun returned the court to Thebes about three years after Akhenaten's death.

sampleAnswers.answer: Akhenaten’s motives for moving the capital to Akhetaten were primarily religious, but political and personal concerns also played a part. The king’s own words in the boundary stela, which swear an oath ‘to the Aten my father in all eternity’, show that his devotion to a single sun god was at the centre of his plans. The stela’s insistence that the inscription ‘shall not be erased’ and ‘shall not be made to disappear’ reveals a king determined to make the new city a permanent sacred place. Relocating to a site with no earlier god or town allowed Akhenaten to found a city dedicated only to the Aten, free from the temples of Amun at Karnak and Thebes. The Amun priesthood was wealthy and powerful, and a move away from Thebes reduced its influence over the king and the state. Other sources support this reading: the boundary stelae set out the city’s limits and describe the Aten as the creator of the site, while the Great Hymn to the Aten celebrates the god as the sole source of life. The Amarna Letters show that Akhenaten maintained diplomacy with foreign rulers from his new capital, suggesting the move did not isolate him from the political world. However, the source is a religious and self-presenting text. The boundary stela is a royal statement of piety, written to proclaim the king’s devotion and the permanence of the Aten cult, so it cannot show the practical reasons for the move, such as the cost of building or the reaction of officials. Its claim that the land belonged to no other god or ruler is also a royal assertion that should be treated with caution. The stela’s wording also needs to be placed in the political context of the king’s reign. The boundary stelae were set up around the new city in its early years, and they fixed its limits as a sacred space. Their language emphasises permanence and the king’s oath, so they were designed for a continuing audience, including officials and priests, rather than only for the king. This makes the stela a deliberate statement of policy, even though it is not a neutral account of his motives. Taking these sources together, religious motives were the most important, because Akhenaten explicitly placed the Aten above all other gods, and the move gave him control of a new sacred centre. Political motives, including the reduction of the Amun priesthood’s power, were a significant secondary factor. Personal motives, such as the king’s wish to establish his own legacy, cannot be proven from the sources but are consistent with the stela’s language of permanence. Akhenaten’s motives were therefore a combination of faith and power, though the stela makes faith the most visible.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 13–15 row: a reasoned judgement that ranks religious, political and personal motives, tests the stela as a royal claim, and integrates the Great Hymn and the Amarna Letters. The answer is complete for fifteen marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Akhenaten moved the capital mainly for religious reasons, to found a city dedicated to the Aten. The boundary stela records his oath to the Aten and says the inscription ‘shall not be erased’, which suggests he saw the new city as a permanent sacred place. The move also took him away from Thebes and the temples of Amun, whose priests were powerful, so political motives may have played a part. The stela is a royal text that presents the king’s piety, so it does not explain the practical reasons for the move, such as cost or the reaction of officials. Other evidence, such as the Great Hymn to the Aten, supports the view that the god was central to his plans. The sources therefore suggest that religion was the main motive, though the evidence for political motives is less direct.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7–9 row: some judgement on religious and political motives, with use of the stela as evidence. Weighing the Amun priesthood’s power against the stela’s religious language, and naming the Great Hymn as support, would lift it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Akhenaten moved the capital because he wanted to worship the Aten, and the stela shows his devotion to this god. The source does not say much about other reasons for the move.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1–3 row: a general statement that refers to the source without explaining the motives or judging them. Explaining why the Amun priesthood mattered and weighing the stela as a royal text would lift it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Akhenaten’s reign brought a deliberate change to the afterlife beliefs and funerary customs that had shaped Egypt for centuries. The traditional model centred on Osiris, the god who ruled the dead, and on spells from the Book of the Dead that guided the deceased through the underworld. Akhenaten replaced this focus with the Aten, the visible sun disc, whose daily rising and setting was presented as the source of all life, including the life of the dead. Funerary art at Amarna shows the royal family and officials bathed in the rays of the Aten, which end in hands offering the ankh sign of life, so the sun’s blessing reached the living and the dead alike. In the Amarna tombs, such as those of Meryre and Huya, the scenes emphasise the king’s rewards and the Aten’s care, while the Osiris imagery that had filled earlier tombs was largely absent. The king’s own rock-cut tomb in the Royal Wadi at Amarna was begun on a new site, reflecting that the Amarna capital was itself the king’s new religious centre. Akhenaten also ordered that the name of Amun be erased from monuments, including funerary texts, so the older gods that had protected the dead were no longer named. These changes were concentrated in a short reign, so the Amarna tombs were abandoned soon after his death and the traditional beliefs were restored. The changes also reached the tombs of the officials who served the king, whose cliff tombs at Amarna place the Aten at the centre of their funerary decoration.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 9–10 row: a well-developed description of the change from Osiris to the Aten, with specific funerary evidence from the Amarna tombs and the erasure of Amun. The answer is complete for ten marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Akhenaten changed the funerary customs and afterlife beliefs of Egypt by focusing on the Aten rather than Osiris, the traditional god of the dead. Tomb scenes at Amarna show the royal family under the rays of the Aten, which end in hands offering the ankh, so the sun god was seen as giving life to the living and the dead. The name of Amun was erased from monuments, and the traditional funerary texts that named older gods were no longer used in the same way. Because the reform was tied to one reign, these changes ended with Akhenaten’s death and the capital was abandoned.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5–6 row: a sound description of the Aten, the tomb scenes and the erasure of Amun, but the tombs are not named and the funerary practice is only briefly covered. Naming Meryre or Huya and the Royal Wadi tomb would lift it.

sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1–2 row: a general statement about the change with no specific funerary detail. Naming Osiris, the Aten’s rays or an Amarna tomb would lift it.

markerNotes: Account for asks for reasons, so each change in titles or images needs a cause placed in its stage of the reign.
Show how the titles (religious and political declarations) and the images (artistic expression of the same message) changed together.
The top band weighs interpretations, such as whether the policy was planned in advance or developed over the reign.
commonStudentErrors: Treating the change of name as the only change and ignoring the images, or the reverse.
Presenting the Aten cult as straightforward monotheism without noting that the religious claims and the political aims are debated.
Describing the images as naturalistic without giving any reason why the style changed.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Akhenaten's titles and images changed in stages, and the changes followed the development of his religion. Early in his reign he presented himself in the conventional way. Tombs such as those of Ramose and Parennefer show him in traditional style, with the Aten appearing only as a sun disc above the royal couple. He worshipped the older gods, and at Karnak he had himself shown worshipping Ra-Horakhty on the Third Pylon. His birth name, Amenhotep, meant 'Amun is satisfied'.

The first decisive change came in regnal year five, when he adopted the name Akhenaten, meaning 'effective for the Aten', and decreed a new capital, Akhetaten. The new name replaced the Amun element in his identity and was the outward sign of a religious change. The reasons were theological and political. The Aten was presented as the sole god, the creator who renews life at each sunrise, and the king was the one through whom its power reached Egypt. Politically, the move weakened the Amun priesthood at Karnak, which had long dominated religious life in the capital. Historians differ on the sequence. Redford argues that the religious policy was not conceived in advance and developed during the reign. The early Sed festival, where offerings were made only to the Aten, fits that gradual shift.

The images changed too. The Amarna style of the early years was exaggerated and expressionistic, and it reflected the Aten's role in creating and sustaining the natural world. Artists portrayed plants, animals and people with a naturalism and movement that traditional art did not allow. Royal images changed most strikingly: the king, queen and daughters were shown in intimate, relaxed scenes that had no precedent in royal art. The exaggerated style was later softened, which suggests the images were adjusted as the regime settled. The tension between the new message and the conventions of royal art explains why the images were so distinctive.

Both titles and images were reversed after his death. Tutankhamun, born Tutankhaten, changed his name, and the court returned to Thebes. Akhenaten was excised from the king lists, and his monuments were defaced. This shows that the titles and images had been tied to one king and his authority rather than forming a fixed tradition.

Overall, the titles changed because Akhenaten's religion changed, and the images changed because the Aten's message needed a new visual language. Religious conviction, the wish to curb the Amun priesthood and artistic experiment together account for the changes, and their later destruction reflects how closely they were bound to one king.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 13-15 row: a well-developed explanation that accounts for both the titles and the images, linking each to religious and political reasons and to the sequence of the reign. The answer weighs the debate over whether the policy was planned, and uses accurate detail (regnal year five, the Sed festival, the Third Pylon) with precise terms.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Akhenaten's titles and images changed because his religion changed. At first he kept the traditional style of royal art, and his birth name, Amenhotep, honoured Amun. In his fifth regnal year he took the name Akhenaten, meaning effective for the Aten, and founded a new capital at Akhetaten dedicated to the Aten. The Aten became the only god worshipped, and Akhenaten presented himself as the king through whom its power reached Egypt.

His images changed to match this message. The new style showed the royal family in relaxed, intimate scenes, and plants and animals were drawn with more natural forms. The style was exaggerated in the early years, and it reflected the Aten's role in creating and sustaining the natural world. The changes were also political, because by moving away from Amun he weakened the priests at Thebes, who had long dominated religious life in the capital.

After his death the old order was reversed. Tutankhamun, who was born Tutankhaten, changed his name, and the court returned to Thebes. Akhenaten's monuments were defaced, so the changes did not last.

The sentence ‘The changes were also political’ gives a reason without showing how it shaped the images. Weighing how the titles and images changed at different stages, and a historian's view, would lift it to 10-12.

sampleAnswers.answer: The representations of Akhenaten and the royal family were innovative because they broke with the idealised style of earlier pharaonic art. Artists depicted the king with an elongated head, narrow face and heavy hips, and showed family scenes in which Akhenaten, Nefertiti and their daughters appeared at home, affectionate and informal. The Aten, shown as a sun disc, had rays that ended in hands offering the ankh sign to the royal family, which expressed a direct link between the god and the king. Such scenes appeared in temples and private tombs, and the talatat blocks, small standard sandstone blocks, allowed the new imagery to be built quickly across the city. These innovations reflected Akhenaten’s religious teaching that the Aten was the sole god, and they presented the royal family as a model of that faith.

prompts.question: What do ancient and modern sources reveal about Akhenaten’s foreign policy?
markerNotes: The top band reads the Amarna letters as evidence of diplomacy and weakening control in the Levant, and it sets the tomb scenes of tribute against the letters rather than treating either as a complete record.
It recognises that the letters are one-sided and the tomb scenes idealised, and it uses this to explain why modern historians reach different conclusions about the king’s intentions.
Answers in the lower bands describe Akhenaten’s religious reform without linking it to his foreign relations, or present the sources as proof of one view.

Stating that Akhenaten lost the empire, rather than showing that the letters reveal weakening control in the Levant.
Treating the Amarna letters as a neutral record without noting that they were written by vassals making requests.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The sources reveal a foreign policy that was less militarised than that of his predecessors, although the evidence is incomplete and debated. The most important ancient source is the Amarna letters, a collection of diplomatic correspondence sent to Akhenaten by rulers and vassals in the Levant. These letters complain about rival city-states and raids by groups known as the Habiru, and they request Egyptian troops, which were rarely sent in large numbers. They suggest that Akhenaten’s authority over the Levant was weakening, although Egypt kept its formal control of the region.

Scenes in the tombs at Amarna show tribute being brought from Nubia and the Levant, including gold, animals and goods. These scenes demonstrate that foreign wealth still flowed to Egypt and that the king maintained the ideal of rule over foreign lands under the Aten. Nubia was governed through a viceroy, and its gold remained important to the royal treasury. Akhenaten’s policy in the south therefore appears to have been more stable than in the north.

Modern historians disagree about how to interpret this evidence. Some argue that Akhenaten neglected the empire to concentrate on his religious reform at Akhetaten. Others argue that the letters show Egyptian officials trying to hold the Levant together with limited resources, and that the king’s policy was shaped by the difficulties he faced. Because the letters are mostly one-sided and the tomb scenes are idealised, the sources cannot show exactly what Akhenaten decided.

Overall, the sources reveal a foreign policy marked by diplomacy, tribute and a decline in Egyptian control of the Levant, rather than by new campaigns. Akhenaten’s devotion to the Aten shaped his relations with other rulers, but the full extent of his policy remains uncertain.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 9–10 row: it reads the Amarna letters and the tomb scenes together, weighs the modern interpretations against them and explains why the evidence is limited. Naming one specific Levantine ruler from the letters would make the evidence more precise.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Amarna letters show that Akhenaten’s foreign policy was mainly diplomatic. Rulers in the Levant wrote to the Egyptian king asking for troops and protection against rival city-states, but Egyptian help was limited. Tomb scenes at Amarna show tribute from Nubia and the Levant, which suggests that the Egyptian empire still brought in wealth. Historians disagree on whether Akhenaten neglected the empire or faced problems he could not solve. Because the letters are one-sided, it is hard to judge his intentions, and this is why the evidence supports more than one interpretation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5–6 row: it identifies the Amarna letters and the tomb scenes and notes the debate, but the explanation of Egyptian limits is general. Linking the requests in the letters to the decline of control would lift it to the 7–8 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Akhenaten received letters from the Levant, and some of them ask for Egyptian help. His foreign policy is shown in these letters, although the evidence is limited.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1–2 row: a general statement that names one source without explaining what it reveals. Describing what the letters show about Egyptian control would reach the 3–4 row.

prompts.question: To what extent did Akhenaten influence his time? Support your response using evidence from relevant sources.
markerNotes: The top band reaches a qualified judgement: Akhenaten's influence on religion, court and art was intense but narrow, and it was largely reversed by his successors.

sampleAnswers.answer: Akhenaten influenced his time more deeply than most New Kingdom rulers in religion, the court and art, but the influence was narrow in scope and short-lived. His most important act was the promotion of the Aten, the sun disc, above the other gods. Early in his reign he changed his name from Amenhotep IV, built the new capital of Akhetaten on a virgin site, and closed or neglected the temples of Amun and other gods. The hymns to the Aten and the tomb reliefs at Amarna show a religion centred on the king and his family. Nefertiti and the royal daughters appear beside him in Amarna art, which departed sharply from earlier conventions and shaped the court's image for the rest of the reign. The reforms also reshaped the economy, as wealth formerly given to the older temples was redirected to the Aten, and the administration was reorganised around the new city. These changes affected officials, priests and craftsmen who moved to Amarna. Outside Egypt, his influence is harder to measure. The Amarna letters show that Akhenaten corresponded with rulers such as those of Babylon, Assyria and Mitanni, and that vassal rulers in the Levant sent urgent appeals for help against rivals. Some scholars argue that the king's neglect of military support weakened Egypt's hold on its Levantine territories. This claim rests on the letters themselves, which are one-sided because the surviving correspondence comes from Egypt's files and from petitioners who wanted aid. The strongest evidence for influence is therefore internal and religious. The priesthoods of the older gods lost wealth and status during the reign, and officials who depended on them had to adapt to a new order that centred on the king. The limits of this influence are clear. Within a generation of his death, Smenkhkare, Tutankhamun and later Horemheb had restored the traditional gods, abandoned Akhetaten and defaced many of his monuments. The Restoration Stela of Tutankhamun records the reopening of the temples, and it is the official account that reversed the revolution. Later rulers such as Horemheb issued decrees against corruption in the administration, which shows that the crisis of the Amarna period had weakened the state's institutions. Nefertiti's prominence in the Amarna reliefs also raises questions about the queen's own role, which the surviving evidence cannot resolve. Akhenaten's reforms changed his court and capital and influenced the artistic style of the period, but they did not reshape the state or the religion of Egypt in the long term. He influenced his time more than most rulers, but his legacy was narrow, and the evidence for its reach is uneven.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 13–15 row: gives a well-reasoned judgement and integrates the Amarna letters, the Amarna art and the Restoration Stela. To go further, test the claim about the Levant more rigorously against the letters' own bias.

sampleAnswers.answer: Akhenaten influenced his time mainly through religion and the court. He promoted the Aten above the other gods, moved the capital to Akhetaten and redirected temple wealth to the new god. The art of Amarna, with its images of the royal family, reflects the court's new religious outlook. These changes affected officials, priests and craftsmen, who moved to the new city. His influence on the wider empire is harder to judge. The Amarna letters show that rulers in the Levant asked Egypt for help, and some historians argue that the king's neglect of these requests weakened Egypt's position. The reforms were short-lived, however, as later kings abandoned Akhetaten and restored the older gods. The religious changes were also confined to a small elite, so the wider population may have experienced them very differently. The art of Amarna, though striking, was a court style rarely seen beyond the royal centres. Overall, Akhenaten influenced his court deeply, but his influence on the wider state was limited.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7–9 row: gives some judgement and refers to relevant sources such as the Amarna letters and Amarna art. To reach 10–12, sharpen the judgement and weigh the evidence for the Levant rather than asserting it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Akhenaten influenced his time because he changed the religion of Egypt. He built a new city and worshipped the Aten. These changes were important, and later kings removed his name from many monuments. The Amarna period is widely studied because of its unusual art and the letters found at the site.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1–3 row: makes general statements about the reforms with little evidence and no judgement. To lift it, say how far the reforms affected his time and support the point with one source.

prompts.question: Assess the significance of Akhenaten’s legacy. Support your response using evidence from relevant sources.
markerNotes: The top band judges the legacy in two parts, the deep but short-lived religious and political change of his reign and the limited long-term effect after his successors reversed it.
It uses the new capital at Amarna, the restoration under Tutankhamun and the later removal of the king’s name as evidence, and it shows that the reform depended on the king’s personal authority.
Answers in the lower bands describe the Aten and the capital without assessing whether the change lasted or how far it affected the monarchy.

Claiming that Akhenaten introduced monotheism in the full modern sense, without noting that the question of his beliefs is debated.
Ignoring the restoration under Tutankhamun, which is essential evidence for assessing the legacy.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Akhenaten’s legacy is significant mainly because his religious reform altered the relationship between the king, the state and the gods. Yet the reform’s impact was short-lived, because his successors dismantled much of it. The most accurate judgement is that his legacy lies in the boldness of the change and in the questions it raised about royal authority, rather than in lasting institutional change.

The religious reform was his most distinctive achievement. He promoted the Aten, the sun disc, as the central god, closed or neglected the temples of rival deities and built the new capital Akhetaten, now known as Amarna. In the city, the king and his family were shown in intimate scenes of worship, which made the royal family central to the religion. These changes gave the monarchy a new religious identity and show how far a king could reshape the priorities of the state.

In the short term, the legacy was political and administrative. The move of power to Akhetaten and the neglect of the traditional priesthoods weakened the established elites, particularly at Thebes, and increased the importance of officials who depended on the king. Foreign relations were also affected, since the Amarna letters show that Egypt’s control of the Levant was weakening during his reign. The king’s legitimacy, which had rested on maintaining Ma’at and the cults of the gods, was therefore challenged.

The long-term legacy was limited. Tutankhamun, who began life as Tutankhaten, returned the state to the worship of Amun, and his advisers restored the temples. Later rulers, including Horemheb, removed many references to Akhenaten from official records, which is why later tradition came to call him a heretic king. The restoration shows that his reform depended on his personal authority and did not survive him.

The legacy also shaped how later rulers understood kingship. The idea that a king could reshape the official religion, and the caution that Tutankhamun and Horemheb showed in restoring the old gods, both became part of how Egyptian rulers were judged. Akhenaten therefore left a precedent as well as a reform: a warning that religious change needed the support of the priesthood and the elite.

Modern assessments remain divided. Some historians see Akhenaten as a visionary who introduced an early form of monotheism, while others argue that his reform was shaped by royal and priestly politics and that control of the state mattered more than the idea of a single god. The evidence from Amarna, including the buildings, tombs and letters, supports both readings. Overall, his impact was deep for a short period and remains one of the most debated episodes in Egyptian history.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 13–15 row: it judges the reform’s depth against its short life, uses the Amarna evidence and the restoration under Tutankhamun, and weighs modern interpretations. Setting the Amarna letters against the restoration more explicitly would sharpen the final judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Akhenaten’s legacy is significant because of his religious reform, which made the Aten the central god and moved the capital to Akhetaten. This changed the relationship between the king and the gods, and the royal family became central to worship. However, his legacy was short-lived. Tutankhamun restored the old gods, and later rulers removed many references to Akhenaten. The reform therefore depended on the king’s authority rather than on lasting institutions.

The Amarna letters show that the reform also coincided with weakening Egyptian control in the Levant, which suggests that its consequences reached beyond the religious sphere. Historians remain divided on whether the reform was a religious vision or a political strategy, and the Amarna evidence supports both views. For this reason the significance of his legacy is real but limited, and its importance lies in the questions it raised about kingship.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7–9 row: it assesses the reform and the restoration and links the legacy to the Amarna letters, but the judgement is brief. Weighing the lasting elements against the reversed ones more directly would lift it to the 10–12 row.

markerNotes: The top band reaches a reasoned judgement on how successful Akhenaten was by separating his aims, such as the promotion of the Aten and a new capital, from what endured after his death.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Judged by his own aims, Akhenaten was successful in establishing the Aten as the central focus of royal religion and in building a new capital, but he was not successful in creating a lasting change. His reform was reversed within a generation, and his lasting impact lies mainly in art and architecture. The judgement depends on whether success is measured by the boldness of the reform or by its survival.

His success in promoting the Aten is clear. He elevated the sun disc above the older gods and presented the Aten as the source of kingship and life. The Great Hymn to the Aten, which is attributed to his reign, shows a carefully developed theology in which the king and his family stood close to the god. Nefertiti appears in the sources as a powerful royal partner, and the royal family was represented in intimate scenes that expressed the new religion. These sources show a reform that was coherent and deliberate.

The building of Akhetaten, the new capital, was the most visible achievement. The city was laid out as a religious and administrative centre, and the Amarna letters show that the court was active in diplomacy with other kingdoms. The style of Amarna art, with its naturalism and its images of the royal family, was a striking departure from earlier conventions. These achievements were real and changed the visual culture of the period, so they weigh heavily in favour of success.

However, the reform did not endure. After Akhenaten's death the court returned to the older religion, and Tutankhamun restored the cult of Amun and moved the court back to Thebes. The capital was abandoned, and the Aten cult was not continued as the state religion. This is the strongest evidence that Akhenaten's aims were not achieved in the long term. On balance, he was successful in his own reign and in the creation of a distinctive art, but his religious programme failed to outlast him.

The judgement that Akhenaten was unsuccessful in the long term does not mean that his reign had no effect. The Amarna period changed the way the royal family was shown, the way the king's body was portrayed and the way the gods were imagined in art. These changes were visible in the sculpture and relief work of the period, and they survived in fragments long after the city was abandoned. Historians therefore weigh the evidence differently: the political failure is clear, but the cultural legacy is harder to dismiss. A reasoned judgement must acknowledge both, and must explain why the cultural legacy did not translate into a lasting religious settlement.

Taken together, the evidence supports a balanced conclusion. Akhenaten pursued his aims with unusual determination, and his reign produced a distinctive art and a striking new capital. Yet the religious programme was not supported by the wider elite, and the restoration of Amun shows how fragile the reform was. The strongest answers therefore reach a clear judgement that separates the boldness of the reform from its endurance.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 13-15 row: a well-developed and reasoned judgement that separates the reform's achievements from its lasting failure, supported by the hymn, the art and the restoration under Tutankhamun. It would lift further by weighing the diplomatic evidence more precisely against the religious evidence.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Akhenaten was partly successful. He made the Aten the focus of religion and built the new city of Akhetaten, which is shown in Amarna art and in the letters of the period. The royal family, including Nefertiti, was presented in a new style that expressed the reform. However, his reforms did not last. The court went back to Thebes after his death, and Tutankhamun restored Amun, so his influence was largely limited to his own reign and to the art that survived from it.

The evidence of failure is strong. The capital was abandoned, and the older temples and their priesthoods regained their place in the state. The Great Hymn to the Aten shows the depth of his theology, but it did not become the basis of a religion that the next generation was willing to keep. His success was therefore real in its own time and in its art, but it was not a success in the long-term religious order of Egypt.

It would reach 10-12 by weighing the Great Hymn and the Amarna letters against the evidence of failure and explaining why one kind of success was stronger than another.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The source by Darnell and Manassa argues that Akhenaten could be as aggressive as any pharaoh and that his military prowess matched the expectations of Egyptian kingship. The claim is only partly justified. Egyptian kings were expected to defend the empire, and the source is right that a pharaoh was judged by his ability to confront threats. Akhenaten did carry on the imperial structure that his predecessors had built, and the role of the military in his reign is part of that continuity.

However, the evidence for an aggressive foreign policy is thin. The Amarna letters, the diplomatic correspondence between the Egyptian court and rulers in Syria and Canaan, show vassal rulers complaining that the king did not send troops or money to protect them. Some local rulers, such as Abdi-Ashirta, were able to extend their territory with little response from Egypt. These letters suggest a king who was distant from military affairs, and they weaken the claim that he confronted threats as aggressively as other pharaohs. The source’s argument may reflect an interpretation of kingship as much as the evidence of this reign.

The judgement is also limited by the nature of the sources. The religious texts and the art of the Amarna period focus overwhelmingly on the Aten and the royal family, and they say little about the army or foreign affairs. This means that the claim of military aggression must be inferred from a small body of evidence, and the Amarna letters are themselves a partial record. A reader who wants to test the source must therefore ask what the absence of military scenes means: it may reflect a deliberate choice of religious imagery, not a lack of military capacity. This is why the claim cannot be fully confirmed or rejected on the available evidence.

The source also needs to be read against the wider evidence of Akhenaten’s reign. The king’s inscriptions focus on the Aten, the new city and the royal family, and they say little about the army. The absence of military scenes is therefore not conclusive, because the programme of religious art may have deliberately excluded them. A reader must weigh the claim of military prowess against the fact that the surviving evidence reflects the king’s religious priorities. The assessment can be justified in its claim that Akhenaten followed the expectations of kingship, but the evidence for aggression is weak.

The judgement must also consider the nature of the evidence. The Amarna letters are the best source for foreign policy, but they are partial, because they survive from the Egyptian archive and reflect the complaints of subordinates. Modern historians who emphasise the military duties of kingship may be reading the source through the standard image of the pharaoh. Overall, the assessment is justified in its claim that Akhenaten was expected to act as a warrior king, but it is not well supported by evidence that he did so in practice.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 13–15 row: a well-developed and reasoned judgement that integrates the source with the Amarna letters and a clear view of its limits. To lift it further, use one specific letter or place name to test the source’s claim directly.

sampleAnswers.answer: Darnell and Manassa argue that Akhenaten could be as aggressive as any pharaoh, and their claim is partly justified. Egyptian kings were expected to defend the empire, and Akhenaten continued the structure of imperial control that his predecessors had built. The source is right that the pharaoh’s military role was central to royal ideology. However, the Amarna letters show vassal rulers complaining that Egypt did not send troops or money, and local rulers were able to extend their territory with little apparent response from the court. This suggests a king who was distant from military affairs rather than a warrior who confronted threats. The judgement must also take into account the limits of the evidence, since the letters are partial and reflect the complaints of subordinates. The source is therefore a useful interpretation of kingship, but it is not well supported by the evidence of this reign.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Akhenaten's reputation as a radical religious reformer is only partly deserved, because the evidence shows a real and sustained change in worship alongside a reign whose lasting impact was limited. His reform centred on the Aten, a sun disc worshipped as the sole god. Sources such as the Great Hymn to the Aten, inscribed in the tomb of Ay at Amarna, and the buildings at Akhetaten show that the reform was carefully planned and enforced. These sources support the view that he was an unusually innovative ruler.

However, many of the images that present him as a visionary were produced by his own court, so they show royal ideology rather than an independent judgement. The collapse of the Aten cult after his death, and the later removal of his name from monuments, suggests that the reform did not win lasting support. The Amarna Letters show Egypt's international relations continuing, but they also reveal problems with Egypt's allies in the Levant, which suggests that his foreign policy was less effective than his religious policy.

Modern interpretations have varied. Early twentieth-century writers often praised him as an early monotheist, while others have seen the reform as a political move centred on the king. Modern historians tend to be more cautious, stressing the limits of the evidence and the role of the court. The modern image of Akhenaten, shaped in part by the opera Akhnaten by Philip Glass, is also a product of later interpretation rather than ancient evidence.

On balance, Akhenaten deserves credit for an innovative religious program and striking art, but the reputation as a successful reformer overstates what he achieved. His reign is best judged as a bold experiment whose failure was shown by the rapid return to the older gods.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 9–10 row: a detailed and well-developed assessment of how far Akhenaten deserves his reputation, using a range of sources. To lift it, the answer could sharpen the distinction between the reform's religious and political aims.

sampleAnswers.answer: Akhenaten deserves some credit for his religious reform, which is shown by the Great Hymn to the Aten and the new capital at Akhetaten. These sources show a ruler who was determined to change worship. However, the reform collapsed quickly after his death, and his name was later removed from monuments. This suggests that his reputation depends on sources produced by his own court, so historians should weigh the reform against its lack of lasting success. Modern interpretations of him have varied, so a balanced view is needed. The reputation is best judged as the product of his reform, his court's presentation of it and the limited success that followed. Historians should therefore avoid both hero and villain labels.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5–6 row: a sound assessment that refers to the Great Hymn and the Amarna evidence. To lift it, the response should weigh the reform against its lack of lasting success more explicitly.

sampleAnswers.answer: Akhenaten was an important pharaoh who changed Egyptian religion. Many people think he was a great leader, and his capital at Amarna is famous.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1–2 row: a general statement about his importance with little use of sources. To lift it, the response needs to assess the evidence for his reform and cite one source.

sampleAnswers.answer: Ridley's source identifies a paradox in the evidence for Akhenaten. At Amarna, the city he founded as Akhetaten, there is a wealth of material: palace and house remains, tomb reliefs, boundary stelae and the Amarna letters, the diplomatic correspondence of the period. Yet, as Ridley argues, many basic matters remain unknown. Outside Amarna the record is thin, and the absence of data from much of Egypt means that definite conclusions about the king, his policies and their success or failure cannot be reached with confidence. The evidence is therefore concentrated in one place and reflects the court's own view of its king. The hymns to the Aten and the tomb scenes present Akhenaten as the centre of a religious revolution, and it is difficult to test that picture against sources from other regions. A second problem is the erasure that followed his reign. Under Tutankhamun and later rulers, many of Akhenaten's monuments were defaced and his religious reforms were reversed. The Restoration Stela of Tutankhamun records the return of the traditional gods, and this official account shapes how historians understand the king. Much of what we know about Akhenaten therefore comes from sources produced by his own court or deliberately damaged by his successors. Historians must weigh these sources carefully. The Amarna letters, for example, show Egypt's foreign correspondence and the king's dealings with rulers abroad, but they are letters that Egypt kept or received, so they cannot show how the wider world understood him. Large gaps remain in their knowledge of the reign.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 9–10 row: presents a well-developed explanation of the Amarna concentration and the erasure, and integrates the Ridley source with the Amarna letters and the Restoration Stela. To go further, weigh the reliability of the Amarna letters against the tomb reliefs more directly.

sampleAnswers.answer: The evidence for Akhenaten is concentrated at Amarna, which the source describes as a wealth of material. The Amarna letters and the tomb reliefs at the site give historians a detailed picture of the court and its religion. However, Ridley says that evidence from the rest of Egypt is limited, so conclusions about the king's policies and their success cannot be reached with confidence. After his death, Tutankhamun's restoration stela shows that the traditional gods were returned, and this official account also shapes what historians know about him. Ridley's point, that much of Egypt is missing from the record, means that the picture of the reign is drawn largely from one city.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5–6 row: refers to the source and gives a sound explanation of the Amarna concentration. To reach 7–8, explain why the Amarna record is one-sided and use the later erasure as a second source for the problem.

sampleAnswers.answer: Akhenaten's evidence is a problem because most of it comes from Amarna, and the source says there is little information from the rest of Egypt.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1–2 row: makes a general statement with some reference to the source. To lift it, explain why a record concentrated in one city limits what historians can conclude.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Xerxes was shaped by the problems he inherited from Darius and by the expectations placed on Persian kings. Stoneman argues that Xerxes lived under the shadow of his great father and had to prove himself a great conqueror, and this is a persuasive reading of the evidence. Xerxes' reign was defined by the need to complete what Darius had left unfinished.

The most immediate context was Darius' unresolved conflict with the Greeks. The Ionian Revolt and the defeat at Marathon in 490 BC were failures that Darius never reversed. When Xerxes came to power in 486 BC, he faced rebellion in Egypt and Babylon, which he suppressed, and this gave him a reputation for resolve. The invasion of Greece in 480 BC, which culminated in the Battle of Thermopylae, can be read as an attempt to achieve the conquest that his father had failed to complete. In this sense, the expectations of Persian kingship shaped the decision to invade.

The interpretation also has limits. Xerxes was not only a figure of his father's making. He was responsible for the scale of the invasion, for the bridging of the Hellespont and for the policies that followed. Stoneman's reading of the shadow of Darius is therefore useful, but it should not reduce Xerxes to a son who followed a plan. The building at Persepolis shows a king who wanted to project his own authority and to display the empire's wealth.

Xerxes' context, then, combined inherited obligations with his own ambitions. The Persian tradition of royal conquest and display made the invasion of Greece almost required, while his father's unfinished business gave it a clear purpose. Shaped by both, Xerxes was driven to prove himself, and the invasion became the defining feature of his reign.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 9-10 row: a well-developed and informed explanation that interacts with Stoneman's claim about the shadow of Darius and supports it with the revolts, Marathon and the invasion. It would lift further by testing the claim against the evidence of Xerxes' own choices more directly.

sampleAnswers.answer: Xerxes was shaped by Darius' unfinished business with the Greeks, especially the failure at Marathon in 490 BC. Stoneman suggests that Xerxes lived under his father's shadow and had to prove himself a conqueror, and the invasion of Greece fits that view. The expectations of Persian kings, which included conquest and display, also shaped his decisions. He had already shown in the revolts in Egypt and Babylon that he would use force to hold the empire together, and this made the invasion of Greece a natural extension of his authority.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-6 row: an explanation relevant to the question that refers to the interpretation and to the context of Darius' reign. It would reach 7-8 by using a second source and explaining how the invasion reflected his inheritance more fully.

sampleAnswers.answer: Xerxes was born into the Achaemenid royal family, the ruling dynasty founded by Cyrus the Great. He was the son of Darius I and Atossa, who was a daughter of Cyrus, so his mother gave him a direct claim to the royal blood of the founder of the empire. His status was strengthened by the fact that he was born after Darius had become king, which meant he was not the eldest son. Herodotus records that Darius’ eldest son, Artobazanes, was born before the accession, and that Xerxes was chosen as heir because his mother was a daughter of Cyrus. This succession decision shows that the royal family valued maternal lineage as well as age, and that the king’s choice could override the normal order of birth. As heir, Xerxes was trained for kingship in the royal court, and he became king in 486 BCE after Darius’ death, with full authority over the empire. His family background therefore gave him the legitimacy needed to rule, though it created tension with his elder brother and his supporters. The royal inscriptions of Xerxes present him as a son of Darius and a member of the Achaemenid line, which reinforced his authority. The combination of royal blood, a maternal link to Cyrus and the king’s own choice made Xerxes the most secure candidate for the throne. The dynasty’s prestige also rested on the monuments that Darius and Xerxes commissioned at Persepolis, which presented the Achaemenid line as the legitimate heirs of Cyrus.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 9–10 row: a well-developed account of his parents, the maternal link to Cyrus and the succession over Artobazanes, with the Achaemenid status made explicit. The answer is complete for ten marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Xerxes was the son of Darius I and Atossa, the daughter of Cyrus the Great. This gave him royal blood from the founder of the Achaemenid dynasty. He was not Darius’ eldest son, but he was chosen as heir, which suggests that his mother’s royal lineage was important. He became king in 486 BCE after his father’s death, so his family background gave him a secure position. The dynasty’s status also depended on its monuments. Darius and Xerxes commissioned inscriptions and palaces at Persepolis and Susa that presented the Achaemenid line as the successors of Cyrus, and these texts gave Xerxes a public claim to the throne.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5–6 row: sound information on his parents and succession, but the Achaemenid status and his court role are only touched on. Naming Artobazanes and explaining why maternal descent mattered would lift it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Xerxes was the son of Darius, a Persian king, so he came from a royal family. He later became king.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1–2 row: a general statement about his royal birth, with no detail on his mother, his succession or his status. Naming Atossa and the succession to Darius would lift it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Xerxes administered the Persian empire through the system of satrapies that Darius I had created. Each satrapy was governed by a satrap, who collected tribute, maintained order and raised troops when required. The tribute and taxes from the provinces supported the court and the royal army, and the satraps were answerable to the king. Communication was supported by the Royal Road, which linked Sardis with Susa, and by royal couriers who carried orders quickly across the empire. The king also used local customs and languages in administration, so that Persian rule was accepted in the provinces. This system allowed Xerxes to control a vast territory with a relatively small central bureaucracy, and it explains why the empire remained stable for much of his reign.

Religious policy

prompts.question: What do ancient and modern sources reveal about Xerxes’ religious policy?
markerNotes: The top band sets the Persepolis inscription against Herodotus’s account of Babylon and explains that the Greek report may distort a Persian royal policy.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The sources reveal a religious policy that was more assertive than that of Xerxes’ predecessors, although historians disagree about its aims. The most important ancient evidence is the Daiva inscription at Persepolis, in which Xerxes states that he suppressed a cult of the daivas and honoured Ahura Mazda. This suggests that he saw himself as the defender of the god who was central to royal ideology.

Herodotus, writing in the fifth century BCE, reports that Xerxes acted against the cult of Marduk at Babylon after a revolt and removed a statue from its temple. Herodotus was a Greek writing about a Persian king, so the report may exaggerate or distort the event. Babylonian sources suggest that the revolt of 484 BCE led to changes in the city’s administration, which indicates that religion was closely tied to political control.

Modern scholars disagree about the Daiva inscription. Some argue that Xerxes was attacking rival religious practices that threatened the unity of the empire, while others argue that the inscription reflects a royal strategy to strengthen the position of Ahura Mazda in the state. Because few Persian sources describe his policy directly, historians must read the evidence with care.

Overall, the sources reveal that Xerxes’ religious policy was used to reinforce royal authority and to show loyalty to Ahura Mazda, especially in regions that had revolted. The evidence is uneven, and the exact nature of his actions remains open to interpretation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 9–10 row: it integrates the Daiva inscription with Herodotus and the Babylonian evidence, and it weighs the modern readings against each other. Naming the Babylonian source more precisely would strengthen the use of evidence.

sampleAnswers.answer: Xerxes’ religious policy is shown most clearly by the Daiva inscription at Persepolis, which says that he suppressed the worship of the daivas and honoured Ahura Mazda. This suggests a deliberate effort to reinforce royal religion. Herodotus reports that Xerxes removed a statue of Marduk from Babylon after a revolt, but his account was written by a Greek and may be exaggerated. Historians therefore disagree about whether the policy was a religious reform or a response to political rebellion. Because the sources are limited, the evidence supports several interpretations. The Persepolis inscription and Herodotus therefore give different impressions of the same policy.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5–6 row: it names the Daiva inscription and Herodotus and notes the problem of a Greek source, but the comparison between them is brief. Explaining how the Babylonian revolt links religion to political control would lift it to the 7–8 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Xerxes honoured Ahura Mazda, as the Persepolis inscription shows. He also acted against some Babylonian religious practices.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1–2 row: a general statement with one source named and no evaluation. Explaining what the inscription reveals about royal policy would reach the 3–4 row.
