sampleAnswers.answer: The Hyksos influenced the development of Egypt more through the crisis they caused and the reaction to it than through their own rule, which was confined largely to the north. Their period of control, the Second Intermediate Period, was a time when Egypt was divided. Hyksos kings ruled Lower Egypt from their capital at Avaris in the Nile Delta, while a native dynasty held Thebes in the south. The Hyksos were not simply invaders who destroyed Egyptian culture. They adopted Egyptian royal titles, used Egyptian administrative forms and built in the Egyptian style, so in some respects they absorbed Egyptian culture rather than replacing it. Their rule nevertheless had consequences that shaped the Eighteenth Dynasty. They introduced new military technology to Egypt, most notably the horse-drawn chariot and the composite bow, which gave their armies a decisive advantage and which Egyptian forces later adopted. The Hyksos also linked Lower Egypt with the Levant through trade and settlement, and these contacts gave the Egyptian court a new view of the wider world. The most direct influence was the war that expelled them. The Theban rulers Seqenenre Tao and Kamose challenged Hyksos control, and Kamose's stela records his campaign against Avaris, presenting the war as a struggle to free Egypt from a foreign king. The war was completed by Ahmose, who captured Avaris and pursued the Hyksos into Canaan, where he laid siege to Sharuhen. The biography of Ahmose son of Ebana, a naval officer, records these campaigns and suggests that the conflict was long and demanding. The victory was also presented as the work of Amun, the god of Thebes, which reinforced the ideology of kingship. The Eighteenth Dynasty that Ahmose founded therefore began with a legitimacy rooted in the defeat of a foreign enemy and in the protection of the Theban god. The Hyksos shaped the character of the state that followed. The military ethos of the New Kingdom owed much to the experience of the war and to the adoption of chariot warfare, and the rulers who followed Ahmose, including Thutmose I and Thutmose III, built an empire in Syria and Canaan. Some historians argue that the Hyksos were the catalyst for this expansion, because Egypt learnt that a state could be conquered by an army with better equipment, and that the threat from the north could be met by war in the Levant. Others argue that the New Kingdom empire was driven more by Egypt's own ambitions and by the wealth available from trade and tribute, and that the Hyksos experience was one factor among several. This debate matters because it determines how much of the expansion was a response and how much a choice. The Hyksos also left a legacy in Egyptian memory. Later Egyptian and Greek writers, notably Manetho, presented them as oppressive foreign rulers, and this image gave the Eighteenth Dynasty a useful enemy against whom its own rule could be justified. The contrast between foreign rulers and the native kings of Thebes became a central theme of royal ideology. Historians must treat this evidence with caution, because the Egyptian sources were shaped by the victors. The Hyksos' own culture, known mainly from Avaris, is only partly understood, and the Egyptian picture of them as enemies may exaggerate the difference between the two peoples. The influence of the Hyksos was therefore real but indirect. Their rule disrupted the unity of Egypt and created the conditions in which Theban kings could reunify the country, and their military technology transformed the armies that later conquered an empire. The strongest evidence for influence lies in the military and ideological developments of the Eighteenth Dynasty, while their own administration left fewer lasting marks. Egypt's development in this period was shaped by the Hyksos more than by any other external power before the New Kingdom, but the scale of that influence should be measured by what it caused: the reunification, the professional army and the imperial ambition of the state. To that extent the Hyksos influenced Egypt considerably, though their greatest contribution was to provoke the response that made the New Kingdom.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 21–25 row: presents a perceptive judgement that separates the Hyksos' own rule from the reaction it provoked, and integrates the Kamose stela, the Ahmose biography and the debate over the empire. To go further, test the claim that the Hyksos were absorbed into Egyptian culture against the evidence from Avaris.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Hyksos influenced Egypt mainly by provoking the war that reunited the country. They ruled Lower Egypt from Avaris during the Second Intermediate Period, while Theban kings held the south, and their rule divided the state. Their military technology, especially the horse-drawn chariot and the composite bow, was adopted by Egyptian armies, and it helped make the New Kingdom army more effective. The Theban rulers Kamose and Ahmose drove them out. Kamose's stela presents the war as a struggle against a foreign ruler, and Ahmose's biography records the siege of Avaris and the pursuit of the Hyksos into Canaan. The victory was associated with Amun, the god of Thebes, which strengthened the ideology of the new dynasty. These events shaped the Eighteenth Dynasty, which began with a legitimacy based on the defeat of a foreign enemy. However, the Hyksos were not wholly alien. They used Egyptian royal titles and administrative forms, and Egyptian culture continued in the north. Their influence on the later empire is therefore debated. Some historians argue that the experience of invasion encouraged the Eighteenth Dynasty to expand into Syria and Canaan, so that the Thutmoside kings built an empire partly as a defence and partly as a source of wealth. Others argue that the empire reflected Egypt's own ambitions and resources. The Hyksos were a major influence on Egypt's development, but their importance lies largely in what they provoked rather than in what they built. Overall, the Hyksos influenced Egypt considerably, though the extent of their influence is open to debate.

prompts.question: How successful were the reigns of Amenhotep II and Thutmose IV?
markerNotes: The top band reaches a qualified judgement that both reigns succeeded in holding the empire rather than extending it, and it separates Amenhotep II's visible campaigns from Thutmose IV's legitimising monuments.

sampleAnswers.answer: The reigns of Amenhotep II and Thutmose IV were successful in maintaining the empire that their predecessors had built, but they were less decisive than the reigns of Thutmose I and Thutmose III, and their achievements are best measured by continuity rather than expansion. Amenhotep II inherited an empire that extended into Syria and Canaan, and he set out to demonstrate that he could hold it. His inscriptions present him as a warrior of extraordinary physical strength, and his campaigns into Syria were designed to reassert Egyptian control over rebellious cities and to secure the loyalty of vassal rulers. The campaigns displayed Egypt's military power and brought prisoners and tribute back to Egypt. They show a king who was active in the field, but the sources for them are royal propaganda and cannot be taken at face value. Their scale and long-term effects are harder to assess than the propaganda suggests. Amenhotep II's most important achievement was probably the consolidation of the empire at home. His administration maintained the system of provincial governors and tribute, and his reign was stable enough for the royal workshops and temples to continue producing monuments. He presented himself as a pious king, and the construction and decoration of temples reflected the cult of Amun at Thebes. His reign was not without problems. The Syrian campaigns required constant effort, and the vassal cities were not always loyal, so the empire depended on the king's presence and the strength of its garrisons. The fact that the Egyptian state could sustain these demands for decades shows its capacity, and that capacity was itself a measure of his success. Thutmose IV's reign is harder to assess because his achievements were smaller and his sources are fewer, but his Dream Stela, set between the paws of the Great Sphinx at Giza, is one of the most important documents of the period. The stela records that the young prince fell asleep in the shade of the Sphinx and that the god promised him the kingship if he cleared the sand from the monument. The text legitimised his accession and presented the royal line as chosen by the gods. Whether the story reflects a real event or a constructed justification for a king whose claim may not have been straightforward, it shows the importance of religious legitimacy in securing the throne. The restoration of the Sphinx also reflects a concern with the monuments of earlier kings and with the continuity of royal ideology. Thutmose IV also maintained foreign relations, including a relationship with the kingdom of Mitanni, a major power in northern Mesopotamia and Syria. Diplomacy was an essential part of Egypt's control of the Levant, because vassal rulers depended on Egyptian support and Egypt's rivals sought to win them over. The success of his foreign policy is visible in the stability of the Syrian territories during his reign, although the evidence for detailed events is limited. His reign passed to his son Amenhotep III, who inherited a stable empire, and this continuity suggests that the Thutmoside system worked well in the short term. To compare the two reigns, Amenhotep II was the more active military figure, and his campaigns and inscriptions give the clearer picture of Egyptian power in Syria. Thutmose IV was less visible militarily, but his reign secured the succession and maintained Egypt's diplomatic position. Both kings were successful in preserving the empire, and neither lost the territories gained by earlier rulers. Their reigns did not produce major new conquests, and the empire was held rather than expanded. This was a considerable achievement, given the difficulty of ruling distant provinces and the threat of rival powers. The judgement that both reigns were successful is therefore qualified: they preserved Egypt's position, but they did not extend it, and the sources for their achievements are shaped by royal ideology.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 21–25 row: presents a perceptive judgement that measures success by continuity, and integrates the Syrian campaigns, the Dream Stela and the Mitanni relationship. To go further, test the claim of diplomatic success against the evidence for the vassal cities.

sampleAnswers.answer: Amenhotep II and Thutmose IV were moderately successful. Amenhotep II campaigned in Syria to reassert control over rebellious cities, and his inscriptions present him as a powerful warrior. These campaigns show that Egyptian power was still effective, although the royal propaganda that describes them should be read with caution. Thutmose IV's reign is documented mainly by the Dream Stela between the paws of the Sphinx at Giza, which claimed divine approval for his kingship. The stela shows the importance of religious legitimacy, and it suggests that his claim to the throne needed support. He also maintained relations with Mitanni, which was important for the stability of the Levant. Neither king expanded the empire, but both held the territories that earlier rulers had won. The administration of provincial governors and tribute continued under both kings, and the temples at Thebes continued to receive royal patronage. Their success was therefore mainly one of maintenance, and it depended on the Thutmoside system of government. The sources are uneven, and the detail of many events cannot be recovered. Amenhotep II's campaigns also reveal the logistics of holding a distant province, since troops, supplies and tribute all had to be moved across long routes. Thutmose IV's Dream Stela shows that the government wished to present his accession as divinely approved, which is a useful measure of the political pressures he faced. The historian must balance the propaganda of royal inscriptions against sparse administrative evidence, so judgements about success remain provisional. Neither reign produced a crisis, which suggests that the Thutmoside system was stable enough to absorb two uneven reigns. Overall, the two reigns were successful in keeping the empire stable, although they achieved less than the kings who had founded it.

sampleAnswers.answer: The view that Ahmose made the greatest contribution to Egypt between his reign and the death of Thutmose IV is persuasive, though it must be qualified. Ahmose’s achievement was foundational: he expelled the Hyksos rulers of the Second Intermediate Period, reunified Egypt under Theban rule and founded the eighteenth dynasty. Without this reunification, the later kings could not have raised the wealth and army that made an Egyptian empire possible. His queen, Ahmose-Nefertari, also gave the new dynasty legitimacy and remained an important figure in the royal cult, which shows that the foundation was not only military. Against this view stands Thutmose III, whose campaigns extended Egyptian control across Nubia and the Levant to the Euphrates, and whose victory at Megiddo around 1457 BCE brought the Canaanite city-states under Egyptian authority. Thutmose I had already campaigned in Nubia and reached the Euphrates, so the imperial programme was started before Thutmose III. The scale of this expansion is the strongest argument against Ahmose, because empire is the most visible form of contribution. However, expansion depended on the stable Egyptian state that Ahmose had created. Thutmose III’s army, administration and tribute system all rested on a kingdom that had been reunited and freed from foreign rule, so his achievements were built upon Ahmose’s. Amenhotep I and Thutmose I consolidated the new order, and Hatshepsut’s reign, which included a trading expedition to Punt and a large building programme, kept the state prosperous. Thutmose IV’s reign, which ended the period, was less expansive, but it maintained the empire’s position in the Levant and the diplomatic network that followed. The evidence for Ahmose is limited, since few inscriptions survive from his reign, and the account of the expulsion of the Hyksos depends on the later autobiographical texts of officials such as Ahmose son of Ebana, which praise the king and his servants. These texts are valuable but partial, because they were written to honour the dynasty. Thutmose III’s annals, carved at Karnak, record his campaigns in detail, but they also present the king as an all-conquering ruler, so they exaggerate the uniformity of Egypt’s success. The early reigns show how the foundation was used. Ahmose’s biography, recorded by his official Ahmose son of Ebana, describes the siege of Avaris and the pursuit of the Hyksos into southern Canaan, which shows that the Egyptian army could operate beyond the Nile valley within a generation of the expulsion. His successors inherited a professional army, a centralised administration based at Thebes and the wealth of a reunited kingdom. Amenhotep I maintained this order, and Thutmose I’s campaigns, which took the army to the Euphrates, depended on the resources that Ahmose had restored. The argument that the foundation was decisive can therefore be tested against what followed: the conquests of the next half-century were possible only because the Egyptian state had been put back together and its enemies removed from its borders. A further test is the role of the Egyptian religious institutions. The temple of Amun at Karnak received much of the booty from the campaigns of Thutmose I and III, and the dedications recorded in these reigns show that the priesthood was a partner in the new imperial order. Ahmose’s restoration of Thebes as a royal centre therefore linked the state’s military success to the temples, so the foundation was political and religious at once. This helps explain why later rulers, including Thutmose IV, sought to keep the favour of the gods that had brought victory. Taken together, Ahmose’s contribution was the essential foundation, because it created the unified state, the army and the confidence that later kings used to build an empire. Thutmose III’s achievement was greater in scale and in visible territory, but it was made possible by Ahmose’s work. Therefore Ahmose made the greatest contribution in the sense that the rest of the period depended on him, although Thutmose III’s conquests were the most impressive result of that foundation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 21–25 row: a perceptive judgement that answers the view directly, places Ahmose’s foundation against the conquests of Thutmose I and III, and evaluates the evidence for each ruler. The answer is complete for twenty-five marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Ahmose made an important contribution to Egypt, because he expelled the Hyksos and reunited the country under Theban rule, which gave the eighteenth dynasty a secure base. This foundation allowed later kings to build a larger state. However, Thutmose III’s conquests were more visible, and they extended Egyptian power to the Euphrates and across the Levant. Thutmose I also campaigned in Nubia and reached the Euphrates, which shows that the imperial programme had begun before Thutmose III. Ahmose’s role was essential, because a divided Egypt could not have supported an empire, but the view that he made the greatest contribution is only partly persuasive, since the rulers who followed achieved far more outward expansion. The sources for Ahmose are limited, and his achievements are known mainly from later inscriptions that praise the dynasty. Thutmose III’s annals present his conquests in great detail, but they exaggerate his success. Ahmose’s contribution is therefore the most fundamental, while Thutmose III’s is the most visible. Thutmose III’s annals at Karnak record campaigns in which Egyptian armies took the tribute of Syrian cities, but the rulers who won those victories depended on the army, the treasury and the temple resources that Ahmose had restored. The foundation also gave later kings a legitimate claim: a dynasty that had driven out foreign rulers could present its conquests as the defence of Egypt and the restoration of order. Ahmose’s contribution was less visible than the campaigns of his successors, but it made their visibility possible.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Thutmose III can be considered the most successful pharaoh of the period from the expulsion of the Hyksos to the death of Thutmose IV, but only if success is measured by imperial reach, military achievement and the organisation of tribute. By the standards of territorial expansion and the control of the Levant, his record is unmatched in the period. Judged by prosperity, religious building or the stability of a peaceful reign, however, rulers such as Hatshepsut have a strong claim. The judgement therefore rests on which criteria are used, and Thutmose III is the strongest candidate when the criteria are military and imperial.

The military record is the foundation of his reputation. The Annals of Thutmose III, carved on the walls of the Karnak temple, list a long sequence of campaigns in Syria-Palestine, and historians commonly count some seventeen campaigns in the Levant during his reign. The best known is the campaign against a coalition of Canaanite and Syrian princes at Megiddo, where the king chose a difficult route through the Aruna pass and forced the enemy to fight. The Annals present the capture of the city as a decisive victory, and the detail of the siege and the spoil shows the scale of the Egyptian effort. Redford's description of a watershed in the military history of the eastern Mediterranean rests on this record, because the Egyptian army was now able to campaign in the north year after year.

Imperial control, however, depended on more than battles. The Annals and the later tribute lists show that the conquered princes sent gold, silver, timber, horses and other goods to Egypt. Thutmose III also required the sons of Levantine rulers to be educated at the Egyptian court, which tied the local elites to the king. This system of tribute and hostages gave Egypt a steady flow of resources and a degree of loyalty that made the empire durable for a generation. The organisation of the empire is therefore as important as the campaigns, and it is one reason why Thutmose III can be seen as a builder of the Egyptian empire rather than a conqueror alone.

Redford's argument is persuasive but needs testing. His claim that Thutmose III's accomplishments represent a substantial advance over the activities of his predecessors is supported by the scale of the campaigns, yet the Annals were written to glorify the king. Each campaign is presented as a success, and the ability of the enemy to rebel repeatedly is only partly acknowledged. The evidence for a true watershed therefore depends on whether the claims of the Annals can be trusted, and the archaeology of Syria-Palestine, where Egyptian garrisons and administrative centres are visible, offers independent support for the reach of the empire.

Comparison with the other rulers of the period shows the limits of his claim. Hatshepsut presided over a peaceful reign in which trade with Punt, a major building program and the Deir el-Bahari temple brought prestige and wealth to Egypt, and her reputation for prosperity is well supported by the monuments. Thutmose I had already extended Egyptian power into Nubia and to the Euphrates, so Thutmose III inherited a foundation. Thutmose III's success was therefore built on the work of his predecessors, and his greatest achievements came in the north rather than in internal peace.

On balance, Thutmose III can be considered the most successful pharaoh of this period in terms of military reach, imperial control and the organisation of tribute, and his claim is stronger than that of any other ruler. However, the claim depends on the criteria chosen. In terms of prosperity, religious building and a peaceful reign, Hatshepsut has a strong case, and the Annals must be read as a royal account that presents victory as inevitable. Thutmose III was the most successful imperial ruler of the period, but not the only measure of success.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Thutmose III was a very successful military pharaoh. His campaigns in Syria-Palestine are recorded in the Annals at Karnak, and the victory at Megiddo is the best known. These campaigns show that the Egyptian army could reach the north year after year, which supports Redford's view that he marked a turning point. The Annals also suggest that conquered princes sent tribute to Egypt, so the empire brought wealth to the king.

However, the Annals were written by the Egyptian court, so they present every campaign as a success. Their picture of tribute and loyalty may be exaggerated, and the repeated rebellions suggest that the control was not as complete as the texts claim. Hatshepsut's reign was more peaceful and was also successful in its own way, with trade to Punt and great building projects. Thutmose III's record is strong in imperial terms, but it is not clear that it makes him the most successful pharaoh in every sense.

The judgement also depends on the period. The Annals and the military record show a king who was active in Syria-Palestine for most of his long reign, and the scale of his campaigns exceeds that of any predecessor in the period. However, his reign also depended on the work of earlier rulers who had restored order after the Hyksos period, and on the economic resources of a state that was already rich. This means that his success was built on a foundation, rather than created from nothing.

sampleAnswers.answer: Queens made a real but largely supporting contribution to the reunification of Egypt. Their influence was greatest in the war against the Hyksos, when a royal woman could hold the family’s claim together, and in the religious and dynastic legitimacy that the Eighteenth Dynasty drew on afterwards. The military victories that expelled the Hyksos and reunited the Two Lands were won by the kings, so the queens’ contribution was substantial but secondary. The clearest case is Ahhotep I, mother of the brothers Kamose and Ahmose. A stela set up in her honour credits her with looking after Egypt in a time of conflict and with caring for its soldiers, and her burial contained gold flies and axes of the kind given to soldiers for valour. These objects suggest that she was seen as a war leader. She is generally thought to have acted as regent at Thebes while her sons campaigned against Avaris, and her role in holding the Theban power base together was essential. Whether she commanded in the field is unknown, but her authority in the war years is well attested. Ahmose-Nefertari contributed differently. As Ahmose’s wife she was linked with the god Amun of Thebes at a time when the cult was rising in importance, and later tradition honoured her as a pious and powerful queen. Her religious role connected the new dynasty with the god whose temple at Karnak the kings enlarged, helping to legitimate a family that had risen from Thebes. Tetisheri, Ahmose’s grandmother, gave the line a royal ancestry that the family could use to claim the throne. These contributions shaped the dynasty’s image without deciding its wars. The limits of the queens’ contribution should be stated. Almost all surviving evidence was commissioned by kings or by male officials, so queens appear mainly as honoured family members in stelae and tomb equipment rather than as decision-makers, and historians must infer their influence from indirect evidence. Reunification was decided on campaigns that the kings led, against the Hyksos at Avaris and in the southern and Nubian territories, and the kings controlled the army and the administration. A queen’s support could strengthen a campaign, but it could not replace the king’s command of the troops. The queens’ roles also changed with the dynasty’s needs. Once the Hyksos were gone and the Eighteenth Dynasty was secure, the emphasis moved from wartime support to the religious and dynastic image of the royal family, which was displayed in temples at Thebes. This suggests that queens were most useful to the dynasty when its legitimacy was in question, and less visible once victory had secured it. The contrast with the Amarna period, when Nefertiti was prominent in royal art, shows how far queenly visibility depended on the circumstances of each reign. On balance, queens contributed significantly, though indirectly. Ahhotep I’s regency and her sons’ dependence on Theban loyalty, Ahmose-Nefertari’s religious prominence and the dynasty’s use of its ancestry all helped make reunification possible. Yet the decisive military and political action was the kings’, and the queens are best understood as supporting that work rather than driving it. The contribution is therefore real but secondary, and its extent depends on how much weight is given to evidence that is limited and shaped by royal propaganda.

sampleAnswers.answer: Queens contributed to the reunification of Egypt in some ways, although the kings were more important. Ahhotep I is the clearest example. She was the mother of Ahmose and probably held authority at Thebes while her sons fought the Hyksos, and a stela set up for her praises her care for Egypt. This shows a queen in a position of authority during the war years, which supported the family’s claim to the throne. Ahmose-Nefertari also helped the dynasty. As Ahmose’s wife she was connected with the cult of Amun, which was important at Thebes, and this religious role gave the new dynasty legitimacy. Tetisheri, Ahmose’s grandmother, was remembered as an ancestor, so the family could present a long line of royal claims. However, the kings did the fighting. Ahmose drove the Hyksos out of Avaris and campaigned in the south and in Nubia, and it was his army that restored the north. Queens could support the war but could not command the army themselves. The evidence for queens is also limited because most inscriptions were made by kings, so it is hard to say how much queens actually decided. Their support was also visible in the religious life of the court. Ahmose-Nefertari’s association with Amun gave the dynasty a religious message that complemented the king’s military success. Because the kings depended on the god for victory, a queen who served the cult could show that the royal family was pious and blessed. This made the queen a useful partner in the dynasty’s claims, even though the decisions remained with the king. Overall, queens helped reunification mainly through religion and family legitimacy, while the kings made the military decisions. Their contribution was important but was not the most important one.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The cult of Amun was central to the pharaoh’s power and authority in the New Kingdom, because it gave the king a divine legitimacy that no other institution could provide. Amun, the chief god of Thebes, was identified with the sun god Re as Amun-Re, and the pharaoh was presented as the son of Amun, chosen to rule Egypt. This ideology was expressed in the great temple complex at Karnak, which grew into the largest religious building in Egypt, and in the festival of Opet, when the king’s divine kingship was renewed through a procession from Karnak to Luxor. The cult therefore linked the pharaoh’s personal authority to the divine order of Egypt.

The cult also had practical political value. Royal decisions were often presented as divine choices, and oracles of Amun were used to confirm the succession and legitimise important acts. Hatshepsut claimed that Amun had chosen her to rule, and her building at Karnak, including the obelisks, expressed that claim. Thutmose III used the victories of his campaigns to show that Amun granted him conquest, and the wealth of the temple, supported by booty and endowments, showed the god’s favour. The pharaoh’s authority was reinforced by these displays of divine approval, and the priesthood of Amun depended on royal patronage for its wealth and position.

However, the cult was not simply a tool of the king. The priesthood of Amun at Karnak grew very wealthy and powerful, controlling land, labour and the god’s oracle. By the late New Kingdom, the high priests of Amun had considerable influence in Thebes, and this was a potential rival to royal authority. The Amarna period showed how the king could attempt to replace the cult, and the restoration of Amun under Tutankhamun shows that the king could not rule without the god’s support. The relationship was therefore one of mutual dependence rather than simple control.

The cult also shaped the way the king was represented in art and architecture. Royal temples were built to house the god, and the pharaoh appeared in reliefs making offerings to Amun, receiving life and victory from him. The festival of Opet, which took the cult image in procession from Karnak to Luxor, allowed the people of Thebes to witness the renewal of royal power in a public setting, and it reinforced the idea that the king’s authority depended on the god. These displays were not simply religious in purpose, since they also expressed the pharaoh’s control over the resources and the labour that sustained the temples.

The cult’s importance can also be measured by the wealth it commanded. The temple estates, the offerings from royal campaigns and the land donated by successive kings made the Amun temples among the richest institutions in Egypt. This wealth reflected the close link between the king’s military success and the god’s prosperity, and it gave the priesthood a stake in the stability of the throne. The cult therefore supported royal power in material as well as ideological terms, and its endowments were a visible sign that the pharaoh’s authority was shared with, and sustained by, the god.

Overall, the cult of Amun was very important to the pharaoh’s power and authority, because it provided divine legitimacy, a ritual framework and a visible expression of royal favour. The priesthood’s independence was a limit, but the king remained the central figure of the cult. The cult’s importance can be assessed most clearly in the reigns that depended on it, and in the crisis that followed when it was challenged.

Royal decisions could be confirmed by the god’s oracle, and the festival of Opet renewed royal authority in a public procession. These displays made the god’s approval visible to the population. However, the priesthood grew wealthy from royal endowments, and by the late New Kingdom its high priests had considerable influence in Thebes. This wealth could become a rival to royal authority. The cult was therefore important to the pharaoh’s power, but it was also a source of tension that could limit the king’s control.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The cult of Amun was very important to internal developments in New Kingdom Egypt, but its importance lay less in political control than in the way it gave the monarchy a religious foundation, a source of wealth and a public stage. The crown depended on Amun for legitimacy, and the priesthood at Karnak gained resources that reflected the military success of the kings. Yet the cult did not dictate policy, and the monarchy retained the decisive authority over appointments, building and the distribution of wealth. The judgement is that Amun was central to the internal life of the period, but that its significance was shaped by the choices of the crown.

The cult's religious role gave the kings a clear basis for their authority. Amun was the king of the gods at Thebes, and the kings presented their rule as the will of the god. The divine birth reliefs of Hatshepsut at Deir el-Bahari show how a ruler could draw on Amun's authority to justify an unusual claim to power. This use of religion was an internal development in its own right, because it shaped how Egyptians understood the king and his place in the world. The cult therefore provided the language in which internal politics was conducted, and the monarchy depended on it to present its authority as legitimate.

The cult's economic weight was even more significant. The temple at Karnak was among the largest religious institutions of the period, and it received land, labour and goods from the crown. Military success brought booty, and much of it was dedicated to Amun. The campaigns of Thutmose III, in particular, enriched the temple and the priesthood, and this created a powerful institution with its own estates and workforce. The priesthood's wealth gave it influence over the administration of the temple estates, and it also gave it a stake in the stability of the monarchy. The development of this economic base was one of the most significant internal changes of the era.

The interdependence of crown and cult, however, had limits. The king appointed the high priest and controlled the major decisions about building and endowments, so the priesthood's influence was exercised within a framework the monarchy defined. Thutmose I, Hatshepsut and Thutmose III all used the temple to display their power, and Amenhotep II's reign reinforced the same pattern. The cult therefore shaped internal developments by providing the ideological and material foundations of royal power, but the decisive authority remained with the king. Its importance is best understood as a partnership in which the monarchy used religion to strengthen its position, and in which the priesthood gained wealth and status as a result. On balance, the cult of Amun was central to the internal development of New Kingdom Egypt, though its influence depended on the crown's willingness to share resources and authority with the god's temple.

The limits of the cult's influence also appear in the way the monarchy managed the temple's resources. The crown could grant or withhold land, and it could promote or replace the high priest, so the priesthood's wealth was never fully independent of royal will. Even the great building programmes at Karnak were directed by kings who used them to display their own achievements, and the temple's walls record the campaigns and dedications of the monarchs rather than the priests. The relationship was one of mutual dependence in which the god's house gave the kings legitimacy and the kings gave the god his wealth, and each side defined the terms of that exchange. This is why the cult's importance is best described as structural rather than autonomous. It shaped the institutions through which the state worked, including the economy, the ideology of kingship and the public life of Thebes, but the decisions that gave these institutions their form were usually made in the royal palace rather than in the temple. A judgement that the cult was very important must therefore recognise that its power was real but derived from the crown, and that the crown's willingness to fund and honour the god was itself a choice with political consequences for the whole kingdom.

The crown depended on the god to justify its rule, and the priesthood grew in wealth as the kings won military success. However, the monarchy kept control over appointments and building, so the cult's importance was shaped by royal decisions rather than by the priesthood alone.

The cult supported royal legitimacy. Amun was the chief god of Thebes and the kings presented their authority as the god's will. The reliefs of Hatshepsut at Deir el-Bahari show her divine birth from Amun, which helped her claim the throne. This use of religion shaped how Egyptians understood the king. Karnak also received land and goods from the crown, and the booty of military campaigns was dedicated to the god. These dedications show a close relationship between the crown and the temple, and they helped the priesthood become a major economic force in the period.

The priests were also part of the administration of Thebes. Their estates and workshops employed large numbers of people, and they kept records of the goods that passed through the temple. This gave the cult an administrative weight that extended beyond religion, and the monarchy needed this administrative capacity to manage the wealth of the New Kingdom. The cult therefore mattered to the working of the state as well as to its ideology.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Pharaohs of the New Kingdom used their building programmes to serve political and religious purposes at the same time, and the two aims were closely connected. A king’s legitimacy rested on maintaining the order of Ma’at and on the favour of the gods, so monuments that honoured the gods also displayed the king’s authority to the people. Building was therefore one of the main ways in which a pharaoh justified his rule, and the great temples of the period, especially at Karnak and Deir el-Bahari, show how political and religious aims worked together.

The temple of Amun at Karnak was the centre of this programme. Successive pharaohs added pylons, halls and obelisks to the complex, and the scale of the work made the temple one of the largest religious sites in the ancient world. Religious purposes were clear: the building honoured Amun, the chief god of the state, and it ensured that the god’s favour continued. Political purposes were equally clear, because the most prominent monuments were inscribed with the king’s name and titles, so that the temple proclaimed his right to rule. The temple thus linked the king to the god and to the state.

Hatshepsut’s mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari shows the political use of building most strongly. Its terraces, colonnades and reliefs presented her as the legitimate ruler chosen by Amun, and they recorded her divine birth and the expedition to Punt. The temple was designed to support a claim to kingship that was unusual for a woman, so the political purpose was to establish her legitimacy in the eyes of the elite and the people. Its religious purpose was equally important, since the temple was a place of offerings and of rituals for the dead king and for the god who had approved her rule.

Thutmose III continued these aims in a different way. His Festival Hall at Karnak, which shows the ritual of the Jubilee and the offerings made to Amun, presented him as a king who renewed the order of the state through ritual. This is a clear example of religious purpose serving political ends, because the ceremonies in the hall confirmed the king’s role as the mediator between the gods and the people. The building also reminded the priesthood and the officials of the king’s authority.

The programme was not only a matter of religion and legitimacy. Building also expressed the wealth that the empire brought to Egypt. Materials such as gold, incense and exotic woods, which came through trade and conquest, were used in the temples, and the scale of the work showed that the pharaoh controlled the resources of Egypt and its foreign dependants. In this sense, the monuments celebrated military and economic success as much as piety.

The purposes of building were also shaped by the need to show continuity with the past. Pharaohs often reused earlier monuments, and they inscribed their own names on the work of their predecessors. This practice linked the present king to the line of rulers who had maintained Ma’at, and it suggested that the authority of the dynasty was unbroken. Political purposes were therefore served by the appearance of tradition as much as by innovation.

Overall, the building programmes of the period show that the pharaoh’s legitimacy depended on both religion and politics. Temples honoured the gods, displayed the king’s authority, celebrated the wealth of the empire and linked the present ruler to the past. The most successful pharaohs used these monuments to combine the favour of Amun with the authority of the state, so that the two purposes could not easily be separated.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Pharaohs of the New Kingdom used building programmes for political and religious purposes, and the two were closely linked. A king’s legitimacy rested on maintaining Ma’at and on the favour of the gods, so temples that honoured the gods also displayed the king’s authority. The temple of Amun at Karnak was the main example, because successive pharaohs added halls and obelisks there. Its religious purpose was to honour Amun, and its political purpose was to proclaim the king’s right to rule.

The political function of the monuments was clearest in the Festival Hall, where the king’s ritual role was shown to the officials and priests who entered. Religious purposes were served by the offerings and the honour paid to the god, so the programme worked on both levels at once. Such buildings made the king’s authority visible to a wide audience, and they remained in use long after the reign ended.

Hatshepsut’s mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari shows the political use of building. Its reliefs presented her as the ruler chosen by Amun, and they recorded the expedition to Punt. The temple supported a claim to kingship that was unusual for a woman, so its political purpose was to establish her legitimacy. Thutmose III’s Festival Hall at Karnak presented him as the king who renewed order through ritual, and it confirmed his role as mediator between the gods and the people. Overall, the monuments show that religion and politics worked together, rather than as separate aims.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Egyptian imperialism in this period was less a single system than a set of arrangements that varied by region, and the nature of the empire was shaped by both opportunity and deliberate policy. Ellen Morris argues that the empire occurred almost by accident, as plunder, glory, recognition and revenue from new conquests proved exciting. This is a persuasive explanation of the early expansion, but the evidence for later stages shows a growing degree of planning. The empire was therefore a combination of opportunism and organisation, and the balance changed over time.

The early conquests were driven by opportunity and the prospect of plunder. Ahmose's campaigns against the Hyksos and the early expansion into Nubia rewarded the army with gold and captives, and the Egyptian state gained wealth that made further campaigns possible. Thutmose I's campaigns in Nubia and in the north, which reached the Euphrates, show a readiness to exploit weakness in neighbouring states. The Annals of Thutmose III, carved at Karnak, describe these wars in terms of glory and divine favour, which supports Morris' view that prestige and revenue were powerful motives.

However, the empire could not have been held together by opportunism alone. In Nubia, Egypt built fortresses such as Buhen and Semna, controlled the gold-producing regions and placed an official in charge of the southern territories. This shows deliberate administration, and it suggests that the Nubian conquest was planned to secure resources as well as to bring plunder. In Syria-Palestine, the Egyptians relied on local rulers who sent tribute and whose sons were educated at the Egyptian court. The system of vassals and hostages is evidence of a settled imperial policy rather than an accident.

The interpretation also needs to be tested against the limits of Egyptian control. Vassal rulers rebelled, and Egypt had to campaign repeatedly to restore authority, so the empire was not secure. The Amarna Letters, written in the reign of Akhenaten, show local rulers complaining of Egyptian officials and asking for troops, which reveals that the system could fail when the king's attention was elsewhere. Imperialism in this period was therefore uneven, combining planned administration in some regions with a loose and sometimes fragile control in others.

On balance, Egyptian imperialism in this period was largely opportunistic in its origins, as Morris suggests, but it developed into a more organised system with fortresses, officials, tribute and hostages. Its nature changed over time, and its strength depended on the ability of the king to maintain control. The empire was not an accident, but it was not a fully secure system either, and the balance between opportunity and organisation is the key to understanding it.

The administration of the northern and southern territories shows the same mixture of planning and opportunism. In Nubia, the Egyptian state developed a governor of the southern lands who oversaw the gold mines and the fortresses, and the placing of garrisons along the Nile was a deliberate policy of control. In the Levant, the Egyptians preferred to rule through local princes, and the cities that sent tribute were expected to supply troops and goods. The contrast suggests that Egypt chose different methods for different regions, which is not what an accidental empire would produce. Morris's argument is therefore strongest for the early wars and weakest for the mature empire, where the evidence points to a conscious and sustained system of imperial management.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 21–25 row: perceptive judgement on the nature of Egyptian imperialism, with comprehensive use of the interpretation and other sources. To lift it further, the answer could separate more clearly the Nubian and Levantine systems of control.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Egyptian imperialism began with opportunity and plunder, and Morris argues that the expansion was almost accidental. The early wars against the Hyksos and in Nubia brought wealth and prestige to the Egyptian state. However, the empire was not only accidental. Fortresses such as Buhen and Semna show that Egypt planned to control Nubia, and the Syrian tribute system shows some organisation. The nature of Egyptian rule was therefore partly opportunistic and partly deliberate, and this explains why the empire lasted for a time.

Vassal rulers did rebel, and the Amarna Letters show that the Egyptian system was not secure when the king was distracted. This suggests that imperialism depended on the attention of the ruler, and that the empire was weaker than the Annals describe. A judgement must weigh the planned administration against the fragility of control.

The administration of the empire also shows planning. In Nubia, fortresses and a southern governor controlled the gold-producing regions, and in the Levant, Egypt relied on local princes who sent tribute. The methods differed by region, which suggests that the empire was not simply accidental. Morris's argument fits the early wars, but the later administration shows conscious management. The empire was therefore partly opportunistic and partly organised, and its strength depended on the king's attention.

The sources for the Levant are mainly Egyptian royal texts, which describe the tribute as a sign of the king's success, so their picture of loyalty should be treated with some care. Even so, the existence of fortresses and officials in the south confirms that the state had a plan for at least part of its empire.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The pharaohs of the New Kingdom established a form of empire in Nubia and Syria-Palestine, but the extent of their control was more limited than the word ‘empire’ might suggest. The establishment of empire rested on military campaigns, above all those of Thutmose III, who fought numerous campaigns in Syria-Palestine and reached the Euphrates. His victory at Megiddo around 1457 BCE was decisive, because it allowed him to take the rebel leaders’ cities and gain tribute from the Canaanite states. Amenhotep II later campaigned in the same region to reinforce Egyptian authority. These campaigns created an empire of tribute rather than of direct rule, because the Egyptian state did not administer most of the territories it conquered.

The maintenance of empire depended on the system of vassal states. Local rulers were required to send tribute and to accept Egyptian garrisons and officials, and their sons were sometimes taken to Egypt as hostages to ensure their loyalty. In Nubia, Egyptian administration was more direct, with fortresses, governors and the exploitation of gold mines. This system gave the pharaohs wealth and prestige, and it allowed the court to display the spoils of empire in temples and tombs. The empire was therefore a network of control based on coercion, tribute and the loyalty of local elites.

However, the empire was fragile. The Amarna letters, the diplomatic correspondence of the late 14th century BCE, show vassal rulers in Syria complaining that Egyptian support was insufficient, and several Canaanite cities were lost to rival states. The pharaohs could not always enforce control, and the reign of Amenhotep III and his successor shows that empire depended on the king’s active leadership. Whether the pharaohs established an empire in this period is therefore a question of definition. They created a large system of tribute and dominance, but the extent of direct control and its durability were limited.

The empire was also sustained by the presence of Egyptian officials and garrisons in key centres. Commissioners were sent to supervise the collection of tribute, and the sons of local rulers were educated at the Egyptian court so that they would become loyal to the pharaoh. The booty from the campaigns was displayed in temples at Karnak and Thebes, which showed the population that the conquest had brought wealth to Egypt. These mechanisms made the empire function as a system of extraction rather than settlement, and they explain how the pharaohs could hold distant territories without a large permanent army in each province.

The question of empire can also be tested by the way Egyptian culture was spread through the conquered lands. Egyptian artisans and scribes worked in Nubian and Canaanite centres, and Egyptian temples were built in Nubia at places such as Soleb and Sesebi. These buildings were a means of expressing the pharaoh’s presence and of integrating the local elites into a common religious framework. The empire was therefore not only a system of tribute, but also an attempt to make conquest appear legitimate through religion and architecture.

Overall, the pharaohs established an empire of tribute and dominance in the period, rather than a fully administered territorial state. The campaigns of Thutmose III and the vassal system gave them great power, but the Amarna letters reveal the limits of that control. The question depends on the criteria applied, and the best judgement recognises both the achievement and its limits.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 21–25 row: a sustained discussion that defines empire and weighs the campaigns, the vassal system and the Amarna evidence. To lift it, compare the depth of control in Nubia with that in Syria-Palestine more directly.

The gold of Nubia was a particularly valuable resource for the crown. However, the empire was fragile. The Amarna letters show vassal rulers complaining that Egyptian support was insufficient, and several cities were lost to rival states. The empire was therefore real but limited, and its strength depended on the king’s active leadership and on the loyalty of local elites.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Egypt administered its empire effectively in the period from the New Kingdom to the death of Thutmose IV, but the effectiveness varied across regions and over time. Thutmose III’s campaigns brought large areas of the Levant and Nubia under Egyptian control, and the administrative system that followed used garrisons, tribute and the appointment of loyal officials. The sources are largely produced by the Egyptian state, so they present the empire in a favourable light. Judging its effectiveness therefore requires weighing the military achievement against the structures that held the territory together.

Military success was the foundation of the empire. Thutmose III defeated a coalition of Levantine rulers at the battle of Megiddo, and his later campaigns brought a steady flow of tribute from cities in Syria and Canaan. The victory at Megiddo was recorded in detailed royal annals, and it showed that the pharaoh could destroy a major coalition. Yet a single victory did not secure control, and the Egyptians had to return to the region repeatedly to maintain their position. This suggests that the empire depended on regular campaigns, which were costly and disruptive.

Tribute was the main economic link between Egypt and its dependencies. Conquered rulers were required to send gold, silver, horses, timber and craft goods to the royal court, and the tribute lists in the temples record the scale of these payments. Tribute strengthened the Egyptian economy and displayed the pharaoh’s power, but it also depended on the willingness of local rulers to comply. Where the flow of tribute was interrupted, the administration had to return to military action, which shows the limits of this system.

Nubia was governed more directly than the Levant. The viceroy of Kush administered the region, and fortresses were built along the Nile to control the routes and to protect the gold mines. These garrisons allowed Egypt to exploit the resources of the south, and they gave the state a practical means of controlling the population. The Nubian system was therefore one of the most effective parts of the empire, because it combined a clear administrative office with military control.

The Levant was administered more loosely. Local rulers remained in place, and their loyalty was secured by oaths, the exchange of gifts and the presence of Egyptian officials and garrisons in key cities. The sons of local rulers were sometimes taken to Egypt to be educated at the court, which created a link between the elites of the two regions. This arrangement was flexible, but it was fragile, because it depended on the continued loyalty of the rulers and on the presence of Egyptian forces.

The Dream Stele of Thutmose IV, which describes the king’s restoration by the god, shows how the state presented its authority to the people. It is a religious text, but it also reflects the dynasty’s need to justify its claims over foreign lands. Such propaganda was an important part of the administration, because it made the empire appear natural and divinely ordained.

The effectiveness of the empire also depended on the reputation of the pharaoh. Victory at Megiddo and the tribute lists allowed Thutmose III to present the empire as the reward of divine favour, and this image helped to bind local rulers to the court. Where the image failed, as in periods of revolt, the administration had to rely on force once more. The sources thus show that effectiveness was a product of ideology as well as of military and economic means.

Overall, Egypt administered its empire with considerable effectiveness in the sense that it extracted tribute, controlled the routes and maintained loyal rulers over long periods. Its effectiveness was limited, however, because it relied on repeated campaigns, on the loyalty of local elites and on the presence of garrisons. The empire was held together by a combination of force, economic dependence and royal ideology, and its success was therefore real but never secure.

sampleAnswers.answer: Egypt’s relations with other societies changed considerably between Ahmose and the death of Thutmose IV, because its dealings with foreign powers moved from defence to empire and then to diplomacy, but the change was one of method and scale rather than a complete transformation. Under Ahmose, the main concern was the security of the reunited kingdom, and contacts with Nubia and the Levant were largely shaped by the need to remove the Hyksos and their supporters. Thutmose I marked a decisive shift. He campaigned into Nubia, which brought gold and labour, and he reached the Euphrates, establishing Egyptian power over Syria and confronting the Mitanni, the Hurrian kingdom that controlled northern Mesopotamia and wanted the same territory. Thutmose III built on this by winning the battle of Megiddo around 1457 BCE, after which Canaanite city-states sent tribute and princes to Egypt, so that Egypt became the dominant power in the Levant. This shows a change from defensive to imperial relations, but it was not a simple one, because Egypt’s control of Syria depended on negotiation with rival powers as well as on force. The relationship with the Mitanni was the central foreign relationship of the period. Rivalry for Syria led to repeated campaigns, but by the reign of Thutmose IV the two powers had settled into a diplomatic relationship in which gifts, letters and dynastic contacts became as important as warfare. The change from campaign to diplomacy is therefore one of the clearest shifts in the period. Egypt’s wider contacts also changed in form. Trade with Punt continued under Hatshepsut, and gifts from Cyprus and the Aegean were exchanged for Egyptian gold and goods. These contacts are visible in tomb scenes showing foreign envoys bearing tribute, so the Egyptians presented their relationships as the submission of other peoples. This is a continuity, since the tribute system ran in the same way from Thutmose I to Thutmose IV, though its scope grew as Egypt’s territory expanded. The sources for these relations are uneven. The annals of Thutmose III at Karnak describe campaigns in detail but present Egypt’s victories in a heroic form. Tomb paintings show envoys and tribute but are an idealised picture of the king’s dominance. Diplomatic correspondence from the later Amarna period, though it falls after this period, reveals the importance of letters between kings, and it suggests the diplomatic habits that were developing under Thutmose IV. These sources are valuable, but they must be read against Egyptian propaganda, which claimed universal rule. The Mitanni evidence comes mainly from Egyptian and Hittite sources, and it is fragmentary. The pattern of contact was also shaped by Egypt’s internal politics. Hatshepsut’s reign, which combined regency and sole kingship, emphasised trade over conquest, and her expedition to Punt brought incense and exotic goods to the temple of Amun at Karnak. Thutmose III’s later campaigns followed a period of relative restraint, which suggests that the scale of foreign relations depended on the king’s needs and the stability of the court rather than on a single policy. The Mitanni, meanwhile, were a sophisticated power that exchanged gifts and envoys with Egypt, and their rivalry with the Hittites in northern Syria meant that Egypt had to manage relations with several powers at once. Taken together, Egypt’s relations with other societies changed from defensive contact under Ahmose to imperial control under Thutmose I and III, and then to a more diplomatic balance under Thutmose IV. The change was substantial, but it was shaped by continuing trade, tribute and rivalry for Syria, so it is best described as a transformation in the methods and scale of contact rather than in its basic character.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 21–25 row: a perceptive judgement on the shift from conquest to diplomacy, with continuity in trade and tribute weighed against it, and specific evidence for Nubia, the Levant and the Mitanni. The answer is complete for twenty-five marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Egypt’s relations with other societies changed in this period, moving from defensive contact under Ahmose to conquest under Thutmose I and III. Thutmose I campaigned in Nubia and reached the Euphrates, while Thutmose III won the battle of Megiddo and brought Canaanite city-states under Egyptian control. These campaigns show a major change. However, the rivalry with the Mitanni over Syria continued, and by the reign of Thutmose IV relations had become more diplomatic. Trade with Punt and the exchange of gifts with Cyprus and the Aegean also continued through the period. The change was real, but it was not a complete break from earlier contacts, and the sources for the period are often shaped by Egyptian propaganda. Nubia illustrates the change in method. Under Thutmose I, Egyptian control was extended into Nubia, and the gold of the region supported the state’s wealth and its foreign policy. Egypt governed Nubia through fortresses and officials who collected tribute and supervised local rulers, which made foreign relations partly a matter of internal government. The Levant was governed through local rulers bound to Egypt by oaths and tribute, and their correspondence reveals a diplomacy of gifts and obligations that continued alongside the campaigns.  Thutmose III’s campaigns against the Mitanni and their allies in northern Syria show that the rivalry was military as well as diplomatic, and the Egyptian army’s presence in the region made Egypt a power that other states had to negotiate with.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Egypt's relations with Nubia, Syria-Palestine and Mitanni were all important in this period, but they differed greatly in character. Nubia was a region to be controlled and exploited, Syria-Palestine was a zone of military contest and tribute, and Mitanni was a rival great power whose relations with Egypt moved from war to diplomacy. The judgement is that relations with Syria-Palestine and Mitanni shaped Egypt's wider position more than Nubia did, because they determined the balance of power in the north. Nubia's importance was real but more limited, since it provided gold and manpower rather than a strategic rival.

Nubia was the most directly controlled of the three regions. Egyptian kings from Thutmose I onwards campaigned in the south and established an administration that was headed by a viceroy of Kush. The region provided gold, which was essential to the Egyptian economy, and it supplied soldiers and labour. Control of Nubia gave the kings a secure southern frontier and a source of wealth that supported the cult and the court. Its significance was therefore economic and administrative, and it did not generate the sustained rivalry that the north did.

Syria-Palestine was the second arena and the most contested. The Egyptian kings sought to control the coastal cities and the routes to the Euphrates, and they used campaigns to secure tribute from local rulers. Thutmose III's victory at Megiddo was a decisive moment, because it allowed him to bring many cities under Egyptian control and to receive their tribute and their princes as hostages. The region was important both for its wealth and for its strategic position between Egypt and its northern rivals, and it made the Egyptian empire a major power in the Near East.

Mitanni was the most significant rival. Mitanni was a state on the upper Euphrates, and its control of northern Syria put it in direct competition with Egypt. The relations between the two powers included war, but they also became diplomatic over time. Thutmose IV is associated with a diplomatic marriage to a princess of Mitanni, which marked a shift from open conflict to an arrangement that stabilised the frontier. This change showed that Egypt was prepared to use marriage and alliance as well as force, and it made the relationship with Mitanni one of the most important of the period.

On balance, Egypt's relations with Syria-Palestine and Mitanni were more significant than those with Nubia, because they determined the stability of the northern frontier and the balance of power across the Near East. Nubia provided wealth and security, but the northern regions shaped the strategic choices that the kings made, and the shift from war to diplomacy with Mitanni was the most important change in the period. The judgement therefore rests on the way the Egyptian state balanced force and diplomacy in its relations with its rivals.

The judgement must also consider the impact of these relations on Egypt's internal stability. The campaigns in Syria-Palestine brought captives, tribute and goods that funded the temples and the court, and they gave the kings prestige that strengthened their authority at home. The viceroy of Kush and his administration ensured that the gold and labour of Nubia reached Thebes, and this supported the wider economy on which royal power depended. Relations with Mitanni, by contrast, were less a source of wealth than a source of risk, because a powerful rival on the Euphrates could threaten the northern provinces and the routes that Egypt relied upon. The diplomacy that developed later in the period reduced this risk, and it allowed the kings to focus their resources on the security of the region they already controlled. The sources therefore suggest that the north was significant for Egypt's political stability, while the south was significant for its economic strength. A judgement that weighs these two functions reaches a more balanced view than one that treats Nubia as a mere periphery. The strategic and economic weight of the three relationships, taken together, explains why Egypt pursued them with such persistence over the period, and why the shift from war to diplomacy was so important for the stability of the state.

It would lift further by weighing the economic value of Nubia more explicitly against the strategic value of the north.

sampleAnswers.answer: The ‘warrior pharaoh’ image was important for the New Kingdom monarchy, though its importance lay more in ideology than in the day-to-day conduct of war. The image justified the kings’ right to rule, explained the empire that Egypt held in Nubia and the Levant, and gave rulers a public role that could be displayed in temples. Its significance must be weighed against the fact that the image was carefully constructed, and that other aspects of kingship, especially religious ones, competed with it. The image mattered because royal legitimacy rested on maintaining order, or ma’at, against foreign enemies. The period began with the expulsion of the Hyksos, a narrative that made the king a liberator, and the kings who followed were shown as heirs of that victory. Scenes of the king smiting enemies, which became a standard subject on temple walls, presented the pharaoh as the guarantor of Egypt’s security. Such images were repeated across Karnak and other temples, so their message reached officials, priests and the wider population who could see them. The clearest expression came under Thutmose III, whose annals carved at Karnak describe his campaigns with a strong sense of personal command. His account of the battle of Megiddo, where he is said to have led the attack in person, shaped how later Egyptians remembered him. The image was important because it reinforced an empire that relied on tribute and on loyal vassal rulers in the Levant. Without some display of military success, the kings could not easily claim the tribute, the gold from Nubia or the loyalty of the local princes on which Egyptian power depended. The image was not the only or the dominant form of kingship. Hatshepsut, who ruled in the same period, presented herself as king in traditional forms, but her monuments at Deir el-Bahari emphasised divine birth, building and the expedition to Punt, and a warrior image was less prominent in her programme. Thutmose IV, whose claim to the throne rested on a dream recorded on a stela between the paws of the Great Sphinx at Giza, also emphasised divine favour. These cases show that rulers chose which aspects of kingship to display, and that the war image was one option among several. The image also shaped how officials understood their roles. A king shown leading his troops encouraged the loyalty of an army whose officers were rewarded by royal favour, so the image tied military service to the crown rather than to any single commander. This made the warrior image a practical tool of government as well as a claim about the king’s character. Its effect on the elite was therefore as important as its effect on the wider population. The importance of the image is best assessed by its effects. It helped legitimise rulers whose claims were not always strong, justified the cost of an empire and encouraged officials to see military service as honourable. But it was constructed for particular audiences, and historians must treat royal accounts of victories with caution because they stress royal valour while the army, the chariot corps and local administrators did much of the work. Overall, the warrior image was important for legitimacy and ideology, and its significance was greatest where it reinforced the monarchy’s control of the empire, but it was one element of a broader kingship rather than its defining feature.

sampleAnswers.answer: The warrior pharaoh image was important to the New Kingdom kings because it presented them as protectors of Egypt. Ahmose drove out the Hyksos, and scenes of kings defeating enemies on temple walls showed that the pharaoh could defend the country. This gave the monarchy legitimacy at a time when Egypt was building an empire in Nubia and the Levant. Thutmose III is the best example. His campaigns are recorded in annals at Karnak, and the battle of Megiddo is described as a major victory won by the king in person. These records helped the king show that he was a strong ruler, and they allowed officials and the public to see the empire as the result of royal success. The image therefore supported control of an empire that depended on tribute from vassal rulers. However, the image was not always the most important part of kingship. Hatshepsut, who ruled in the same period, did not stress war in her building programme and was more concerned with trade and religion. Thutmose IV used a dream to claim the throne, which shows that religious legitimacy could be just as important as military success. The image also had practical uses. Showing the king as a successful commander reassured officials that the throne could protect them, and it encouraged soldiers to see their service as a route to royal favour. These purposes gave the image a political value that the reality of each campaign could not fully match. The warrior image was important, but it was one part of how the kings presented themselves. It helped with legitimacy and control of the empire, though other features of kingship mattered as well.

sampleAnswers.answer: Ramesses II’s contribution to Egypt was considerable, though uneven, and it is best judged by separating what he achieved from how he chose to present it. He ruled for about sixty-six years, from around 1279 to 1213 BCE, during the 19th Dynasty of the New Kingdom, and his reign combined a lasting monumental legacy, a long period of foreign stability and a strong administration. His achievements were partly a matter of image, however, and the evidence for them is largely monumental and propagandistic, which makes it difficult to separate reality from display. The assessment must therefore weigh each area of contribution against the evidence that survives for it, and recognise the costs and problems that the reign also produced. His building programme was the most visible contribution. The temples at Abu Simbel, cut into the cliffs of Nubia, the Ramesseum at Thebes, his mortuary temple on the west bank, and additions at Karnak and Luxor displayed royal power to Egyptians and visitors and gave the monarchy a lasting presence in the landscape. The Great Temple at Abu Simbel, with its four colossal seated figures of the king, asserted his authority in the south, and these temples were later moved in the 1960s when the Aswan High Dam threatened to submerge them. He also founded Pi-Ramesses in the eastern Delta, a new royal residence close to the Levantine frontier, which reflected the growing importance of the north and of the Near East. Its position linked the administration of the country to the routes into Asia. These projects were expensive, and their value lay in display as much as in function, but they remain the reign’s clearest legacy. In foreign policy Ramesses preserved and reasserted Egypt’s position. His campaigns in Syria, including the battle of Kadesh in about his fifth year, kept key cities and vassal rulers under Egyptian influence, even though Kadesh was not a clear victory: the Hittite king Muwatalli II was not decisively defeated, and Ramesses withdrew without taking the city. The treaty with Hattusili III, a later Hittite king, secured peace for most of his reign, and copies of it survive in both Egyptian and Akkadian versions. In Nubia, a network of temples and a viceroy, the King’s Son of Kush, kept the gold-producing region under control and drew its wealth into the royal treasury. Nubian gold also helped to finance the building work that displayed the king’s power. The Egyptian presence in Syria depended on repeated campaigns and on fortresses along the coastal routes, which held the key roads through the Levant. These arrangements gave Egypt stability in its empire for decades. Ramesses also maintained the administration. His long reign produced a stable bureaucracy and a generation of officials, including viziers and treasury officers, who served his successors. His large family, however, brought problems: he had a great many children, and many of his older sons died before him, so the succession passed to an elderly son, Merenptah, which shows how much the system depended on the king’s personal authority. The strains of the reign were visible in the years after his death, when rival claimants contested the throne. His reign also shows the difficulty of measuring a king’s contribution by monuments alone. The reliefs of Kadesh and the great temples were designed to show a victorious and divinely supported king, and historians must read them as statements of ideology. The Kadesh inscriptions, carved on several temples, presented the battle as a personal triumph in which the king had acted alone against the enemy, a version the wider evidence does not fully support. The administrative records of the period give a fuller picture of how the state worked day to day. They suggest a functioning bureaucracy, but they also show the costs of maintaining a large building programme across the country, which is part of why his achievements look different when viewed from the state rather than from the temple. A qualification is needed here. The monuments were not only display: the great temples were centres of worship and administration, and royal projects employed large numbers of workers, craftsmen and officials, so the building programme had economic and social effects as well as symbolic ones. Yet the costs were real, and the succession problems that followed his death show how far the system relied on his own authority. Ramesses II made a major contribution to Egypt through a long period of stability, a monumental legacy and a durable peace with the Hittites. His achievements were partly a matter of image, and the Kadesh accounts exaggerate his personal role. He preserved the empire and the monarchy’s prestige but did not expand it significantly. His contribution is therefore best assessed as considerable: his building and diplomacy outlived him, although the system he left depended heavily on his own long rule.

sampleAnswers.answer: Ramesses II made a significant contribution to Egypt. He reigned for a very long time and built many temples, including Abu Simbel and the Ramesseum, which show his power. These buildings were meant to impress Egyptians and visitors. Abu Simbel is cut into rock in Nubia, and the Ramesseum was the temple where the king was remembered after his death, so the buildings did more than one job. In foreign policy he kept Egypt’s position in Syria and the Levant. He fought the Hittites at Kadesh and later made a treaty with them. This brought peace for much of his reign. The treaty is known from copies in two languages, which shows how seriously it was recorded. He also controlled Nubia, which was important for gold. Egyptian officials were sent there to run the region and collect what it produced. He also founded a new capital, Pi-Ramesses, in the Delta. This shows that he thought the north was important, and the city was close to the routes into Asia. Its buildings gave the court a setting for ceremony that matched the king’s wider claims to power. His sons helped run the country, although many of them died before him. The royal family was large, and some of his children were given important roles, but the succession was not always simple. His reign also had a long-term effect on how later Egyptians remembered the monarchy. The temples and statues he set up remained visible for centuries, and his name became a standard for royal achievement. This memory shaped later Ramesside kings, who tried to match his scale of building and display. Some of them reused parts of his monuments. Ramesses II was therefore an important king whose building and foreign policy helped Egypt. His reign was long and gave stability, but some of his achievements were about image rather than real change. Many of the monuments were meant to make the king look successful, and it is not always easy to tell what they did for the country itself.

His buildings were also visible to visitors and to later generations, which made them an important part of his legacy.
