sampleAnswers.answer: The treatment of subject peoples reveals that the Persian empire was a pragmatic and decentralised system, which combined toleration and the preservation of local elites with a readiness to use overwhelming force when revolt threatened the king's order. The empire was too large and diverse to be governed uniformly, and the kings relied on local cooperation as much as on direct control. The clearest statement of this policy is the Cyrus Cylinder, a Babylonian-style inscription of 539 BCE, in which Cyrus presents himself as a legitimate ruler who restored the cults of the Babylonian gods and allowed deported peoples to return to their homes. The text is propaganda, aimed at Babylonian audiences, but it reflects a real policy of accommodating local religion and elites, and the biblical account of Cyrus' decree permitting the Jews to rebuild the Temple is consistent with it. The empire's toleration of religious practice and local institutions was therefore a central element of its governance. Local rulers, priests and communities kept their customs, and taxation was often assessed through existing structures. The satrapy system organised the empire into provinces governed by satraps, who collected tribute, maintained garrisons and commanded local forces. The tribute lists carved on the Apadana at Persepolis show the subject peoples bringing goods and animals to the king, and this record suggests that the empire was held together by the regular extraction of wealth in exchange for protection and order. The royal road, which linked Susa with Sardis and the Aegean, facilitated communication and the movement of troops and officials, and it allowed the king to project authority across the empire. Yet toleration was never unconditional. Revolts threatened the empire repeatedly, and the response to them was severe. In 522 and 521 BCE Babylon revolted, and Darius I defeated the rebels, executed their leaders and displayed the outcome in the Behistun inscription, which shows the king trampling the rebel leader and describes the punishment of his followers. Egypt also revolted during the reigns of Darius and Xerxes, and the suppression of these revolts was accompanied by the reassertion of Persian control over its administration and its temples. The Persian kings used force to make an example of rebels, and the message was intended for the wider empire. The contrast between toleration and terror is therefore a central feature of Persian rule. The Behistun inscription is itself a key source for this relationship. It presents Darius as the restorer of order against rebellious usurpers, and it stresses that the rebellions were the work of liars and impostors. This framing is a royal construction, and historians must treat the account of the revolts with care, because the Persian sources present the rebels as enemies of the divinely ordered empire. Greek writers, notably Herodotus, provide a different perspective, describing the Persian empire as a system of tribute and obligation, but also as a power that treated Greek cities with contempt when they resisted. The biblical and Babylonian texts show the Persian kings as protectors of religion, while the Greek texts show a more hostile image, and historians must weigh each account against the others. The most accurate view of the Persian empire is therefore that it was a federation of diverse peoples held together by royal authority, local cooperation, tribute and the threat of force. The treatment of subject peoples reveals that the empire did not seek to impose a single culture or administration, and that its kings were willing to accommodate local elites in return for loyalty and wealth. At the same time, the frequency of revolts shows that loyalty could not be assumed, and that the empire's stability depended on the capacity to punish rebellion. The empire was therefore neither a centralised state nor a loose confederation, but a system in which toleration and coercion were balanced according to the threat at hand. The treatment of subject peoples thus reveals the pragmatic nature of Persian rule, its dependence on local cooperation and its reliance on the king's reputation for power.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 21–25 row: presents a perceptive judgement that Persian rule combined toleration with coercion, and integrates the Cyrus Cylinder, the Behistun inscription, the tribute reliefs and the Greek accounts. To go further, weigh more precisely how far the Behistun account can be trusted on the scale of the revolts.

Local rulers and communities kept their customs, and the satrapy system organised tribute and garrisons through provincial governors. The tribute reliefs on the Apadana show subject peoples bringing gifts to the king, and the royal road linked distant provinces to the centre. However, toleration had limits. Babylon revolted in 522 and 521 BCE, and Darius I suppressed the rebellion and displayed his victory in the Behistun inscription. sampleAnswers.answer:
Religious policies were not more significant than economic policies in the maintenance of the Persian empire, although they were closely linked. Economic policies, especially the system of tribute and taxation, provided the wealth that paid for the army and administration, and without this revenue the empire could not have been held together. Darius I organised the empire into satrapies that paid fixed tribute, and the royal roads and standard coinage allowed trade and payments to move across the empire. The tribute was the foundation of royal power, and the army that defended the empire was paid from it.

Religious policies were also important, because they helped to win the loyalty of subject peoples. Cyrus II’s conquest of Babylon was accompanied by the Cyrus Cylinder, which presented the king as the restorer of the gods’ cults, and Cyrus allowed exiled peoples, including the Jews, to return to their homelands and rebuild their temples. Darius I presented his rule as the will of Ahuramazda, and this religious claim helped to justify Persian authority. These policies reduced the risk of revolt and made Persian rule more acceptable to the elites of conquered cities. However, religious tolerance was not uniform, and the rebellions in Egypt and Babylon show that religious concessions did not always prevent resistance.

The comparison therefore depends on the purpose of the policies. Religious policy secured legitimacy, while economic policy provided the means of control. Each depended on the other, because the cults that the king supported required resources, and the economic system depended on the loyalty of local elites that religious policy helped to secure. Economic policy was more directly responsible for the maintenance of the empire, but religious tolerance was an essential instrument of stable rule.

Economic policy also depended on the stability that religious tolerance helped to maintain. Subject cities that were allowed to keep their temples and their local customs were more likely to pay tribute without resistance, and the elites who ran local administration were more willing to serve the king. Cyrus’ restoration of the cults in Babylon, and the support given to the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem, were both economic and religious measures, because they kept the local economies functioning and reduced the costs of control. The distinction between religious and economic policy is therefore harder to sustain than the question suggests.

The question can also be considered from the perspective of the Persian elites. The satraps and the local dynasties were rewarded with land, office and honours, and their loyalty was secured by a system of exchange that was economic and political at once. The gift of estates and privileges was as much an economic policy as a political one, and it shows how closely the management of resources and the maintenance of loyalty were connected. The distinction between religious and economic policy is therefore hard to sustain in practice.

Overall, economic policies were more significant than religious policies in the maintenance of the Persian empire, because they provided the revenue and the administrative structure on which the empire depended. Religious policies were a valuable complement that secured the acceptance of subject peoples, but they could not replace the material basis of Persian power.

sampleAnswers.answer: Darius I had a major impact on the administration of the Persian empire, because he created a system of provincial government, taxation and communication that gave the state a unity it had not previously possessed. The satrapy system was his most significant structural reform. He divided the empire into provinces, some twenty by Herodotus’ count, each governed by a satrap who collected tribute and maintained order. The satraps were answerable to the king, and their authority was balanced by military commanders and royal secretaries, which prevented any one official from gaining too much power. The reform was not wholly original, since Cyrus and Cambyses had established provincial rule, but Darius systematised it and extended it to new regions. His tribute system was also significant. Herodotus describes the assessment of tribute by province, and the Behistun inscription, which records Darius’ suppression of revolts, shows that the king regarded control of the provinces as the basis of his authority. Tax assessment linked the empire’s administration to its economy, and this allowed Darius to fund the royal court and the great building projects at Persepolis. Darius also created a standard coinage, including the gold daric and the silver siglos, which made payments and taxation easier across the empire. The Royal Road from Sardis to Susa, with its relay stations and royal messengers, linked the provinces to the centre and allowed the king to communicate with his officials quickly. Aramaic became the language of administration, which gave the empire a shared written language for its records. These reforms were significant because they created an administrative framework that lasted until Alexander’s conquest. The Behistun inscription is a royal text, and it presents Darius as a legitimate king who restored order, so it reflects his own claims. Its account of revolts and rebels is propaganda, which is designed to justify his rule. Herodotus provides a detailed account of the satrapies and tribute, but he was writing for a Greek audience and was interested in Persian customs and royal extravagance. Persepolis provides archaeological evidence of the court and the administration, including the Fortification Tablets, which record payments and rations in Elamite and show the working of the state, though they are not a full account. The administrative records, in Aramaic and Elamite, provide a more direct view of how the system worked, but they are fragmentary. Darius’ administration also depended on the regions and their traditions. The Persians did not impose a uniform culture; they allowed local elites to keep their law and language where this served the empire, and the Aramaic papyri from Elephantine show local administration functioning within the imperial framework. Persepolis itself was a ceremonial centre in which representatives of the subject peoples were shown bringing tribute, as the reliefs of the Apadana show, which reinforced the idea of a unified empire. This ceremonial dimension complemented the administrative system and gave the king a visual claim to universal rule. The administration also left a lasting imprint on the regions. The provinces were assessed for tribute according to their resources, and the Persian road and courier system carried royal orders to the satraps and returned reports to the centre. The Royal Road and its relay stations were the means by which the king could respond to revolts quickly. Darius’ achievement was to combine local autonomy with central control, and the system he created allowed the empire to function for more than two centuries. Taken together, Darius I’s impact on the administration of the empire was substantial. He systematised the satrapies, the tax system and the communications, and he gave the empire a monetary and administrative framework. His reforms were built on earlier foundations, but their scale and organisation made Darius the decisive figure in the administration of the Persian empire.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 21–25 row: a perceptive assessment of Darius’ administrative reforms, with the satrapies, taxation, coinage and the Royal Road, weighed against the earlier roots and the evidence from Behistun, Herodotus and Persepolis. The answer is complete for twenty-five marks.

Herodotus describes some twenty satrapies, each governed by a satrap who collected tribute. The Royal Road linked Sardis and Susa, allowing royal messengers to communicate quickly with the provinces. Aramaic became the language of administration, which gave the empire a shared written language. The Behistun inscription presents Darius’ suppression of revolts as legitimate, so it reflects his claims. Persepolis evidence shows the working of the state, but it is fragmentary. Darius built on earlier foundations, but his reforms gave the empire its administrative framework. The effectiveness of Darius’ system depended on the balance between local power and central control. Satraps governed their provinces with their own staffs and collected tribute, but the king’s secretaries and military commanders reported directly to the court. Tribute was often assessed in the goods and silver each province could supply, which tied the administration to the economic character of the regions. The Persepolis Fortification Tablets record payments of rations and goods, showing how the state distributed its wealth to workers and officials. The system was a network of accounts and commands rather than a single chain of authority, and this complexity is the strongest evidence of Darius’ administrative design.  The Behistun inscription also shows the king’s claim to restore order across the provinces, which confirms the importance of the satrapies to the royal authority.

sampleAnswers.answer: Issues of dynastic succession weakened Persia, but they were not the decisive cause of its collapse. Succession disputes repeatedly drained the empire’s resources and split its elite, and they made the Persian state more vulnerable when Alexander invaded in 334 BCE. The most damaging episode before the invasion was the civil war between Artaxerxes II and his younger brother Cyrus the Younger, which ended in 401 BCE with Cyrus’ death at the battle of Cunaxa. Cyrus had recruited a large Greek force, and Xenophon’s account of the Greek retreat shows how far Persian authority had been challenged. Later, the reign of Artaxerxes III was marked by the murder of rivals and relatives, and his successor Arses and his children were killed by the chamberlain Bagoas, who then placed Darius III on the throne. These killings created instability at the centre, weakened the loyalty of officials and allowed provincial governors to pursue independent policies. The Persian empire’s strength depended on the king’s authority over the satraps, and each succession crisis reduced that authority. In this sense, dynastic problems weakened the state and made it less able to resist external challenge. However, the collapse of the empire was caused by Alexander’s military success. Persia had survived earlier civil wars and rebellions, including the revolt of Cyrus the Younger, because its administrative system and its army could be mobilised quickly. The defeats at the Granicus in 334 BCE, at Issus in 333 BCE and at Gaugamela in 331 BCE were decisive because Darius III lost the armies and the battles that held the empire together, and the capture of Babylon, Susa and Persepolis followed. These defeats show that the empire could not recover from the loss of its main army, even though its structure remained. The sources for succession disputes are mainly Greek. Herodotus describes the succession to Darius I and the Persian court, but his account is shaped by his interest in Greek and Persian contrasts. Xenophon, who fought for Cyrus, presents the civil war as the story of Greek courage and Persian weakness, so his account is partial. Diodorus and Arrian, writing much later, rely on earlier histories and portray the Persian court as corrupt. The Persian sources, such as the royal inscriptions, rarely describe the murders and disputes, which were politically sensitive, so the evidence for succession is largely external. Archaeology at Persepolis and Susa shows the wealth and organisation of the empire, but it does not reveal the internal politics of the court. The internal dimension of succession can be tested against the record of the Achaemenid kings. Darius I came to power after a sequence of revolts and the murder of Bardiya, and he had to suppress rebellion across the empire before his position was secure. The Behistun inscription records these revolts and shows how the dynasty justified its claims through royal lineage. The revolts in Egypt in the fourth century show that rebellions remained a constant threat. Each succession crisis therefore added to the pressure on a state that relied on the king’s personal authority to manage its distant provinces. The succession problems also weakened the cohesion of the Persian army. Royal princes and provincial governors commanded forces that could be turned against the king, and the reliance on Greek mercenaries, such as those who fought for Cyrus the Younger, showed that the empire had to hire foreign troops to contest royal claims. Once Alexander had defeated the main Persian armies, the rival factions at court could not agree on a common defence, and the murders that had brought Darius III to power left his authority fragile. The collapse was thus accelerated by the same divisions that had weakened the state earlier. Taken together, succession disputes weakened Persia by dividing its elite and exhausting its resources, but the collapse of the Persian Empire was caused by Alexander’s conquest, which destroyed the armies and the central authority that holds the empire together. Dynastic weakness made Persia vulnerable, but the decisive reasons for its collapse lie in the military failure against Alexander.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 21–25 row: a perceptive argument that dynastic weakness made Persia vulnerable but Alexander’s victories were decisive, supported by the Cyrus the Younger and Bagoas episodes and tested against the Greek sources. The answer is complete for twenty-five marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Succession disputes weakened Persia, because rivalries such as the revolt of Cyrus the Younger drained resources and divided the elite. The murders of Arses and his children by Bagoas brought Darius III to the throne, and the instability at the centre encouraged satraps to act independently. However, the collapse of the empire was caused mainly by Alexander’s victories at the Granicus, Issus and Gaugamela, which destroyed the armies that held the empire together. The Greek sources, including Xenophon and Diodorus, are partial in their portrayal of the Persian court. Succession problems made Persia vulnerable, but Alexander’s conquest was the decisive cause of its collapse. The Greek evidence and the Persian record can be compared on this point. The Behistun inscription shows that Darius had to fight many revolts in the first years of his reign, which suggests that the instability after Cambyses’ death was widespread. Later succession disputes were less frequent but more destructive when they occurred, since rival princes could draw on satraps and foreign mercenaries. Cyrus the Younger’s use of Greek hoplites in 401 BCE shows that the empire’s military strength could be turned against itself, and the murders of the late fourth century show a court in which the king’s survival depended on powerful eunuchs and officials such as Bagoas.  The Achaemenid court was also a place where royal women and eunuchs played a part in succession disputes, which made the dynasty vulnerable to intrigue.

The Macedonian invasion was successful mainly because of Macedonian military strength and Persian failures of policy, rather than a general decline of the Persian empire. George Cawkwell rejects long-drawn moral decline as an explanation, and asks instead whether the empire could have checked the Macedonian advance and whether there were failures of policy. The evidence suggests that the failures of policy were decisive. The Persian empire in 334 BCE was still wealthy and large, and its problems lay in the choices of its rulers and commanders. The judgement is that the idea of decline explains the Persian weakness in part, but that the success of Alexander depended on decisions made in the battles.

The notion of decline has to be defined. The Persian empire had internal problems in the years before Alexander's invasion. Artaxerxes III was murdered in 338 BCE, and the succession of Darius III in 336 BCE followed a period of court intrigue. Egypt had rebelled in the previous decades and the empire had fought a long struggle to recover it. These were signs of instability, but they do not show that the state had lost its capacity to field large armies or to raise revenue. The empire remained the largest state in the known world, and this is the first point against a simple decline argument.

The military record shows that Persian policy was the decisive weakness. At the Granicus in 334 BCE, the Persian satraps fought in a disorganised manner and lost their cavalry and their Greek mercenaries, and the battle was decided by the Macedonian heavy cavalry. Persian commanders had advised a scorched-earth strategy that would have denied Alexander supplies, but this advice was not followed. At Issus in 333 BCE, Darius III chose to fight in terrain that favoured the Macedonians and fled the field, which left his army to be destroyed. These are failures of policy and command, not signs of an empire that had lost its strength.

Gaugamela in 331 BCE was the decisive battle. Darius III again had a large army, but he chose a flat plain that suited his chariots and his numerical advantage, and he again fled. The Persian army was defeated, and Darius was murdered by his own satrap in 330 BCE. The death of the king and the flight of the court show that the leadership of the empire had broken down. The question is whether this breakdown came from a long decline or from the immediate choices of a king who could not hold his army together under pressure.

The Macedonian forces also deserve credit. Alexander's army was well trained and experienced, and the Macedonian phalanx and cavalry, developed under Philip II, were more cohesive than the Persian levies. Alexander's tactics, including the cavalry charge against the centre at Gaugamela, were effective. These advantages were not created by Persian decline, and they would have been important even if the Persian empire had been strong. The Macedonian victories therefore reflect Alexander's skill as much as Persian weakness.

On balance, the Macedonian invasion was successful because of Persian failures of policy and command, which Cawkwell identifies as the key question, and because of the strength of the Macedonian army. A general decline of the Persian empire is not sufficient to explain the outcome, since the state retained its wealth and size. The judgement is that Persian decline was a contributing factor, but the decisive causes were the choices made by Darius III in the battles and the military superiority of the invader.

Cawkwell's question about whether the empire could have checked the Macedonian advance is central. The Persian state had resources, a large army and a navy in the Aegean, and it could have used these to defend the coast or to deny Alexander supplies, as the scorched-earth advice shows. The failure to do so was a failure of policy and command. The empire did not collapse before Alexander arrived; it was defeated by the choices made in the crucial years between 334 and 331 BCE.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The unification of the Warring States was of decisive importance to the success of the Qin, because it gave the state a single system of government, a large and disciplined army and the resources of the conquered states. The Qin's reforms, especially those associated with Shang Yang, prepared the state for conquest, and unification was the outcome of that preparation. The judgement is that unification was the most important reason for Qin's success, but that it was only durable because the Qin built the institutions that allowed the empire to be governed, and these institutions were inherited by the Han.

The Qin state's reforms made unification possible. Shang Yang's reforms in the fourth century BCE reorganised land and taxation, built a system of rewards for military service and created a legal framework based on strict rules and collective responsibility. These changes gave Qin a stronger economic base and a more effective army than its rivals. The legalist ideas that supported the reforms emphasised the power of the state and the obedience of the people, and they provided the justification for a state organised for war and control.

Unification itself was the decisive achievement. The conquest of the six rival states between 230 and 221 BCE gave the Qin control of the whole of the Chinese world as it then existed. The unification ended a long period of conflict and created a single empire under one ruler. This was a turning point in the history of the region, and it shows that the Qin's ability to conquer its rivals was the most important reason for its success.

The importance of unification also lay in the standardisation that followed. The Qin standardised weights, measures, currency and the writing system, and built roads and a common administrative structure across the empire. These measures created a unity that was more than military, and they allowed the central government to communicate and to collect taxes across a vast territory. Without these institutions, the conquest would have been difficult to hold, and the Qin would have remained a conqueror rather than a state.

However, the Qin's collapse in 206 BCE shows that unification alone was not enough. The empire was governed harshly, and its legalist policies provoked resistance. Yet the Han dynasty that replaced the Qin, founded by Liu Bang, inherited the centralised administration and much of the structure that unification had created. In this sense, the importance of unification extended far beyond the Qin. On balance, unification was the most important factor in Qin's success and the foundation of the imperial state that followed it, even though the Qin dynasty itself was short-lived.

The importance of unification must also be judged by its costs. The Qin state required heavy labour and taxation to sustain its campaigns and its projects, and its legalist system punished offences with severity that many people found intolerable. Historians disagree about how much of this harshness was a product of the Qin's principles and how much was a response to the difficulty of ruling a newly conquered population. The sources, many of them written by later scholars who were hostile to the Qin, emphasise the brutality of the regime. Even so, the evidence suggests that the Qin's institutions were effective, and that the speed of their collapse owed more to the failure of the succession and the revolts that followed the First Emperor's death than to the institutions themselves. A reasoned judgement must therefore weigh the efficiency of the state against its costs, and conclude that unification was the decisive reason for Qin's success while acknowledging that the regime's methods made its survival precarious.

It would lift further by assessing the legalist harshness more precisely against the durability of the institutions.

sampleAnswers.answer: The establishment of Qin power transformed China in this period by replacing the aristocratic and competitive politics of the Warring States with a centralised state governed by appointed officials. The Qin rise was a process of reform and conquest rather than a single event. Under Shang Yang, whose reforms were introduced in the middle of the fourth century BCE, Qin reorganised land registration, rewarded military merit with rank rather than birth, and introduced strict penal laws. These changes produced a state that could mobilise large armies and resources more effectively than its rivals. The reforms were based on Legalist principles, which held that clear laws, rewards and punishments were the best means of ordering society, and they redirected the aristocracy's power toward the ruler. The result was a state whose military and administrative capacity exceeded that of the other Warring States. Qin power was also built through conquest. In the decades after 247 BCE, when Ying Zheng became king of Qin, the state defeated its rivals one by one, first Han, then Zhao, Wei, Chu, Yan and finally Qi, which it conquered in 221 BCE. The conquests destroyed the independent kingdoms that had competed for centuries, and they brought a vast population and territory under a single government. The military successes depended on the reforms that had prepared the state for war, and on the ability to sustain long campaigns and to supply armies over great distances. The political transformation that followed the conquests was equally important. The unified state abolished the hereditary rule of the former kingdoms and divided the empire into commanderies and counties administered by officials appointed by the centre. This system replaced the feudal and quasi-feudal arrangements of the Warring States and gave the emperor direct control over the appointment, transfer and dismissal of local officials. The standardisation of weights, measures, script and axle widths followed, and these reforms made communication, taxation and the movement of goods more uniform across the empire. They also made the state more capable of mobilising labour for public works, including roads, canals and the frontier walls that were later linked into a northern barrier. Yet the transformation was not simply beneficial. The Qin state relied on severe laws and punishments, and its demands for labour and military service were heavy. Resentment built among the conquered peoples, and among the population that bore the costs of the great projects. The burning of certain books in 213 BCE and the suppression of rival doctrines show a regime that sought to control ideas as well as territory, and this contributed to the instability that followed. The collapse of the dynasty within four years of the First Emperor's death in 210 BCE shows that the Qin system was more effective at conquest and administration than at securing consent. The evidence for these developments is uneven. The reforms of Shang Yang are known in part from later texts, and the Qin achievements are largely recorded by Sima Qian, who wrote under the Han and had reasons to condemn the Qin. The archaeological evidence, including the administrative bamboo slips found in Qin tombs, confirms the importance of legal and administrative documents, but it does not reveal the experience of ordinary people. The historian must therefore use the administrative sources to confirm the structure of the Qin state while treating the moral judgements in the literary sources with caution. The most accurate judgement is that the establishment of Qin power transformed China by creating the institutions of a centralised empire, and that these institutions outlasted the dynasty that created them. The Han dynasty retained much of the administrative system, which shows the depth of the change. The transformation was nonetheless achieved at a high human cost, and its durability depended on the lessons later rulers drew from its failure. Qin power therefore changed China fundamentally, but the change was shaped as much by the methods of its rulers as by the scale of their conquests.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 21–25 row: presents a perceptive judgement that Qin power transformed China structurally at a heavy human cost, and integrates the Shang Yang reforms, the conquests, the commandery system and the administrative slips. To go further, test the claim that the Han retained the system against the evidence for Han revisions.

sampleAnswers.answer: Legal reforms were more significant than cultural reforms for the Qin dynasty during its short life, because the legal system made the state possible and the rulers’ control depended on it. Cultural reforms had longer-lasting effects, especially the standardisation of script, which outlasted the dynasty. The question therefore depends on whether significance is measured by the Qin’s own survival or by its legacy. On the first measure legal reforms were clearly more important, while on the second cultural reforms were more enduring. The legal reforms built on the reforms of Shang Yang in the state of Qin in the fourth century BCE. Qin law, enforced through a hierarchy of officials, collective responsibility among households and harsh penalties, made it possible to assess taxes, raise labour and conscript soldiers across a unified territory. The large public works of the dynasty, including the Great Wall and the palace and tomb complexes, depended on these powers. Legal texts found in tombs, such as the bamboo slips from Shuihudi, show how detailed the administration was, and the law gave the emperor a system for controlling officials. The cultural reforms were broader in intent. The first emperor standardised the writing system, adopting a small seal script for official use, and introduced common standards for weights and measures, the width of carriage axles and the coinage. These measures made administration and trade across the empire easier. The reforms also had a darker side: the burning of books and the burial of scholars in 213 and 212 BCE, recorded in the Shiji, aimed at removing rival traditions and centralising ideas. Such cultural policies showed that the state intended to shape not only conduct but also thought. The durability of these reforms is difficult to separate from the fall of the dynasty. The legal system’s severity contributed to unrest, and the rebellion of Chen Sheng in 209 BCE grew from conscription and forced labour that the legal system imposed. The Qin collapsed in 206 BCE, and its legal structure was partly moderated under the early Han, which kept an administrative framework and a degree of legalism but reduced the harshest penalties. The standardised script, by contrast, survived the collapse and remained a basis of Chinese unity, so the cultural reforms outlasted the dynasty that created them. The two kinds of reform also differed in their reach. The legal system applied to officials and households across the state, and its enforcement shaped daily life through taxes, labour and punishment. The cultural measures reached a smaller and more literate audience at first, but over time the script and standard weights and measures affected commerce and administration across the empire. This difference in reach is part of why the legal reforms shaped the dynasty’s fate while the cultural reforms shaped its legacy. Legal reforms were more significant for the Qin dynasty itself, because they gave the state the power to unify, to fight wars and to build, and their harshness is part of the reason the dynasty fell quickly. Cultural reforms had a greater and longer legacy, because the standard script and standard measures outlived the Qin. The Qin’s significance for the later Chinese state therefore rests largely on its cultural unification, while its significance as a political system depended on the legal foundations. To the extent that the question asks about the dynasty’s own period, legal reforms were the more significant.

sampleAnswers.answer: The legal reforms and the cultural reforms were both important to the Qin dynasty. The legal reforms came from Shang Yang’s earlier changes in the state of Qin, and they gave the government control over taxes, labour and soldiers. Without them the Qin could not have built the walls and palaces that the dynasty needed. The cultural reforms standardised things across the empire. The script was made uniform, and weights, measures and coins were also standardised. These changes made administration easier and helped trade. The burning of books in 213 BCE shows the government also wanted to control ideas. The Qin did not last long. The legal system was harsh, people rebelled against conscription and forced labour, and the dynasty fell in 206 BCE. The Han dynasty kept some of the Qin system but changed the harsh punishments. The legal reforms also had a clear purpose in the state’s competition with rival kingdoms. Strict law and collective responsibility made it easier to mobilise resources in war, and Qin used these powers to defeat its rivals in the Warring States period. The cultural reforms were less about winning wars than about holding the empire together afterwards. The standardised script lasted longer than the Qin dynasty. This suggests that the cultural reforms were more important in the long run. However, the legal reforms were important for the Qin itself, because they made the state work while it lasted.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Li Si was highly important to the success of the Qin, but his importance lay mainly in the institutions that held the empire together rather than in the conquests that created it. Paul Goldin argues that the imperial institutions of later China were indebted to Li Si's model of centralised bureaucracy, and this claim is strong. The Qin's military success came from the king, the generals and the economic resources of the state, while Li Si's contribution was the administrative system that turned conquered territory into an empire. On balance, Li Si was the architect of the Qin state's institutions, and his importance is greatest in the years after unification.

The conquests of the Warring States period were the work of the king and his generals, such as Meng Tian, who led the armies in the north. The Qin state had been prepared for these wars by earlier reforms and by its resources, and the king made the decisions to attack the other states. Li Si was a counsellor who supported the policy of unification, and the Shiji shows him advising the king on the strategies that would weaken the rival states. This was an important role, but it was one of advice rather than command, so his influence on the conquests was indirect.

After unification, Li Si's importance was much greater. He is credited with the standardisation of the script, which the Shiji and later sources describe as part of the reforms that followed 221 BCE. The standardisation of weights, measures and axle widths was part of the same administrative program, and these measures allowed the central government to communicate, tax and move goods across the empire. The system of commanderies and counties, which placed officials under the control of the capital, reflected the centralised model that Goldin describes. These institutions made it possible to govern a vast territory with a relatively small administration.

Li Si's support for the harsh policies of the state also had a cost. The proposal to burn books in 213 BCE, which the Shiji records, was part of a campaign to suppress the rival doctrines of the scholars and to make the legal system the only authority. The policy reflected the legalist philosophy that Li Si championed, and it made the state more feared than respected. The Shiji presents Li Si as a traitor and opportunist, and later writers repeated this judgement, so the sources themselves are hostile. A historian must therefore treat the portrait with caution, while recognising that the policies were real.

The limits of Li Si's influence are shown by the succession crisis after the death of the First Emperor in 210 BCE. Li Si joined the eunuch Zhao Gao in a conspiracy to place the younger son Huhai on the throne, and the Shiji records that he was later executed in 208 BCE. The crisis shows that Li Si was a powerful minister, but his power depended on the emperor and on court politics. The collapse of the Qin in the following years shows that the institutions he built were strong, but that the dynasty's stability depended on the ruler.

On balance, Li Si was crucial to the success of the Qin as the architect of its administrative state, which allowed the conquests to be turned into a lasting empire. His importance was greater in governing than in conquering, and his influence was limited by the power of the king and the intrigues of the court. The judgement is that Li Si was very important, but that the success of the Qin rested on a combination of the king's leadership, the army and the institutions that Li Si helped to design.

Li Si's role also shows the costs of the system he helped to build. The Shiji records that the centralised administration depended on the penalties of the law, and the harshness of the system contributed to the discontent that followed the First Emperor's death. The rebellions of 209 BCE, which began among conscripted labourers, show how the state's demands could turn against it. Li Si cannot be blamed for every cost, but his institutions were the framework within which these demands were made, and his importance cannot be separated from the cost of the empire he built.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Problems of succession were a major cause of the fall of the Qin, but they worked together with the harshness of the regime and the burdens of its policies. When Qin Shi Huangdi died in 210 BCE, his chancellor Li Si and the eunuch Zhao Gao concealed the death and forged an edict that placed the younger son Huhai on the throne in place of the eldest son Fusu, who was forced to take his own life. The illegitimacy of the new emperor weakened the authority of the court, and the regime lost the legitimacy that the first emperor had built through conquest. The disputed succession therefore opened the way for opposition that had been building for years.

However, the succession crisis was not the only cause. The Qin had imposed heavy labour service on the population to build the Great Wall, the palaces and the mausoleum, and its legal system was harsh, with severe penalties for minor offences. The unification of China had required enormous military and economic effort, and by the end of the first emperor’s reign many people were exhausted. The rebellion of Chen Sheng and Wu Guang in 209 BCE was a response to these burdens, and the revolt spread quickly across the old states. Discontent with the regime was therefore already deep, and the succession crisis gave it a focus.

The succession crisis also shaped the form of the collapse. Zhao Gao’s power at court created a struggle between factions, and Huhai was forced to take his own life in 207 BCE. The Qin court could not organise an effective response to the rebels, and regional leaders, such as Liu Bang and Xiang Yu, were able to take advantage of the disorder. The fall of the dynasty came within four years of the first emperor’s death, and this speed shows how fragile the system had become. The succession was a trigger for collapse, but the scale of the revolt reflected the weight of earlier grievances.

The court politics that followed the succession crisis also made the dynasty more fragile. Zhao Gao controlled access to the emperor and used his position to remove those who opposed him, and his struggle with the court officials left the administration divided at the moment when the rebel armies were gathering. The Qin had built a centralised state, but this state depended on the loyalty of its officials, and the uncertainty over the succession removed that loyalty. The collapse was therefore as much a failure of government as a military defeat.

The judgement can be tested by the nature of the sources. The main account of the fall of the Qin comes from Sima Qian, who wrote a century later under the Han, and his narrative stresses the moral failings of the Qin court and of its officials. This interpretation gives weight to the succession and to the cruelty of Zhao Gao, and it may underplay the economic and social causes that the records only partly show. A historian must therefore weigh the moral narrative against the evidence of the labour burdens and the uprisings, and this makes the question of the succession only one part of a larger picture.

Overall, problems of succession were a major reason for the fall of the Qin, because they destroyed the legitimacy of the court at the moment when the empire faced revolt. However, they were most significant as a catalyst for existing causes, such as the burdens of labour and the harshness of the laws. The fall was produced by the combination of a weak succession and a regime that had exhausted its people.

sampleAnswers.answer: Gaozu contributed decisively to the development of the Han Empire, because he won the civil war that followed the fall of the Qin, established a new dynasty and set the political framework within which the empire operated. However, his contribution was foundational rather than complete. The institutions that defined the Han in its mature form were refined by later emperors, including Jingdi, and his personal achievement must be measured against the compromises he made and the problems he left for his successors. Liu Bang, later known as Gaozu, rose from humble origins in the state of Pei to become a local official and then a rebel leader in the chaos that followed the death of the Qin ruler and the collapse of the dynasty in 206 BCE. The struggle against Xiang Yu, the leader of the rival Chu forces, was the decisive contest. Gaozu's military and political skill, and his ability to win the support of commanders and local leaders, allowed him to defeat Xiang Yu, who died in 202 BCE, and to proclaim the Han dynasty. This victory was his most significant contribution, because it ended a period of division and created a new imperial government. The political framework he established was a compromise. Gaozu granted large territories to kings, many of them loyal generals and members of his own family, and this created a system of feudal kingdoms alongside commanderies governed directly by the court. The compromise was pragmatic: it secured the loyalty of his commanders and reduced the immediate risk of rebellion. Yet it also created a source of instability, because the kings had their own power bases and eventually challenged the centre. Gaozu's policies towards the Xiongnu, the nomadic confederation of the northern steppe, were a further example of pragmatism. The treaty of heqin, agreed in 198 BCE, provided for a royal marriage alliance and for regular payments of goods, in exchange for peace on the frontier. This policy was a response to the military weakness of the new dynasty, and it shows that Gaozu was willing to accept a humiliating arrangement in order to secure the empire. The later Han used the treaty as the basis of a more assertive policy, and the settlement of the northern frontier was a continuing question for his successors. Gaozu also drew on a range of advisers, and his government mixed Legalist administration with a growing respect for Confucian ideas. The Han did not reject the Qin system, but it made it more flexible and less harsh, and Gaozu's reputation for leniency was part of his political appeal. The evidence for his reign comes largely from Sima Qian, who wrote a biography of Gaozu in the Historical Records and was himself a court official under the Han. This source presents Gaozu in a favourable light, and historians must consider its bias. The later reigns of Huidi and the empress dowager Lü show that the power of the court could be captured by factions after Gaozu's death, and this exposed the weaknesses of his settlement. Jingdi, who reigned from 157 to 141 BCE, faced the problem of the feudal kingdoms directly. The rebellion of the Seven States in 154 BCE, which was crushed, showed the danger of the kingdoms and encouraged the court to reduce their power. This reform was the work of Jingdi and his advisers, and it shows that the Han structure was reshaped by later rulers. Gaozu's contribution must therefore be weighed against the institutions that grew from his foundations. The Han Empire lasted for four centuries, and its longevity owed much to the stable framework he created, but the balance between centre and kingdoms was a problem that his successors had to solve. The most accurate judgement is that Gaozu contributed decisively to the Han by winning power and establishing the core framework of the empire, but that the mature Han institutions were the product of later reforms. His contribution was therefore essential but incomplete, and its lasting value depended on the work of those who came after him.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 21–25 row: presents a perceptive judgement that Gaozu's foundation was decisive but incomplete, and integrates the defeat of Xiang Yu, the feudal kingdoms, the heqin treaty and the reforms of Jingdi. To go further, test the claim that the Han continued Qin institutions against the evidence for Gaozu's Confucian sympathies.

Liu Bang rose from humble origins to defeat Xiang Yu, the leader of the Chu forces, who died in 202 BCE. His victory ended the division of the period and created a new imperial government. His political framework was a compromise: he granted territories to kings, including loyal generals and members of his family, alongside commanderies governed by the court. This secured the loyalty of his commanders but created kingdoms that later challenged the centre. His treaty with the Xiongnu, agreed in 198 BCE, provided a marriage alliance and payments in exchange for peace, which shows a pragmatic willingness to accept an uncomfortable settlement. Gaozu's government mixed Legalist administration with growing respect for Confucian ideas, and it made the Qin system more flexible. However, the feudal kingdoms remained a problem after his death, and Jingdi was required to reduce their power after the rebellion of 154 BCE. Overall, Gaozu laid the foundation of the Han Empire, but its mature institutions were shaped by later reforms. The settlement's problems, especially the kingdoms, shaped the politics of the following generation. Historians therefore weigh his achievement not only by what he won but by the questions he left unresolved for his successors. Jingdi's reforms confirmed that the kingdoms had to be curbed if the court was to hold authority, and later rulers, including Wudi, extended central control further.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Emperor Wendi made a substantial contribution to the establishment of the Han dynasty, though his achievement lay more in consolidating a fragile regime than in founding it. Gaozu had founded the dynasty after the fall of the Qin, and Wendi came to power after the downfall of the Lü clan, which had threatened the dynasty's stability. His reforms in taxation, agriculture and punishment, together with his management of the Xiongnu, gave the dynasty a legitimacy and a stability that it had not yet possessed. The judgement is that Wendi's contribution was decisive for the survival of the dynasty, even though its foundations had been laid by Gaozu and its later expansion came under Wu Di.

Wendi's accession followed a crisis. The Lü clan had attempted to seize power after the death of Empress Lü, and its defeat left the throne in doubt. Wendi was a member of the imperial family who was chosen by the officials who had removed the Lü, and this gave him a fragile legitimacy that he needed to strengthen. His early policies were directed at securing the loyalty of the officials and the people, and the sources show him as a cautious ruler who was aware of the dangers of overreach. This context frames the rest of his contribution, because it explains why he chose moderation rather than bold action.

His agricultural and fiscal policies were central to his achievement. Wendi reduced the land tax and later abolished it for a period, which relieved the burden on peasant farmers. He also encouraged agriculture through ritual ploughing and attention to the land. These measures strengthened the rural economy on which the state depended for tax and labour, and they reduced the risk of unrest. A dynasty that had emerged from civil war needed the support of the peasantry, and Wendi's policies provided it.

His legal and military policies also mattered. Wendi reduced the severity of punishments, including the abolition of some mutilating penalties, which softened the image of the Han state. His management of the Xiongnu relied on marriage alliances and payments of goods, which kept the northern frontier relatively quiet. This policy was a pragmatic response to a powerful nomadic confederation that the Han could not yet defeat, and it allowed the dynasty to concentrate on consolidation at home.

On balance, Wendi's contribution was real and important. He stabilised a dynasty that had emerged from crisis, and he built the economic and political foundations that allowed his successors to expand. His caution limited his ambitions, but it gave the Han the time it needed to become a secure state. Gaozu established the dynasty, but Wendi made it durable, and this is the sense in which his contribution to the establishment of the Han was decisive.

The judgement must also consider Wendi's relationship with the policies of his successor, Jingdi. Jingdi continued the moderate course of his father, and the stability of the early Han state owed much to the continuity between them. The reduction of the land tax, the caution in foreign affairs and the attention to agriculture formed a pattern that Jingdi did not disrupt, and this pattern gave the state the resources and the stability needed for the later expansion under Wu Di. Wendi's own contribution was therefore part of a longer development in which the early Han rulers learned to rebuild the state after the Qin collapse. The sources record a government that valued moderation and the welfare of the peasant population, and these values were built into the institutions of the dynasty. A reasoned evaluation sees Wendi as a consolidator whose policies gave the dynasty the time and resources it needed to establish itself, and whose successors built on his foundations.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Confucianism was highly significant in the government of China during the Qin and Han periods, but its importance grew over time. The Qin dynasty rejected Confucian scholarship and ruled through Legalist principles of law, punishment and reward. The Han dynasty, after an early period in which Legalist and Daoist ideas were influential, adopted Confucianism as the moral basis of government under Emperor Wu. The ideas of Confucius were used to train officials, to justify the authority of the emperor and to define the duties of the family and the state. Its significance lay in its use as a framework for government rather than in a simple adoption of the teachings of the sage.

The Qin rejection of Confucianism was the clearest contrast. The Qin ruler Shihuangdi adopted Legalism as the basis of government, and the Shiji records the burning of books and the burying of scholars in 213 and 212 BCE. These events show that the Qin regarded Confucian learning as a threat to the unity of the state, and that its rulers preferred law and force. The Qin’s harsh rule and rapid collapse made Confucian scholars critical of Legalism, and this criticism shaped how the Han later understood the dynasty.

The early Han rulers did not immediately adopt Confucianism. Their government relied on a mixture of Legalist administration, Daoist ideas of restraint and the practical needs of a new empire. Confucian scholars were consulted, but they did not dominate the court, and the early emperors were cautious about reforms that would reduce their own power. This shows that Confucian ideas were not automatically accepted by the new dynasty, and that their adoption was the result of a deliberate choice.

The decisive shift came under Emperor Wu, who reigned from 141 to 87 BCE. Dong Zhongshu, a Confucian scholar, argued that the emperor’s authority rested on moral virtue and on the cosmic order, and that the government should be guided by the classics. The emperor accepted these arguments in part, and he founded an Imperial Academy in 124 BCE, where students studied the classics and prepared for official service. This institution linked Confucian learning to the recruitment of officials, which gave the ideas a lasting place in government.

The Five Classics became the core of the examination of officials and the moral education of the elite. Officials were expected to know the texts, and the classics provided the language in which they justified their decisions. Filial piety, the duty of respect for parents and superiors, was used as a model for loyalty to the emperor. Recommendation of candidates for office often emphasised their filial conduct, which made the family a model for the state. Confucian values therefore became part of the everyday practice of government.

Confucianism was not the only element of Han government, however. Legalist laws, punishments and administrative methods continued to be used, and the Han penal code was in many respects a continuation of the Qin system. The emperors combined moral language with strict law, so the Confucian ideal of benevolent rule coexisted with the practical use of force. This combination shows that Confucianism was significant as a framework of legitimacy rather than as a complete system of government.

The evidence for this significance comes from the Han histories, especially the Shiji and the Hanshu, which present Confucian government as the ideal. These texts were written by scholars who supported the Confucian cause, and their accounts may therefore exaggerate its influence. The Imperial Academy and the role of the classics in official training are, however, confirmed by the institutions and practices that followed.

Overall, Confucianism was significant in the government of China because it provided the moral language, the training of officials and the justification of imperial authority during the Han. Its importance was greatest from the reign of Emperor Wu onward, and it was combined with Legalist methods rather than replacing them. The Qin’s rejection of Confucian learning shows what its adoption meant, and the Han’s use of the classics made it a lasting part of Chinese government.

sampleAnswers.answer: The empress dowagers made real contributions to the Han dynasty, though their influence varied greatly and was often judged harshly by male historians. Their most important contribution was to maintain continuity at court during periods when emperors were young or weak, but some used their position to advance their own families. The contributions were therefore mixed, and the judgement depends on whether stability or the interests of a family are given priority. The most powerful was Empress Lü, widow of the founder Gaozu. After her son Emperor Hui died in 188 BCE, she ruled as regent for the young emperors who followed until her death in 180 BCE. She appointed members of her own family to high posts and attempted to secure the Lü clan’s position, a policy that the Shiji, in its annals of Empress Lü, portrays as dangerous for the Liu house. Her regency preserved the court’s stability and kept the structures of the new dynasty in place, but after her death the Lü were overthrown by officials and Liu relatives, which suggests that her policy had made enemies. Empress Dou, consort of Emperor Wen and mother of Emperor Jing, was influential during the reigns of her husband and son, and into the reign of Emperor Wu. Her preference for Huang-Lao thought, which favoured quietist government, is recorded in later sources, and she is said to have opposed Confucian-minded officials who wanted to reform the court. Her influence blocked some of the reforms that Wu’s advisers proposed in the 130s BCE, but her death in 135 BCE removed the obstacle and allowed the emperor to pursue more active policies, including the promotion of Confucian scholars. Her contribution was a conservative one: she protected existing policies while delaying change. The contributions of the empress dowagers can be evaluated in two ways. Stability was the most important: Empress Lü kept a dynasty with young rulers on its throne, and Empress Dou prevented sudden changes during a period when the empire was still consolidating. Against this, both women used their positions to shape appointments and policy, and the historians who recorded their careers, writing within a male and Confucian tradition, portrayed them as threats to legitimate rule. Their reputations therefore say as much about later perspectives on women’s power as about their actual decisions. The empress dowagers’ influence also shows the limits of imperial authority. The dynasty depended on a small circle of relatives and officials, and when an emperor was young or weak the court needed someone to hold it together. The women who filled this role were those closest to the throne, but their authority was provisional and could be challenged by officials and other members of the imperial family. Their careers therefore show how the Han system relied on personal networks as well as on formal institutions. Overall, the empress dowagers were significant to the Han, particularly in providing continuity during succession crises and in shaping the pace of reform. Lü Zhi’s regency sustained the dynasty in its early years, while Dou’s influence slowed the move towards more active government. Their contributions are most accurately evaluated as mixed rather than simply negative or positive, and the record of their achievements is shaped by the sources that judged them.

Overall, the empress dowagers made some contributions to the Han, but their influence was mixed. They mostly helped stability but were sometimes a problem for the emperors.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The empress dowagers were significant to the maintenance of power and authority in the Han dynasty, especially during periods when emperors were young or weak. The position of the dowager gave a woman legal authority over the court and the young emperor, and it allowed her to act as regent. Empress Lü, the widow of Liu Bang, dominated the court from 195 BCE to 180 BCE. She appointed members of her family to key offices and used her position to protect the dynasty against those who opposed her, and her actions preserved the Liu line on the throne when she was regent. Her power depended on the regency, which gave her the authority to make decisions in the emperor’s name.

The dowagers also helped to keep the balance of power at court. Empress Dou, the widow of Emperor Wen, exercised considerable influence during the reign of Emperor Jing, and she shaped policy by supporting the Huang-Lao ideas that favoured restraint. Her influence shows that the dowager could act as a stabilising figure, mediating between the emperor and the officials. The dowagers’ authority thus contributed to the continuity of the dynasty, especially when the succession was disputed or the emperor was too young to govern.

However, their power was limited and usually temporary. The bureaucracy was staffed by officials who had their own loyalties, and the dowagers depended on the support of a faction at court. After Empress Lü’s death, her relatives were removed in a coup that restored the Liu line, which shows that the dowager’s power could be challenged. In the late Western Han, the empress dowagers and their families, such as the Wang family under Wang Zhengjun, became significant again, and their dominance contributed to the instability that led to the rise of Wang Mang, who usurped the throne in 9 CE.

The late Western Han also shows the risks that a dowager posed when she was associated with a powerful family. The Wang family of Empress Dowager Wang Zhengjun held the major offices at court in the decades before 9 CE, and their dominance encouraged the factional conflict that weakened the dynasty. The power of the dowager was therefore a double-edged asset. It could maintain continuity during a regency, but it could also concentrate authority in a family that was not accountable to the court, and this contributed to the ambitions that led to the usurpation of Wang Mang.

The judgement can be tested by the ways in which the dowagers used the rituals of the court. As the mothers of emperors, they held the seal and the authority to name heirs at certain moments, and the formal confirmation of the succession gave them a legal basis for action. These powers were exercised within the framework of Confucian ideas about filial duty and the family, which made it difficult for officials to oppose them openly. The dowager’s authority therefore rested on both law and ritual, and it could be used to sustain the dynasty in periods of uncertainty.

Overall, the empress dowagers were significant to the maintenance of power and authority in the Han, because they provided continuity during regencies and stabilised the court. Their significance was real, but it was limited by the bureaucracy and by the factional politics of the court. Their power sometimes weakened the dynasty, and the regencies of the later Han show that the dowagers’ authority could destabilise as well as preserve the state.

sampleAnswers.answer: Emperor Wudi made a greater contribution to the Han than any other ruler of the dynasty after its founder, though his contribution is best understood as the creation of a lasting political and intellectual system rather than as conquest alone. Wudi’s reign, from 141 to 87 BCE, transformed the Han from a state recovering from the Qin and the early wars into a centralised empire with a bureaucracy trained in a shared ideology. His most important reform was the promotion of Confucian learning. He established an imperial academy, the Taixue, in 124 BCE, where students studied the Five Classics, and this created a body of officials who were trained in a common moral and political language. Over time this training became the basis for appointment to office, so the state’s administration rested on learning rather than inherited privilege. This is a lasting political and cultural reform, and its effects were felt for centuries. Wudi’s economic reforms were equally significant. In 119 BCE he created state monopolies on salt and iron, which funded the wars against the Xiongnu, and he introduced a new coinage in 118 BCE, the wuzhu, which replaced the earlier currency and stabilised the money supply. The equable marketing system, which used state agencies to buy and sell goods across regions, shows an attempt to control prices and supply. These reforms were effective, but they were resented by merchants and officials, and the debate over monopolies, recorded in the Discourses on Salt and Iron, shows that they were controversial. Wudi’s contribution must be weighed against the costs of his wars and the expansion of the state. His campaigns against Nanyue, Korea and Dayuan extended Han power but drained the treasury. The campaigns against the Xiongnu opened the Hexi Corridor and began the contacts that became the Silk Road, after the missions of Zhang Qian. These achievements were significant, but they were expensive and their results were uneven. The earlier Han emperors had already laid the foundations for the dynasty. Han Gaozu established the imperial state after the fall of the Qin, and Emperor Wen and Emperor Jing had built a stable economy and administration. Wudi’s contribution was therefore a development of these foundations, though his reforms gave the Han its distinctive system. The evidence for Wudi’s reign is mainly from the Shiji of Sima Qian and the Hanshu of Ban Gu. Sima Qian was a court historian who was critical of Wudi’s extravagance and his punishment of officials, and his account reflects that disappointment. Ban Gu wrote a century later and praised the Confucian order that Wudi established, so his portrait is shaped by the later ideology. Archaeological evidence, including coins and tomb goods, supports the account of the coinage reform and the economy, but it does not reveal the views of the officials or the peasants who bore the costs. The judgement must also address how Wudi’s policies affected later Han government. The examination system that grew from the Imperial Academy shaped the bureaucracy for centuries, and the emphasis on Confucian texts became a standard for officials. Later rulers looked back to Wudi’s reign as a model of a strong state, though the debate of 81 BCE recorded in the Discourses on Salt and Iron led to partial reversals of the monopolies, showing that the costs of his policies were recognised by his successors. Taken together, Wudi’s greatest contribution was the creation of a bureaucratic and ideological framework that gave the Han its long-lasting character. His military expansion extended the empire, but the lasting political and cultural reforms were the more significant contribution. The view is persuasive, though the costs of his policies must be recognised as part of his legacy.

His economic reforms, including the salt and iron monopolies and the wuzhu coinage, funded the state and stabilised its money. However, his wars were expensive, and the monopolies were resented, as the debates on salt and iron show. Earlier emperors had laid the foundations for the dynasty, so Wudi built on their work. Sima Qian was critical of his extravagance, and Ban Gu later praised the order he created, so the sources reflect different views. Wudi’s reforms were his most lasting contribution, though his conquests extended Han power. The Discourses on Salt and Iron, a record of a debate held in 81 BCE, shows that Wudi’s monopolies were challenged by scholars and merchants who argued that the state was taking too much from the people. The debate did not end the monopolies, but it shows that the reforms were political as well as economic. Wudi’s reliance on officials trained in the Five Classics also meant that the state was served by a new class of scholars whose loyalty depended on the ideological framework he had established.  Wudi’s reign also saw the expansion of state control over trade and the coinage, which affected the wealth of merchants throughout the empire.

sampleAnswers.answer: The wars against the Xiongnu were highly significant to the expansion of the empire, because they opened the western and northern frontiers and made possible the contacts that became the Silk Road. The Xiongnu were a nomadic confederation that had dominated the steppe and had forced the early Han into a humiliating peace, with the marriage alliances and the annual tribute that the dynasty had been obliged to pay. Under Emperor Wudi this arrangement was abandoned, and the Han went on the offensive. In 121 BCE the general Huo Qubing led campaigns that drove the Xiongnu from the Hexi Corridor, the route to Central Asia. This opened the corridor to Han control, and the commanderies of Jiuquan, Zhangye, Wuwei and Dunhuang were established in the territory, which extended the empire to the Gobi and gave the Han a military base in the west. This was the first decisive step of territorial expansion beyond the traditional heartland. The campaign of 119 BCE, in which Wei Qing and Huo Qubing struck the Xiongnu at Mobei, drove the Xiongnu leader north and weakened his power in the steppe. The Han then sent envoys to the western regions, most notably Zhang Qian, whose missions to the Yuezhi and beyond opened contacts with Central Asia and Ferghana. These contacts were the origin of the trade routes that connected China with the wider world. The expansion of the empire was therefore a direct result of the Xiongnu wars, since the campaigns secured the routes and made possible the first systematic knowledge of the west. However, the wars were costly. They required large armies, long supply lines and heavy taxation, and the state monopolies on salt and iron were partly created to fund them. The cost led to protests at court and to debates about the value of the war, which the Discourses on Salt and Iron record. The expansion also left the Han committed to defending a long frontier. Its significance was therefore both territorial and financial. The Xiongnu themselves split in 53 BCE, when one faction submitted to the Han, which shows that the wars had changed the balance of power on the steppe. The main evidence for the wars is the Shiji of Sima Qian, a Han historian who wrote about a century after Wudi’s campaigns and who was critical of the costs of war. His account of Zhang Qian and the campaigns is detailed but reflects the court’s debates. The Hanshu of Ban Gu presents the campaigns from a later, more favourable perspective. Xiongnu sources are rare, which means that the nomads’ view is largely absent, and the Chinese account presents them through the lens of Han superiority. Archaeological evidence from the Hexi forts and the Gansu wall lines supports the account of the frontier expansion, but it does not reveal the Xiongnu’s internal politics. The consequences of these wars also extended beyond the frontier. The Han campaigns pushed the Xiongnu away from the Gansu corridor, and the Han’s relations with the Western Regions became part of its diplomatic system. Han forces established a presence at Dunhuang and along the Gansu corridor, which was essential for controlling the caravan routes. These frontiers required sustained garrisons, and their supply became a major component of state spending for the rest of the dynasty. Taken together, the wars against the Xiongnu were central to the expansion of the empire. They secured the Hexi Corridor, created the commanderies and opened the western routes, though the costs of the wars shaped the later limits of Han power. The wars were therefore a turning point in the expansion of the empire, even though their long-term results were uneven.

The Shiji criticises the costs of war, while the Hanshu presents the campaigns more favourably, so the sources must be read with care. The wars were a turning point, though their costs limited the long-term gains. The campaigns were also a test of Han logistics, since armies advancing into the Gobi and the Hexi Corridor depended on supply convoys across hundreds of kilometres of desert. The establishment of garrisons and beacon towers along the Gansu corridor was a response to these needs, and the surviving watchtowers show how the Han turned conquest into a permanent military system. The wars therefore changed the state’s administration as much as its boundaries.  The campaigns also gave the Han access to horses from Ferghana, which the court valued for its army, and this shows that the wars had economic as well as military purposes.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The Han were highly effective in expanding their empire, particularly under Emperor Wu, but their success in maintaining it was more uneven. The expansion was driven by campaigns against the Xiongnu and by conquests to the south and east, while maintenance depended on the replacement of rebellious kings with members of the Liu family, as Grant Hardy and Anne Kinney describe. The judgement is that the Han were effective in both respects, but the costs of expansion and the persistent threat of the Xiongnu limited the security of the state. The empire lasted for more than two centuries, which is evidence of real effectiveness.

Expansion under Emperor Wu, who ruled from 141 to 87 BCE, was the most striking achievement. Campaigns against the Xiongnu, the nomadic confederation to the north, were launched in the 120s BCE and drove the Xiongnu away from the Ordos region. Zhang Qian's missions to Central Asia, recorded in the Shiji and the Han histories, opened contacts with the states of the west, and this laid the foundations of the trade routes later called the Silk Road. Han armies also conquered the kingdom of Nanyue in the south in 111 BCE and extended control over parts of northern Korea in 108 BCE. These conquests show a state that could raise large armies and sustain campaigns over long distances.

The Xiongnu were never fully defeated, and their threat shaped Han policy throughout the period. Campaigns against them were expensive, and in the decades after Emperor Wu the Han turned to diplomacy and to marriage alliances in the north. The effectiveness of the Han in expansion therefore depended on the ability to sustain military costs, and this ability was limited. The Han gained territory and prestige, but the Xiongnu remained a powerful neighbour, so the security of the frontier was never complete.

Maintenance of the empire depended largely on control of the kingdoms. Hardy and Kinney describe how Liu replaced rebellious kings with his own brothers and sons, so that the kingdoms were ruled by members of the imperial family. The Rebellion of the Seven States in 154 BCE showed the danger of the kingdoms, and the Han subsequently reduced their size and power. These measures strengthened central control, and the kingdoms remained large and prosperous, but they were no longer able to challenge the throne. This is a clear example of effective maintenance, though it required constant attention.

The limits of Han maintenance are visible in the continuing autonomy of the kingdoms and in the pressure on the frontier. The kingdoms were not fully loyal, and Hardy and Kinney note that even relatives might be tempted to break away. The Han's strategy of marriage and gifts to the Xiongnu was a form of diplomacy that helped to keep the peace, but it was costly and depended on the goodwill of the nomad leaders. These weaknesses show that effectiveness was real but qualified.

On balance, the Han were highly effective in expanding their empire, especially under Emperor Wu, and they were reasonably effective in maintaining it through the control of the kingdoms and the management of the Xiongnu. The costs of expansion and the continuing threat on the frontier limited their security, but the longevity of the dynasty shows that their methods of government worked.

The Han effort at maintaining their empire also relied on their ability to manage finances and to reward officials. The state expanded its bureaucracy and its tax base, which paid for the armies and the frontier garrisons. Emperor Wu's reforms of the monopolies and the currency were a response to the costs of war, and they show a state that had learned to fund expansion without ruining its economy. This financial capacity was as important to the success of the Han as the armies themselves, and it allowed the dynasty to maintain control for more than a century after the great campaigns.
