sampleAnswers.answer:
The Han administered their empire with considerable effectiveness, but the system was a compromise that changed over time. The Western Han inherited a mixed structure of commanderies governed by central officials and feudal kingdoms ruled by relatives and allies of the emperor. Its effectiveness depended on how well the central government could control the kingdoms, and this problem was resolved gradually. The Han achieved long-term stability and a strong central administration, but the process was slow, and the system was shaped by the need to balance central authority with the power of the kings. The judgement depends on whether the Han system is compared with the Qin or with the later imperial state.

The basic structure of Han government rested on commanderies and counties, whose officials were appointed by the central government. These units were responsible for tax collection, justice and the maintenance of order, and they provided the empire with a network of officials. This system was effective in the core regions, where the central government could enforce its decisions, and it allowed the Han to draw revenue and labour from the population. Its efficiency was therefore strongest where the commanderies were directly administered.

The feudal kingdoms were a different element of the system. Early Han emperors enfeoffed their relatives and followers as kings, who ruled large territories with their own officials and armies. This arrangement was intended to protect the dynasty, but it created a power base that could challenge the emperor. The kings were semi-autonomous, and their courts could resemble miniature versions of the imperial court. The system was therefore a source of both support and instability.

The Seven Rebellions of 154 BCE showed the danger of the kingdoms. Several kings rebelled against the central government, and the rebellion was crushed by the Han army. The rebellion was a turning point, because it led the court to reduce the power of the kings and to remove their control of administration. This event shows that the Han government was willing to use force to strengthen central authority, although the change was not immediate.

Emperor Wu, who reigned from 141 to 87 BCE, completed the process of centralisation. He divided the realm into regions supervised by inspectors, who checked the conduct of officials and reported to the court. He also reduced the territories of the kings by allowing their lands to be divided among their heirs, which weakened their power. These measures gave the central government much greater control over the provinces, and they made administration more uniform.

The Han also strengthened the bureaucracy through recruitment and training. Officials were increasingly drawn from the educated elite, and the Imperial Academy was used to train candidates for office. This created a body of officials who were loyal to the central government and who were familiar with its procedures. The effectiveness of the administration therefore depended on the quality of its officials as well as on its structure.

Han administration also relied on a system of records, legal codes and communication. Official documents from the period, including wooden slips found in frontier garrisons, show how the government managed grain, labour and military supply. The network of roads and postal stations allowed messages to be carried across the empire. These arrangements allowed the central government to coordinate the administration of a large territory, although the speed of communication was limited.

The Han histories present the administration as a successful model of government, but the sources were written by officials who served the dynasty and who may have exaggerated its achievements. The records of the Seven Rebellions and of Emperor Wu’s reforms are also shaped by the viewpoint of the central court. Historians therefore use archaeological evidence, such as the administrative documents, to test the claims of the written accounts.

Overall, the Han administered their empire effectively in the sense that they maintained a large territory for more than four centuries and built a bureaucratic system that outlasted the dynasty. Their effectiveness was uneven, however, because the feudal kingdoms created tension until Emperor Wu’s reforms reduced their power. The Han therefore combined the Qin model of centralised officials with a flexible structure of kingdoms, and this combination gave the state its strength and its difficulties.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Persian imperialism was the main cause of the Persian Wars in the sense that it created the conditions of conflict, but it was not the only cause, and the Ionian Revolt was the immediate trigger. Oswyn Murray argues that the causes of the Persian Wars lay in the psychology of the Persian ruling class and in the necessities of the Persian imperial system, and that both Greeks and Persians were aware of the coming conflict. This is a persuasive view of the long-term causes. However, the decisions of individuals and the choices of Athens and the Ionian cities also shaped the outbreak of war. On balance, Persian imperialism was the main structural cause, but the wars were produced by the interaction of imperial ambition and Greek responses.

Persian imperialism created the framework for conflict. Cyrus II conquered Lydia in 546 BCE, and the Ionian Greek cities of the coast came under Persian control. Darius I extended Persian power into the Balkans and against the Scythians, which showed that the empire expanded by conquest and was ready to campaign at a distance. The Persian system required the continued loyalty of subject peoples, and it used tribute, garrisons and the appointment of local tyrants to maintain control. This system made conflict with the Greek cities likely, because the Ionian cities were subject to a power that expected obedience and resources.

The Ionian Revolt of 499 BCE was the immediate cause of the war. The Ionian cities rebelled against Persian rule, and the Athenians and Eretrians sent ships in support. Herodotus records that Athens' intervention angered Darius, who ordered that the Athenians be remembered in his court, and that he resolved to punish Athens and Eretria. The revolt was crushed by 493 BCE, but it made the Persian king determined to extend his control over the Greek mainland. This shows that the immediate trigger was Greek resistance to Persian rule, which Persian imperialism had made necessary.

Murray's emphasis on the psychology of the Persian ruling class adds a further dimension. The Persian court expected the continued submission of the Greeks, and Herodotus records demands for earth and water sent to the Greek states in 491 BCE. These demands were a symbolic assertion of imperial authority, and the refusal of Athens and Sparta to submit reflected a Greek awareness of what Persian rule meant. Murray is right that both sides expected a conflict, and that Persian ambitions made war likely even if the Ionian Revolt had not occurred.

However, Greek actions and choices also mattered. The Athenian decision to support the Ionian revolt was a major decision, and it brought the Persian army into the heart of Greek affairs. The Greek states were not simply victims of imperialism; their rivalries and their own ambitions shaped the war. The decision of Athens and Sparta to resist, rather than submit, was a choice that could have gone differently. Persian imperialism therefore set the conditions, but the decisions of the Greeks determined the course of the conflict.

On balance, Persian imperialism was the main cause of the Persian Wars in that it created the framework of conflict, the demands for submission and the Persian ambition to control the Greek world. The Ionian Revolt and the Athenian intervention were the immediate triggers, and the choices of the Greek states shaped the outbreak of war. The judgement is that imperialism was the main underlying cause, though not the sole one.

The Persian demands for earth and water are a further test of Murray's argument. Herodotus records that the Persian envoys sent to the Greek states in 491 BCE demanded symbolic submission, and that Athens and Sparta refused in ways that became famous. This shows that the Persian court expected acknowledgement of its authority, and that the Greek states understood the demands as a challenge. The demands do not prove that Persia planned an invasion of Greece at that time, but they show the expectation of imperial obedience that made conflict likely. The structure of the empire, rather than any single decision, was the underlying cause.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 21–25 row: a perceptive judgement on the causes of the Persian Wars, supported by Murray's interpretation and a comprehensive account of the Ionian Revolt and Persian demands. To lift it further, the answer could make the link between imperial structure and individual decisions more explicit.

However, the Ionian Revolt was the immediate trigger, and the Athenian decision to support it shaped the outbreak of war. The Greek states also chose to resist, and their decisions mattered. sampleAnswers.answer: Miltiades’ role was important for the Athenian victory at Marathon in 490 BCE, but it was one of several decisive factors. He shaped the decision to fight, chose the tactics and secured the support of the other generals, while the Athenian hoplites, the Plataean contingent and the Persian army’s own choices also determined the outcome. Assessing his importance therefore requires separating the planning of the battle from the conditions that made it succeed. Herodotus gives Miltiades the central role in the decision to engage the Persian army. There were ten generals, the strategoi, who shared command, and the polemarch Callimachus had the casting vote. Herodotus reports that Miltiades persuaded Callimachus to vote for battle, which was decisive when the generals were divided. Miltiades’ experience made him persuasive: he had fought in the northern Aegean and had earlier ruled in the Chersonese, so his knowledge of Persian forces was greater than most generals’. Without his argument the Athenians might have waited for reinforcements, in the hope of Spartan help that in fact arrived after the battle. Herodotus describes Miltiades’ tactical arrangement in some detail. He drew up the Athenian and Plataean hoplites in a line matched to the Persian front, weakened the centre so that the wings could hold, and ordered a rapid charge across the open plain to reduce the time under Persian archery. The Persians broke through the centre, but the wings then turned inwards and destroyed the force that had advanced. This plan exploited the Persian reliance on archers and light troops, and it was not merely brave. The tactics suggest that Miltiades’ role was crucial, although the account is shaped by Athenian tradition. Other factors were equally important. The Plataeans sent about a thousand hoplites, which gave the Athenians numerical strength and political backing in the battle. The Athenian hoplites were well trained and disciplined, and their close formation told in hand-to-hand fighting in a way that the Persian light troops could not match. The Persians’ choice of landing at Marathon exposed their army to attack on the plain, and the Spartans arrived too late to take part. Hippias’ presence as a guide shows how the Persians relied on local knowledge that proved insufficient. The victory was thus the product of many factors. The importance of Miltiades can also be judged by what followed. His role was therefore significant for Athenian self-image, but less so for his own career. Miltiades’ importance was substantial because he drove the decision to fight and devised the tactics that exploited the Persian formation. However, the victory depended on the discipline of the hoplites, the support of the Plataeans, the Persian choice of ground and the late arrival of the Spartans, which deprived the Athenians of help but also left them to win on their own. Miltiades was therefore a decisive figure in the victory, but his role was one of planning and persuasion within a wider set of conditions that made success possible. Judged as a whole, his role was important, though not sufficient on its own.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The battle of Plataea was highly significant to the Greek victory in the Persian Wars, because it destroyed the main Persian army that remained in Greece and ended the threat of a land invasion. In 479 BCE a Greek army of Spartans, Athenians, Tegeans and others, led by the Spartan regent Pausanias, faced the Persian army under Mardonius near the city of Plataea in Boeotia. After a long standoff, the Greeks attacked, and the Persian forces were defeated. Mardonius was killed in the fighting, and the Persian camp was taken. The victory removed the military threat to central Greece and gave the Greeks a decisive success on land.

The battle followed earlier Greek defeats at Thermopylae and the naval victory at Salamis, which had already weakened the Persian position. Salamis in 480 BCE forced Xerxes to withdraw most of his fleet, but Mardonius remained in Greece with a substantial army, and it was this army that Plataea destroyed. Without the battle, the Persians could have regrouped and renewed the campaign in the following season. Plataea therefore completed the sequence of events that ended the invasion, and its importance lies in ending the land war.

The battle was also significant for the Greeks’ confidence and unity. The Greek cities had been divided by fear and by the decision of some to submit to Persia, and the success at Plataea showed that a coalition could defeat the Persian army in the field. The victory helped to create the alliance that later became the Delian League, and it gave Sparta and Athens a shared achievement that they celebrated. The battle thus had political as well as military consequences.

However, the battle must be placed in the wider sequence. Mycale, fought the same year, destroyed the remaining Persian fleet and the Ionian revolt was revived, and Salamis was the decisive naval engagement that prevented the Persian navy from supporting the land army. Plataea was the decisive land battle, but it was not the only factor in the victory.

The Greek victory also depended on the coordination of the allied forces, which was difficult to achieve. The Greeks had to agree on a commander, supply their armies and keep the coalition together while the Persian army waited in Boeotia. The decision to fight at Plataea, rather than to retreat, reflected the confidence that the earlier victories had created. The battle therefore shows how a military success on land could depend on political unity among the Greek cities, and this unity was itself a product of the war’s earlier events.

The judgement can be tested by the Persian perspective. Herodotus, whose account is the main source, describes the defeat with a sense of divine retribution, and the Persian losses at Plataea were seen by the Greeks as a moral vindication of their freedom. Persian records of the campaign are scarce, so the significance of the battle must be judged largely from Greek evidence. A careful historian should therefore recognise that the victory was real and decisive, while noting that the story of its meaning was shaped by the victors.

Overall, the battle of Plataea was very significant to the Greek victory, because it ended the Persian threat on land and secured the freedom of central Greece. Its significance depended on the earlier battles, but it was the decisive event that ended the invasion and confirmed the Greek success.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Salamis was a major turning point of the Persian invasion of Greece, because the naval defeat weakened Xerxes’ strategy and encouraged the Greeks to fight on, but it was not the sole turning point. The invasion of 480 BCE had begun with Persian successes at Thermopylae and in the north, and the Greek fleet had not yet defeated the Persians decisively. The battle of Salamis changed the strategic balance, and the Persian king withdrew most of his forces. Yet the war was finally decided on land at Plataea and Mycale in 479 BCE, so Salamis was a turning point in a longer sequence rather than the single decisive moment.

The case for Salamis as the turning point rests on its consequences. Themistocles persuaded the Greek fleet to fight in the narrow straits, where the Persian ships could not use their numbers effectively. Herodotus records that the Persians were lured into the strait and suffered heavy losses, and the defeat forced Xerxes to reconsider his position. The Persian fleet was not destroyed entirely, but its failure meant that the king could not guarantee the supply of his army in Greece. This loss of control at sea was the decisive change.

The Persian withdrawal confirms the importance of the battle. Xerxes returned to Asia with a substantial part of his forces, and he left Mardonius with an army in Greece. This decision shows that the king had lost confidence in the campaign, and that the naval defeat had made the situation untenable. The withdrawal changed the nature of the invasion, because the Persian army in Greece was now cut off from its base and dependent on the Greek response.

Thermopylae and Artemisium were earlier engagements that delayed the Persians but did not stop them. The Greek defeat at Thermopylae, with the death of the Spartan king Leonidas and his force, showed that the Persians could break a defensive line. Artemisium was a naval engagement that was indecisive, and it allowed the Greek fleet to withdraw to Salamis. These battles were important because they gave the Greeks time to prepare, but they did not change the strategic balance in the way Salamis did.

The land campaign of 479 BCE shows the limits of the Salamis argument. The Greek victory at Plataea destroyed the main Persian army under Mardonius, and the battle of Mycale on the Ionian coast removed the Persian fleet from the Aegean. These victories ended the invasion and freed the Greek cities of Asia, so Plataea and Mycale were decisive in the final sense. Salamis made these victories possible, but the war was not finished until the Persian army was defeated on land.

The Greek accounts of Salamis must be read with care. Herodotus presents the battle as a Greek triumph shaped by divine favour and the wisdom of Themistocles, and Aeschylus’s play The Persians, staged within a few years of the battle, presents the Persian defeat as a moral lesson about hubris. These sources emphasise Athenian leadership and the Greek unity that the battle supposedly created. Modern historians therefore question how far the victory was decided by Greek skill, and how far it depended on the Persian fleet’s weaknesses and the logistics of the invasion.

The Persian perspective offers little direct evidence, because the Persian king’s records of the campaign are limited. The Persian withdrawal, however, suggests that Xerxes regarded the naval defeat as decisive for his position. The fact that he left Mardonius in Greece also indicates that he did not regard the war as lost. This ambiguity shows that the Persian view of the battle is hard to reconstruct.

Overall, Salamis was a turning point of the Persian invasion because it destroyed the Persian control of the sea and led to the withdrawal of Xerxes. Yet it was not the final turning point, since the Greek victories at Plataea and Mycale ended the war. The battle is best understood as the decisive moment in a sequence of engagements, and its significance lies in the change of strategy that it forced upon the Persian king.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The Battles of Thermopylae and Artemisium were a success for the Greeks in strategic terms, although they were defeats in tactical terms. At Thermopylae, Leonidas and his force held the narrow pass for several days and were finally overwhelmed after a Greek was revealed to have shown the Persians a path around the defence. At Artemisium, the Greek fleet fought the Persian navy to a standstill in a series of engagements. The judgement is that the two battles were a success because they delayed the Persian advance, gave the Greek states time to organise and made the later victories at Salamis and Plataea possible, even though the Greek losses were real and the immediate outcome favoured Xerxes.

The tactical outcome of Thermopylae was clearly a defeat for the Greeks. Leonidas and his Spartans, together with allied contingents from several states, were killed or overwhelmed, and the pass was lost to the Persian army. Herodotus records that the defence was decided by the betrayal of a local man who guided the Persians along a mountain path, and this shows how fragile the Greek position was. Yet the defence had a clear purpose. It forced Xerxes to spend several days on a narrow front, and the Persian losses in the early assaults were heavy. The sacrifice made the Greek resistance a symbol of determination that spread through the allied states.

Artemisium was a naval engagement that was indecisive. The Greek fleet, drawn largely from Athens and the other states of the Greek alliance, fought the Persian navy in the narrow waters off the north of Euboea. The Persians lost ships in storms and in combat, and the Greeks were able to withdraw in good order when news of the defeat at Thermopylae arrived. The stalemate prevented the Persian fleet from sailing south to cut off the Greek forces and allowed the Greeks to regroup at Salamis. This was an important strategic result, even though the fleet was not victorious in an absolute sense.

The value of these battles was realised at Salamis, where Themistocles drew the Persian fleet into the narrow waters of the strait and destroyed it, and at Plataea, where the Greek land army defeated the Persian forces in 479 BCE. The Greek delay at Thermopylae and the survival of the fleet at Artemisium made these victories possible. Without the time gained, the Athenians could not have evacuated their city, and the Greek states could not have organised a combined force. The success of the Greeks in the wider war therefore depended on the delay that these two battles imposed on the invaders.

On balance, the Battles of Thermopylae and Artemisium were a success for the Greeks, but a success measured in time and morale rather than in territory. The defeat at Thermopylae cost the lives of many brave men, and the stalemate at Artemisium did not destroy the Persian navy. Yet the Greek resistance slowed the invasion, preserved the fleet and encouraged the allies to fight on, and these results made the decisive victories of the following year achievable. The judgement is that the battles were a strategic success, and an essential part of the Greek victory over the Persian invasion.

The judgement must also weigh the cost of the Greek defeat at Thermopylae and the damage it did to the Greek alliance's morale in the short term. The Spartan dead and the allied losses were heavy, and the Persian army was able to march south and occupy Athens. Herodotus presents the battle as a moral triumph, and its legend shaped the later memory of the Greek resistance, but the strategic judgement must rest on the outcome of the wider war. The defeat was a loss, and it showed how exposed the Greeks were in the open north. The victory was in the delay it imposed, and in the way it allowed the navy to keep the sea and the allies to gather. A reasoned assessment therefore recognises the tactical defeat and the strategic gain, and it measures success by the outcome of the campaign as a whole.

sampleAnswers.answer: Themistocles contributed decisively to the Greek victory in the Persian Wars, because he created the naval force that defeated Xerxes' fleet and he shaped the strategy that drew the Persians into a battle they could not win. However, the victory was a collective achievement. It depended on Spartan leadership on land, on the sacrifice at Thermopylae, on the Persian errors that followed and on the cooperation of the allied fleets. Themistocles' greatest contribution was the decision to build a navy, and the Athenian fleet it produced was the core of the victory. In 483 BCE, when the Athenians were debating how to use a windfall of silver from the Laurion mines, Themistocles persuaded them to invest in triremes rather than distribute the money. The fleet that resulted gave Athens the largest navy in Greece, and it made Athens the decisive naval power when the Persian invasion came in 480 BCE. Without this fleet the Greek resistance would have lacked the means to challenge Persian sea power, and the defence of Greece would have depended on land forces that could not stop the Persian army. The strategy at Artemisium showed his skill in using naval force to delay the Persians while the allies gathered at Thermopylae. The naval engagement there was indecisive, but it kept the Persian fleet occupied and gave the land defenders time. Thermopylae, where Leonidas and his Spartans and allies held the pass, was a different kind of contribution. It delayed the Persian army, but it did not stop it, and the Greek forces were forced to withdraw after a Persian force found a path around the defenders. Leonidas' stand is therefore a significant element of the victory, but it was Themistocles' fleet that kept the sea open. The decisive moment was the battle of Salamis in 480 BCE. Themistocles, according to Herodotus, arranged for the Persians to believe that the Greeks were divided and planning to flee, and he ensured that the allied fleet fought in the narrow straits, where the Persian ships could not manoeuvre. Herodotus' account of the stratagem may be shaped by later Athenian memory, and the message sent to Xerxes is a literary device, but the outcome is not in doubt. The Persian fleet was defeated, and Xerxes withdrew much of his army from Greece. The Spartan commander Eurybiades held the nominal command of the allied fleet, and the Athenian contribution was the largest, so Themistocles' influence over the battle was considerable even without formal authority. The victory at Plataea the following year, won by the Greek land army under Pausanias, completed the defeat of the Persian invasion, and Themistocles had no role in it. The campaign therefore shows that the victory required both the naval and the land components. The political consequences also show the limits of his contribution. After the war, Themistocles pressed for the rebuilding of Athens' walls, which the Spartans opposed, and his influence declined. He was ostracised in the early 470s BCE, and he later went into exile, ending his days in Persian service. These events show that his role in the victory was controversial even among the Greeks, and that his reputation depended on the Athenians' memory of their navy. The evidence is shaped by Herodotus and by the Athenian tradition, which emphasised Themistocles' cunning and the naval triumph. The historian must balance this account against the strategic realities of the war, in which Spartan land power, the cooperation of the Greek states and the Persian mistakes were all necessary. The most accurate judgement is that Themistocles was essential to the Greek victory because he built the fleet and made the decision to fight at Salamis, but that his contribution was one of several necessary conditions. The victory was therefore a product of collective action in which Themistocles provided the decisive naval strategy.

sampleAnswers.answer: Themistocles contributed significantly to the Greek victory by creating the fleet that fought at Salamis. Herodotus' stratagem may reflect later Athenian memory, but the outcome is not in doubt. The Spartan commander Eurybiades held nominal command, so Themistocles' influence depended on the Athenian contribution rather than on formal authority. The land victory at Plataea under Pausanias completed the defeat, and Themistocles had no role in it. After the war his influence declined, and he was ostracised in the early 470s BCE. His contribution was therefore essential at sea, but it was one of several necessary conditions for the victory. Herodotus' emphasis on Themistocles' cunning reflects Athenian memory of the war, while Spartan and allied accounts gave more weight to Leonidas and Pausanias. The historian must weigh the claims of each tradition, and recognise that the Athenian fleet was the common decisive factor in all of them. The victory also raised the political standing of the poorer citizens who rowed the ships.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Athenian navy made the greatest contribution to Greek victory and Persian defeat, though the argument must acknowledge the wider Greek effort and the role of Sparta at Plataea. The most important Athenian contribution was Themistocles’ decision, taken around 483 BCE, to use the silver from Laurion to build a large fleet of triremes. Without this fleet, Athens would have had no means of resisting Xerxes’ invasion of 480 BCE, and the Greeks could not have fought a sea battle with any hope. The fleet was decisive at Salamis, where the Greek triremes were fought in the narrow strait and the Persian fleet, crowded and disorganised, was defeated. This victory disrupted Xerxes’ supply line and forced him to withdraw most of his army to Asia, which left the land campaign in Greece in the hands of Mardonius. Salamis therefore transformed the balance of the war, because the Persians could no longer rely on the fleet to supply and protect their army. The Athenian navy also contributed to the victory at Mycale in 479 BCE, which removed the Persian fleet from the Aegean. These naval victories were the basis for the Greek success, since they kept the Persian army dependent on a fragile supply line and allowed the Greeks to concentrate on the land campaigns. However, the land victory at Plataea in 479 BCE was equally important, because it destroyed Mardonius’ army and ended the threat of a Persian invasion of mainland Greece. The Spartan-led coalition and its hoplites were decisive there, and without Plataea the naval victories might not have been enough to end the war. This is the strongest argument against the view. Herodotus, the main source, presents Salamis as the turning point, but he also credits the Spartan and Corinthian contingents, so his judgement is partly shaped by the political alliances of the Greek states. Thucydides and the later accounts of Plutarch are also shaped by Athenian interests, since they present Athens as the saviour of Greece. Archaeological evidence, including the Themistoclean walls and the naval inscriptions, supports the view that Athens built a large navy, but it does not establish the relative importance of the battles. The importance of Salamis is also clear from the Persian response. After the defeat, Xerxes withdrew most of his army to Asia, and the surviving Persian fleet retreated to Samos, which left Mardonius with a smaller army and no secure line of supply by sea. Mardonius’ decision to remain in Boeotia in 479 BCE was a consequence of this naval defeat, because the Persians could no longer expect reinforcements by sea. This shows that the navy shaped the land campaign as well as the sea war. The Athenian fleet also held the sea lanes around the Greek mainland, which allowed the allied army to move to Plataea and to strike at the Persian camp. The judgement can also be tested against the Spartan contribution. Sparta’s army won the decisive land battle at Plataea, and its leadership of the allied command gave the Greeks a unified strategy in the later campaigns. The Peloponnesian states, however, had few warships of their own and depended on Athens for much of the naval strength the coalition needed. The navy and the army were therefore complementary parts of a coalition, and the question of which made the greatest contribution depends on whether Persian failure is measured by the defeat of the fleet or the defeat of the army. Taken together, the navy made the greatest contribution because it created the strategic conditions for the Greek victory, by destroying the Persian fleet, securing the Aegean and forcing Xerxes to withdraw. Plataea was the decisive land battle, but it depended on the naval war having first removed the Persian supply line. The view is therefore persuasive, though it must be qualified by the importance of the Greek coalition on land.

sampleAnswers.answer: Relations between Athens and Sparta changed during this period because the victory over Persia created two states with different ambitions and different fears. The alliance that won the war was never comfortable. Sparta led the land forces and was the most prestigious power in Greece, but it had no appetite for an overseas war. Athens, which had lost its city and rebuilt its navy, took the lead at sea and in 478 BCE formed the Delian League, which united the Aegean states against any renewed Persian threat. The League's treasury was at Delos and was later moved to Athens, and its members were gradually converted from allies into subjects. The growth of Athenian power was therefore the central cause of change. The early friction arose from the rebuilding of Athens' walls. Sparta opposed the fortification of Athens on the ground that it would make the city a base for future domination, and the Athenians, under Themistocles, delayed the work until their own safety was assured. This episode, recorded by Thucydides, revealed that the two cities had different ideas about the post-war order. Sparta wanted a Greek league under its leadership, while Athens wanted security and the freedom to act. The Athenian response was to strengthen its position through its navy and alliances, and this gave Sparta a reason to fear it. The turning point came in 464 BCE, when a major revolt of the helots broke out in Messenia. Sparta asked its allies for help, and the Athenians sent a force under Cimon, whose policy favoured cooperation with Sparta. Yet the Spartans then sent the Athenian contingent home, perhaps because they feared the political radicalism of the Athenian troops or because they distrusted Athens' motives. The insult was deeply felt in Athens, where the democrats turned against Cimon and the pro-Spartan policy. The episode showed that the Spartan alliance was no longer reliable and that Athens had to look to its own interests. The breakdown followed quickly. Athens allied with Argos and with Thessaly, and it became involved in a war with Corinth and Aegina. Sparta and Athens fought the First Peloponnesian War in the 450s BCE, and the Athenians suffered reverses in Egypt and elsewhere before the conflict was settled. The Thirty Years' Peace of 446 or 445 BCE ended the open war and recognised the spheres of the two powers, but it did not resolve the underlying rivalry. The Athenian empire continued to expand in the Aegean, and Spartan allies, especially Corinth, grew increasingly alarmed at it. The Corinthian complaints before the war of 431 BCE, which Thucydides records, identified Athenian expansion as the cause of the crisis, and the Spartan assembly voted for war. The evidence for these developments comes largely from Thucydides, who was an Athenian and wrote with a clear understanding of the causes of the war. His account of the Pentecontaetia, the period of fifty years between the Persian Wars and the outbreak of the Peloponnesian War, shapes the way historians understand the change. Yet the speeches he records are reconstructions, and the Athenian perspective is strong in them. The inscriptional evidence of Athenian alliances and tribute lists supports his account of imperial growth, but it does not reveal Spartan motives. The historian must weigh these sources carefully. The most accurate judgement is that relations changed because the post-war settlement created a power that Sparta did not trust, and that Athens' expansion made the rivalry permanent. The Ithome episode was the turning point rather than the cause, and the war of 431 BCE was the result of accumulated tensions. The change in relations was therefore driven by the growth of Athenian power, by Spartan fear and by the specific incidents that revealed their divergent goals.

Early friction arose when Sparta opposed the rebuilding of Athens' walls, and the Athenians delayed the work until their safety was assured. The turning point came in 464 BCE, when a revolt of the helots broke out at Ithome. Sparta asked its allies for help, and the Athenians sent a force under Cimon. The Spartans then sent the Athenian contingent home, which was deeply insulting in Athens and led to Cimon's removal. Athens allied with Argos and Thessaly, and a war with Sparta followed in the 450s BCE. The Thirty Years' Peace of 446 or 445 BCE ended the open war but did not resolve the rivalry, and Corinth's complaints about Athenian expansion helped to bring about the war of 431 BCE. The change in relations was therefore driven by Athenian growth and Spartan fear, with the Ithome episode revealing their divergent goals. Thucydides' account of the Corinthian complaints and the Spartan vote for war suggests that the two cities had reached an impasse that neither could resolve peacefully, so historians see the change as cumulative rather than sudden. sampleAnswers.answer:
The Delian League achieved some of its aims, particularly the removal of Persian forces from the Aegean, but it did not achieve its aim of a free and equal alliance. The League was founded in 478 or 477 BCE to continue the war against Persia, and it succeeded in driving the Persians back from the Aegean and in freeing many Greek cities. Yet Athens gradually transformed the League into an Athenian empire, and the allies lost their autonomy. The extent of its success therefore depends on whether the aims of the League are judged by its military purpose or by its political ideals.

The original aim of the League was to continue the struggle against Persia after the defeats of Xerxes. The allies swore an oath to share the same friends and enemies, and the members contributed ships or money to a common fund kept on the island of Delos. This arrangement allowed the Greek states to pursue the war at sea, and it gave the Athenians a leading role because of their fleet. The early campaigns were directed against Persian garrisons and cities in the Aegean and the Hellespont.

The League’s military success was real. Under Cimon, the Athenian commander, the allied fleet defeated the Persians at the Eurymedon River, probably around 466 BCE, and this victory removed the Persian fleet from the Aegean for a period. The campaign freed Greek cities in the region, and it strengthened the League’s reputation as a force that could protect its members. This success shows that the League achieved its most important military aim.

The League’s political aims were less successful. Thucydides records that some allies, such as Naxos and Thasos, tried to leave the League, and that Athens used force to bring them back. Naxos was forced to remain, and Thasos was besieged and compelled to surrender its fleet and walls. These events show that the League’s members were not free to withdraw, and that the alliance had become a means of Athenian control. The allies had been promised equality, but they were treated as subjects.

The treasury of the League illustrates this change. The money was originally kept at Delos, where the sanctuary of Apollo provided a religious centre for the alliance. In 454 BCE the treasury was moved to Athens, and Thucydides presents this move as a sign of Athenian dominance. The Athenians used the tribute to fund their navy, their public buildings and their own needs, and this use of the tribute made the League an instrument of Athenian power.

The Athenian justification for the League was the threat of Persian revival. Athenian speakers, as recorded in Thucydides, argued that the empire was necessary to protect the allies and to maintain security in the Aegean. This argument had some force, because the Persians remained a threat, but it was also a means of justifying the control of the allies. Thucydides, however, presents the Athenian arguments with some scepticism, and this suggests that the empire was maintained by force as well as by necessity.

The allied view of the League is less well preserved. The surviving sources are mostly Athenian or written from an Athenian perspective, so the complaints of the allies are known mainly through the actions taken against them. The revolts of Naxos, Thasos and Samos show that some allies resented the imposition of Athenian control, and that the League’s aims were understood differently by its members. The lack of allied sources makes it hard to judge how far the League was supported by its members.

Modern historians disagree about when the League became an empire. Some argue that the change occurred gradually, as Athens used its naval power to suppress revolts and to impose its judicial authority. Others see the transfer of the treasury as the decisive point, because it showed that the League no longer served the common purpose. The evidence supports both views, since the League’s aims changed over time.

The League’s aims must also be measured against its wider consequences. The alliance brought prosperity to Athens and transformed the city into the leading power of the Greek world. It also created a model of imperial control that later shaped the Peloponnesian War. The League therefore had a lasting effect that went beyond its original aims, and this effect was the source of the tensions that led to the war.

Overall, the Delian League achieved its military aim of removing the Persians from the Aegean, as the victory at Eurymedon shows, but it did not achieve its political aim of a free and equal alliance. Athens converted the League into an empire, using tribute, force and the transfer of the treasury to maintain control. The League’s success was therefore real in its original purpose and unsuccessful in its political promise.

Testing the dating of Eurymedon against a second source would strengthen the evidence.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Cimon and Aristides the Just both contributed to the development of Athens and its empire, but their roles were different in kind and in period. Aristides was important in the foundation of the Delian League and in the early organisation of its tribute, while Cimon was the dominant general and political leader of Athens for almost two decades. Donald Kagan argues that Cimon gained so much political support that he became the leader of the Athenians in fact, if not in law, and this claim is well supported by the evidence. The judgement is that Cimon was the more important figure in the development of the empire in practice, while Aristides was important in establishing its structure.

Aristides' contribution was the foundation of the League. After the Persian Wars, the Greek states that had resisted Persia formed an alliance against any renewed threat, with its treasury at Delos. Plutarch and Aristotle attribute to Aristides the assessment of the tribute that each member was to pay, and this assessment gave the League a settled basis. The evidence for his role is later and partly anecdotal, and the stories of his justice and honesty are likely to be idealised. Nevertheless, the League's early organisation shows the importance of a figure who could negotiate and assess the contributions of the member states.

Cimon's career was more clearly documented. Kagan notes that Cimon was elected general each year between 479 and 462 BCE, led every important expedition and persuaded the assembly to support his policies at home and abroad. His campaigns, including the capture of Scyros and the victory at Eurymedon around 466 BCE, brought Athens wealth and extended its control of the Aegean. The Thasian revolt of 465 BCE was suppressed under his leadership, which showed that the League could be used to coerce members. These campaigns made Athens the dominant naval power in the Aegean.

Cimon's policy also had a political dimension. He favoured cooperation with Sparta and the maintenance of the aristocratic order at home, and his opposition to the democratic reforms of Ephialtes was an important part of Athenian politics. The ostracism of Cimon in 461 BCE, when Athens turned against his Spartan policy, shows that his position depended on the support of the assembly. His successors, including Pericles, followed a more democratic and more aggressive policy, which transformed the League into an Athenian empire.

The sources for both men have limitations. Kagan's account is strongly shaped by the wish to explain Athenian policy, and Plutarch's biographies of Cimon and Aristides are later and idealised. A historian must therefore weigh the clearer evidence for Cimon's campaigns against the more uncertain evidence for Aristides' early role. The judgement depends on which stage of the League's development is emphasised, and the two men represent successive phases of its growth.

On balance, Aristides was important to the foundation and early organisation of the Delian League, while Cimon was the leader who made Athens the dominant power in the Aegean and extended its control through campaigns and coercion. Cimon's role in the development of Athens and its empire was greater in practice, but both men were necessary to the transformation of an alliance into an empire.

The evaluation of the two men also depends on how the empire itself developed. Aristides' tribute system gave the League a basis of fair contributions, and this encouraged the members to pay. Cimon's leadership turned the League into a more coercive instrument, as the campaigns against Thasos show. Later, Pericles completed the transformation into an Athenian empire. The development of Athens and its empire was therefore a sequence, and each of these men represents a stage. Their contributions must be judged in relation to the stages they helped to create.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The Delian League transformed into the Athenian Empire because Athens used its naval strength to turn a voluntary alliance into a system of control. The league was founded in 478 or 477 BCE to continue the war against Persia, with the allies contributing ships or money to a common treasury on the island of Delos. Its early success depended on the consent of its members, and the allies were expected to share the cost of the war. Athens provided most of the fleet and the leadership, and this gave it a growing influence over the decisions of the league.

The threat of secession was a major pressure. When allies such as Naxos and Thasos wished to leave the league, Athens responded by forcing them to remain, and the revolt of Thasos around 465 BCE was crushed. Athens began to treat the allies as subjects who owed obedience, and the members were required to pay tribute in place of ships, which reduced their ability to resist. This shift from voluntary contributions to compulsory tribute was a decisive step in the transformation of the league.

The financial and political pressures of the war against Persia also encouraged the change. The treasury was moved from Delos to Athens in 454 BCE, which made the funds directly accessible to the Athenian state. The money was used for Athenian projects and for the naval campaigns that Athens led, and this blurred the line between the league’s interests and those of Athens. The Athenian Empire was therefore a consequence of the funds, the fleet and the threat of revolt.

However, the transformation was not entirely planned. Aristides, who organised the early assessment of contributions, sought a fair system, and the early league was a genuine alliance. The change came from the need to maintain unity and from the ambition of Athenian leaders, such as Cimon and later Pericles, who pursued an active policy in the Aegean. The shift reflected the power of Athens rather than a single intention to create an empire.

The change was also driven by the political choices of the Athenian leadership. Athenians saw the Aegean as their sphere of influence, and their navy protected the trade routes on which the city depended. The use of the allies’ money to pay for the fleet made Athens the dominant naval power, and the allies, who had lost their own fleets to the Persian wars, could not easily build alternatives. This dependence on Athens explains why the transformation proceeded so smoothly once compulsory tribute was established.

The judgement can be tested by the reactions of the allies. Many of the smaller island states were reluctant to contribute money rather than ships, and Athens responded by using its fleet to enforce payments. The allies’ dependence on Athenian protection against Persia gave Athens a strong position, but it also created resentment, and this resentment shaped the later revolts. The transformation was therefore driven by the interaction of Athenian pressure and allied reluctance, and it was not a single decision taken at the league’s foundation.

Overall, the Delian League transformed into the Athenian Empire because Athens’ naval power, the treasury and the threat of secession made the alliance into a system of tribute and control. The transformation was driven by the pressures of war and by Athenian ambition, and it marked the end of the league as a voluntary union.

sampleAnswers.answer: The impact of empire on Athenian democracy was profound, because Athenian imperialism produced the tribute that allowed the state to pay its citizens for public service, which broadened political participation, while the empire also limited the democracy’s moral and political foundations. The Delian League was founded in 478 BCE as an alliance against Persia, but Athens gradually turned it into an empire, and the treasury was moved from Delos to Athens in 454 BCE. The tribute of the allies then funded the navy, public works and the pay for the citizens who served in the courts and the Assembly. This payment, the misthos, allowed poorer citizens to take part in government without losing their livelihood, which was a major change for democratic participation. The thetes, the poorest citizens, rowed the fleet that held the empire together, and their service gave them a political importance that the older hoplite class had lacked. The democracy therefore rested on imperial revenue, and the navy made the poorest citizens central to the empire’s power. This was a direct impact of empire on the citizens. However, the same empire also changed the character of Athenian democracy. In 451 or 450 BCE, Pericles’ citizenship law restricted citizenship to those with two Athenian parents, which narrowed the political community even as it gave the citizens who remained more power. The allies, who paid the tribute, had no voice in the Assembly, and the cities that revolted, such as Mytilene in 428 BCE, were punished harshly. The decision to execute the men of Mytilene, although later reversed, shows how the imperial demands affected the democratic process. The Athenians used their democracy to govern subject cities, which meant that the democratic citizens were complicit in the empire’s oppression. The evidence for this impact is partly from Thucydides, who was an Athenian general and who wrote about the Mytilene debate and the Melian dialogue. His account is detailed but reflects the Athenian view of power. The Old Oligarch, a critic of the democracy, argued that the poor benefited from the empire because they were paid, and this is a biased but contemporary judgement. Inscriptions recording the tribute lists and the Athenian decrees provide direct evidence, but they show the administration rather than its effect on the citizens. Comedy, such as the plays of Aristophanes, offers a satirical view of the democracy and its politicians. The empire also affected the citizens’ identity and their relationship with the state. Athenian citizens who served in the navy or on juries became members of an imperial system that rewarded them with pay, and this gave them a stake in the empire’s continuation. Public building projects, such as the Parthenon, were funded from the imperial treasury, and they displayed Athens’ power to citizens and visitors. However, the same system generated fear when rebellion threatened, as the debate over Mytilene shows, and the willingness to use force against allies raised questions about the democracy’s character that later writers debated. The impact can also be seen in the changing composition of the Assembly and the courts. As the empire brought wealth to Athens, pay for jurors and officials allowed citizens with limited means to attend the courts and the Assembly for long periods, which altered the social base of political participation. Critics such as the author of the Old Oligarch complained that the poor controlled the city because the empire paid them, and this complaint shows that contemporaries saw a direct link between imperial revenue and the political power of the poor. Taken together, empire gave Athenian democracy its financial base and its widest participation, but it also narrowed the citizen body and turned democratic power into an instrument of imperial control. The impact was therefore double-edged, enriching the citizens at the cost of the allies and the democracy’s own principles.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 21–25 row: a perceptive assessment of the impact on democracy, separating the gains from the misthos and the navy from the narrowing of citizenship and the treatment of allies, tested against Thucydides, the Old Oligarch and the inscriptions. The answer is complete for twenty-five marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The impact of empire on Athenian democracy was considerable. Tribute from the allies paid for the navy and for the wages of citizens who served in the courts and the Assembly, which allowed poorer citizens to take part in government. The thetes rowed the fleet and gained political importance. However, the empire also changed democracy in less positive ways. Pericles’ citizenship law of 451 or 450 BCE narrowed the citizen body, and the allies had no voice in the Assembly. The treatment of revolting cities such as Mytilene shows the cost to the allies. Thucydides, who was an Athenian, presents the empire from the Athenian view, and the Old Oligarch judged the empire’s benefits to the poor. The impact was therefore double-edged. Imperial revenue also changed the structure of the democracy. The payment of jurors, which Pericles is said to have introduced, allowed citizens who worked for a living to serve in the courts, and the courts became the principal arena in which Athenian citizens exercised political power. The empire thus supplied the financial basis of a democracy in which ordinary citizens judged cases and shaped policy, though this participation depended on the allies’ tribute and on the Athenians’ willingness to use force against them.  The Athenians also used the empire to fund the Parthenon and other public works, which made the democracy’s power visible in the city and linked citizens to the imperial treasury.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The key democratic developments within Athens in the mid fifth century were highly significant, because they widened the participation of ordinary citizens in government and made the Athenian democracy the most participatory of the Greek states. The reforms of Ephialtes, the payment for public service and the citizenship law of 451/450 BCE each extended the political role of the poorer citizens. However, these developments were paid for by the empire, and the tribute of the allies funded the institutions that gave the citizens their power. The judgement is that the democratic developments were significant in transforming the citizen body, but that their significance was inseparable from the imperial system that financed and sustained them.

The reforms of Ephialtes in 462/461 BCE were the first major step. Ephialtes curtailed the powers of the Areopagus, the council of former magistrates that had been the most powerful body in the state, and transferred its functions to the council and the assembly and the courts. This was a shift of power from an aristocratic body to institutions in which ordinary citizens took part. The reform was significant because it made the democracy less dependent on the goodwill of the old elite, and it gave the citizens a stronger voice in the decisions of the state.

The payment for public service, associated with Pericles, allowed poorer citizens to serve on juries and in the council without losing their income. This measure was a practical condition of democratic participation, because it enabled citizens who worked for a living to take part in the courts and the government. Its significance lies in the way it made the democracy more inclusive, but it was an expensive measure, and its cost was met in part by the resources that the Delian League had brought to Athens.

The citizenship law of 451/450 BCE restricted citizenship to those whose parents were both Athenian. This law defined the citizen body more narrowly, and it made the privileges of the democracy more exclusive. Its significance is ambiguous, since it strengthened the identity of the citizens while excluding many who had previously been regarded as Athenian. The Funeral Oration of Pericles, preserved by Thucydides, presents the democracy as a model of equality and freedom for the citizens, but the citizenship law shows the limits of that equality.

The Delian League's tribute was the essential financial basis for these developments. The treasury had been moved to Athens in 454 BCE, and the allies' payments funded the building programme, the navy and the pay of public officials. The impact of imperialism on Athenian democracy was therefore profound: it made the democratic institutions possible, and it also made the citizens dependent on an empire that they ruled over others. On balance, the democratic developments were the most significant feature of Athenian political life in this period, but their significance depended on the empire that financed them.

The judgement must also weigh the democratic developments against the experience of the allies. The tribute paid by the Delian League was enforced by Athenian officials and garrisons, and the cities that tried to leave the league were punished. The revolt of Samos in 440 BCE, which Athens crushed, shows that the empire was maintained by force as well as by the benefits of membership. Citizens who benefited from pay and public office depended on this revenue, and the democracy's stability was bound up with the empire's continuing income. A reasoned evaluation therefore recognises that the democratic developments were significant for the citizens who took part in them, and that the same developments were supported by a system that subjected other Greeks to Athenian control.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 21-25 row: a perceptive judgement that weighs the widening of citizen participation against the dependence on the tribute of the empire, with evidence from Ephialtes, jury pay, the citizenship law and the transfer of the treasury. It would lift further by assessing how the allies experienced the empire in relation to the democratic gains of the citizens.

sampleAnswers.answer: The activities of the Peloponnesian League were largely a response to Athenian imperialism between the 470s and 440s BCE, but they were not solely a response. Sparta’s leadership reflected long-standing concerns about its own position, including the helot population and its rivalry with Argos, which also shaped its policy. Athenian power provided the main pressure, but Sparta’s actions were also driven by internal and regional factors, so the response was real but not the sole explanation. In the years after the Persian Wars the Peloponnesian League was dominated by Sparta, which was reluctant to pursue a war of liberation and preferred to keep its alliance intact. When Athens turned the Delian League into an empire, Sparta’s response was cautious. Thucydides argues that the growth of Athenian power and the fear it caused in Sparta made war inevitable, which suggests that the League’s posture was a response to Athenian expansion. Yet Sparta’s concerns also included the helots: in 462 BCE, during a helot revolt, Sparta asked Athens for help and then sent the Athenian force away, an insult that Thucydides records as turning Athens towards Argos. The League’s activities in the 450s and 440s show a pattern of response. Spartan-led forces defeated the Athenians at Tanagra in 457 BCE, and in 446 BCE, after revolts in Boeotia and Megara, the Spartans invaded Attica and pressed Athens to accept the Thirty Years’ Peace of 446 or 445 BCE. In 432 BCE Corinth’s complaints at Sparta about Athenian actions against Potidaea and the Megarian decree prompted a Spartan assembly that led to war. These episodes suggest that Sparta responded to Athenian power with military and diplomatic action. Other activities cannot be explained by Athenian imperialism alone. Corinth and Megara had their own commercial interests and rivalries with Athens, which drew Sparta into conflicts that were not only about imperial control. Corinth pressed Sparta to act partly to protect its trade and its colonies, not only to counter an empire, and the League’s members often pursued their own disputes through Sparta’s authority. The League’s response was thus shaped by the interests of its members as well as by Athenian power. The League’s responses also show the limits of Spartan power. Sparta was reluctant to act against Athens without the support of its allies, and its decisions depended on the politics of its assembly and its anxieties about the helots. Thucydides’ account suggests that Sparta often acted only when Athenian expansion threatened its allies directly. This reluctance means that the League’s responses were shaped as much by the limits of Spartan willingness as by the pressure of Athenian power. To a considerable extent, the League’s activities were a response to Athenian imperialism, especially in the 450s and 440s, when Athenian expansion and the treatment of its allies provoked Spartan and allied action. However, Sparta’s concerns about the helots, the rivalries among its allies and Corinth’s commercial interests also shaped the League’s conduct. The response to Athenian imperialism was the most visible driver, but not the only one. The League’s activities are therefore best understood as a response filtered through its own internal divisions and interests.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Spartan hegemony was successful for a generation, but its success was fragile, because it rested on the power of a small ruling state over unwilling allies and its dominance ended in a decisive defeat at Leuctra in 371 BCE. Lysander's victory over Athens at Aegospotami and the surrender of 404 BCE gave Sparta control of the Greek world. Agesilaus II's campaigns and the King's Peace extended that control, but they also provoked the resistance that destroyed it. The judgement is that Spartan hegemony was successful in the short term, and that its failure came from the policies that made it possible.

Lysander's role was decisive in the early years. His defeat of the Athenian fleet at Aegospotami in 405 BCE, and the subsequent siege of Athens, brought the Peloponnesian War to an end. He installed pro-Spartan governments in many of the cities and supported the regime of the Thirty at Athens, which shows how Sparta used oligarchies to secure its dominance. These policies gave Sparta control, but they relied on local collaborators and on the threat of Spartan force, and they created enemies in the cities that Sparta had defeated.

Agesilaus II, who became king in 399 BCE, pursued a more ambitious policy. His campaigns in Asia Minor against the Persians in the 390s brought him prestige, and his conduct in the Corinthian War of 395 to 387 BCE showed the resources that Sparta could mobilise. The Corinthian War was a serious challenge to Sparta, since Athens, Thebes, Corinth and Argos allied against it, and Sparta was forced to seek Persian money to continue the war. The King's Peace of 387 BCE, which was negotiated with Persia, recognised Spartan dominance and imposed its terms on the Greek states.

The King's Peace is the strongest evidence of Spartan success, because it secured the recognition of Sparta's leadership by the Persian king and the other Greek states. Yet it also revealed the price of that success. The peace depended on Persian support, and it required Sparta to enforce terms that many Greeks resented. The garrisons and pro-Spartan governments in the cities made Sparta unpopular, and its policies increased the number of states that were hostile to its rule.

The battle of Leuctra in 371 BCE, in which Epaminondas and the Theban army defeated the Spartans, ended the hegemony. The defeat showed that Sparta's army could be beaten, and the subsequent Theban liberation of Messenia destroyed the economic base of Spartan power. On balance, Spartan hegemony was successful as a system of control for a generation, but it was built on coercion and on Persian support, and its collapse at Leuctra shows that its success could not be sustained.

The judgement therefore rests on the contrast between the short-term control that Sparta achieved and the long-term instability that its methods produced, and it is this contrast that makes the hegemony a qualified success.

The judgement must also weigh the impact of the hegemony on Sparta itself. The Spartan citizen body was small and its army depended on a limited number of full citizens, while the population of the helots who worked the land was large and resentful. The demands of empire increased the strain on this system, and the commitment of troops to distant campaigns and to garrisons in the cities reduced the reserves available for the defence of Laconia. The sources suggest that Sparta's leaders were aware of these weaknesses, but they were unable to resolve the tension between imperial commitments and the limited manpower of the state. The hegemony was therefore successful for a generation, but its foundations were narrow, and the collapse at Leuctra exposed a structural weakness that had been building since the Spartan victory over Athens.

It would lift further by assessing Lysander's and Agesilaus' policies more directly against the outcome at Leuctra.

sampleAnswers.answer: The King’s Peace of 387 or 386 BCE was significant for developments in Greece between 387 and 362 BCE because it set the terms of diplomacy, gave Persia a role in Greek affairs and encouraged a system in which Sparta’s enforcement of autonomy generated new rivalries. Its importance lies less in the peace itself than in the ways its principles were used and contested. The period from 387 to 362 was shaped by the tension between autonomy and hegemony that the Peace created. The King’s Peace was brokered by the Spartan envoy Antalcidas with the support of the Persian king Artaxerxes II. Its terms recognised Persian control of the Greek cities of Asia Minor and Cyprus and declared that the other Greek cities should be autonomous, which Sparta presented as a principle of freedom but which in practice allowed Sparta to intervene against cities it chose to suppress. The Peace marked a new Persian role in Greek politics, since Persia could now set terms for the Greek states, and this role was used to balance Sparta and Athens against each other. Sparta enforced the Peace selectively and used it to strengthen its own position. It broke up the union of Mantinea in 385 BCE and seized the Theban citadel, the Cadmea, in 382 BCE, which was justified as an enforcement of autonomy but was widely seen as an abuse. Such actions were significant because they showed that the Peace could be turned against those who had accepted it, and they created resentment that Thebes later exploited. The Spartan garrison was expelled from Thebes in 379 BCE by exiles, which marked the start of Theban independence. Athens also responded to Spartan power by founding the Second Athenian Confederacy in 378 or 377 BCE. Its charter declared respect for the autonomy of its members, which echoed the Peace’s language, and the Confederacy allowed Athens to rebuild a sea power. The alliance was significant because it gave the Peace’s principles a new meaning: an anti-Spartan league could claim to defend autonomy. Thebes, meanwhile, built a Boeotian league and defeated Sparta at Leuctra in 371 BCE. Leuctra ended Spartan hegemony and was the most important consequence of the Peace’s disputed principles. The Peace also shaped the political thinking of the Greek states. The principle of autonomy allowed cities to claim the right to govern themselves, and it could be invoked against Sparta, Athens or Thebes depending on who held power. Such a principle was flexible, and its meaning shifted with each new alliance. The King’s Peace therefore created a language of diplomacy that outlasted the Peace itself, and its significance for 387 to 362 lies partly in the arguments it made possible. The King’s Peace was significant mainly as the framework within which these conflicts took place. It legitimised Persian involvement, justified Spartan interventions and gave later powers a principle to invoke. Its effects were determined by how Sparta, Athens and Thebes used the principle of autonomy, and the collapse of Spartan hegemony at Leuctra showed that it could not secure lasting order. Between 387 and 362 BCE the Peace was therefore highly significant for the shape of Greek politics, though its significance lay in the disputes it generated rather than in the stability it provided.

sampleAnswers.answer: Persian intervention was highly significant for developments in Greece in this period, because Persian money, fleets and diplomacy decided the outcome of the Corinthian War and set the terms of the peace that ended it. Yet the intervention worked through Greek rivalries, and its success depended on the conflicts that Greek states were already fighting. Sparta emerged from the Peloponnesian War as the dominant power in Greece, but its ambitions alarmed Thebes, Corinth and Athens. Sparta's commanders engaged in aggressive campaigns in Asia Minor against the Persian satrap Tissaphernes, and the Persians responded by supporting Sparta's enemies. This was the context in which Persia became the decisive external factor. In 395 BCE the Corinthian War broke out, and Thebes, Corinth and Argos joined with Athens against Sparta. The Persian satrap Tiribazus and the Persian court provided money to these states, enabling them to resist Sparta. The gold that Persia gave to the anti-Spartan coalition was the most important single factor in keeping the war going, because Sparta depended on its own resources and on the support of its allies in the Peloponnese. The Persian fleet, commanded by the Athenian Conon, decisively defeated the Spartan navy at Cnidus in 394 BCE, which ended Sparta's naval supremacy. Conon used Persian money to rebuild the Long Walls of Athens, which restored the city's defences and its political independence. This episode shows that Persian support could restore an Athenian power that had been broken by the Peloponnesian War. Persian diplomacy then shifted its policy. By the 380s BCE the Persian court wished to end the war in a way that favoured Persian interests in Asia Minor and restored Spartan power as a counterweight to Athens and Thebes. Sparta, which had suffered heavily, accepted Persian mediation, and the peace negotiated by Antalcidas in 387 or 386 BCE, known as the King's Peace, was imposed on the Greek states. Its terms required the Greek cities of Asia Minor to be handed over to Persia, and it stated that the other Greek cities should be independent. This autonomy clause gave Sparta a legal basis for intervention, because it allowed Sparta to enforce the peace and to break up federations such as the Boeotian League. The King's Peace was therefore a Persian settlement enforced by Sparta, and it shows the scale of Persian influence. The sources for Persian policy are fragmentary. Most of the evidence comes from Xenophon, who was an Athenian sympathetic to Sparta, and from Diodorus, who wrote centuries later and relied on sources of uneven quality. These writers present Greek motives and battles in detail but say little about the Persian court. The Persian role must therefore be reconstructed from the outcomes and from the few references to royal policy, and historians must acknowledge the uncertainty. The significance of Persia is also shown by the way Greek states sought its support. Athens, Thebes and Sparta all looked to Persia for money and ships, and each accepted Persian terms when it needed them. The Greek cities were therefore not independent actors in a closed system, but participants in a wider Achaemenid policy. Yet Persia could not have dictated events without Greek cooperation. The rivalries between Sparta and Thebes, and the ambitions of Athens, provided the reasons for the conflicts, and Persian gold could only sustain wars that Greek states were already determined to fight. Persian intervention was therefore a decisive amplifier of Greek conflict rather than its sole cause. The most accurate judgement is that Persian intervention was highly significant because it determined the outcome of the Corinthian War and the terms of the peace, which had lasting effects on Greek politics. Its significance lay in the combination of money, naval power and diplomatic leverage that it brought to Greek rivalries. The King's Peace shows that the Persian court could set the terms of Greek politics when it chose, and that Greek states accepted this in return for the support they needed.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The collapse of Spartan hegemony over Greece had several linked causes, but the defeat at Leuctra in 371 BCE was the decisive event that ended Sparta’s claim to dominate the Greek states. Sparta had won the Peloponnesian War in 404 BCE, yet its power rested on a small citizen body, on the subjection of the helots and Messenians, and on alliances that depended on Persian support and the good conduct of its allies. Over the following decades these weaknesses combined with Theban military innovation and the revival of Athens to end Spartan supremacy. The collapse was therefore the result of structural weakness, external pressure and a single crushing defeat.

Sparta’s structural problems were already serious before 371 BCE. The Spartan citizen body had shrunk considerably, and the Spartiates who were full citizens could not easily replace their losses. The helots, who worked the land, outnumbered the Spartans and had to be controlled by force. Sparta’s military system depended on a small elite of trained soldiers, so each defeat was costly. This shortage of manpower made it difficult for Sparta to maintain garrisons and armies across a wide region.

The Corinthian War of 395 to 387 BCE showed the limits of Spartan power. Athens, Thebes, Corinth and Argos fought against Sparta, and Persian money helped to finance the anti-Spartan alliance. The Athenian naval victory at Cnidus in 394 BCE destroyed Spartan naval power in the Aegean, and the Persian king later imposed the King’s Peace in 386 BCE. The peace allowed Sparta to keep its position in the Peloponnese, but it depended on Persian authority and on Sparta’s willingness to accept the terms, so Spartan hegemony was dependent on external support.

The Theban rise was the most direct challenge. Under Epaminondas, Thebes developed a new military approach at Leuctra, where the Theban line concentrated its strongest troops on the left and broke the Spartan army. The Spartan king Cleombrotus was killed, and the defeat shattered the myth that Spartan soldiers could not be beaten. The battle was decisive because it removed the military basis of Spartan hegemony and gave Thebes a dominant position in central Greece.

The consequences of Leuctra were far-reaching. The Thebans invaded the Peloponnese, and they liberated Messenia from Spartan rule in 369 BCE, founding the city of Messene as its new capital. This loss deprived Sparta of the fertile land that had supported its citizens and its helots for centuries. The founding of Messene was a clear sign that the old order had collapsed, and it allowed the Messenians to rebuild their identity after generations of subjection.

The battle of Mantinea in 362 BCE confirmed the collapse, although it did not restore Theban supremacy. Epaminondas was killed in the battle, and the Theban hegemony he had created did not survive him. Sparta remained a major state, but it could no longer dominate Greece, and the Greek cities moved towards a more fragmented system of alliances. The outcome showed that no single state could hold the leadership of Greece for long.

The sources for this period are uneven. Xenophon’s Hellenica is the main narrative and reflects the views of an admirer of Sparta, so its account of Spartan failures may be selective. Diodorus, writing much later, relies on earlier sources and gives a different emphasis. Theban accounts were shaped by the victors, and they stress the genius of Epaminondas. Historians must therefore weigh these accounts against each other and against the evidence of the Spartan military system.

Modern assessments differ on the relative weight of the causes. Some historians emphasise the internal weakness of Sparta, especially the shortage of citizens, while others stress the military innovations of Thebes and the role of Persia. The evidence suggests that Sparta’s structural problems made it vulnerable, but that Leuctra was the event that turned vulnerability into collapse. The battle and its consequences therefore provide the clearest explanation for the end of Spartan dominance.

Overall, the collapse of Spartan hegemony resulted from the combination of a small citizen body, the subjection of Messenia and the helots, the reliance on Persian support and the military defeat at Leuctra. The loss of Messenia and the death of the Spartan king showed that the Spartan system could no longer sustain the claim to leadership. Leuctra was the decisive turning point, but it was the product of problems that had been building for decades.
