sampleAnswers.answer: Theban hegemony ended in the 360s BCE mainly because it depended on a small number of men, above all Epaminondas, and because the states that Thebes had dominated and the rivals that it had provoked were able to combine against it after his death. The hegemony was a remarkable achievement. Thebes had been a minor power in the early fourth century, but after the King's Peace it challenged Sparta, and at Leuctra in 371 BCE the Theban army under Epaminondas defeated the Spartan army, which had been regarded as invincible on land. The victory destroyed the Spartan claim to hegemony, and Thebes was able to invade the Peloponnese, liberate Messenia and help to found Megalopolis as a counterweight to Sparta. These achievements made Thebes the dominant power in Greece for a brief period. Yet Theban hegemony rested on a narrow foundation. Thebes was a city of limited manpower, and its power depended on the leadership of Epaminondas and Pelopidas, who held office in the Boeotian federal structure and commanded its armies. The Boeotian League that Thebes led was a federation, but Thebes dominated it, and the other Boeotian cities were not always willing partners. The hegemony therefore depended on the political and military skill of its leaders and on the continued loyalty of its allies, and neither was assured. The first sign of weakness came in 364 BCE, when Pelopidas was killed at Cynoscephalae in Thessaly fighting against the tyrant of Pherae. His death removed a key commander, and it shows the strain of Theban operations beyond Boeotia. The decisive blow came at Mantinea in 362 BCE. Epaminondas led the Theban army against a coalition of Sparta, Athens and other Peloponnesian states, and he won a tactical victory, but he was killed in the battle. His death ended the Theban leadership, because no comparable figure emerged to direct Theban policy. The coalition that had opposed Thebes was then able to make peace on terms that restored the independence of the Peloponnesian states, and Thebes' allies began to drift away. The ancient sources emphasise the personal role of Epaminondas, and this emphasis is justified, because the hegemony was built on his leadership and reputation. The sources for the period are mainly Xenophon, who was hostile to Thebes, and Diodorus, who wrote centuries later. Their accounts are coloured by their own views of Thebes and of Epaminondas, and historians must treat their assessments of the hegemony with caution. Structural factors also contributed to the end of Theban power. The Theban army depended on the Sacred Band and on citizen hoplites, and it could not sustain the campaigns that the hegemony required without the support of allies. Athens resented Theban dominance of the Greek states, and Sparta, though weakened, remained a formidable force. The loss of Messenia and the spread of Theban garrisons in other states created resentment that Thebes could not contain. The rise of Macedonia was a later development, and Philip II did not become a major factor until the 350s BCE. The threat from Macedon therefore played little part in the end of the hegemony in the 360s BCE, and it is a mistake to read later events back into this period. The King's Peace of 387 or 386 BCE, which had been imposed by Persia and enforced by Sparta, had already shaped the political landscape, and Thebes' challenge to it was a result of Sparta's overreach rather than a planned revolution. Theban hegemony was therefore a product of particular circumstances, and it ended when those circumstances changed. The most accurate judgement is that the death of Epaminondas at Mantinea was the decisive event, because it removed the leadership on which the hegemony depended. The structural weaknesses of Thebes made it impossible for its successors to maintain the position, and the allies, once their confidence was lost, were willing to return to their earlier alignments. The hegemony ended not because Thebes was defeated in a single battle, but because the personal and political foundations of its power collapsed when its leader died.

To go further, weigh the structural explanation more directly against the death of Epaminondas.

sampleAnswers.answer: Epaminondas and Pelopidas were both significant to developments in Greece after 404 BCE, because together they created the Theban hegemony that broke Spartan power and dominated the Greek world for a decade. Their importance lay in complementary roles: Epaminondas was the military and political architect, while Pelopidas was a commander and diplomat who extended Theban influence. Their victory at Leuctra in 371 BCE was the turning point. Epaminondas used a deep formation on the left wing, supported by a strong force led by Pelopidas, which defeated the Spartan king Cleombrotus and the Spartan army. This defeat ended the belief that Sparta was invincible on land, and it allowed Thebes to take the lead in the Greek world. Pelopidas’ Sacred Band of picked soldiers, which he is said to have formed and which fought in pairs of lovers, was a key element in the army and reinforced the Theban military reputation. After Leuctra, Epaminondas led invasions of the Peloponnese in 370 and 369 BCE, which freed Messenia from Sparta and led to the foundation of Messene. The creation of Megalopolis in 368 BCE as a counterweight to Sparta also reflected Theban policy in the region. Epaminondas also reorganised the Boeotian League, which gave Thebes a stronger federal base and increased its military resources. Pelopidas’ diplomacy extended the hegemony beyond Greece. In 367 BCE he travelled to Persia and obtained a royal rescript that recognised Theban leadership, which increased Thebes’ prestige and gave it a useful counter to Athens and Sparta. The hegemony was fragile, however. Thebes depended on the abilities of its two leaders, and Pelopidas was killed at Cynoscephalae in 364 BCE. Epaminondas died at Mantinea in 362 BCE, a battle in which he won a tactical victory but was killed, and after his death Thebes lost its commander and its leadership. The Theban hegemony therefore depended on these two men, and its collapse showed the limits of a state built around individual leaders. The sources for these men are largely literary. Xenophon’s Hellenica is hostile to Thebes and portrays Epaminondas with some reserve, while Diodorus relies on the earlier histories and gives a more favourable picture. Plutarch’s lives of Pelopidas and Epaminondas are later and rely on anecdotes, which make the story vivid but may exaggerate. Inscriptions, including the treaties and the decrees of the Boeotian League, provide evidence for the political changes but say little about the men themselves. The leadership of both men also depended on the Boeotian federal system. Epaminondas’ reforms of the Boeotian League, including the redistribution of power among the Boeotian cities and the organisation of a common army, gave Thebes a resource base that rivals could not match, and the army could campaign in the Peloponnese for long periods. Without this federal structure, the victories at Leuctra and Mantinea would have been difficult to sustain. The Theban position was also reinforced by the divisions between Athens and Sparta, which prevented a common peace and allowed Thebes to exploit their rivalry. Epaminondas also transformed the Theban army. He used a deeper formation on the left, which gave the Theban attack decisive weight at Leuctra, and he trained the army to hold together over long campaigns. These changes were reflected in the Theban victories of the 360s, while Pelopidas’ political role at home kept Thebes united during the campaigns abroad. The combination of military innovation and political leadership gave Thebes a short-lived ascendancy, which ended once the two men were lost. Taken together, Epaminondas and Pelopidas were significant because they transformed a minor Boeotian city into the leading power of Greece, creating the hegemony that ended Spartan dominance, though its fragility shows that their achievements depended on their own lives and abilities.

Their victory at Leuctra in 371 BCE, in which the Sacred Band under Pelopidas played a part, broke Spartan power on land. Epaminondas then invaded the Peloponnese, freed Messenia and helped found Messene and Megalopolis, while Pelopidas’ mission to Persia recognised Theban leadership. However, the hegemony depended on the two leaders. Pelopidas died in 364 BCE and Epaminondas at Mantinea in 362 BCE, and after their deaths Thebes lost its power. The sources, especially Xenophon and Plutarch, present the men with different degrees of bias. The character of Theban leadership also explains its fragility. Epaminondas built his policy around the Boeotian League and a small group of trusted commanders, while Pelopidas led the Sacred Band and conducted diplomacy in Persia. The hegemony was held together by the personal authority of these men and by the fear that Sparta would recover, so when they died, the Theban federal structure had no leader of comparable standing. The Boeotian cities also resented Theban domination, and their loyalty could not be assumed.  Epaminondas’ tactical innovations at Leuctra and Mantinea showed that the Theban army could defeat the Spartan hoplites, and his reorganisation of the Boeotian League made the military gains durable for a time. Pelopidas’ diplomacy in Persia, which won royal recognition of Theban leadership in 367 BCE, gave the hegemony an international standing that Sparta and Athens could not easily ignore.

sampleAnswers.answer: Philip II was a highly successful Macedonian king, and by the standards of his time his achievements were exceptional. He restored a kingdom that was close to collapse, built an army that could defeat the Greek city-states, and laid the foundations for his son’s conquest of Persia. His success was not complete, however. His control over Greece rested on force and alliances that depended on his personal authority, and his assassination left his kingdom to a succession crisis. Philip came to the throne in 359 BCE in a kingdom threatened by Illyrian and Thracian enemies and by rival claimants, and he acted quickly to secure his position. He first served as regent for his nephew and then took the throne himself, using the army’s support to deal with rivals. His kingship drew on Macedonian traditions of personal leadership, and his skill as a commander and diplomat allowed him to build a stable state from a fragile inheritance. Philip’s reforms of the army were central to his success. He developed the phalanx with longer spears, the sarissa, and professional soldiers who were paid and trained, which gave the Macedonian army a flexibility that combined infantry and cavalry. His expansion followed: Amphipolis was taken in 357 BCE, Methone in 354 BCE, where he lost an eye, and the Chalcidian city of Olynthus in 348 BCE. These conquests secured Macedonia’s resources, especially timber and silver, and made Philip the dominant power in the north Aegean. Philip’s relations with Greece were built on diplomacy as well as force. The Peace of Philocrates in 346 BCE recognised his position, and he used the Third Sacred War to extend his influence into central Greece. The decisive victory at Chaeronea in 338 BCE over the Athenians and Thebans brought the main Greek resistance under his control, and the League of Corinth in 337 BCE gave him a formal leadership of Greece. Yet Philip’s position depended on his army and on the willingness of Greek states to accept his terms, and Demosthenes’ opposition shows that resistance remained strong until the end. Philip’s success also depended on his handling of his court and his neighbours. He used marriage alliances, rewards and the threat of force to bind the Macedonian nobility and the peoples of the north to his rule, and his diplomacy with Thessaly and Thrace gave him security while he campaigned in the south. These arrangements show that his kingship was more than military strength: it was a system of loyalty that held the kingdom together and allowed his conquests to be sustained. Philip’s limits were significant. His attempts on Perinthus and Byzantium in 340 BCE failed, and his Greek policy was never fully accepted. His assassination in 336 BCE, at the wedding of his daughter at Aegae, showed that his court was not secure, and the succession passed to Alexander without a settled structure. Still, Philip’s achievements were remarkable: he transformed a weak kingdom into the strongest power in the Greek world and created the army and resources that Alexander used. Judged as a king, his success was very substantial, though his greatest ambitions were completed by his son.

sampleAnswers.answer: Philip II was a successful Macedonian king because he made Macedon the strongest state in Greece. He came to the throne in 359 BCE when the kingdom was in trouble, and he dealt with rivals and enemies. His army reforms were important. He trained a phalanx with long spears and paid his soldiers. This army allowed him to win battles, such as the battle of Chaeronea in 338 BCE, where he defeated the Athenians and Thebans. Philip also took many cities, including Amphipolis and Olynthus, and he gained control of silver mines. He also made a treaty with Athens in 346 BCE. These achievements show he was a successful king. His reign was also significant for the way he used Macedon’s resources. Control of mines and the revenue from new territories gave him money to pay the army and to outlast his rivals. This financial basis is one reason his achievements lasted beyond the campaigns that won them. However, Philip was murdered in 336 BCE, so his plans were not completed. Alexander then carried them out. So Philip was successful, but his son achieved the most.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Macedon rose to dominance in Greece because of a combination of royal authority, military reform and diplomacy, and the accession of Philip II in 359 BCE was the turning point. The Macedonian kingdom had long been a regional power on the northern edge of the Greek world, but it had been weakened by civil war, invasion and rival claims to the throne. Philip used his position to unify the kingdom, to reform its army and to exploit the divisions among the Greek states. The rise of Macedon was therefore the product of personal leadership and structural strength, although the most decisive step was the victory at Chaeronea in 338 BCE.

The nature of Macedonian kingship was central to its strength. The Argead kings ruled through personal authority, supported by a nobility of landowners and companions who served in the royal army. The king’s relationship with the nobles was based on shared service and loyalty, and the army assembly could acclaim or reject a new king. This structure gave the monarchy strength, because it could mobilise the aristocracy and the peasant soldiers, but it also created the risk of rival claims to the throne. Philip’s accession was made possible by the death of his brother Perdiccas III in battle, and he took power when the kingdom faced invasion and disorder.

Philip’s military reforms were a decisive factor. He reorganised the army around a heavy infantry formation, the phalanx, armed with a long spear called the sarissa, and he supplemented it with cavalry and skirmishers. Training and discipline were improved, and the phalanx became a flexible force that could hold a front and then strike decisively. These reforms gave Macedon an army that could defeat the Greek city-state armies in open battle, and they allowed Philip to campaign across a wide area.

Diplomacy and conquest were equally important. Philip extended Macedonian control over Amphipolis, which gave access to the gold and timber of the region, and he used marriages, alliances and bribery to secure the cooperation of rival rulers. His marriage to Olympias, the daughter of the king of Epirus, created an alliance with a neighbouring power, and the birth of Alexander strengthened the dynasty. These policies allowed Philip to expand Macedon without relying solely on force.

Demosthenes, the Athenian orator, warned against Philip in a series of speeches known as the Philippics, and his speeches show how Athenians viewed the growing power of Macedon. These speeches are a valuable source for Athenian fears, but Demosthenes was an opponent who wanted to rally Athens against Philip, so his portrayal of the king is partisan. The speeches reveal the anxieties of Athens rather than a neutral account of Macedonian policy.

The evidence of Diodorus, writing centuries later, supplements the picture, although his account depends on earlier sources. Diodorus presents Philip’s growing dominance as the result of his ability and his use of the army, and he records the sequence of campaigns that brought Thessaly, Thrace and the cities of the north under Macedonian control. These accounts are useful for the chronology of the rise, but they tend to present the king as the sole architect of Macedonian success.

The battle of Chaeronea in 338 BCE was the decisive step. Philip defeated a combined army of Athenians and Thebans, and his son Alexander is said to have commanded the cavalry on one wing. The victory gave Philip control over central Greece, and it allowed him to create the League of Corinth in 337 BCE, which made the Greek states subject to his leadership. This settlement was the clearest sign that Macedon had become the dominant power in Greece.

Modern historians debate how far the rise of Macedon depended on Philip’s personal qualities and how far it reflected the strengths of the Macedonian state. The evidence suggests that both were important, since Philip used the existing structures of kingship and the army, but reshaped them. The structural strength of the kingdom gave him the means, and his leadership gave the means their purpose.

Overall, the rise of Macedon was the result of a monarchy that could mobilise its army, a king who reformed that army and diplomacy that exploited Greek divisions. Philip’s accession in 359 BCE began the process, and the victory at Chaeronea completed it. The rise was therefore driven by Philip’s leadership, but it depended on the strength of the Macedonian kingship and the army that sustained it.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Changes in Greek warfare were highly influential in the developments in Greece and Macedon from 404 BCE, because they altered the balance of power between the city-states and the Macedonian kingdom. In the early fourth century, the traditional hoplite phalanx of citizen-soldiers was challenged by new tactics. Epaminondas of Thebes, at the battle of Leuctra in 371 BCE, used a deeper formation on his left and defeated the Spartan army, which showed that the old Spartan dominance could be broken. These innovations encouraged the Greek states to rely on more specialised forces, but many city-states were unable to sustain the expense and the discipline that the new methods required.

Philip II transformed these developments into a decisive advantage for Macedon. He reorganised the Macedonian army around a longer pike, the sarissa, which allowed his phalanx to hold a line against opponents, and he combined this infantry with cavalry and light troops in coordinated attacks. The professional, well-paid army that Philip built could fight throughout the year, and it could be sustained by the wealth of Macedon and the gold of its mines. This allowed Philip to campaign effectively against the Greek cities and to exploit their rivalries.

The victory at Chaeronea in 338 BCE demonstrated the effect of these changes. Philip’s army defeated the combined forces of Athens and Thebes, and the battle ended the independence of the Greek states in any real sense. The military innovations had therefore made Macedon the dominant power, and the city-states lost the ability to resist. The Greek states could not match Macedonian armies in organisation or numbers, and this led to the creation of the League of Corinth under Philip’s leadership.

However, the influence of changes in warfare must be weighed against political factors. The Greek cities were divided by rivalries, and Philip used diplomacy, bribery and marriage alliances as well as force. The changes in warfare gave Macedon the means to win, but the political divisions of the Greek world made the outcome possible. Warfare was the decisive instrument, but it worked through the weaknesses of the city-states.

The changes also affected the internal politics of the Greek states. Armies that relied on professional soldiers and mercenaries were expensive, and the cities that tried to keep up with the new methods often fell into debt or faction. Macedon, with its mines and its royal control of the army, did not face the same constraints. The gap between Macedonian and Greek forces therefore widened, and this helped Philip to exploit the divisions between the city-states, as the diplomacy of the 340s BCE shows.

The judgement can be tested against the record of the Greek states’ responses. Several cities tried to build professional forces and fortify their positions, but the expense was heavy and the discipline difficult to maintain. Athens relied on mercenaries and on its navy, while Thebes depended on the skill of a few commanders. Macedon, by contrast, combined royal control of the army with the resources of its mines and its agricultural land. The result was that the changes in warfare favoured the state with the most unified command, and this helped Macedon to shape the politics of the south.

Overall, changes in Greek warfare were the most important influence on developments in Greece and Macedon in this period, because they gave Macedon a military advantage that the city-states could not match. The reforms of Philip II and the example of Leuctra transformed the balance of power, and the battle of Chaeronea confirmed that the age of the independent polis was ending.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Philip's reforms of the army were central to the rise of Macedon, but they were not sufficient on their own. Hugh Bowden argues that Philip transformed the fortunes of Macedonia in less than three years through diplomacy, military reorganisation and skilled generalship, and that the extent of his personal responsibility for the army's innovations is debated. The judgement is that the army reforms were the most important single factor, because they gave Macedon a military advantage that its rivals could not match, but they worked alongside diplomacy and financial measures. Without the army, the diplomacy would have had less force; without diplomacy, the army would have had fewer opportunities to act.

The reforms of the infantry were decisive. Philip reorganised the Macedonian infantry around the phalanx and equipped the front ranks with a longer pike, the sarissa, which allowed a deep formation to present a wall of points. Training was made more regular, and soldiers were paid, which encouraged loyalty and discipline. The phalanx could hold ground against opponents who relied on the hoplite spear, and the combination of this infantry with a strong companion cavalry gave Philip a flexible force. These innovations were not invented wholly by Philip, but he organised and exploited them more effectively than any predecessor.

The battle of Chaeronea in 338 BCE shows what the reforms achieved. The Macedonian army defeated the combined forces of Athens and Thebes, which had been the strongest military powers in Greece. The victory was decisive for the rise of Macedon, because it gave Philip authority over the Greek states and allowed him to establish the League of Corinth. The battle depended on the infantry and the cavalry working together under Philip's command, and it demonstrated that the reforms had produced an army capable of defeating the best of the Greek hoplites.

Diplomacy was equally important. Bowden emphasises that Philip used marriage alliances, bribery and the exploitation of rivalries among the Greek states to weaken his opponents before they fought. Philip's control of Thrace, the Chalcidice and the gold mines of Mount Pangaeus gave him resources that paid for the army and bought allies. These measures show that military reform was one part of a broader strategy, and that the rise of Macedon depended on the combination of force and political manoeuvre.

The debate over Philip's predecessors qualifies his personal responsibility. Earlier Macedonian kings had already begun to modernise the army, and some of the innovations may have been introduced before Philip came to the throne in 359 BCE. Bowden notes that some of the changes may have been completed by Alexander, which means that Philip's reforms were the starting point of a longer process. The evidence for these developments is limited and largely derived from later writers, so historians must be cautious about attributing everything to Philip alone.

On balance, Philip's army reforms were largely responsible for the rise of Macedon, because they provided the military instrument that made his victories possible. However, the reforms were part of a wider strategy that included diplomacy, finance and the exploitation of Greek divisions. The judgement is that the reforms were essential but not sufficient, and that the rise of Macedon was the result of a combination of military, political and financial measures under a single ruler.

The reforms also need to be seen in the context of the Macedonian kingdom's finances. Philip's control of the gold mines of Mount Pangaeus gave him the wealth to pay soldiers and to maintain a professional army, which was a condition of the reforms. Without the resources, the infantry could not have been equipped and trained on the scale that Chaeronea required. The reforms and the finances were therefore linked, and Philip's ability to combine them made Macedon the strongest state in the north.

sampleAnswers.answer: Macedonian expansion into Greece was effective because Philip II combined diplomacy and war in a way that allowed him to isolate his enemies and defeat them one at a time, though war was the decisive instrument in the final stage. When Philip came to the throne in 359 BCE, Macedonia was weak and surrounded by enemies. He reformed the army, creating a disciplined phalanx armed with the long sarissa and supported by cavalry and light infantry, and this gave him the military force to act decisively. His use of diplomacy was equally important. He made alliances, paid bribes and exploited the rivalries of the Greek states, which allowed him to intervene in disputes without facing a united opposition. In the Third Sacred War, from 356 to 346 BCE, he presented himself as the defender of the god’s sanctuary at Delphi, which gave him a religious justification for intervening in central Greece. The Peace of Philocrates in 346 BCE with Athens was a diplomatic triumph, because it recognised his gains and allowed him to strike at other enemies while Athens was distracted. The destruction of Olynthus in 348 BCE was the decisive war of this phase, since the city’s fall ended the Chalcidian League and removed a rival power in northern Greece. Diplomacy and war thus worked together, with each supporting the other. However, the effectiveness of diplomacy had limits. Athenian and Theban resistance was stubborn, and Demosthenes’ Philippics warned repeatedly against the danger of Philip’s growing power. The final test came at Chaeronea in 338 BCE, when Philip defeated an alliance of Athens and Thebes. Here war was decisive, because the victory removed the last effective opposition in mainland Greece. After Chaeronea, Philip formed the League of Corinth in 337 BCE, which united most Greek states under his leadership and gave his expansion a legal and institutional form. The League combined diplomacy with compulsion, since its members were bound to accept Macedonian hegemony. This shows that Philip’s effectiveness depended on the combination of the two methods, with diplomacy creating the conditions for war and war securing the results of diplomacy. The sources for this period are partly Athenian. Demosthenes’ speeches are passionate and partisan, and they present Philip as a threat that Athens failed to meet. Diodorus and Justin, writing later, describe the campaigns in more neutral terms but rely on earlier histories. Inscriptions, including the treaty texts and the decrees of the League of Corinth, provide direct evidence of the diplomatic arrangements. The Macedonian kingdom’s resources also explain the effectiveness of Philip’s methods. Macedonia had timber, grain and access to the gold and silver mines of Mount Pangaeus, which Philip exploited to pay soldiers and to reward the Greek leaders who supported him. Diplomacy depended on these resources as much as on the army, and the combination of gold and force made his expansion more effective than the rival alliances of the Greek city-states, which lacked a unified command or an equivalent treasury. Philip’s diplomacy also depended on his ability to offer terms that rivals could accept. The Peace of Philocrates allowed Athens to keep its territory while accepting the gains Philip had already made, and it gave Philip time to campaign against his other enemies. Diplomacy therefore bought freedom of action rather than settling every dispute, and the war that followed showed that Philip was ready to use force when talks failed. Taken together, diplomacy and war were both effective, but war was decisive in its final results, because Chaeronea and the destruction of Olynthus ended the resistance that diplomacy alone could not overcome. Philip’s expansion was therefore a combined strategy in which diplomacy prepared the ground and war completed the conquest.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The Macedonian expansion under Philip II had a profound impact on Greece, because it ended the independence of the major city-states and created a new political order in which Macedon led the Greek world. Philip used diplomacy and war together, and the combination was more effective than either alone. The judgement is that the impact was decisive and lasting: the autonomy that the Greek states had enjoyed for centuries was lost, even though the Greeks retained their cultural life and their local institutions. The Macedonian settlement shaped the Greek world for the following generation, and it prepared the ground for Alexander's conquests.

Philip's early expansion was built on diplomacy and opportunism. He took advantage of the divisions among the Greek states and the weakness of Athens and Thebes, and he used alliances, marriages and bribery to advance his interests. His seizure of Amphipolis and his conflicts with the cities of Chalcidice brought Macedonian power to the northern Aegean. The Peace of Philocrates in 346 BCE, which Athens accepted, recognised his position in the north and gave him a status that Athenian politicians had difficulty opposing.

The war against Olynthus was the most decisive act of force before Chaeronea. Olynthus, a powerful city of the Chalcidic League, resisted Philip, and the Athenians sent help that proved insufficient. Philip captured and destroyed the city in 348 BCE, and its population was enslaved or dispersed. The destruction showed the Greek states that resistance could be fatal, and it made Philip's threat real in the minds of their leaders. Demosthenes' speeches against Philip, the Olynthiacs and the Philippics, expressed the alarm of Athens and the call for resistance.

The battle of Chaeronea in 338 BCE ended organised resistance. Philip defeated an alliance of Athens and Thebes, and his victory opened the way to the settlement that followed. The League of Corinth, formed in 337 BCE, brought the Greek states into a union under Macedonian leadership. Its members swore not to change their constitutions, and the league's purpose was to support Philip's campaign against Persia. The independence of the Greek cities was thereby reduced to a formal autonomy within a system controlled from Pella.

On balance, the Macedonian expansion transformed Greece. Diplomacy gave Philip the means to divide and control his rivals, war gave him the decisive force, and the League of Corinth made his leadership permanent. The impact on Greek autonomy was profound, but the Greek states retained their cities, their cultural achievements and their local institutions, and these survived the Macedonian domination. The expansion therefore changed the political order of Greece without destroying its civilisation, and it created the foundation for Alexander's campaign against Persia.

Taken together, the evidence shows that the impact of Macedonian expansion was a fundamental change in the structure of Greek political life, and the judgement rests on that change rather than on any single battle or treaty.

The judgement must also consider the internal consequences of Macedonian expansion for the Greek states. Many cities were governed by pro-Macedonian factions, and political life in them was shaped by the need to deal with Pella. The Greek citizens who opposed Philip were exiled or executed, and the states that resisted lost their leaders. This political reorganisation changed the nature of civic life, because the old debates between democrats and oligarchs were now conducted in the shadow of an external power. Yet the Macedonian settlement also brought a degree of peace after decades of warfare between the Greek states, and some Greeks welcomed the order that Philip provided. A reasoned judgement recognises both the loss of autonomy and the experience of order, and it concludes that the impact of Macedonian expansion was profound for the political structure of Greece, even if its cultural life continued.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 21-25 row: a perceptive judgement that weighs the loss of autonomy against the survival of Greek culture, with evidence from Amphipolis, the Peace of Philocrates, Olynthus, Chaeronea and the League of Corinth. It would lift further by evaluating Demosthenes' Philippics more critically as a partisan source.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The Macedonian expansion under Philip II had a major impact on Greece, because it ended the independence of the leading city-states and placed the Greek world under Macedonian leadership. Philip used diplomacy and war together. The destruction of Olynthus in 348 BCE and the defeat at Chaeronea in 338 BCE showed that resistance was dangerous, and the League of Corinth organised the Greek states under Macedon.

The impact was real, although the Greek states kept their cities and their culture. Demosthenes' speeches show the alarm of Athens, and the Peace of Philocrates recognised Philip's position in the north. The judgement is that Macedonian expansion ended Greek autonomy, but it did not end the civilisation of the Greek cities, and this made it a lasting but not complete transformation.

The destruction of Olynthus and the victory at Chaeronea showed Greek states that resistance could be fatal, and the League of Corinth then gave Philip a permanent framework to lead them. Demosthenes' speeches reveal the alarm of Athens at this loss of independence.

The judgement is that the expansion was decisive for the political order of Greece, because it ended the independence of the leading states. The Greek cultural life survived, but the cities were now subject to a power that controlled their foreign policy.

The Peace of Philocrates shows how diplomacy could secure Philip's interests without a formal conquest, and this approach made the Greek states more inclined to accept his leadership.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Demosthenes was only partly successful in opposing Philip II. He was one of the most effective orators of his age, and his speeches, the Philippics and the Olynthiacs, persuaded many Athenians to resist Philip’s expansion. However, he was unable to prevent Philip’s growth of power, and his greatest opposition ended in defeat at Chaeronea in 338 BCE. His success therefore lay in rhetoric and mobilising opinion, while his failure lay in the military and political conditions that favoured Macedon.

Demosthenes’ achievements were considerable. In the Olynthiacs of 349 BCE he urged Athens to support the city of Olynthus against Philip, and his arguments encouraged the Athenians to send help, although the city was eventually destroyed in 348 BCE. In the Philippics, delivered over the following years, he argued for a consistent policy of resistance and for the strengthening of Athens’ military. His speeches made the threat of Macedon a central issue in the Athenian Assembly, and they shaped the opinions of the citizens who voted on policy.

However, his opposition was constrained by Athenian divisions. Many Athenians distrusted war and preferred the peace that Philip offered, and the Peace of Philocrates in 346 BCE was accepted partly because of this preference. Demosthenes himself had opposed that peace, but he could not prevent the Assembly from accepting it, and Philip used it to strengthen his position in central Greece. The failure to stop Philip was therefore not only Demosthenes’ failure but a result of the Athenians’ own reluctance and the Macedonian army’s superior strength.

The defeat at Chaeronea in 338 BCE was the decisive point. Athens and Thebes fought together against Philip, and they were defeated. Demosthenes had persuaded the Athenians to fight, and his policy was vindicated in the sense that Athens had resisted, but the outcome showed that the alliance he sought could not overcome Macedonian power. His success in rousing Athens did not extend to the military achievement that would have checked Philip.

Demosthenes’ speeches also had a longer-term effect on the Athenian political culture. He presented the struggle against Philip as a defence of freedom and of the democratic order, and this message remained powerful in Athens long after the defeat. Its influence shows that his success lay as much in shaping the values of the citizens as in the immediate policy outcomes, although the failure at Chaeronea limited the practical value of that influence.

The judgement can be tested by the length of Demosthenes’ opposition. He began to warn the Athenians about Philip in the 350s BCE and continued for more than a decade, and this persistence kept the question of resistance alive when many Athenians wanted to avoid war. His policy was not consistent in every detail, and his speeches show a shifting balance between diplomacy and force. The verdict on his success depends on whether one values the sustained public argument or the failure of the policy, and a balanced judgement must consider both.

Overall, Demosthenes was successful in opposing Philip in the sense that he shaped Athenian resistance and kept the issue before the Assembly, but he was unable to stop Macedon’s expansion. His rhetoric was effective, but the political divisions of Athens and the strength of Philip’s army limited what he could achieve.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Sulla’s legacy was highly significant for political developments in the late Republic, because his dictatorship and his use of the army set precedents that shaped the conflicts of the following decades. In 82 BCE Sulla marched on Rome with his legions after the civil war with Marius and his supporters, and he was appointed dictator to restore order. He used proscriptions to eliminate his opponents and reformed the constitution to strengthen the Senate. His reforms increased the number of senators, limited the powers of the tribunate and fixed the order of public offices. These measures were designed to restore the traditional authority of the Senate, and they were the most direct expression of his legacy.

However, the most important element of his legacy was the precedent of military force in politics. Sulla had shown that a commander with an army loyal to him could take Rome and govern by force, and this example was followed by later generals. Marius had already used the army for political purposes, and Sulla’s march on Rome made the link between armies and politics permanent. Pompey, Crassus and Caesar all relied on the loyalty of their soldiers, and the civil wars of the late Republic were shaped by this model. The legacy of Sulla was therefore less his constitutional settlement than the practice of using legions for political ends.

The constitutional reforms did not survive in their original form. Sulla resigned the dictatorship in 79 BCE and died in 78 BCE, and the tribunes regained their powers within a decade. The Senate found that its authority depended on the cooperation of ambitious men, and it could not control the generals who commanded the armies. The reforms were therefore a short-term settlement that did not address the underlying tensions of the Republic, such as the power of military commanders and the competition for office.

The legacy of Sulla also extended to the institutions of the Senate. He increased its membership and gave senators a clear role in the courts and in the public offices, which was meant to restore the traditional leadership of the aristocracy. These changes showed the conservative purpose of his reforms, but they did not give the Senate control over its own members or over the generals who commanded the armies, and this gap contributed to the crises of the following decades.

The judgement can be tested by the later use of Sulla’s example. Pompey and Caesar each claimed to be following a precedent of military order or of settling the state, and the image of Sulla as the general who had restored the Senate by force was invoked by later politicians on both sides. The legacy was therefore not a fixed set of laws but a model of behaviour, and its significance lay in how others interpreted it. The judgement that Sulla’s example mattered more than his reforms is supported by the way his successors used it.

Overall, Sulla’s legacy was very significant for political developments in the late Republic, but its significance lay more in the precedent of military dictatorship than in the constitutional reforms he introduced. The reforms were quickly undone, while the example of Sulla’s march on Rome shaped the political conflicts that led to the end of the Republic.

sampleAnswers.answer: Pompey was a highly influential figure in the political developments of the late Republic, but he was not the most significant individual, because his power depended on commands and alliances that were granted or undermined by others. His rise was built on loyalty to Sulla in the civil wars of the 80s BCE, and on his success in the Sertorian War in Spain, which earned him the title of Magnus and made him a useful military figure for the Senate. His consulship of 70 BCE, held with Crassus, restored the powers of the tribunes that Sulla had reduced, which shows his willingness to work with popular politicians. The extraordinary commands that followed made Pompey the most powerful commander in the Roman world. The lex Gabinia of 67 BCE gave him control of the Mediterranean to suppress piracy, and the lex Manilia of 66 BCE gave him the Mithridatic command in the East. He defeated Mithridates, reorganised the eastern provinces and established the Eastern Settlement of 62 BCE, which regulated the kingdoms and cities of the region. These achievements were significant, but they also revealed the weakness of the Senate. When Pompey returned to Italy in 62 BCE, the Senate delayed ratifying his settlement and refused land for his veterans. This was a political mistake, because it drove Pompey into an alliance with the men who could deliver what he wanted. The First Triumvirate of 60 BCE, which united Pompey, Caesar and Crassus, was a private arrangement that bypassed the Senate, and it made Pompey dependent on Caesar's consulship and on Caesar's subsequent command in Gaul. Caesar's influence was therefore greater than Pompey's in the years that followed. Caesar's Gallic campaigns brought him wealth, loyal troops and political standing, and they allowed him to challenge the Senate on terms Pompey could not match. Pompey's marriage to Caesar's daughter Julia in 59 BCE bound the two men, and Julia's death in 54 BCE removed the link that had kept the alliance together. Pompey drifted towards the Senate in the following years, and his appointment as sole consul in 52 BCE, after the disorder caused by the murder of Clodius, showed that the Senate now looked to him as a defender of order against Caesar. This position made Pompey the leader of the Senate's resistance, but it also meant that he became the focus of Caesar's ambition. When Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE, Pompey's forces were not prepared, and he withdrew from Italy. His defeat at Pharsalus in 48 BCE and his death in Egypt show that his authority rested on the military resources of the commands he had been granted, and that these were no longer sufficient. The political developments of the late Republic were therefore shaped by many individuals and by structural problems. Sulla's precedent of using armies for political ends, the Senate's refusal to accommodate its leading men and the growing wealth and ambition of commanders all contributed to the crisis. Crassus' wealth and his Parthian campaign, which ended in defeat at Carrhae in 53 BCE, removed a key member of the triumvirate, and Cicero and Cato defended the Senate's authority with different methods. Pompey's significance lay in his extraordinary commands, which gave him unmatched resources, and in his alliances, which shaped the balance of power for a decade. His significance was real, but it was a product of the opportunities that the Senate and the political system gave him, and Caesar used those opportunities more effectively. The most accurate judgement is that Pompey was one of the most influential figures in the political developments of the late Republic, but that he was not the most significant individual, because Caesar's ambition, the Senate's failures and the precedents of the civil wars were more decisive. Pompey's career illustrates how the Republic's system of commands and alliances could make a single man powerful, but it also shows how little that power could withstand a rival with greater resources and a clearer purpose.

sampleAnswers.answer: Pompey’s extraordinary commands were significant to developments in the late Republic, because each command set a precedent that weakened the constitutional limits of the Senate and magistracies, and each brought him power that he could use against his rivals. The first of these was the lex Gabinia of 67 BCE, which gave Pompey an extraordinary command against the pirates across the Mediterranean, with wide powers over the coast and the seas. The law was passed despite the Senate’s opposition, and its success showed that the popular assemblies could grant a commander powers that the Senate had refused. The command was completed within months, and it made Pompey popular with the people and with the eastern provinces. The lex Manilia of 66 BCE then gave him the command against Mithridates VI of Pontus, with authority over the east that the Senate had not been able to prevent. This command led to the Eastern Settlement of 63 BCE, which reorganised the eastern provinces and client kingdoms, and it made Pompey the most powerful man in the Roman world. The commands also gave Pompey a military following that was loyal to him, which was a source of future conflict with the Senate. The consulship of 70 BCE, which Pompey held with Crassus, had already shown that he could use the people’s assemblies to restore the powers of the tribunes and overturn the Sullan constitution, so the commands built on this political success. The significance of the commands for the late Republic lies in the precedent they set. The Senate had previously granted extraordinary commands in emergencies, but Pompey’s commands were given by the people in defiance of the senatorial establishment, and this made the Republic’s constitutional order less stable. Caesar followed the precedent with his Gallic command, and this made the extraordinary command the basis of military power in the civil wars. The Eastern Settlement also gave Pompey the resources to recruit clients and wealth that he later used in the civil war. However, Pompey himself did not seek to overthrow the Republic, and his commands were not an attempt at monarchy. He sought recognition for his achievements, and the Senate’s refusal to ratify the Eastern Settlement drove him into alliance with Caesar. The sources for the commands are largely Roman. Cicero, who supported the lex Manilia, presents Pompey favourably, while Plutarch’s life of Pompey, written later, portrays him as a great general. Dio provides a fuller narrative, but he writes with hindsight. Inscriptions and coins provide some evidence of Pompey’s eastern settlement and his military achievements. Pompey’s command also changed the relationship between the military and the state. The soldiers recruited for the eastern campaign owed their loyalty to Pompey personally, and the land grants he requested for them became a political issue when the Senate refused to ratify his settlement. The refusal to provide land for his veterans was a central reason Pompey turned to Caesar in 60 BCE, and the alliance showed how personal armies could be used to pressure the Senate. The commands also show the limits of Pompey’s own aims. He did not use his power to overthrow the Senate, and he accepted a triumph in 61 BCE under the constitutional settlement. But the Senate’s refusal to ratify the arrangements of his eastern command created a grievance that made him vulnerable to rivals who wanted to limit his influence. His decision to work with Caesar shows how the commands had created an incentive for alliance rather than independence. Taken together, Pompey’s extraordinary commands were significant because they showed that the people could grant great power outside the Senate’s control, and they created the military and financial basis for the civil wars. Their significance was therefore structural, even though Pompey’s own aims were conservative.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Cicero was significant in the political developments of the late Republic, but his significance lies less in his success than in the way he defined the political debates of his age. Kathryn Tempest argues that Cicero's reputation has suffered because he often backed the losing side, that his political beliefs have been seen as short-sighted and that he offered no effective solutions to the pressing needs of his times. These criticisms have some force, but they measure him by outcomes alone. Cicero's consulship, his speeches and his later writings shaped the terms of the political argument, and his influence on the Republic's final crisis was considerable. On balance, Cicero was a central figure whose importance came from his voice in the debates, even though his political strategy often failed.

Cicero's most important early moment was his consulship in 63 BCE, when he exposed and suppressed the Catilinarian conspiracy. His speeches against Catiline, and his decision to have the conspirators executed without a trial, presented him as the defender of the Republic against revolution. This claim of protection shaped his career, but the execution of citizens without trial later led to his exile in 58 BCE, when his opponents passed a law against him. The episode shows both the strength and the vulnerability of his political position, and it made him an important symbol of the conflict between the senate and popular politicians.

Cicero's political beliefs were rooted in the ideal of the concord of the orders, in which the senate and the equestrian order worked together under the authority of the best men, the optimates. This was a conservative vision, and Tempest is right that it had little to offer the urban poor or the military leaders who came to dominate the Republic. Yet the ideal shaped Cicero's speeches and his political writings, which set out a theory of the state that later generations read as a justification of the Republic. Significance can come from a coherent argument even when it is not adopted in practice.

Cicero's choices in the civil wars illustrate the difficulties of his position. He joined Pompey in the conflict with Caesar, and after Pharsalus he accepted Caesar's pardon and returned to political life, though he kept his distance from the dictator's politics. His Philippics against Mark Antony in 44 and 43 BCE were an attack on the new power of Antony and a defence of the Republic. Antony's agents murdered him in 43 BCE, and his head and hands were displayed in Rome, which shows how seriously his opponents took his influence. This final act made him a martyr of the Republic in the eyes of many contemporaries.

The evidence for Cicero is unusually rich, because his letters, speeches and treatises survive in large numbers. This makes him one of the best sources for the late Republic, though the letters were written to private correspondents and reflect his moods and self-interest. A historian must therefore weigh his own presentation of events against the record of his actions. Tempest's critique is valuable because it shows how his self-presentation shaped the judgement of later writers.

On balance, Cicero was highly significant in the political developments of the late Republic. His consulship, his exile, his writings and his opposition to Antony all shaped the debates of his time and the understanding of the Republic that followed. His political beliefs were often impractical, and his strategy repeatedly failed, but his significance lies in the way he articulated the values of the Republic and in the influence he had on those who followed.

Cicero's significance is also visible in the way later generations read the late Republic. His letters and speeches provide much of what we know about the period, so his own presentation shaped how the crisis was understood. His defence of the senate's authority and his denunciation of Antony became a model for opponents of tyranny. Tempest's critique is valid, but it must be balanced against the lasting influence of his writings. Cicero was not a successful politician in the sense of achieving his aims, but he was a central figure whose words shaped the debate over the Republic.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The First Triumvirate played a more significant role than the Second Triumvirate in the fall of the Roman Republic, because it created the political conditions for civil war, whereas the Second Triumvirate completed the work of destroying the Republic’s institutions. The First Triumvirate, formed in 60 BCE, was a private agreement between Pompey, Crassus and Caesar. Caesar obtained the consulship in 59 BCE with the support of Pompey and Crassus, and then received command of Gaul, which gave him an army and a power base. The agreement allowed the three men to override the Senate, and it shaped the politics of the following decade.

The Triumvirate’s significance lay in the military commands that followed. Caesar’s conquest of Gaul made him the most powerful commander in the Republic, and the wealth and loyalty of his army gave him a means to challenge the Senate. Pompey’s command in Spain and his later alliance with the Senate created a rivalry with Caesar, and Crassus’ death at Carrhae in 53 BCE removed the balance that had held the agreement together. The breakdown of the alliance led directly to Caesar’s crossing of the Rubicon in 49 BCE and to the civil war between Caesar and Pompey.

The Second Triumvirate, formed in 43 BCE between Octavian, Antony and Lepidus, was given a legal basis to rule for five years, and it used this authority to carry out proscriptions that killed many senators and supporters of the Republic. Its role was decisive in ending the remaining opposition, including the forces of Brutus and Cassius, who were defeated at Philippi in 42 BCE. The Second Triumvirate thus completed the destruction of the Republic’s independent politics, but it did so after the Republic had already been undermined by the civil wars.

The comparison therefore favours the First Triumvirate. Its agreement made possible the military power of Caesar and the conflicts that destroyed the old constitutional balance, while the Second Triumvirate operated in a state already transformed by civil war. The First Triumvirate was the cause of the political breakdown, and the Second Triumvirate was its final expression. A reader must judge the fall of the Republic as a process, and the First Triumvirate was the more significant stage in that process.

The Second Triumvirate also used legal authority more openly than the First. Its members were granted the power to make laws and to hold office for a fixed term, and this gave the agreement an appearance of constitutional legitimacy. The proscriptions of 43 BCE, which killed many senators and equestrians, were carried out under this authority, and they removed the political class that had resisted the triumvirs. The contrast with the First Triumvirate shows that the later agreement was a settlement reached after the Republic had already collapsed into civil war.

The judgement can be tested by the political conduct of Crassus and Pompey after the agreement. Crassus sought military glory in the east and died at Carrhae, while Pompey drifted between the Senate and the triumvirs, and neither acted as a steady partner in the arrangement. These shifts show that the First Triumvirate depended on personal interests as much as on any shared programme, and that its collapse was driven by the rivalry of its members. The fall of the Republic was therefore shaped by the personal dynamics of this agreement.

Overall, the First Triumvirate played a more significant role in the fall of the Roman Republic, because it created the military commands and rivalries that led to civil war, while the Second Triumvirate completed a settlement that was already the product of that war. The first alliance was the foundation of the Republic’s collapse, and the second was its end.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The relationship between Pompey and Crassus was highly significant in the politics of the late Republic, because their rivalry and eventual cooperation shaped the course of Roman politics and prepared the way for the civil wars that ended the Republic. They were both wealthy and powerful men who had competed for influence, and their alliance under Caesar's guidance produced the First Triumvirate in 60 BCE. The judgement is that the relationship was significant less for its personal warmth than for the way it allowed the most powerful men in Rome to bypass the Senate and dominate public life, and that its collapse made civil war inevitable.

Their rivalry began in the 70s BCE, when both men competed for prestige and command. Crassus had made his fortune through property and speculation, and he had defeated the slave rebellion led by Spartacus in 71 BCE. Pompey was celebrated for his campaigns against the pirates and against Mithridates, and he had a large military following. The two men were jealous of each other's achievements, and their competition created a dangerous instability in the Senate, because each sought to outdo the other with the support of the people and the army.

Their reconciliation was the outcome of their joint consulship in 70 BCE, when they both held the highest office and used it to restore the powers of the tribunes that Sulla's reforms had curtailed. This cooperation was a sign that the two men could act together when it suited them, and it prepared the ground for the alliance that followed. Their common interest was to secure the support of the people and to advance their own commands, and this interest made them receptive to the approach of Caesar.

The First Triumvirate of 60 BCE linked Pompey, Crassus and Caesar in a private agreement. Caesar's consulship in 59 BCE and his marriage of his daughter Julia to Pompey strengthened the bond. Julia's death in 54 BCE removed the family link that had held the alliance together, and Crassus's death in battle against the Parthians at Carrhae in 53 BCE removed the third member of the triangle. The loss of these two figures left Pompey and Caesar as rivals, and the rivalry led to the civil war of 49 BCE.

On balance, the relationship between Pompey and Crassus was significant because it helped to create the conditions in which the Senate's authority could be bypassed by powerful individuals. Their alliance and rivalry showed that the institutions of the Republic could be overridden by private agreements, and the consequences of this development were enormous. Their relationship did not cause the fall of the Republic on its own, but it was a major step in the process, and it shows how personal ambition and public power were becoming inseparable in the late Republic.

The judgement must also consider how far the relationship between Pompey and Crassus shaped the political culture of the late Republic. Their agreement demonstrated that the most powerful men could use their wealth, clients and armies to secure outcomes that the Senate could not block, and it set a precedent that later generals followed. The consulship of 70 BCE, the Triumvirate and the successive commands showed that the Senate's authority could be overridden when the leading men agreed. Yet their relationship was never a settled friendship, and each sought to use the alliance to advance his own position. The contest between them for influence over the Senate and the people was a source of instability, and it made any future settlement fragile. A reasoned judgement must therefore recognise that the relationship was significant because it changed the rules of politics, even though its personal basis was unstable.

sampleAnswers.answer: Foreign wars and expansion contributed significantly to the fall of the Roman Republic, but their effect was indirect. They created the conditions in which ambitious generals could command loyal armies, accumulate wealth and challenge the Senate's authority. The fall of the Republic was the product of these military and financial changes working through domestic political conflicts. Expansion across the Mediterranean had brought Rome enormous wealth, slaves and provinces, and it had made the Senate's government of the provinces a major source of profit and corruption. Governors who were sent abroad often used their posts to enrich themselves, and the prosecution of Verres in 70 BCE, which Cicero conducted, exposed the scale of provincial exploitation. The Senate's failure to control the provinces gave generals the opportunity to build personal power bases, and the wealth from war was the means by which they could reward their soldiers and win political support. The most important military change was the reform of the army by Marius around 107 BCE, which opened recruitment to the poorest citizens and made the army dependent on its general for pay, land and discharge. This made the soldiers loyal to their commanders rather than to the state. The Republic's armies were therefore no longer citizen militias that returned to civilian life, but professional forces whose loyalty could be bought. Sulla's march on Rome in 88 BCE, during the Mithridatic command, was the first clear demonstration of this new power. He used his army to seize Rome and to impose his will on the state, and his subsequent dictatorship set a precedent that others followed. The Mithridatic Wars that Sulla fought in the East, and the later campaigns of Pompey, brought vast commands and enormous revenues, and they gave generals a claim to independent authority that the Senate could not easily check. Pompey's settlement of the East, the wealth it produced and the armies it commanded created an unprecedented concentration of resources in the hands of one man. Crassus, who was defeated and killed by the Parthians at Carrhae in 53 BCE, shows the risks and the ambitions of such commands. His defeat removed a counterweight to Pompey and Caesar, and the campaign was undertaken in the hope of matching their military glory. Caesar's Gallic War from 58 to 50 BCE was the most consequential of these conflicts. It brought Caesar a huge army, loyal to him through years of campaigning and shared hardship, and enormous wealth from plunder and the sale of captives. Caesar used these resources to challenge the Senate directly, and his crossing of the Rubicon in 49 BCE was the decisive act of the civil war. The Gallic War therefore shows how foreign conquest could be turned into domestic power. Yet foreign wars did not destroy the Republic on their own. The civil wars were the product of political conflicts about land, debt, the powers of the tribunes and the position of the Senate, and these disputes were made more dangerous by the armies that foreign wars had created. The Senate's inability to reward its generals, to settle its veterans or to control its provincial governors was as important as the wars themselves. The evidence for these developments comes largely from Cicero, Caesar and later writers such as Plutarch and Appian. Caesar's own Commentaries present the Gallic War as a series of lawful campaigns, and this self-presentation must be read with care. Cicero's letters and speeches, though contemporary, were shaped by his own political interests. Historians must therefore treat the military and financial explanation as one of several interpretations, and weigh it against the political evidence. The most accurate judgement is that foreign wars and expansion contributed to the fall of the Republic by creating loyal armies, enormous commands and the wealth that rewarded them, but that these effects became decisive only through the domestic political failures that the Senate could not resolve. The wars provided the means, and the political crisis provided the motive, and the collapse of the Republic followed from their combination.

To go further, weigh the claim about domestic failure against the evidence for the Gallic War's own role in Caesar's ambition.

sampleAnswers.answer: Foreign wars contributed to the fall of the Republic mainly by creating loyal armies and the wealth that rewarded generals. Marius' reform of the army around 107 BCE made soldiers dependent on their general for pay and land, so their loyalty shifted from the state to the commander. Sulla's march on Rome in 88 BCE, after his Mithridatic command, showed how such an army could be used against the Senate. The Mithridatic Wars and Pompey's eastern commands brought vast revenues and independent authority. Crassus' defeat and death at Carrhae in 53 BCE removed a counterweight to Pompey and Caesar. Caesar's Gallic War from 58 to 50 BCE gave him a huge army and enormous plunder, and he used these resources to challenge the Senate directly, crossing the Rubicon in 49 BCE. However, foreign wars did not destroy the Republic alone. Disputes over land, debt and the tribunes, and the Senate's failure to reward its generals, were equally important. The Marian reforms and the Mithridatic campaigns show a pattern that repeated over several decades: generals gained armies and money abroad, then used them against rivals at home. Carrhae removed Crassus, and the Gallic War made Caesar the richest and most loyal commander of his age. Provincial exploitation, documented by the prosecution of Verres, had also made the Senate's authority look self-interested, which weakened its ability to restrain generals. Historians therefore tend to see foreign wars as an accelerating force rather than a cause in themselves. Overall, foreign wars created the means of the Republic's collapse, while domestic political failure supplied the motive.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The military activities of Pompey and Caesar were central to developments in the late Republic, because their commands gave them armies, their campaigns brought wealth and loyalty, and their rivalry turned a political struggle into a civil war. David Shotter describes Caesar's warfare as a means of keeping his troops employed in lucrative campaigns while securing frontiers that would better defend the empire. This interpretation is persuasive, but the judgement must also consider Pompey's eastern settlement and the way the provinces and commands were used in politics. On balance, Caesar's military activities were the more decisive, because they produced the army that ended the Republic's political order.

Pompey's career was built on military commands that were granted by the people rather than the senate. His campaigns against the pirates in 67 BCE and against Mithridates VI in the east brought him great prestige, and his settlement of the eastern provinces, including the capture of Jerusalem in 63 BCE, gave him clients and resources across the Mediterranean. These achievements made him the most powerful man in Rome, but the settlement also alienated some senators, who opposed his land grants and his ratification of his arrangements. Pompey's military success therefore created both loyalty and resentment.

Caesar's Gallic campaigns from 58 to 50 BCE were the decisive military achievement of his career. The conquest of Gaul brought him an army of experienced veterans, enormous wealth from the spoils and the captives, and a reputation that rivalled Pompey's. His crossings of the Rhine and his expeditions to Britain showed a commander who could plan operations beyond the normal limits of Roman expansion. Shotter's point that Caesar planned warfare to keep his troops employed and to secure frontiers is supported by the scale and continuity of the Gallic operations. The army he built in Gaul was loyal to him and was the instrument of his later struggle with the senate.

The civil war was the consequence of this rivalry. When the senate ordered Caesar to give up his command, he crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE, and the war that followed was fought across Italy, Spain, Greece and Egypt. Pompey's defeat at Pharsalus in 48 BCE and his murder in Egypt, followed by Caesar's campaigns against Pompey's sons in Spain, which ended with the battle of Munda in 45 BCE, show that the military activities of the two men were now the basis of politics. The war was not simply a clash of armies but a contest over who would control the Republic.

Historians have debated how far the military activities were the cause of the Republic's collapse rather than its symptom. The commands, the provinces and the armies were the product of a political system that allowed individuals to accumulate power through war, so the wars reflected deeper problems. Yet the generals' decisions turned those problems into a collapse, and their rivalry made the political order impossible to maintain.

On balance, the military activities of Pompey and Caesar were essential to developments in the late Republic. Pompey's eastern settlement and Caesar's conquest of Gaul created the armies and the clients that made their rivalry possible, and the civil war that followed ended the Republic's competitive politics. Caesar's campaigns were the more decisive because they produced the victorious army, but both men's military activities were necessary to the crisis.

The military activities of both men also shaped the political language of the period. Caesar presented his campaigns in Gaul as a service to the Republic, and his Commentaries made the case for his achievements to the Roman public. Pompey's military reputation gave him authority in the senate, while his clients in the East supported his claims for ratification of his settlements. These uses of military success show that the campaigns were not only about conquest but about the political legitimacy of the commanders.

sampleAnswers.answer: The optimates and populares were significant as the main political labels of the late Republic, though they were less rigid than the labels suggest. The optimates defended the authority of the Senate and the traditional leadership of the aristocracy; the populares were leaders who sought popular support, often through the assemblies and the tribunes. Their significance lies in the way the labels shaped alliances and hostilities, rather than in fixed parties with programmes. The distinction explains much of the period’s conflict, but it must be used with care. The optimates were significant because they gave the Senate a coherent defence against individuals who used popular support to gain power. Cicero, who spoke for the boni, the good men of the Senate, opened his prosecution of Catiline with the words ‘How long, Catiline, will you abuse our patience?’, and his suppression of the conspiracy in 63 BCE was a defence of senatorial authority. Cato the Younger was the most uncompromising defender of the Senate, and his opposition to Pompey’s arrangements and to Caesar’s consulship of 59 BCE shows the optimates’ role in resisting personal power. Their significance was greatest when they could unite behind the Senate’s authority. The populares were significant because they challenged the Senate’s monopoly of political initiative. Caesar, as consul in 59 BCE, used a popular assembly to pass land laws, and he allied with Pompey and Crassus in the First Triumvirate. Clodius, as tribune in 58 BCE, passed laws that provided grain and exiled Cicero, and his gangs were a form of popular mobilisation. The populares were not a unified movement, and several of them, including Clodius and Caesar, were themselves members of the aristocracy who used popular methods for personal ends. Their significance was in demonstrating the power of the assemblies and the tribunate when the Senate was divided. The labels should not be overstated. Pompey moved between the two camps, allying with the populares in the 60s BCE and with the optimates after 52 BCE, and many senators supported popular measures for their own advantage. The optimates and populares were therefore coalitions and styles of politics rather than settled parties. The labels were significant, but they served political argument as much as they described fixed groups. The labels also matter for how the sources were written. Cicero’s speeches and letters use the language of the good men against popular leaders, and his portrayal of his opponents shapes how historians have read the period. Caesar’s own commentaries present him as a defender of the tribunes and the people, which gives a different account of the same conflicts. Historians must weigh both perspectives, and the significance of the labels depends partly on who is using them. The optimates and populares were significant because they framed the political conflicts that brought down the Republic. They gave the Senate a defence and gave ambitious leaders a means of challenging it, and the failure of the optimates to accommodate Caesar, together with the populares’ use of the assemblies and the tribunate, combined to drive the crisis of 49 BCE. Their significance was real, but it was as political language and loose alliances rather than as organised parties, and historians who treat them as parties risk exaggerating their coherence.

To go further, it could assess the role of the tribunate in the populares’ success more precisely.

Cato was also an optimate and he was strongly against Caesar. Caesar and Clodius were populares. Caesar passed land laws as consul in 59 BCE, and Clodius passed a law on grain as tribune in 58 BCE. These men used popular support to challenge the Senate. The labels also shaped how contemporaries acted. Politicians who wished to be seen as defenders of the Senate could oppose popular laws, while those who sought popular support could use the tribunes to pass measures the Senate disliked. The labels gave the arguments a shared vocabulary even when the men using them were pursuing their own ambitions. The labels were not always clear, because Pompey changed sides and some senators supported popular laws too. The two groups were important, but they were not fixed parties.
