sampleAnswers.answer:
The Senate was responsible for some of the political crises of the late Republic, but its responsibility was shared with the individual leaders who used its procedures for their own ends. The Senate’s rigidity, its reliance on the optimates and its willingness to use extraordinary measures against opponents all contributed to the instability. Yet the crises also came from the extraordinary commands of Pompey and Caesar and from the ambitions of men who saw the Senate as an obstacle. The Senate was a central player in the crises, but it was not the sole cause, and its role must be judged against the actions of its most powerful members.

The Senate’s authority rested on tradition, on the magistracies and on its control of finance and foreign policy. Its members were drawn from families of wealth and status, and they expected the Republic to be governed by collective decision. This system worked well when power was shared among the elite, but it became unstable when individual generals commanded large armies for long periods. The Senate’s difficulty was that it could not easily control men who had the loyalty of their soldiers.

The Senate’s use of extraordinary measures was a source of instability. The senatus consultum ultimum, a decree that allowed magistrates to take emergency action against threats to the state, was used against the Gracchi and later against Catiline in 63 BCE. Sallust’s account of the Catilinarian conspiracy shows how the Senate and Cicero acted against those they considered enemies of the state, and it suggests that the decree was used to silence opponents as well as to defend the Republic. This use of extraordinary power weakened the principle of legal process and made political conflict more violent.

The optimates, the conservative senators led by figures such as Cato the Younger, opposed the ambitions of popular leaders and of generals who wanted special commands. Their resistance was principled, but it also made them inflexible. When Pompey and Caesar sought favourable terms for their veterans and their own careers, the optimates refused to compromise, and this refusal pushed the rivals towards alliance and then conflict.

The extraordinary commands given to Pompey were a clear example of the Senate’s limited control. The Gabinian law of 67 BCE gave him command against the pirates of the Mediterranean, and the Manilian law of 66 BCE gave him command against Mithridates. These commands were approved by the people, not by the Senate, and they showed that the Senate could not prevent the assembly from granting powers to a single man. The commands also gave Pompey the means to build a personal following, which he used to dominate politics.

The First Triumvirate of 60 BCE, formed by Pompey, Caesar and Crassus, was a private arrangement that bypassed the Senate. Caesar’s consulship in 59 BCE was carried by force and the support of the assembly, and the Senate was unable to resist. This episode shows that the Senate could not control the political process when its leading members were divided, and it made the Senate’s authority depend on the goodwill of the dynasts.

The Senate also failed to address the causes of unrest, such as debt, land and the status of the veterans. Its unwillingness to settle these questions left many citizens dissatisfied, and it allowed demagogues to use the grievances for their own purposes. The crisis of 63 BCE and the disorder that followed reflected this failure, as Catiline exploited the discontent of the poor and of debtors.

The final crisis in 49 BCE illustrates the Senate’s position. When Caesar crossed the Rubicon, the Senate declared him an enemy of the state and called on Pompey to defend the Republic. Its refusal to negotiate, and its reliance on Pompey’s army, made war almost inevitable. The Senate was therefore responsible for the decision to confront Caesar, but Caesar’s ambition and his army made him willing to challenge it.

Overall, the Senate was responsible for some of the political crises of the late Republic, because its rigidity, its use of extraordinary measures and its failure to resolve grievances made conflict more likely. Yet the crises were also driven by the ambitions of Pompey and Caesar and by the extraordinary commands that gave them armies. The Senate was therefore a central player in the crisis, but its responsibility was shared, and the decisive factors were the individuals who used the Senate’s weaknesses for their own purposes.

Testing the claim about the Gabinian and Manilian laws against Cicero’s speeches would strengthen the argument.

sampleAnswers.answer: The use of the army was a major contributor to political developments in the late Republic, and it was central to the collapse of the Republic’s institutions. Commanders who used legions for political ends altered the balance between the Senate and individual generals, and the Civil War of 49–45 BCE grew directly from this shift. However, army use was not the only cause. Political rivalry, the failure of compromise and economic pressures also shaped events, so the army’s contribution was significant but not exclusive. The precedent was set by Sulla, whose march on Rome in 88 BCE to secure a command against Marius was the first time a Roman general had led his army against the city. Marius’ reforms, which recruited poorer citizens into the legions and made them dependent on their commanders for land and pay, deepened the link between soldiers and generals. Pompey’s extraordinary commands in the 60s BCE and Caesar’s Gallic army gave both men personal forces, which allowed them to exercise political power that the Senate could not easily check. The crisis of 49 BCE showed the consequences most clearly. The Senate’s final decree, which authorised action against Caesar, was answered by his crossing of the Rubicon with his army, a decision recorded in Suetonius as ‘the die is cast’. Caesar’s legions gave him the advantage over the Senate and Pompey, and the victories at Pharsalus in 48 BCE and Munda in 45 BCE confirmed that the army, not the institutions of the Republic, decided the contest. The Civil War was therefore the direct result of commanders’ armies being used against the state. The army was not the only military element in Roman politics. Clodius and Milo employed armed gangs in Rome in the 50s BCE, and the violence that followed Clodius’ death in 52 BCE led the Senate to ask Pompey to take up the consulship alone and to station troops in the city. This is a sign that the political system had become dependent on force, and that the line between armies and urban violence was thin. The Senate’s turn to Pompey, and the use of troops to restore order, shows that political crises could be resolved only by military power. The consequences of army use can also be seen in the fate of the Republic’s institutions after 49 BCE. Caesar’s dictatorship and then the Second Triumvirate showed that the political system could be run through the power of commanders and their armies, and the Senate’s authority was subordinated to men with troops. Even when the Republic’s forms were preserved, the army had become the decisive factor in deciding who held power, and this shift shaped the transition to the principate. The use of armies contributed greatly to political developments, because it allowed commanders to override the Senate and reshaped the Republic’s balance of power. But the army’s role depended on the political crisis that preceded it: the failure of the First Triumvirate to hold together, the Senate’s refusal to accept Caesar’s terms and the rivalries among leading men had created the conditions for force to decide the outcome. Overall, the use of the army was the most decisive means by which the late Republic fell apart, but its contribution was to accelerate developments rather than to originate them.

The army was also used in Rome itself. In 52 BCE, after Clodius was killed, the Senate asked Pompey to become sole consul and he brought troops into the city. This shows the use of force in politics. The army also changed the relation between commanders and their soldiers. Veterans expected land and pay from the generals who led them, which made soldiers loyal to individuals rather than to the state. Such loyalty made it easier for commanders to act against the Senate, and it was one reason the civil wars were so difficult to end. However, the army was not the only cause of the Republic’s fall. Other things, such as rivalries between leaders, also mattered. So the army was important, but it was not the only reason.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Urban violence contributed significantly to the fall of the Roman Republic, because it made the Senate dependent on extraordinary measures and it opened the way for powerful men to use armed force in politics. Yet the violence was a symptom as much as a cause. It revealed the weakness of the institutions that were supposed to keep order and the readiness of ambitious leaders to use private armies. The judgement is that urban violence was an important contribution to the collapse, but that it was the ability of commanders to use armies, rather than the street fighting in Rome, that proved decisive.

The street violence of the 50s BCE was the most visible feature of political life in Rome. Clodius and Milo, who had organised gangs in the city, fought for control of the streets and the elections, and in 52 BCE Milo's men killed Clodius on the Appian Way. The violence that followed caused the Senate to pass its emergency decree and to demand order, and it made the city's political institutions appear incapable of governing themselves. The disorder gave the Senate a reason to look for a strong man, and this was the most immediate effect of the violence on the Republic.

The response to the violence revealed the dangers of the Senate's position. Pompey, who had been given extraordinary commands in the East, was appointed sole consul in 52 BCE to restore order, and this was an unprecedented concentration of power in the hands of a single man. The Senate's willingness to accept such a measure showed that it had lost confidence in its own ability to govern, and Pompey's power was now dependent on the army and the support of the optimates. The violence therefore strengthened the position of the most powerful individuals rather than the institutions of the Republic.

The use of the army in politics was the more fundamental danger. Sulla had marched on Rome in 88 BCE with his legions, and this precedent showed that an army could be used to decide political disputes. Catiline's conspiracy in 63 BCE had already revealed how a discontented faction could threaten the state, and the rivalries of the 50s made it likely that commanders would turn their armies against the Senate. Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon in 49 BCE, with the army he had commanded in Gaul, was the decisive act, and it shows that violence in the streets had prepared the political climate in which armed force became acceptable.

On balance, urban violence contributed to the fall of the Republic by making the Senate dependent on extraordinary powers, by strengthening the hand of individual leaders and by creating a climate in which force was normal. However, the decisive factor was the willingness of commanders to lead their armies against the state. The violence in Rome exposed the weakness of the Republic's institutions, but it was the army that destroyed them, and the judgement is that urban violence was a significant contributing factor rather than the principal cause.

The judgement must also consider the attitude of the Senate and the elite to the violence. Many senators supported the use of force against their opponents, and the Senate's emergency decrees were applied in ways that favoured the optimate faction. This willingness to use disorder against political rivals meant that the violence was not only a product of the gangs but also of the elite's own choices. The Senate turned to violence when it suited its interests, and it was then unable to control the consequences. Cicero's own prosecution of Catiline's supporters and his reliance on force in 63 BCE show that the elite accepted extraordinary measures as normal. A reasoned judgement must therefore place the violence within a political culture in which order and force were used interchangeably, and conclude that this culture made the later use of armies by commanders far easier to justify.

sampleAnswers.answer: Political crises were responsible for the outbreak of civil war in 49 BC to a considerable extent, because the First Triumvirate broke down and the constitutional structure of Rome could no longer manage the rivalry between its leading men. The Triumvirate was formed in 60 BCE by Caesar, Pompey and Crassus, an informal alliance that allowed each to pursue his aims. The arrangement depended on personal ties, and these were severed in quick succession. Julia, Caesar’s daughter and Pompey’s wife, died in 54 BCE, which removed the family bond that had joined the two men. The death of Crassus at Carrhae in 53 BCE removed the third member, who had been a counterweight to both. Without Crassus and Julia, the alliance lost its stability, and Pompey moved towards the Senate and its conservative leaders. The violence in the city between the followers of Clodius and Milo in 52 BCE, including the murder of Clodius, created a climate of disorder that Pompey exploited. Pompey became sole consul in 52 BCE, a position that gave him extraordinary power and put him at the head of the Senate’s resistance to Caesar. This was a decisive crisis, because it made Pompey a rival rather than an ally. Caesar’s position was also at stake. His command in Gaul was due to expire, and he sought the right to stand for the consulship in absence. The Senate demanded that he give up his army before he entered the city, while Pompey and the optimates insisted on this. The crisis came to a head in January 49 BCE, when Caesar crossed the Rubicon with his army. The sequence shows that the political breakdown created the conditions for war, but the choice to fight was made by Caesar and by the senators who refused his demands. The structural problem was that the Republic lacked a means to settle disputes between men with armies and personal followings. However, the crises were not inevitable. Caesar might have accepted a compromise, and Pompey might have worked with him, and the personal ambition of each man was a decisive element. The sources for this period are mainly Caesar’s own Commentaries, which present his case, and Cicero’s letters, which record the anxieties of an observer who was himself tied to the Senate. Plutarch’s Lives of Caesar and Pompey, written later, rely on earlier histories and present the rivalry as a tragedy of two men. Dio’s history, written in the third century CE, provides a broader narrative but is written with hindsight. The breakdown was also shaped by the legal and constitutional disputes over the Gallic command. Caesar’s position depended on the legal arrangements that allowed him to stand for the consulship without entering the city, and the Senate’s demands that he dismiss his army threatened to remove that protection. The tribunes Mark Antony and Quintus Cassius, who fled to Caesar’s camp in January 49 BC, were a sign that the constitutional balance had collapsed, since the tribunes’ sacred status had been violated. Public violence and financial crisis also weakened the Republic’s institutions. The death of Crassus at Carrhae removed a major financial and political weight, and the consular elections of the early 50s BC were marked by bribery and disorder. The Senate’s attempts to restrain Caesar relied on laws and decrees whose enforcement depended on the consuls, who could not act decisively while the rivalry between the leading men was unresolved. Taken together, political crises were a major cause of civil war, because the Triumvirate’s collapse and Pompey’s sole consulship made the Republic’s institutions unable to contain the rivalry. Yet the decisive factor was the individual decision of Caesar to cross the Rubicon, which turned a political crisis into a civil war.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The assassination of Caesar on the Ides of March in 44 BCE did not restore the Republic, but it was the event that led to the civil wars that ended it. The assassins believed they could restore the traditional government of the Senate, but they lacked a broad base of support, and the power vacuum allowed Mark Antony and Octavian to seize control. The Second Triumvirate of 43 BCE, the proscriptions and the battles of Philippi and Actium led to the rule of Octavian. The assassination therefore marked the end of the Republic in practice, although its formal end came later, and the question depends on how the events of 44 to 31 BCE are interpreted.

The assassins’ aim was the restoration of the Senate’s authority, and they sought to remove Caesar as a tyrant. Brutus and Cassius believed that the Republic could be revived if Caesar were removed, and they were supported by senators who opposed his dictatorship. Yet the conspirators had no plan for the aftermath, and their action alienated many citizens who had benefited from Caesar’s policies. The assassination was therefore a political act with no means of securing the peace that followed.

Mark Antony, as Caesar’s consul and friend, was the first to seize the initiative. He read Caesar’s will to the people and used the crowd’s grief to turn opinion against the assassins, and he secured control of Caesar’s papers and money. Octavian, Caesar’s adopted heir, returned to Italy and claimed his inheritance, and he raised troops from Caesar’s veterans. These two men competed for the leadership of Caesar’s following, and their rivalry shaped the next years.

The Second Triumvirate, formed in 43 BCE by Octavian, Mark Antony and Lepidus, was a formal arrangement that gave the three men extraordinary powers for five years. It was not a restoration of the Republic but a dictatorship shared by three men. The triumvirs proscribed their opponents, executing many senators and equestrians and confiscating their property. The proscriptions showed that the new rulers were willing to use terror to secure their position, and they killed Cicero, the leading defender of the Republic.

The battle of Philippi in 42 BCE destroyed the armies of Brutus and Cassius, and it removed the main republican resistance. The victory showed that the assassins could not defeat the armies of Caesar’s heirs, and it left Antony and Octavian in control of the east and the west. The division of the empire between them became the basis of the next conflict.

The final struggle came between Octavian and Mark Antony, who had allied himself with Cleopatra and the eastern kingdoms. The battle of Actium in 31 BCE ended the rivalry, after the fleet of Octavian defeated the combined forces of Antony and Cleopatra. The victory gave Octavian control of the whole Roman world, and it removed the last rival to his authority. The end of the civil wars meant that one man now controlled the Roman state.

The sources for these events are shaped by the outcome. Cicero’s letters and speeches show the anxieties of the Republican elite and the hopes that the assassins had raised, but they were written before the final victory. Suetonius’s Life of Augustus, written much later, presents Octavian as a restorer of order, and this portrayal reflects the claims that the Augustan regime made about itself. The historians of the period must therefore read these accounts critically.

Modern historians debate whether the end of the Republic was caused by the assassination or by the longer crisis that had already undermined the Senate. Some argue that Caesar’s dictatorship had already ended the Republic in practice, and that the assassination merely brought the crisis into the open. Others see the murder as the decisive act, because it provoked the civil wars that destroyed the old order. The evidence supports both views, since the assassination was the immediate trigger for a crisis that had deep roots.

The assassination also changed the political language of Rome. The appeal to liberty and the Republic was used by both sides, but the leaders who survived the wars presented their rule as a restoration of order. Octavian’s later settlements of 27 and 23 BCE built the principate on the outcome of these civil wars, and they showed that the Republic had been replaced by a monarchy in all but name.

Overall, the assassination of Caesar did not restore the Republic, and it set off the civil wars that ended its traditional form. The Second Triumvirate, the proscriptions and the battles of Philippi and Actium created the conditions for Octavian’s rule. The assassination was therefore the decisive event that led to the end of the Republic, although the final settlement came from the victory of Octavian over his rivals.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The settlements of 27 and 23 BCE were key to Augustus’ power and authority, because they gave him the legal and military powers that the Republic had never granted to a single citizen in peacetime. Augustus presented them as a restoration of the Republic, and the Res Gestae records that he handed back his extraordinary powers to the Senate and the people. Yet the powers he retained made him the dominant figure of the state. The settlements were therefore central to the principate, although their importance depends on how far the formal restoration is set against the actual concentration of power.

The settlement of 27 BCE was the first formal step. Augustus gave up the extraordinary commands that he had held during the civil wars, and the Senate conferred on him the name Augustus. The Res Gestae describes this as the restoration of the Republic to the Senate and the Roman people, and it presents the act as a return to traditional government. Augustus retained command of the provinces where the legions were stationed, including Spain, Gaul and Syria, while the Senate kept the more settled provinces. This division gave him control of the army, which was the basis of his authority.

The settlement of 23 BCE was more important for the constitutional basis of his power. Augustus gave up the consulship, which he had held repeatedly, but he received tribunician power for life. This gave him the right to veto legislation and the sacrosanct status of the tribunes, and it allowed him to act in the interests of the people without holding office. He also received proconsular imperium over all the provinces, which gave him authority above the governors of the Senate’s provinces. These powers were held permanently, and they allowed Augustus to dominate politics without the appearance of an autocrat.

The combination of these powers was the real foundation of the principate. The tribunician power gave Augustus a legal basis for intervention in the city, and the imperium maius gave him authority over the governors in every province. The army, which he commanded through his provincial legates, gave him the means to enforce his authority. The Senate retained its formal role and its magistracies, but its decisions were shaped by an emperor who held the most important powers of the state.

The Res Gestae is the key source for Augustus’ own view of the settlements. He records the honours, the grants of the Senate and the gifts he made to the people, and he presents his rule as one of restoration and moderation. This account is valuable because it reveals the official ideology of the regime, but it was written by Augustus to present his achievements in the best light, so it cannot be taken as an objective record of how his power worked.

The Roman historians describe the settlements in ways that show their significance. Suetonius records the honours and the political changes of Augustus’ reign, and Cassius Dio explains how the powers granted to Augustus were combined in one figure. These accounts show that contemporaries recognised the settlements as the creation of a new constitutional order, even though the language of the Republic was preserved. They also show that the Senate’s role was real but limited.

Modern historians debate whether the settlements were a genuine compromise or a disguised monarchy. Some argue that Augustus skilfully preserved the forms of the Republic while concentrating power, and that the settlements were a pragmatic way to end the civil wars. Others see the settlements as the decisive step towards an autocracy, because the powers granted made the emperor independent of the Senate. The evidence supports both readings, since the forms of the Republic were kept while the substance of power changed.

The settlements were also key to Augustus’ authority because they were accepted by the elite and the people. The Senate gave him honours, the people supported his policies, and the provinces came to depend on his governance. This acceptance was based on the peace and stability that followed the civil wars, and it gave Augustus a legitimacy that was not purely formal. Stability and prosperity, rather than the legal powers alone, made the settlements durable.

Overall, the settlements of 27 and 23 BCE were key to Augustus’ power, because they gave him the army, the tribunician power and the proconsular imperium that made him the dominant figure in the state. The Res Gestae presents them as a restoration, but the powers that remained made the principate a new constitutional form. The settlements were therefore central to Augustus’ authority, although their legitimacy also depended on the peace and the consent that followed them.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The principate was established because the Republic had been destroyed by a century of civil war, and because Octavian was able to control the armies, the loyalty of the people and the acceptance of the Senate. The civil wars had exhausted the Roman state and created a desire for stability, and Octavian's victory at Actium in 31 BCE gave him the decisive military position. The judgement is that the most important reason was the combination of military control and the political skill with which Augustus presented his power as a restoration, and that the settlements of 27 BCE and 23 BCE were the means by which this combination became permanent.

The exhaustion of the Republic was the background to the principate. The assassination of Julius Caesar in 44 BCE was followed by a long series of civil wars between rival generals, and the Roman elite had seen the Republic's institutions repeatedly overridden by armed men. Many Romans wanted peace and order more than they wanted the restoration of the old constitution, and this desire made them willing to accept a single leader who could guarantee stability. The principate was therefore a response to a crisis that had made the Republic unworkable.

Octavian's control of the armies was the decisive military reason. His victory at Actium over Antony and Cleopatra in 31 BCE removed his last serious rival and gave him command of the Roman legions. The loyalty of the soldiers, who had been paid and settled by Octavian, meant that he could not be displaced by force. This military dominance was the foundation on which the political settlement was built, and it made the Senate's acceptance a matter of choice rather than necessity.

Augustus's political skill was equally important. His settlement of 27 BCE, in which he surrendered his extraordinary powers and was granted the name Augustus, presented the restoration of the Republic as a gift to the Senate and the people. The settlement of 23 BCE gave him tribunician power and an authority over the provinces that made him the dominant figure in public life. These arrangements preserved the forms of the Republic, including the consulships and the Senate, while concentrating real power in his hands. The language of auctoritas, which expressed his moral influence rather than legal command, made his power acceptable to the political elite.

On balance, the principate was established because of the exhaustion caused by civil war, Octavian's control of the armies and Augustus's skill in presenting his power as a restoration. The military and political reasons were closely linked, and the settlements of 27 and 23 BCE gave them a lasting constitutional form. The principate was therefore not simply imposed by force, but built on a combination of coercion, consent and the desire for stability, and this combination explains why it lasted for the next century.

The judgement must also consider the role of Augustus's personal qualities and the expectations of his contemporaries. Augustus presented himself as a restorer of the Republic and as a leader who had avenged his adoptive father, and this image appealed to many Romans who wanted security after decades of violence. His use of religion, including his priesthoods and the cult of the divine Julius, gave his authority a sacred dimension that reinforced his political position. The settlements of 27 and 23 BCE were carefully designed to avoid the appearance of monarchy, but they gave him powers that no other citizen possessed. A reasoned evaluation therefore recognises that the principate was shaped by the conditions of the civil wars, by the control of the armies and by the personal skill of Augustus, and that these factors combined to make the new system acceptable and durable.

It would lift further by assessing the role of the Senate's own choices more explicitly.

sampleAnswers.answer: The roles and responsibilities of the Senate changed considerably in this period, though its formal standing was preserved. Before Augustus, the Senate had controlled the government, directed the provinces and dominated the magistracies, and its authority rested on its collective judgement of the state. After the civil wars, Augustus claimed to restore the Republic in 27 BCE, and he kept the Senate as a body of great prestige. Its formal responsibilities continued: it passed decrees, which were called senatus consulta, it heard legal cases and it retained the right to grant triumphs and honours. The Senate also kept its role in the administration of the provinces, since Augustus divided the provinces into senatorial and imperial categories, and the senatorial provinces were governed by proconsuls who were chosen by lot. This preserved the Senate’s place in government, but it was a subordinate place, since the emperor controlled the army and the most important provinces. The change was most visible in the powers that moved to Augustus himself. In 23 BCE he received tribunician power for life, which gave him the right to veto and to act in the people’s name, and this made him the central political authority. The Senate’s role in elections was also reduced. Augustus recommended candidates, and the Senate and assemblies generally accepted his choices, so the traditional process of electing magistrates became a formality. In 18 BCE, Augustus revised the Senate’s membership, reducing its size and removing members whose conduct was unsuitable, which asserted his control over its composition. The Senate therefore kept its roles but lost its independent authority. However, the change was not total. Augustus consulted the Senate on major decisions, and his legislation, such as the laws on marriage in 18 BCE, was passed through the assemblies with senatorial approval. The Senate remained the body through which the emperor’s authority was legitimised, and its members held the highest posts. The evidence for this change is mainly Augustus’ own Res Gestae, which presents him as restoring the Republic and giving the Senate its proper dignity, a claim that must be treated as propaganda. Tacitus, writing about a century later, describes the Senate as a shell of its former self, and this judgement reflects his own view of the emperors. Suetonius provides detail on the Senate’s reform and Augustus’ conduct, but he writes as a biographer. Coins and inscriptions record the emperor’s honours and the Senate’s decrees, but they show the formal structure rather than the real balance of power. The Senate’s financial and judicial roles also changed in form. Augustus established the aerarium militare in 6 CE to pay veterans, a new financial institution outside the traditional treasury, while the Senate continued to administer the aerarium Saturni. This division of finance shows the Senate’s formal functions surviving alongside new imperial structures. Its judicial role remained significant, since senators sat in the courts, but the emperor could intervene in cases and could influence the penalties for senators. The Senate’s role in the provinces and the army also shows the balance of change. Senators continued to hold many offices, and the career pattern of the cursus honorum remained a senatorial path, but the emperor had the power to appoint men to provincial commands and to decide who held the most important legions. Augustus’ own account in the Res Gestae claims that he gave the Senate its dignity, yet his control of the army made the Senate’s independence formal rather than real. Taken together, the roles of the Senate changed in substance, because it lost its independent control of the state and its elections, but it kept its formal functions and its prestige. The change was therefore a transformation of its place in government rather than its abolition, and it set the pattern for the principate that followed.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Augustus's relationship with the Senate was a managed partnership in form and a relationship of domination in substance. The Senate retained its honours, its offices and some of its provinces, and Augustus worked through its institutions to give his authority a legitimate appearance. Yet the armies, the most important provinces and the tribunician power remained in his hands, and the Senate could not act against his wishes. The judgement is that Augustus evaluated the Senate carefully: he preserved its dignity and used its consent, but he made sure that real power rested with himself.

The settlement of 27 BCE set the terms of the relationship. Augustus surrendered his extraordinary commands and was granted the name Augustus, and the Senate took back the provinces that had been unsettled. In return he received control of the frontier provinces where the legions were stationed, and the senatorial provinces were governed by proconsuls chosen by lot. This division preserved the Senate's role while giving Augustus command of the army, and it shows that the relationship was defined by an arrangement that suited both parties.

The settlement of 23 BCE strengthened Augustus's position. He received tribunician power, which gave him the right to veto Senate decisions and to act for the people, and he was granted an authority over the provinces that exceeded that of the other senators. These powers were held for life, and they gave him a permanent legal basis for influence in the Senate. The Senate's acceptance of these grants shows its willingness to cooperate, but it also shows that its independent authority had been reduced.

Augustus's own account, the Res Gestae, presents the relationship as one of mutual respect, in which the Senate honoured him and he restored the Republic. This is an important source for his aims, but it is a self-presentation, and it must be read critically. The Senate's honours and decrees were real, yet they were shaped by the emperor's wishes, and the senators who opposed him were often removed from office or forced into exile. The partnership was real in form but its terms were set by Augustus.

On balance, Augustus's relationship with the Senate was cooperative in appearance, carefully managed in practice and dominated in substance. He treated the Senate with respect and gave it real roles, but the control of the armies, the provinces and the tribunician power meant that the Senate's independence was limited. The judgement is that the relationship was one of skilled partnership under the emperor's authority, which allowed the Senate to keep its dignity while it accepted the emperor's leadership.

The judgement therefore rests on the balance between the honours that the Senate retained and the powers that the emperor held, and it is this balance that defined the relationship for the rest of the Augustan period.

The judgement must also consider the fact that the relationship changed over time. In the early years, Augustus was careful to consult the Senate and to present its decisions as collective, and the senators who held the consulship and governorships were treated with respect. As the principate matured, the emperor's dominance became more evident, and the Senate's role in appointments and in the provinces was increasingly shaped by his wishes. The Senate's loss of influence was gradual rather than sudden, and it was accepted by many senators who preferred security and honour to the risks of independence. This suggests that the relationship was a negotiated settlement, in which the Senate kept its prestige and gained a secure place in the new order, while the emperor kept control of the instruments of power. A reasoned judgement therefore sees the relationship as a skilful partnership that tilted towards the emperor, rather than as simple domination.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The titles, honours and images of Augustus were important to his principate because they gave a monarchy a legitimacy that the Roman tradition would not otherwise accept. Mary Beard argues that the name Augustus evoked authority and religious observance, and that it was a new name that no one had borne before, which made it an ideal title for a ruler who wished to appear as the restorer of the Republic. This view is persuasive, but the honours were important only in combination with real powers. On balance, the titles and images were essential to the appearance of the principate, while its substance rested on the powers Augustus held.

The name Augustus was granted in 27 BCE, and Beard's reading is persuasive for its religious associations. The word was linked to augury, and the augures were one of the great priestly colleges, so the name suggested sacred authority and proper religious practice. Augustus used this to present his rule as legitimate and divinely supported. The name was also new, and this novelty gave it prestige, since no previous Roman had borne it. The title became a central part of his public identity.

The honours Augustus accepted in 27 BCE, including the civic crown, were a public acknowledgement of his service to the state. The title princeps, meaning first citizen, was the key to his presentation, because it suggested that he was the leading member of the senate rather than a king. In 2 BCE he was given the title of father of the country, which further emphasised his role as a protector of the state rather than a ruler above it. These honours allowed Augustus to rule through traditional institutions while exercising a unique authority.

The images were equally important. The Res Gestae, Augustus' own account of his achievements, was inscribed in public places, and the Ara Pacis and the Prima Porta statue presented a carefully chosen image of peace, victory and divine favour. The Prima Porta statue, with its cuirass showing the return of Roman standards from the Parthians, shows how the images combined military triumph with diplomacy. These images were widely seen across the empire, and they created a visual language of the principate that persisted for generations.

However, the honours depended on the powers that supported them. Augustus' tribunician power, his control of the provinces with large armies and his position as the principal patron of the senate gave him the authority to act. The titles and images were effective because the army and the senate accepted his leadership, and the honours did not themselves create that acceptance. Beard's emphasis on the name and its meaning therefore needs to be balanced against the institutional basis of the principate.

On balance, the titles, honours and images of Augustus were important to his principate because they legitimised a monarchy and allowed a new form of rule to be presented as the continuation of the Republic. They were most effective when combined with the powers he held, and their importance lies in the way they made authority acceptable to Romans who were attached to traditional forms. The judgement is that the honours were essential, though not sufficient, for the principate.

Augustus' claim to auctoritas, the moral authority that Romans prized, was the central idea behind the honours. The title Augustus, the civic crown and the status of princeps all presented him as a leader whose influence rested on respect rather than office. Beard's reading makes this clear, and it explains why the images were carefully chosen. The honours allowed Augustus to command the state without appearing to abolish the Republic, and they gave his authority a place in the traditional vocabulary of Roman politics. Without this language, the principate would have been harder to accept.

sampleAnswers.answer: Equestrians were more significant than freedmen for the Augustan principate, though freedmen played a real role in the emperor’s household and finances. Equestrians held public office, commanded troops and governed provinces, which gave them a formal place in the administration, while freedmen’s influence depended on their personal relations with Augustus and was harder to institutionalise. The comparison therefore rests on the difference between public responsibility and private proximity to the princeps. Augustus drew on the equestrian order for many of the new offices the principate required. He gave the order a defined status, including a property qualification of 400,000 sesterces, so that men of that wealth could be trusted with public service. Gaius Cornelius Gallus, an equestrian, was the first prefect of Egypt, a province administered directly for the emperor and kept outside senatorial control. Its wealth, including the grain sent to Rome, was controlled directly by the emperor, which made the post one of the most sensitive in the empire. Equestrian prefects also commanded the praetorian cohorts that guarded Rome, a permanent force whose command gave an equestrian direct influence over the emperor’s safety, and they held charge of the grain supply. Equestrian procurators also collected revenue and managed estates in several provinces, and this gave the order a role in the finances of the empire. Their presence in the provinces extended the emperor’s authority beyond the senatorial governors. Maecenas, an equestrian and close adviser, shaped literature and cultural policy without ever holding a senatorial office, and he gave patronage to poets whose work supported the new regime. These positions gave the equestrians a career path, often built on a sequence of military and civil posts, and their loyalty to the emperor made them an important counterweight to the senatorial aristocracy. Freedmen were important in the imperial household, where they handled correspondence, accounts and personal business. Their role was significant because they dealt directly with the princeps and could influence decisions, and the wealth of some freedmen made them politically visible. Some freedmen were also used in financial administration, where their experience of managing an estate made them useful to the emperor. Their wealth and their closeness to the palace made them visible to the Roman elite, which resented their influence even when it was limited in practice. Yet Augustus did not give freedmen formal high offices, and their power was largely a matter of their position in the household. Accounts that describe freedmen as corrupt or overbearing come mainly from later writers and may reflect the hostility of senatorial writers rather than the working of the household itself, so they should be treated with caution. A counter-argument deserves consideration. Freedmen could shape what the emperor heard and decided, and that access could matter more in practice than a formal post. The reply is that access without office was hard to institutionalise, and it lasted only as long as the favour of the person who granted it. The distinction between equestrians and freedmen should not be overdrawn. Some equestrians rose through office and some freedmen held positions of trust that resembled equestrian responsibilities, and both groups owed their position to the princeps. Augustus’ administration was also still largely dependent on the senatorial class for consuls, governors of senatorial provinces and military commands. Equestrians filled the gaps between the senatorial class and the household, so their significance lay in the middle levels of government. The division between the two groups also reflects the principate’s need for trusted agents. The equestrian order provided men with the education and property to govern, and their careers gave them a stake in the new regime. Freedmen owed their position to the emperor’s personal favour, so they could be favoured or dismissed without the constraints of a formal career. This difference shows why the equestrians were more central to the system, while freedmen were more influential within the household. The later reign of Claudius shows how much the balance could change when power passed more fully to freedmen, but under Augustus the formal offices remained the backbone of the state. Overall, equestrians were the more significant group for the Augustan principate because they held the public offices that made the principate function, from the governance of Egypt to the praetorian guard. Freedmen were important in the emperor’s private administration and finances, and their influence should not be dismissed, but it was less institutionalised and less visible in the formal structure. The difference was partly one of degree, since both groups served the princeps, yet the equestrians’ formal responsibilities give them greater significance for the principate as a system. That judgement is strongest for the period of Augustus himself, when the offices were still being shaped, and it would need revisiting for the reigns that followed.

sampleAnswers.answer: Equestrians were significant for the Augustan principate because they held important offices. Augustus appointed equestrians as prefects, for example Gallus as prefect of Egypt, and the praetorian prefects who commanded the guard in Rome. Freedmen were also important, especially in the emperor’s household, where they handled letters and money. They could influence Augustus because they worked closely with him, but they did not have formal public office. The senators were still the main class of government. They held the consulship and commanded the legions in the senatorial provinces, so Augustus relied on them as well. Equestrians filled some gaps in the administration. Equestrians also served as officers in the army and as governors of some smaller provinces, which gave them direct experience of the frontier. Gallus, for example, fell from favour while still holding the Egyptian post, which shows that such positions depended on the emperor’s trust rather than on a secure career. The praetorian guard was a permanent force in Rome, so its command placed an equestrian close to the emperor’s safety. This made them a link between the military and the civil administration, and their presence in both spheres strengthened the emperor’s control. Equestrians also had a practical role in keeping Rome fed, because the grain supply was placed in their charge. Freedmen worked in the household and handled the emperor’s business, and this gave them a close place in the palace. Some were later sent to manage provincial finances, but they did so as the emperor’s personal agents rather than as holders of a formal office, so their authority could be withdrawn at will. Maecenas, an equestrian, was a close adviser of Augustus and a patron of writers, which shows the range of roles that equestrians could fill. Equestrian men also held commands in the provinces and in Rome, so their roles were spread across the state. The senators had more prestige, and Augustus needed their support to maintain his position. Overall, equestrians were more important than freedmen because they had formal offices, but freedmen were important too.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Augustan reforms were largely successful in stabilising the principate and in creating an administrative system that lasted for centuries, but they were less successful in the areas that depended on social change and on the cooperation of the Senate and the elite. Augustus' reforms are known best from his own account, the Res Gestae, which claims that he restored the Republic, returned power to the Senate and the people, and rebuilt the temples of the city. This account was written to present his achievements in the best possible light, and historians must read it as propaganda as well as evidence. Testing its claims against other sources shows which reforms were effective and which were limited. The most successful reforms were administrative and military. After the civil wars Augustus created a standing army and a system of provinces that were governed either by senators or by imperial legates, which allowed him to control the frontier armies. The Praetorian Guard, established as a permanent force around Rome, gave him a loyal military presence in the capital, and it later became the decisive force in imperial politics. The vigiles, the night watch and fire brigade of Rome, were created in 6 CE, and they gave the city a permanent protection that had been lacking. The aerarium militare, a military treasury funded by new taxes, provided pensions for veterans, which reduced the risk of the kind of veteran crisis that had destabilised the late Republic. These reforms addressed real problems and were effective. The Augustan settlement also made the Senate a partner in government, while the princeps retained the real power. The Senate kept its honours and its role in the provincial governments of the older provinces, and senators were given prestigious posts. This arrangement reduced the conflict that had made the Republic unstable, and it allowed the new system to function without open civil war for four decades. The reforms of public life and religion were also significant. Augustus restored temples, revived religious observances and promoted the cult of the gods of the state, and his building programme, including the Forum of Augustus and the Ara Pacis, presented his regime as the restorer of Roman tradition. Yet these reforms were partly symbolic, and they did not always produce the results that Augustus claimed. The restoration of the Senate's authority was incomplete, because the Senate's power was limited to the favour of the princeps, and the Res Gestae's claim to have restored the Republic was a construction. The moral and marriage legislation was the least successful of the reforms. The lex Iulia de adulteriis of 18 BCE and the lex Iulia de maritandis ordinibus of the same year aimed to encourage marriage and to punish adultery among the upper classes. They provoked widespread resistance and were modified in 9 CE by the lex Papia Poppaea, which shows that the laws could not change behaviour by decree. Augustus' own family life, including the exile of his daughter Julia, suggested that the moral programme was not applied consistently. The succession also reveals the limits of the settlement. Augustus lost his heirs one by one, and he was forced to adopt Tiberius, who did not come to power with the same authority. The principate was therefore created by the personal authority of one man, and its stability depended on finding a successor who could command that authority. The evidence for these reforms is uneven. The Res Gestae and the works of Augustan poets such as Virgil and Horace present the regime in the most favourable light, while the later historians Tacitus and Suetonius offer a more critical view of the settlement and its consequences. Coins, inscriptions and archaeological remains confirm the building programme and the administrative structures, but they do not reveal how the reforms were received by ordinary people. The most accurate judgement is that the Augustan reforms were successful in establishing a stable and enduring system of government, and especially in creating the administrative and military structures of the principate. They were less successful in the moral legislation, in restoring the Senate's independent authority and in solving the problem of succession. The reforms therefore achieved their central purpose, which was to end civil war and to secure the power of the princeps, but they did so by creating a monarchy that depended on the personal authority of its founder.

To go further, weigh the Res Gestae claims about the Senate more directly against Tacitus and Suetonius.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Augustan reforms were largely successful in stabilising the principate, though less so in areas that depended on social change. Augustus' own account, the Res Gestae, claims that he restored the Republic and rebuilt the temples, but it was written to present him in the best light. The administrative and military reforms were effective. The Praetorian Guard gave him a loyal presence in Rome, the vigiles of 6 CE provided fire and night protection, and the aerarium militare funded veterans' pensions. The Senate retained its honours and some provincial governments, which reduced conflict. The moral legislation was less successful: the lex Iulia de adulteriis and the lex Iulia de maritandis ordinibus of 18 BCE provoked resistance and were modified by the lex Papia Poppaea in 9 CE. The succession also remained a problem, since Augustus lost his heirs and had to adopt Tiberius. Overall, the reforms achieved their central purpose of ending civil war, but they relied on the personal authority of Augustus. The reforms of the provinces, including the distinction between senatorial and imperial provinces, reflected a practical division of responsibility that Augustus kept under his own control. The principate also depended on the loyalty of the army, which the Praetorian Guard and the legions supplied. Augustus' legislation on marriage and morals was intended to reinforce the family as the basis of the state, but it was unpopular among the elite and difficult to enforce. Its partial revision in 9 CE shows how far the government had to adjust to resistance. The reforms therefore combined real achievement with limits that Augustus could not remove.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Augustus dealt with challenges to his principate effectively in most cases, but his responses were often improvised, and some of his risks did not pay off. Adrian Goldsworthy argues that the system was created by trial and error, with chance events playing almost as big a role as design. This is a useful qualification of the image of a carefully planned settlement. The judgement is that Augustus was effective because he was adaptable and because he preserved the appearance of consensus, but that his solutions were not always successful, and the frontier disaster of 9 CE shows the limits of his strategy.

The principate faced political opposition from rivals and aristocrats. Conspiracies such as those of Varro Murena and Fannius Caepio in the 20s BCE threatened his life and power, and Augustus responded by pardoning many of the conspirators, which strengthened his reputation for clemency. This was an effective response in the short term, because it avoided the cycle of proscriptions and reprisals that had marked the civil wars. The response shows an adaptable ruler who understood that clemency could be as useful as force.

The succession was a more persistent problem. Augustus' designated heirs, including Marcellus, Gaius and Lucius Caesar, died young, and the question of succession remained unresolved for decades. The exile of his daughter Julia in 2 BCE and of Agrippa Postumus in 7 CE shows that family politics were a continuing challenge. Augustus responded by adopting Tiberius, which secured the succession but did not end the tensions within the imperial family. Here the results were mixed: the system survived, but the dynasty was fragile.

Military and frontier challenges tested the principate more severely. The campaigns in Germany were expensive, and the disaster in the Teutoburg Forest in 9 CE, when Varus lost three legions, was a serious failure of frontier policy. Augustus is said to have been deeply distressed by the news, and he halted expansion beyond the Rhine. This shows a real limit to his effectiveness: the attempt to extend the frontier had failed, and he chose to consolidate instead. The decision was pragmatic, but it was also an acknowledgement that the empire could not be pushed indefinitely.

Goldsworthy's view that Augustus took risks and that not all of them paid off fits these examples. The victory at Actium in 31 BCE was decisive, but the later settlement of the provinces and the handling of the army involved improvisation. The system was not created by a single plan but was shaped by responses to events. This does not reduce his skill, but it shows that his effectiveness came from adaptability rather than from perfect foresight.

On balance, Augustus dealt with challenges effectively in the sense that he kept power, preserved the appearance of consensus and avoided the civil wars that had destroyed the Republic. However, his responses to the succession and to the frontier were less successful, and the Teutoburg disaster revealed the limits of his strategy. The judgement is that his effectiveness was considerable but uneven, and that his adaptability mattered more than any single plan.

The opposition that Augustus faced also tested the limits of his clemency. The conspiracies of the 20s BCE showed that aristocratic rivals would act against him, and his decision to pardon many of the conspirators was a deliberate policy of reconciliation. However, the exile of Julia in 2 BCE and the later removal of Agrippa Postumus in 7 CE showed that family rivalries could be as dangerous as political ones. Augustus' effectiveness was greatest when he could use persuasion and honours, and weakest when the rivalries reached into his own household. Goldsworthy's account of trial and error helps to explain why his responses varied so much in success.

To lift it further, the answer could separate the challenges to the principate's stability from the military and frontier challenges more clearly.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Augustus used building programs to establish and maintain his principate by transforming Rome into a city that displayed his achievements, his piety and his claim to restore the Republic. His programs were not simply decorative. They were designed to present the new regime as the guarantor of peace, religious tradition and the traditions of the Roman people. Augustus famously claimed, as recorded by Suetonius, that he had found Rome a city of brick and left it a city of marble. The monuments of the city became the physical record of his regime, and they encouraged citizens to see the principate as a return to order.

The Forum of Augustus, dedicated in 2 BCE, was the clearest expression of his political message. It contained a temple to Mars the Avenger, which commemorated the murder of Julius Caesar and the defeat of his assassins, and it linked the new regime to the avenging of Caesar and the honour of the dynasty. The statues of the great men of Rome in the forum linked Augustus to the Republican past, and this legitimised his power as the heir of tradition. The forum also displayed his military successes, which allowed the regime to claim victory and peace at once.

The Ara Pacis, dedicated in 9 BCE, was a monument to the peace that Augustus claimed to have established after years of civil war. Its reliefs showed the imperial family in a procession, which presented the dynasty as the centre of Roman religious life and order. The Mausoleum, built in the Campus Martius, expressed the dynastic claim of Augustus’ family and its succession. Such monuments combined public piety with the display of the family, which made the principate appear natural and enduring.

However, the programs were not solely a matter of ideology. They also provided employment, improved the infrastructure of the city and offered the emperor a means to reward those who supported him. The construction of temples, theatres and aqueducts strengthened the loyalty of Rome’s elite and the urban population. Yet the programs also reflected the financial and political power of Augustus, and their significance depended on his control of the resources of the empire.

The programs also had a practical role in the economy of the city. Construction employed large numbers of craftsmen and labourers, and the imperial marble that Augustus brought to Rome was a visible sign of the wealth that the empire now controlled. Such projects linked the emperor’s personal patronage to the daily life of the city, and this made the principate appear beneficial as well as impressive. The programs were therefore a means of securing consent as well as a record of achievement.

The judgement can be tested by the reception of the programmes among the population. The monuments were not only seen by the elite; the processions, the public festivals and the ceremonies at the altars and temples brought the regime’s message to ordinary citizens. The Augustan calendar of festivals, which included the celebration of the Ara Pacis, made these monuments part of the civic year. This shows that the programmes had a practical as well as an ideological function, and that their effect depended on being repeated in the lives of the people of Rome.

Overall, Augustus used building programs to establish and maintain his principate because they combined piety, dynastic display and the claim to restore order in a form that the population could see every day. The monuments were the visual language of the regime, and they linked the emperor’s personal authority with the traditions and security of Rome.

sampleAnswers.answer: Propaganda was highly significant in contributing to Augustus' authority, because it allowed him to present his rule as the fulfilment of Rome's destiny, the restoration of peace and the legitimate heir of Julius Caesar. Yet propaganda worked alongside military control, the Senate's honours and Augustus' own skill in managing rivals, and its influence was strongest where it reinforced real achievements. The foundation of Augustus' authority was his victory in the civil wars. After Actium in 31 BCE, he controlled the armies and the resources of the Roman world, and his position rested on this military reality. Propaganda was then used to justify and to celebrate that position. The most important propaganda claim was his association with Julius Caesar. After Caesar's death in 44 BCE he was deified, and Octavian styled himself the son of the divine Julius, a title that gave him a religious and dynastic legitimacy. The coinage that Augustus issued in the 30s and 20s BCE carried the image of Caesar, with the legend referring to his divine status, and this allowed Augustus to present his power as the continuation of Caesar's cause without the stigma of the civil wars. The Res Gestae, the account of his achievements that was inscribed on bronze tablets at Rome and in the provinces, is the most explicit statement of this propaganda. It presents Augustus as a restorer of the Republic, a benefactor of the people and the defender of Roman peace, and it lists his honours and his building. Its claims are a major source for the period, but they are the self-presentation of the regime, and historians must test them against other evidence. The literary propaganda was equally important. Maecenas, Augustus' adviser, gathered poets around him, and Virgil's Aeneid presented the foundation of Rome as the origin of Augustus' peace and as a divinely sanctioned destiny. Horace celebrated the peace and the restoration of moral order, and the poets helped to make the new regime seem natural and inevitable. The Aeneid, however, was not simply a piece of propaganda. Its ambiguities and its sympathy for suffering have led many readers to see in it a more complex view of imperial power, and the poem reveals the limits of straightforward praise. The monuments were propaganda in a more visual sense. The Ara Pacis, dedicated in 9 BCE, expressed the peace that Augustus claimed to have established, and its processional reliefs placed the imperial family within a religious and civic order. The Forum of Augustus, with its statues of great Romans, presented Augustus as the heir of the Roman past, and the Julian family was prominently placed in the cult. These monuments reached the people of Rome and the provinces, and they made the regime visible. Yet the monuments were built with the money and labour of the state, and their message depended on the power that paid for them. Propaganda could not secure authority on its own. The Senate's grant of the title Augustus in 27 BCE and of the auctoritas that went with it, and the tribunician power and imperium that he held, were the constitutional basis of his position, and they were more important to his authority than any image. The reactions of some elite writers, such as those who wrote about the exile of Ovid or about Augustus' moral legislation, show that propaganda did not silence opposition. Augustus' personal achievements, including the restoration of the public peace and his care for the grain supply, made the propaganda credible to many. Historians also have to recognise that the surviving propaganda reflects the regime's own interests, and that its success is shown partly by how much the later tradition continued to accept its image. The most accurate judgement is that propaganda was highly significant, because it turned military victory into a stable and widely accepted authority, and it gave the new regime a language of peace, tradition and dynasty. Yet it was effective because it reinforced real power, not because it replaced it. Propaganda and military control worked together, and the authority of Augustus rested on both.

To go further, test the claim about the Aeneid's ambiguity against a specific passage.

The coinage of the 30s and 20s BCE carried Caesar's image and a reference to his divine status, which linked Augustus to Caesar's cause without the stigma of the civil wars. The Res Gestae presents him as a restorer of the Republic and a benefactor, but it is his own account and must be tested against other evidence. Maecenas gathered poets, and Virgil's Aeneid presented the foundation of Rome as the origin of Augustan peace, while Horace celebrated the restored moral order. The Ara Pacis of 9 BCE expressed the peace in monumental form, and the Forum of Augustus placed the emperor in the Roman past. However, propaganda could not create authority alone. Augustus' position rested on his victory at Actium and on the Senate's grant of honours and powers, and his achievements gave the propaganda credibility. Overall, propaganda was highly significant, but it worked by reinforcing real power rather than replacing it. Augustus' own avoidance of the title of king, and his use of the modest title princeps, was itself a form of political presentation that the propaganda supported. The regime also used religious ceremony and public games to show the people its benefits, and the Senate's public honours were often given in forms that emphasised tradition. Historians see this presentation as a combination of symbolism and practical power.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Imperial women were significant to the maintenance of power and authority in the Augustan principate, although their influence worked mainly through their dynastic value and their relationship with Augustus rather than through formal office. Women could not hold public office, but they were central to the family strategy by which Augustus secured his succession. Livia, his wife, was the most prominent of these women, and she was honoured with public recognition, including public statues and honours that set her apart from earlier wives. Her influence within the household gave her a role in the decisions that shaped the court.

Livia’s significance lay in her role as the mother of Tiberius and in her network of support, which helped to secure the succession of her son. Her position as the mother of the heir gave her a stake in the regime’s stability, and her advice was valued by Augustus. The honours she received made her a public symbol of the principate’s traditional virtues, such as the Roman matron’s devotion to family and the state, and this image strengthened the regime’s claim to restore moral order. Her role was therefore important both privately and publicly.

Julia, Augustus’ daughter, was also significant as a dynastic instrument. Her marriages to Marcellus, Agrippa and Tiberius were arranged to secure the succession, and her children with Agrippa were adopted by Augustus to strengthen the line. However, Julia’s public conduct led to scandal, and she was exiled in 2 BCE for adultery. The scandal showed that imperial women’s significance depended on their conduct and on their usefulness to the dynasty, and that they could be removed when they threatened the regime’s image of order.

The limits of women’s influence must also be recognised. Augustus remained the source of authority, and women’s power depended on the emperor’s favour. Their influence was exercised through networks, marriages and family ties, and it was constrained by the expectations of Roman society and by the emperor’s control of appointments. Nonetheless, their significance was real, because they embodied the dynastic continuity that the principate required.

Julia’s public image also gave the regime a way to present its values. Her conduct was condemned as a betrayal of the traditional virtues of the Roman matron, and the exile was presented as a restoration of moral order. This shows that imperial women were significant not only as dynastic instruments but also as symbols whose behaviour reflected on the emperor. Their significance therefore lay in the standards that the principate expected them to uphold.

The judgement can be tested by the way the regime used women in its public messages. Livia’s image in public monuments presented her as a model of Roman virtue, while Julia’s fall showed that the same standards could be used against a woman who failed to meet them. Both cases show that imperial women were not only dynastic instruments but also public symbols whose reputations were tied to the regime’s claim to restore moral order.

Overall, imperial women were significant to the maintenance of power and authority in the Augustan principate, because they were the instruments of dynastic succession and the public symbols of the regime’s values. Their influence was indirect, but it was essential to the stability of the principate, and their fate showed how closely their significance was tied to the emperor’s own interests.

sampleAnswers.answer: Agrippa’s role and contribution to the principate was essential, because his military victories secured Augustus’ power, his building works gave Rome a new public face, and his marriage to Julia linked him to the imperial family. However, his role was that of a loyal and capable subordinate rather than an independent founder, so his contribution was real but limited by Augustus’ authority. Agrippa’s military role was decisive. He commanded Octavian’s naval forces at Actium in 31 BCE, where the defeat of Antony and Cleopatra ended the civil wars and made Augustus the sole master of the Roman world. This victory was the foundation of the principate, since it gave Augustus the loyalty of the army and the navy. Agrippa’s campaigns in Gaul and Spain also extended Roman control and gave Augustus a reputation as the restorer of order. The building works in Rome were another major contribution. Agrippa constructed the Pantheon in 27 BCE, and he built the Aqua Virgo, the aqueduct that supplied the city with water, in 19 BCE. These projects were part of the public building programme that made the princeps’ rule visible in the city. They also contributed to the public welfare of the capital, which was essential to the legitimacy of the principate. His marriage to Julia, Augustus’ daughter, in 21 BCE tied him to the imperial family and made him the most important figure in the succession. Agrippa received tribunician power in 18 BCE, which made him a partner in the authority of the princeps, and he was expected to support the succession of Augustus’ sons, Gaius and Lucius. This shows the importance of his role, but it also shows its limits, because the authority remained Augustus’ and Agrippa’s position depended on his loyalty. After Agrippa’s death in 12 BCE, the succession problems revealed how much the principate had depended on him. The sources for Agrippa are mostly literary and monumental. Cassius Dio provides a detailed account of Agrippa’s career, but he wrote in the third century CE and relied on earlier histories. The inscription on the Pantheon records Agrippa’s construction, which provides direct evidence of his building work. Augustus’ own Res Gestae presents the restoration of the Republic and says little about Agrippa, which suggests that Augustus preferred to present his own authority as the source of success. Coins and aqueduct inscriptions give further evidence of Agrippa’s projects, though they are limited. Agrippa’s role also reflected the conditions of the Augustan settlement. He governed the eastern provinces in 23 BCE when Augustus was ill, and he organised the census in Gaul in 27 BCE. These roles tested the principate’s dependence on a loyal deputy. Agrippa was the father of Augustus’ heirs, Gaius and Lucius, and his tribunician power in 18 BCE shows that the succession was being arranged within the family, but Agrippa’s own authority always remained subordinate to Augustus. Agrippa’s public works also changed the city’s relationship with the princeps. His baths, the Pantheon and the Aqua Virgo were gifts to the Roman people, and his benefactions were recorded in public inscriptions. This model of public generosity by senators and members of the imperial family was one that Augustus encouraged, and it helped to bind the elite to the new regime without requiring the emperor to act alone. Taken together, Agrippa’s contribution to the principate was essential in military, building and dynastic terms. He secured Augustus’ victory at Actium, provided the public works that made the principate visible and supported the succession. His contribution was therefore indispensable, but it was always exercised in Augustus’ name and under his authority.

His building works in Rome, including the Pantheon and the Aqua Virgo, made the new regime visible and supplied the city with water. His marriage to Julia linked him to the imperial family, and he received tribunician power in 18 BCE. However, Agrippa remained Augustus’ subordinate, and his authority was exercised in Augustus’ name. Cassius Dio provides a detailed account, but he wrote much later. The inscription on the Pantheon is direct evidence of Agrippa’s building work. Agrippa’s contribution was indispensable, but it always depended on Augustus’ authority. Agrippa’s role also shows how the principate was built from the family and the army together. He commanded the fleet at Actium, and he governed the eastern provinces when Augustus needed a trusted deputy there. His tribunician power in 18 BCE gave him legal authority within the constitutional framework, while his marriage to Julia linked the principate to the imperial family. His death in 12 BCE left Augustus relying on his stepsons Tiberius and Drusus, a change that shaped the succession.  His building of the Pantheon and the Aqua Virgo, together with his public benefactions, gave the Roman people visible evidence of the regime’s generosity, while his military command at Actium showed that the Augustan settlement depended on force as well as consent.
